Psalm 33 is praise with instruments and a reason given for each line. "Sing joyously to the Lord, you righteous ones… Extol the Lord with a harp; sing to Him with a ten-stringed lyre. Sing to Him a new song." Then how things got here: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and by the breath of His mouth all their hosts… For He spoke, and it came to be; He commanded, and it endured." And then the part that belongs to this month: "The Lord has annulled the counsel of nations; He has foiled the schemes of peoples… The king is not saved by a great army, nor a warrior rescued by great might. The horse is a false guarantee for victory; with all its great strength it offers no escape. But the eye of the Lord is directed toward those who fear Him."
Psalm 41 closes: "And I, because of my integrity, You upheld me; You set me before You forever. Blessed is the Lord, the G-d of Israel, to all eternity, Amen and Amen."

77.title: The Stork is Saying
body: The stork opens, and this gathering is wings over a nest while a vow is being made.

"Speak to the heart of Jerusalem, and call to her" meets the cherub — "And He rode upon a cherub and did fly" — and then the eagle: "as an eagle awakens its nest, hovering over its fledglings." The pardon follows, with the sea closing over them: "for her time has arrived, for her sins have been pardoned" / "You blew with Your wind, the sea covered them" / "He was seen upon the wings of the wind" / "it spreads its wings, taking them and carrying them on its pinions."

Then the dove in the rock, and Hannah beginning: "My dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the coverture of the steps" / "if You will look upon the affliction of Your bondswoman" / "for she has taken double from G-d's hand for all her sins."

The foxes come in next, with the forty thousand and the lead: "Seize for us the foxes, the little foxes" / "who destroy the vineyards, for our vineyards are with tiny grapes" / "when the forty thousand went against Israel?" / "they sank like lead in the powerful waters."

Then the vow is laid out across the whole last stretch, a clause at a time, with the psalm's assurances between them. "And she vowed a vow, and said: to Lord of Hosts" / "and no razor shall come upon his head" / "and You will remember me, and You will not forget Your bondswoman" / "with this I shall know that You desire me" / "show me your appearance, let me hear your voice" / "You set me before You forever" / "my beloved is mine, and I am his" / "and You will give Your bondswoman a male child."

It ends with the giving over and the blessing: "and I shall give him to the Lord all the days of his life" / "my heart is toward the lawgivers of Israel" / "Blessed is the Lord, the G-d of Israel" / "who grazes among the roses" — and then the heavens and the earth, and to all eternity, Amen and Amen.

78.title: Revealing Warmth to Those that Are Cold and Indifferent
body: Week twelve, and the raven asks: "Who prepares food for the raven, when his young ones cry out to G-d?" (Job 38:41)

This is the week of Yud Tes Kislev, called the Rosh Hashanah of Chassidism — the day the Alter Rebbe came out of prison, and the yahrzeit of the Maggid of Mezeritch. He had been accused of treason by the opponents of Chassidism, with the death penalty in prospect, and he came out of it. He took the release as a verdict in the Heavenly Court as well as the earthly one, and afterwards he taught far more openly. The effort that followed carried the warmth of Chassidism into the coldest and most indifferent part of a Jew: the intellect. The capital of intellectual Judaism was Vilna, where he had been sent.

The raven is the right creature for that. It was put out of Noah's ark for not keeping the rule of celibacy, and it is known for being cruel and careless toward its own young. And yet when Elijah fled from Ahab, G-d arranged that the raven — which does not even feed its own chicks — should bring him food. Elijah had run out of hope and was complaining about the state of the people, and the lesson was that like the raven, everyone has warmth and good in them; it only has to be brought out.

The word itself says so. *Orev*, raven, is close to *arev* — responsible for another, and sweet, and mixed together, as in *Kol Israel Arevim Zeh LaZeh*, that all of Israel is responsible for, sweet to and mixed up with one another. Which is nearly the whole basis of Chassidism and of the Torah: love your fellow as yourself.

Twelve is the twelve tribes. For all the differences and the setbacks, we are mixed together and answerable for each other. On his deathbed Jacob was worried about exactly those differences, and the Talmud says his twelve sons answered him in unison: "Listen, O Israel" — meaning Jacob — "Hashem is our G-d, Hashem is One."

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Tarfon: "The day is short, the work is much, the workers are lazy, the reward is great, and the Master is pressing." And: "It is not incumbent upon you to finish the task, but neither are you free to absolve yourself from it." Chassidism came to light a fire under people who were low and spiritually asleep. An alarm clock: the time is short, start now.
The pairing is Hod shebeGevurah. Hod belongs to the inner dimensions of the Torah — as Lag Ba'Omer, which is hod within hod, is the yahrzeit of the man who set down the Zohar.

79.title: Nathan and Friendship
body: "So the Lord guided them alone, and there was no alien deity with Him." (Deuteronomy 32:12) One of the first principles of Chassidism is *hashgachah pratit* — that everything that happens comes straight from Him, with nothing else interfering, and that all of it is for the best. And one of the first acts in rededicating the Temple was clearing out the foreign gods the Greeks and their sympathisers had put in it.

The haftorah: "And He fixed darkness about Him as booths; gathering of waters, thick clouds of the skies." (II Samuel 22:12) Chassidus is about turning darkness into light, and darkness is the sign of the Greek exile. Chanukah also runs eight days in order to answer the eight days of Sukkot, which the verse's own word for booths calls up.
The quality is bonding of friends, which may be the main principle of the whole movement: that chassidim are one family, and that all Jews are one.

The prophet is Nathan, who shows what it means from both sides. He is the one who reproves King David with a parable, over an act that was the opposite of bonding with a friend. And it is by that same bonding that he later acts for Batsheva against Adonyah's attempt on the throne: Adonyah had gathered his own friends and allies to declare himself king, so David sends Nathan to join Benaiah ben Yehoyada and Zadok the Kohen and the rest, and declare Solomon.

The Levitical city is Anathoth, which may be the darkest of them. The Zohar says Anathoth means poverty. It was a town of Kohanim gone wrong, whose people wanted to kill the prophet Jeremiah, who came from there, and whose prospects in his prophecy are grim. Chassidus came to teach that even Anathoth can be raised. The name comes from *Anat*, a Canaanite warrior-goddess who looks related to Athena — which suits a month about fighting Greece both ways. And the name has a better side: it is the name of the parent of Shamgar, one of Israel's judges and deliverers, and of a man of the tribe of Benjamin, and of one who signed a covenant in the Book of Nehemiah.

The lesson follows last week's. One of the first things Pirkei Avot says is: make for yourself a rabbi, acquire for yourself a friend, and judge every person favourably — acquiring the friend comes straight after making the teacher. The Talmud puts it harder: either companionship or death. Studying with a partner brings clarity, and lets you see how far you have actually got.
79.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 12.

80.title: Arpachshad and the Fiery Furnace
body: "Who is like You among the powerful, O Lord? Who is like You, exalted in the holy place?" *Mi Chamocha Ba'Elim Hashem* — the acronym that gives the Maccabees their name. And the question comes twice, which answers to the two lights the Alter Rebbe brought: the revealed, in law, and the hidden, in Chassidus. The first half of the verse is His greatness out in the open — *elim* meaning the forces of nature — and the second is the hidden kind.

The haftorah is about giving yourself up willingly, and then: "The riders of white donkeys." Which points at Mashiach, who comes on a donkey. The Alter Rebbe's Tanya belongs to this day, and R. Zusya of Anipoli is said to have foretold: with the Tanya the Jewish people will go out to greet the righteous Mashiach.

Sotah's twelfth daf is Miriam and Moshe. The Talmud says Moshe was also called Tuviah, for the great light revealed about him at his birth — which goes with a man named Shneur for the two lights he brought. And Miriam spoke to her father and so persuaded him, and through him the whole people, not to divorce their wives. The Alter Rebbe's daughter Devorah Leah had a conversation of that kind with her father too, about giving up her own life to add years to his, so that the work could go on.

The generation is Arpachshad, Shem's son, whose name breaks into three words: *ohr*, light; *pach*, a vial; and *shad*, from Sh-dai, one of His names, read as *Shomer Daltot Yisrael*, Guardian of the doors of Israel — the Name that goes on a mezuzah. All three are this festival. Light; the small vial of pure oil that lasted eight days instead of one; and the lamp that is lit beside the mezuzah. A mezuzah's first fixing is called *Chanukath HaBayit*, the dedication of a house. The Midrash also reads Sh-dai as the One who told the world *dai*, enough — who set limits on what He made, being Himself without any. Which is this festival's message from the other direction: He can also do what nature does not allow.

The journey arrives at the mountain: "They journeyed from Rephidim and camped in the Sinai desert." Last week's weakness for want of water turns out to have been for the sake of a larger knowledge — as this week gives the Torah of Chassidus.

Arpachshad is also tied to Ur Chasdim, where Abraham was thrown into the furnace for defying Nimrod. Which brings to mind Rabbi Elimelech of Lizhensk's practice: in any idle moment, lying awake, picture a great fire burning in front of you reaching to the heavens, and for the sake of His holiness go against your nature and throw yourself in. The Holy One joins good intentions to great deeds — so you are no longer idle but keeping a commandment.

81.title: The Rosh Hashanah of Chassidut
body: "And it came to pass, as she prayed long before the Lord, that Eli watched her mouth." She prays at length, and the Kohen Gadol guards her mouth.

Which is the story of this week. Yud Tes Kislev begins with a heavenly decree against the Alter Rebbe for revealing the secrets of Chassidut, and it came out as fifty-three days in prison on invented charges of treason against the Czar. During those days he was visited by the Baal Shem Tov and by the Maggid of Mezritch — whose yahrzeit is Yud Tes Kislev — and told that he was not only absolved of the decree but should teach and reveal more. With his masters having watched his mouth, his teaching afterwards became far more expansive. Chassidim speak of before Petersburg and after Petersburg, Petersburg being where he was held.
The week's quality is that the Torah makes him fit to be *chassid*, pious — and Yud Tes Kislev is the Rosh Hashanah of Chassidut. Hannah in that verse is piety itself.

Proverbs' twelfth chapter keeps contrasting the righteous with the wicked. The difference between a tzadik, last week's word, and a chassid is that the chassid goes past the letter of the law to please the Creator. The chapter is full of that kind of thing: "A good man will obtain favor of the Lord… A righteous man has regard for the desire of his beast, but the mercy of the wicked is cruel… The righteous is more generous than his neighbor… In the road of charity is life, and on the way of its path there is no death."

Two yahrzeits here, both close to the Alter Rebbe. The eighteenth of Kislev is Rabbi Baruch of Mezhibuz, the Baal Shem Tov's grandson, a disciple of the Maggid and one of the leading rebbes of the Alter Rebbe's own day — and it was to him that the Alter Rebbe wrote, once freed, describing the miracles. He once challenged the Alter Rebbe, who is said to have answered: "You may be his grandson in a physical sense; I am his grandson in a spiritual sense."

And the nineteenth is the Maggid of Mezritch himself, the Baal Shem Tov's successor, whose disciples became the leaders of the movement — Rebbe Elimelech of Lizhensk and his brother Rav Zusia of Anipoli, Rebbe Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk, Rebbe Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, Rebbe Aharon of Karlin, Rebbe Shmuel Shmelke of Nikolsburg and his brother Rebbe Pinchas Horowitz of Frankfurt. On his deathbed he turned to the Alter Rebbe: "Zalmanyu, give me your hand. You will remain alone, you are for yourself — you have your own way. You will need a lot of help from Heaven. I will yearn for you very much, and G-d willing, I will save you from all your troubles." And, by the Chabad tradition, he said: "This day is our Yom Tov."

82.title: Longing for G-d
body: "Until the sun spreads, and the shadows flee, go around; liken yourself, my beloved, to a gazelle or to a fawn of the hinds, on distant mountains." Then a new chapter: "On my bed at night, I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him but I did not find him. I will arise now and go about the city, in the market places and in the city squares. I will seek him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but I did not find him."

All of it is ours. The sun spreading is what happened after the release: Chassidut went out across the land — to distant mountains, to a bed at night, which is exile, and into the city, the market, the squares. There was nowhere it could not get into. And taken together the verses are a long ache for Him. The Alter Rebbe's longing for Hashem was such that it gave him a breathing complaint.

Of the seventy souls the twelfth is Saul the son of the Canaanitess. Rashi explains that this is Dinah's son — she had been raped and taken by a Canaanite who meant to marry her. One of the subjects of this month is intermarriage and assimilation, and in Dinah's story Shimon and Levi act with the zeal of Maccabees to get her back. Though their violence and their deceit, unlike the Maccabees', were not right, and Jacob condemned them for it. The tribe of Levi learned in the end what to do with its zeal.

Shevuot's twelfth daf is about buying what is dedicated on condition of using the remainder, and what to do with animals left over from offerings, and then the goat sent to Azazel, which atoned for whatever the inner goat did not. Which has something of Chassidut's own innovation in it: that everything is holy and has a use, that every Jew is holy, and that even the animal soul can be made holy.

Jeremiah's twelfth chapter lays out one disaster after another and rebukes the people — and all the way through calls them "My inheritance" and "My soul's beloved." The Greeks wanted that exact belief gone, that this people had a portion in Him, and the love between them was the thing they could not grasp. "I have abandoned My House, I have forsaken My inheritance; I have delivered My soul's beloved into the hand of her enemies." And later: "after I uproot them, I will return and have pity on them, and I will restore them, each one to his inheritance and each one to his land."

83.title: Reviewing the Fourth Week of Kislev - Psalms 34-36; 42:1-4; 89:13
body: The fourth week of Kislev in psalms: the thirty-fourth, thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth, with the opening of Psalm 42 and a verse of Psalm 89.

Psalm 34 is headed from when David feigned insanity before Avimelech and was driven away. It is mostly instruction, and generous with it. "I bless the Lord at all times; His praise is always in my mouth… I sought the Lord and He answered me; He delivered me from all my fears. Those who look to Him are radiant; their faces are never humiliated." Then the invitation: "Taste and see that the Lord is good." And the teaching, asked as a question: "Who is the man who desires life, who loves long life wherein to see goodness? Guard your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil and do good, seek peace and pursue it." Its best-known line is near the end: "The Lord is close to the broken-hearted, and saves those with a crushed spirit."

Psalm 35 is a lawsuit. "Fight my antagonists, O Lord, battle those who battle against me. Take hold of shield and armor and arise to help me… say to my soul, 'I am your deliverance.'" What stings most in it is the ingratitude: "They repay me evil for good… But I wore sackcloth when they were ill; I afflicted my soul with fasting… As if it were my friend, my brother, I went about; like a mother in mourning, I was bent over in gloom. But when I limped, they rejoiced and gathered." And their words: "They opened their mouths wide against me, they said, 'Aha! Aha! Our eyes have seen his misfortune.'" Against which: "You saw, Lord, be not silent."

Psalm 36 opens inside the head of a man who has stopped being afraid of anything. "Sin says to the wicked, 'There is none who need place the fear of G-d before his eyes.' For Sin makes itself appealing to him… On his bed he contemplates evil, he stands in a path that is not good; he does not despise evil." And then, without a join, the psalm turns and becomes one of the widest things in the book: "O Lord, Your kindness is in the heavens; Your faithfulness is till the skies. Your righteousness is like the mighty mountains, Your judgments extend to the great deep; man and beast You deliver, O Lord. How precious is Your kindness, O G-d; man takes shelter in the shadow of Your wings… For the source of life is with You; in Your Light do we see light."

Psalm 42 begins the thirst: "As a hart cries longingly for rivulets of water, so does my soul cry longingly to You, O G-d… My tears were my bread day and night when they say to me all day long, 'Where is your G-d?'"

84.title: The Raven Is Saying
body: The raven opens, and this gathering is a search carried out in the dark.

"Who prepares food for the raven, when his young ones cry out to G-d?" is answered by the guiding — "the Lord guided them alone, and there was no alien deity with Him" — and then the darkness set about Him as Sukkot, with the gathering of waters and the thick clouds.

Then the great question twice, and the thirst under it: "Who is like You among the powerful, O Lord? Who is like You, exalted in the holy place?" / "My soul thirsts for G-d, for the living G-d; when will I come and appear before G-d?"

And then the searching, with Hannah's long prayer set inside it. "On my bed at night, I sought him whom my soul loves" / "I sought him but I did not find him" / "and it came to pass, as she prayed long before the Lord" / "that Eli watched her mouth" / "I will seek him whom my soul loves" / "I sought him, but I did not find him."

The gazelle on the distant mountains follows, and then the willing offering and the white donkeys, with the hart crying for water across them: "that offered themselves willingly among the people" / "the riders of white donkeys" / "as a hart cries longingly for rivulets of water" / "so does my soul cry longingly to You, O G-d."

Then the taunt, and the going out into the city: "My tears were my bread day and night" / "when they say to me all day long, 'Where is your G-d?'" / "I will arise now and go about the city" / "in the market places and in the city squares."

It ends on the compass and the mountains singing — "the north and the south — You created them; Tabor and Hermon sing of Your Name" — and then the sun spreading, the shadows fleeing, and a maskil of the sons of Korah.

85.title: To Publicize Miracles with Pride and Humility
body: Week thirteen brings in Chanukah, and the starling sings about being seen: "Their seed shall be known among the nations, and their offspring among the peoples; all who see them shall acknowledge them, that they are the seed that G-d has blessed." (Isaiah 61:9)
Which is this week's own mitzvah — *pirsumei nissa*, publicising the miracle, so that everyone can see what was given to this people in the days of the Greeks.

The song's attention to seed points at the kohanim, whose line, unlike nearly everything else in Judaism, runs by the physical male seed; there are even tests for a kohen gene, to tell with near certainty whether a man descends from Aaron. The Maccabees were kohanim, and what they did made the seed of Aaron known among the nations.

And Chanukah comes from *chinuch*. The starling also says that each of us was a seed, planted and tended and blessed by parents and teachers and above all by G-d — and the same or better has to be done for our children and students. Darkness and assimilation are beaten by education in the end.

Pirkei Avot gives Akavia the son of Mahalalel, who is blunt: "Reflect upon three things and you will not come to the hands of transgression. Know from where you came, where you are going, and before whom you are destined to give a judgment and accounting. From where you came — from a putrid drop; where you are going — to a place of dust, maggots and worms; and before whom you are destined to give a judgment and accounting — before the supreme King of Kings, the Holy One, blessed be He."

That is seed again, put much less kindly — and it is pointed straight at what this week defeated. Hellenistic culture valued man, and the human body in particular, above everything. Akavia says the body comes from a putrid drop and ends being eaten by worms, and is then judged by G-d Himself. Keep your eye on G-d, not on man.

Which also shows how much mercy there is in it. Low where we came from and low where we are going, and still in a direct relationship with the King of kings, the way children are with a father. There is a spark of Him in us, and when He punishes it is for our good. Chassidism teaches that we have no idea how precious the body is to Him — precious like the seed in the starling's song.
The pairing is Yesod shebeGevurah, and it could hardly fit better: yesod is foundation, and this week a people held to its foundation, with courage, against a policy of forced assimilation.

86.title: David and Avigail, and the Quality of "Sharp Discussion"
body: "He made them ride upon the high places of the earth, that they would eat the produce of the field. He let them suck honey from a rock, and oil from the mighty part of the crag." (Deuteronomy 32:13) High places, something impossible, and oil — the whole story is in one verse. The word for high places, *bamah*, also means altar. And the oil can be read as the *pintele yid*, the innermost part of a Jew that stays pure whatever happens and shows itself when things get hard.

The haftorah: "From the brightness before Him flamed forth coals of fire." (II Samuel 22:13) Brightness and fire, which is the Menorah — and coals again, which can be burning inside and need one more step before the fire shows.

The quality is sharp discussion with students, *pilpul*. One of the things this people got out of the Greek exile was sharpness and logic. The Greek king's name, *Talmai*, has the same numerical value as *Talmud*, and the Talmud grew greatly out of that encounter — it even carries Greek words.

The prophets are David and Avigail. David is monarchy, and the Maccabees made a dynasty; he is also the proof that a person can be entirely holy and entirely involved in the world at once — Torah and prayer alongside running a government and fighting wars. Chanukah has both halves too: the military victory, and the victory of Jewish wisdom over Greek wisdom, which are David and Solomon respectively. And Avigail kept blood from being spilt by going to David and talking to him about her husband, as the Hasmoneans kept further blood from being spilt by making an alliance with Rome. Both of them had the sharpness this week is about. David's mind was such that the halachah always followed his opinion, and it was Avigail's argument that stopped him.

The Levitical city is 'Almon, which means hidden — from *He'elem*, and from *olam*. Revealing what is hidden is the point of Kislev. Through this miracle you can see that the whole *olam* is a kind of screen and that His power is the real thing. And on Chanukah even the most hidden Jews come out. There are limits on what may be used for Shabbat candles and no such limits for these; every Jew is lit up by it.
86.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 13.

87.title: Shelah and Chanukah
body: "Too awesome for praises, performing wonders! You inclined Your right hand; the earth swallowed them up." Praise for wonders, which is the week's whole work. The haftorah asks for it to be told: "those that sit in judgment, and those that walk on the path, tell of it" — and says the persecution has stopped "between the places of drawing water," which stands for the study of Torah the Greeks were attacking.

Sotah's thirteenth daf is the burial of Jacob and of Joseph, and opens with the room filling with light when Moshe was born. On Jacob's burial, the Talmud notices that the argument with Eisav was not won by reasoning: Eisav was making a baseless claim and demanding proof of this and that, and Chushim son of Dan could not stand to see his grandfather's burial held up, so he went ahead and killed him. Which is almost exactly how the revolt began — Matisyahu, told to slaughter a pig on a pagan altar, refused, and then killed the Jew and the Syrian official who had demanded it.
The generation is Shelah, Arpachshad's son — and Shelah is one of the names of Mashiach. It is also the name of Judah's son, whom he did not give to Tamar.

Rabbi Yosef Jacobson draws the two together. Rabbi Isaac Luryah wrote that the judgment begun on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur is completed some three months later, in the days of Chanukah. Three months after Judah and Tamar, Judah is told what Tamar has supposedly done and the verdict goes against her. And at that moment she sends word: "I am pregnant by the man who is the owner of these articles. Identify, I beg you, these objects. Who is the owner of this seal, cord and staff?"

Read as the Jew speaking to G-d, the timing is exact. At the moment the prosecuting angels have nearly proved the whole experiment a failure, the Jew sends word that the report is false — if he has strayed here and there it is a surface thing, and underneath he belongs to no one else. And he points at the objects: the cord, which is the wick soaked in oil each night, commemorating a sealed cruse found after the Temple was plundered; the seal on that cruse; and the staff, which he has had to pick up over and over for two thousand years, leaving house and security to find somewhere he could still live as a Jew.

Then Judah answers: "She is right; it is from me that she conceived. She did it because I did not give her to my son Shelah." And Shelah is the name of Mashiach. Read that way, it is G-d saying the fault is His: how can I expect a Jew never to sin, never to try his luck with a world that looks so appealing, when I held back the light of Mashiach so long? "It is I who is guilty of treason," not the Jew. Tamar is an innocent palm tree with one heart to her Father in heaven.

The journey is a hard place: "They journeyed from the Sinai desert and camped in Kivroth hataavah" — the graves of craving. Having received the Torah, the work is burying one's desires, through *itkafia* and *itapcha*. The Baal Shem Tov reads the graves of craving as utter self-nullification in cleaving to G-d, where cravings die and are buried with no chance of coming back. Chanukah is, unlike the other festivals, mainly a spiritual one: there is no commandment to make a meal. It is a holiday for praising Him.

88.title: Being Straightforward
body: "Now Hannah, she spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice could not be heard; therefore, Eli thought she had been drunken." This is the clearest demonstration that prayer is a spiritual act before it is anything else. No sound has to leave a person for Him to hear the cry. And this festival is the victory of the spiritual over the material.

The week's quality is that the Torah makes him fit to be *yashar*, correct — literally straight: truthful, straightforward. Yashar is tied particularly to keeping the negative commandments, which draw down revelations beyond the created order. In the story Eli wrongly takes Hannah for drunk, when she was praying out of a broken heart — and praying drunk would break a negative commandment. Her conduct is the conduct of a yashar, past reproach, and what it drew down was a child.

Proverbs' thirteenth chapter carries on setting the righteous against the wicked, and speaks directly about light: "The light of the righteous will rejoice, but the candle of the wicked will ebb away. Only with wickedness does one cause quarrels, but there is wisdom with those who take counsel."

Two yahrzeits. On the twenty-fourth of Kislev, Rabbi Chaim Chizkiya Medini, known for the Sdei Chemed, an encyclopaedic work of law in eighteen volumes. He was born in Jerusalem and lived in Turkey and Crimea before returning; he was considered for Rishon L'Zion, and moved to Hebron to give himself to his studies instead, eventually becoming its Chief Rabbi. Jews and Arabs alike held him a holy man.

And on the twenty-seventh, Rabbi Chaim Tirar of Chernowitz, known for the Be'er Mayim Chayim, his commentary on the Torah, and for Sidduroh Shel Shabat on the holiness of the Sabbath. He was one of the most important disciples of the Maggid of Mezritch, and studied under Rabbi Yechiel Michel of Zlotchov.

89.title: Finding G-d in Exile
body: "The watchmen who patrol the city found me: 'Have you seen him whom my soul loves?' I had just passed them by, when I found him whom my soul loves; I held him and would not let him go, until I brought him into my mother's house and into the chamber of her who had conceived me. I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or by the hinds of the field, that you neither awaken nor arouse the love while it is desirous."

After all the searching and not finding, and after asking the watchmen — Rashi reads them as Moshe and Aharon, and perhaps they are the leaders and prophets and priests of any generation — He is found. That is Chanukah: He shows Himself, in an impossible victory and in oil that burned eight days.
And once found, not let go until He is brought into the mother's house, into the chamber of the one who conceived — which is the rededication of the Temple, the home of the Shechinah.
The third verse is the same one that closed week eight. Standing here instead, after the finding, the hard tone toward the nations reads as a victory shout rather than a refusal.
Of the seventy souls the thirteenth is Levi, and the fit needs no explaining: every kohen and every zealous Maccabee came from him.

Shevuot's thirteenth daf asks whether Yom Kippur atones for everything, repentance or not, and finds three exceptions: one who denies the basis of the Torah, one who ridicules it, and one who annuls circumcision. Denying the Torah's origin and undoing circumcision were two of the sharpest points of conflict with Hellenist culture. The daf also treats the atonement of the kohanim separately from everyone else's.

Jeremiah's thirteenth chapter is the girdle he is told to wear, which rots and becomes useless — and then: "just as the girdle clings to a man's loins, so have I caused the entire house of Israel and the entire house of Judah to cling to Me." The chapter returns to skirts uncovered and pulled over the face, and to darkness: "Give the Lord your God honor before it becomes dark, and before your feet stumble on the dark mountains." Then: "Will a Cushite change his skin, or a leopard his spots?" The leopard, in Jewish tradition, is particularly Greece — for its beauty, its speed, and above all its boldness. The word for its spots also means stains, *kesem*, of the kind tied to impurity. And leopards are known to mate outside their species. The chapter's last line asks when Jerusalem will ever be pure. In the days of the Maccabees, it was.

90.title: Reviewing the Fifth Week of Kislev - Psalms 37-39; 42:5-7; 89:14
body: The fifth week of Kislev in psalms: the thirty-seventh, thirty-eighth and thirty-ninth, with three verses of Psalm 42 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 37 is a long argument against envying people who are doing well out of doing wrong. "Do not compete with the wicked; do not envy doers of injustice. For like grass they will be swiftly cut down." Its instructions are the kind you can act on: "Trust in the Lord and do good… Delight in the Lord, and He will grant you the desires of your heart. Cast your needs upon the Lord… Let go of anger, abandon rage." And it keeps returning to how short the apparent advantage is: "For soon the wicked one will not be; you will gaze at his place and he will be gone… I saw a powerful wicked man, well-rooted like a vibrant, native tree. Yet he vanished, behold he was gone; I searched for him, but he could not be found." The line in it people remember is an old man's testimony: "I have been a youth, I have also aged; yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring begging bread."

Psalm 38 is illness and shame together. "There is no soundness in my flesh because of Your rage, no peace in my bones because of my sin. For my iniquities have flooded over my head; like a heavy load, they are too heavy for me. My wounds are rotted; they reek because of my foolishness." And the loneliness in it is precise: "My friends and companions stand aloof from my affliction; my intimates stand afar." His answer to the people laying traps is silence: "But I am like a deaf man, I do not hear; like a mute that does not open his mouth… Because for You, O Lord, I wait."

Psalm 39 is about holding the tongue and what holding it costs. "I said that I would guard my ways from sinning with my tongue; I would guard my mouth with a muzzle… I became mute with stillness, I was silent even from the good, though my pain was crippling. My heart grew hot within me, a fire blazed in my utterance." Then it asks the size of a life: "O Lord, let me know my end and what is the measure of my days… Behold, like handbreadths You set my days; my lifetime is as naught before You." And: "he amasses riches and knows not who will reap them."

Psalm 42's verses are a memory of walking up: "These do I recall, and pour out my soul from within me: how I traveled in covered wagons; I would walk leisurely with them up to the House of G-d, amid the sound of rejoicing and thanksgiving, the celebrating multitude." Then the question asked twice in that psalm: "Why are you downcast, my soul, and why do you wail within me? Hope to G-d, for I will yet thank Him."

91.title: The Starling is Singing
body: The starling opens, and the gathering is riding high places while a soul is downcast.

"He made them ride upon the high places of the earth" / "that they would eat the produce of the field" comes first, with the starling's seed threaded through it: "Their seed shall be known among the nations" / "and their offspring among the peoples" / "He let them suck honey from a rock" / "and oil from the mighty part of the crag" / "all who see them shall acknowledge them."

Then the telling, and the wonders: "those that sit in judgment" / "and those that walk on the path, tell of it" / "too awesome for praises" / "performing wonders!" / "instead of the noise of adversaries" / "between the places of drawing water" / "You inclined Your right hand" / "the earth swallowed them up."

And then the searching and the mistaken accusation together. "The watchmen who patrol the city found me: have you seen him whom my soul loves?" / "only her lips moved, but her voice could not be heard" / "therefore, Eli thought she had been drunk" / "now Hannah, she spoke in her heart" — and immediately the psalm's own question: "why are you downcast, my soul, and why do you wail within me? Hope to G-d."

The coals of fire come next, and the finding, and the pouring out of the soul: "from the brightness before Him flamed forth coals of fire" / "I had just passed them by, when I found him whom my soul loves" / "these do I recall, and pour out my soul from within me."

The last stretch braids the holding-on with the walking up to the House. "Held him and would not let him go, until I brought him into my mother's house" / "and into the chamber of her who had conceived me" / "I would walk leisurely with them up to the House of G-d" / "amid the sound of rejoicing and thanksgiving, the celebrating multitude."

It ends low and then level: "My G-d! My soul is downcast upon me" / "because I remember You from the land of Jordan" / "and Hermon's peaks, from Mount Mitzar" — and the last line is the love that must not be woken before it wants to be.

92.title: To Believe in Our Own Strength, which Comes from G-d
body: Week fourteen carries on Chanukah and brings in Rosh Chodesh Teveth, and the domestic goose asks for everything at once: "Give thanks to G-d and call upon His name, make His works known amongst the peoples, sing to Him, make music to Him, speak of all His wonders!" (Psalms 105:1-2) Which is last week's mitzvah again — telling the miracle — now sung.

Teveth is a hard month. It holds the fast of the tenth, when Jerusalem was besieged. Its tribe is Dan, whose mark is strength and the power to multiply. Dan had only one child and looked likely to die out, and became one of the largest tribes. Samson came from Dan, and he too is physical strength and that same power.

This week also holds Didan Netzach, "victory is ours," on the fifth of Teveth — the day of the victory of the books, when the Lubavitcher Rebbe's case over the Lubavitch library was won, and a secular court openly recognised what there is between a Rebbe and his chassidim. It sits well beside the Maccabees' victory, and beside a month that is about valuing what is written.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Chanina, deputy high priest: "Pray for the integrity of the government; for were it not for the fear of its authority, a man would swallow his neighbor alive." Taken plainly and taken as a figure, both: without something above them, the strong eat the weak, in body and in money.

It is a striking place for the deputy Kohen Gadol's teaching to fall — the week a people celebrates being freed from a foreign power by a handful of kohanim, and thanks G-d for delivering the strong into the hands of the weak.

The pairing is Malchut shebeGevurah, and it closes another seven. The Maccabees were hard and disciplined, which is gevurah, and when they had won they founded a line of kings, which is malchut. Like them, we are to act inside the material world, with discipline — which is Teveth's own quality.

The goose's lesson: notice the miracles that happen around you daily, and say them out loud. Recalling them and telling them is one of the better ways to be grateful, and gratitude is a source of blessing and of happiness.

93.title: Solomon and Having a Settled Mind
body: "The cream of cattle and the milk of sheep, with the fat of lambs and rams of Bashan and he goats, with kidneys of wheat, and it would drink the blood of grapes which was as the finest wine." (Deuteronomy 32:14) Cattle, sheep, lambs, rams, goats, fat, wheat, wine — every one of them went into the Temple's offerings, in the week the Temple was dedicated again.
The haftorah: "The Lord thundered from heaven; and the Most High gave forth His voice." (II Samuel 22:14) Thunder is light breaking through darkness, and a miracle is His voice in the open.

The quality is calmness, *yishuv* — which also means to settle, to sit, to dwell. All of which this festival is. The Temple is where He dwells on earth; the war with the Greeks was about being able to serve Him quietly in our own land. And *Chanukah* can be read *chanu k"h*, they rested on the twenty-fifth.

The prophet is King Solomon, the wisest of men — and this festival is about wisdom, Jewish chochmah set against Greek. He built and dedicated the first Temple, and his reign was the prosperity Haazinu's verse describes. He is also calmness itself: *shalom* is the root of his name, and the Tanach shows him settling disputes.

The Levitical city is Elteke, of which little is known beyond its being given to Dan. It is known for a battle in which Sancherib beat the Egyptians, after which he laid siege to Jerusalem. When all looked lost Isaiah told the king not to fear, and the next day Sancherib's army was struck by plague. That happened on Passover, with Israel and the angels saying Hallel that night — which is what we do on this festival. It is said that G-d wanted to make Chezekiah the Mashiach and did not, because he failed to say Hallel after the miracle.

The name also resembles Tekoa, both holding the uncommon pair *tav* and *kuf*. Tekoa was known for its olive oil — the only oil chosen for the Temple — and at the rededication, pure oil had to be brought from there. It took eight days to produce, which is how long the Kohen Gadol's small flask lasted, and how many days this festival runs. Oil also stands for chochmah, the highest part of the intellect, from which inspired thought comes. The Talmud notes that in Tekoa, where olive oil was common, chochmah was common too. And as the Psalm says, the beginning of chochmah is the fear of G-d.
93.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 14.

94.title: Eber and Fighting Off Physical Desires
body: "With Your loving kindness You led the people You redeemed; You led them with Your might to Your holy abode." Led, and led to a holy place, which is the week. The haftorah asks for it to be said out loud: "there they will tell the righteous acts of the Lord, the righteous acts of restoring open cities in Israel" — telling the miracle again, and restoring, which is what happened to the Temple.
And this is Rosh Chodesh Teveth, whose power is to multiply when things look hopeless.

Sotah's fourteenth daf is the burial of Moshe, who is buried opposite Baal Peor — as a guard against it — and Baal Peor is promiscuity, intermarriage and idolatry, which is what the Maccabees were fighting. The tractate also opens a new chapter and returns to the Sotah ritual, with the kind of offering she brings: barley, which is animal feed. What she is accused of is an animal's behaviour, so the offering is an animal's too.

The generation is Eber, who with his great-grandfather Shem had set up a yeshiva to study His laws even then. The destruction that falls in Teveth is bound up with Torah study not being given its proper weight. Eber seems to be helping Shem against the values of Yafeth and his grandson Yavan — and it was by learning in Eber's yeshiva that Yaakov prepared himself to face the deceit and the pull of assimilation in Lavan's house.

The journey is to a place with a bad name: "They journeyed from Kivroth haTaavah and camped in Hazeroth." Hazeroth is where Miriam spoke against Moses, and some say where Korach rebelled. Last week was burying the cravings; this week turns to bad speech and to rebellion against one's leaders. Lashon hara is weighed equal to idolatry, immorality and murder — and the Talmud says it was for those three that the first Temple fell.

95.title: Being Faithful
body: "And Eli said to her: Until when will you be drunk? Throw off your wine from upon yourself." The Kohen Gadol telling her to put the wine down. Which is worth sitting with, because this whole festival began with a Kohen Gadol — Matisiyahu — killing a man who wanted to bring a pagan offering in the Temple. Chanukah means dedication, and it is the Temple dedicated again once the idolatry was cleared out. Serving while drunk is also what killed Aaron's sons at the first dedication of the Tabernacle, which was finished on the twenty-fifth of Kislev.

But notice that Eli says *your* wine. What is wine? Rabbi Meir held that the fruit of the Tree of Knowledge was the grape, and so do the Zohar and a Midrash. The Tree of Knowledge stands for secular wisdom, as the Tree of Life stands for Torah. Rabbi Riskin points out that the Menorah is shaped like a tree, and may be the two trees perfectly combined — and that the kohanim's job is to clean and purify its lights.

So this festival is the fight between a culture tied to the Torah and one tied to secular wisdom alone — but the Torah is not against secular wisdom. It has its place, so long as it dwells in the tents of Shem. Adam's sin was not tasting the Tree of Knowledge; it was tasting it before the Tree of Life. Had he given himself to the Tree of Life first, the other would have become permitted in time.

Which may be why Eli says *your* wine. His job is to keep improper influences out of the Temple, including a person too drunk to judge how much of that tree to take in. Noah had the same trouble — the Zohar says he planted a vineyard to repair Adam's sin, and erred, and got drunk. But Eli does not rule the thing out altogether. There is a place for it, and it may still belong to Channah the tzadeket, in the right dose. That is this festival's message too.

The week's quality is that the Torah makes him *ne'eman*, faithful — from *emunah*. Emunah is what separated the Jews from the Greeks, and emunah is above reason, so a person acting out of it can look irrational to others, or even drunk, exactly as in this story. Part of having it is not being thrown by how it looks from outside.

Proverbs' fourteenth chapter runs on the same contrasts: "The wisest of women — each one built her house, but a foolish one tears it down with her hands… A faithful witness does not lie, but he who speaks lies is a false witness."

The yahrzeits are Ishbitz and Peshischa. On the fourth of Teveth, Rabbi Gershon Chanoch Henoch Leiner of Radzin, the Baal HaTecheles, grandson of the founder; and often this week the founder himself, Rav Mordecai Yosef Leiner of Ishbitz, the Mei Shiloach — a childhood friend and colleague of the Kotzker Rebbe, both of them students of Reb Simcha Bunim of Peshischa. He followed Kotzk and taught there, and in the end the two parted and Ishbitz was founded. His own students included Rav Tzadok HaKohen of Lublin.

96.title: Sticking with the Torah and the Temple
body: "Who is this coming up from the desert, like columns of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, of all the powder of the peddler? Behold the litter of Solomon; sixty mighty men are around it, of the mighty men of Israel. They all hold the sword, skilled in warfare; each one with his sword on his thigh because of fear at night."

Coming up out of the desert under the Clouds of Glory — and this festival is eight days in order to answer Sukkot, which is that protection remembered. Rashi takes the verses to the Mishkan, the Temple that moved, and to "the war of Torah, and similarly, the priests who surround it, who camp around the Mishkan, skilled in the order of their service."

And then he says what the swords are. "Each one with his sword: his weapons. These are the Masorah and the mnemonics, by which they preserve the correct version of the Oral Law and the masorah, lest it be forgotten. Because of fear at night: lest they forget it, and troubles will befall them." The night is Greece's darkness. The weapons are the devices for keeping the text and the reading exact — which is both the fight against a perverted law and the respect for Torah whose absence, as this month remembers, brought the first Temple down.

Of the seventy souls the fourteenth is Gershon — the name of one of Levi's sons and of one of Moshe's. It is a name about being a stranger, and about holding on to who you are among foreign influences. Moshe's Gershon was brought up by Yitro as well as by Moshe, and Yitro's influence told in the long run. Gershon's family also had charge of keeping up the Mishkan.

Shevuot's fourteenth daf carries on with the kohanim's atonement, taken separately, and opens a chapter on awareness of impurity and what happens when a person forgets its laws. Impurity against purity is this festival; and ignorance of the law is Teveth's tenth day.

Jeremiah's fourteenth chapter is a drought from beginning to end — and there is no reference to water in Scripture that is not the Torah. Its close comes back to this month exactly: "Do not condemn us for Your name's sake, do not disgrace the throne of Your glory. Remember, do not break Your covenant with us." The throne of His glory, Rashi says, is the Temple.

97.title: Reviewing the First Week of Teveth - Psalms 40-42; 42:8-10; 89:15
body: The first week of Teveth in psalms: the fortieth, forty-first and forty-second, with three verses of the Tikkun HaKlali and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 40 opens with being pulled out. "I put my hope in the Lord; He turned to me and heard my cry. He raised me from the turbulent pit, from the slimy mud, and set my feet upon a rock, steadying my steps. He put a new song in my mouth." Then it says what is actually wanted: "You desired neither sacrifice nor meal-offering, but obedient ears You opened for me… I desire to fulfill Your will, my G-d; and Your Torah is in my innards." And it will not keep quiet about it: "I did not conceal Your righteousness within my heart… I did not hide Your kindness and truth from the vast congregation." Then the weight comes back: "my sins have overtaken me and I cannot see; they outnumber the hairs of my head." It ends plainly: "As for me, I am poor and needy… my G-d, do not delay!"

Psalm 41 is the whole psalm of the man thoughtful of the poor, having been given to us a few verses at a time. "Fortunate is he who is thoughtful of the poor, for the Lord will save him on the day of evil… The Lord will support him on the bed of illness." Then the sickroom visitors: "if one comes to see me, he speaks insincerely, for his heart gathers iniquity for himself, and when he goes out he speaks of it." And the betrayal: "Even my ally in whom I trusted, who ate of my bread, has raised his heel over me."

Psalm 42 is the thirst, whole. "As the deer cries longingly for brooks of water, so my soul cries longingly for You, O G-d! My soul thirsts for G-d, for the living G-d. When will I come and behold the countenance of G-d? My tears have been my bread day and night, when they say to me all day, 'Where is your G-d?'" It remembers walking up to the House in a crowd, and asks itself twice why it is downcast. And it holds the line that is this month's measure of depth: "Deep calls to deep at the roar of Your channels; all Your breakers and waves have swept over me." Then: "By day the Lord ordains His kindness, and at night His song is with me, a prayer to the G-d of my life."
Psalm 89's verse names what the throne stands on: "Righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne; kindness and truth go before Your countenance."

98.title: The Domestic Goose is Saying
body: The domestic goose opens, and this gathering runs the day's kindness against the night's song.

"Give thanks to G-d and call upon His name" / "make His works known amongst the peoples" / "by day the Lord ordains His kindness" / "and at night His song is with me." Then the music, and the prayer: "sing to Him, make music to Him, speak of all His wonders!" / "a prayer to the G-d of my life."

Then the throne, and the depths: "Righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne" / "kindness and truth go before Your countenance" / "deep calls to deep at the roar of Your channels" / "all Your breakers and waves have swept over me."

Solomon's litter comes next with its guard: "Behold the litter of Solomon; sixty mighty men are around it, of the mighty men of Israel" / "they all hold the sword, skilled in warfare" / "each with a sword on his thigh due to fear at night." And then the thunder: "The Lord thundered from heaven; and the Most High gave forth His voice."

The lowest line in the gathering falls here, between the thunder and the wine: "I say to G-d, my rock, 'Why have You forgotten me? Why must I walk in gloom under the oppression of the enemy?'" / "and it would drink the blood of grapes as the finest wine" / "and Eli said to her: Until when will you be drunk? Throw off your wine from upon yourself."

It ends in the desert and the spices, and then in the plenty: "of all the powder of the peddler" / "who is this coming up from the desert" / "like columns of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense" / "the cream of cattle and the milk of sheep" / "with the fat of lambs and rams of Bashan and he goats, with kidneys of wheat."

99.title: Giving Proper Value to Torah and to the Presence of the Shechinah
body: Week fifteen, and the wild goose has two songs. Seeing Israel busy with Torah: "A voice cries out: Prepare in the wilderness the way for G-d, make straight in the desert a path for our G-d." (Isaiah 40:3) And on finding its food out there: "Cursed is the man who trusts in human beings; Blessed is the man who trusts in G-d, and G-d shall be his assurance." (Jeremiah 17: 5, 7)

This is the week of the fast of the tenth of Teveth, when Jerusalem was besieged in the days of the first Temple — the first step toward its destruction and the exile of the Shechinah. It is also the yahrzeit of Rabbi Nathan of Breslov, Rebbe Nachman's chief disciple.

Few survived that destruction, and they multiplied back into a numerous people — like Dan, whose month this is. Much the same happened to Rabbi Nathan: he took up a movement that was tiny, against terrible opposition, and it not only survived but grew beyond measure.

The Midrash says Jerusalem was besieged and the Temple later destroyed because the people did not recite the blessing over Torah study. That is, because of what they did not think the Torah and the holy writings were worth. Which sits beside Didan Netzach, the victory of the books, from last week.

And there is the other half of the goose's song. They also put their trust in the wrong place — in an alliance with Egypt, against which the prophets had warned. In a prophecy made on the twelfth of Teveth, before the siege, Ezekiel calls Egypt "a reed-like support for the House of Israel — whenever they held you in their hand you would snap, piercing their every shoulder." When Egypt fell to Babylon, Israel followed.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Chanina son of Tradyon: two who sit together and let no word of Torah pass between them are a session of scorners; two who sit and exchange words of Torah have the Divine Presence resting between them. And even one who sits alone and occupies himself with it has a reward set aside for him: "He sits alone in meditative stillness; indeed, he receives reward for it."
The pairing is Chesed shebeTiferet. When the siege began it was not yet hopeless — there was still room to turn back and stop the whole thing. Kindness inside mercy, which is tiferet's other name.
What the goose knows is that Torah study matters and that its food comes from Him and not from any person. If we do our part, He will do His.

100.title: The Prophet Iddo and the Importance of Scripture
body: "And Jeshurun became fat and rebelled; you grew fat, thick and rotund; Israel forsook the G-d Who made them, and spurned the Mighty Rock of their salvation." (Deuteronomy 32:15) Rebellion after everything — which is what the tenth of Teveth is about, a people grown fat and not valuing what they had.

But the word for fat, *shemen*, used twice here, is also the word for oil. And oil belongs to the lights of Chanukah, which take in Rosh Chodesh Teveth and so shine through this whole month. So the verse can be read the other way: Jeshurun became full of oil and kicked away the enemy; grew full of oil, thick and rotund in holiness; spread out the knowledge of the G-d Who made them, and made song with the lyre about the Rock of their salvation. Spreading the word is this season's own mitzvah.
The haftorah suits the second reading better: "And He sent out arrows and He scattered them, lightning and He discomfited them." (II Samuel 22:15) Scattering, and light.
The quality is *Mikrah*, scripture — and the first Temple fell over the blessing not said on Torah study, over scripture not being held holy enough.

The prophet is Iddo, and the only thing Tanach says of him is that he wrote: he set down the events of Rehoboam, and the genealogy of the kings of Israel, with Shemaiah the Prophet. He took writing and records seriously. And the Talmud says Iddo is the prophet who went against his own word and was mauled by a lion — which runs painfully close to a people that did not heed the words of the prophets and of scripture.

The Levitical city is Gibbethon, another name attached to disaster: the Talmud says Rabbi Akiva's twenty-four thousand students who died were "from Gibbethon to Antipatris." And then, in the manner of this month and of Dan — out of five more students, Rabbi Akiva rebuilt everything.
100.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 15.

101.title: Peleg and Evil Speech
body: "People heard, they trembled; a shudder seized the inhabitants of Philistia." Years later it would be this people trembling, when Babylon came and laid its siege.

The haftorah: "Then the people of the Lord went down to the cities. Praise! Praise! Deborah." The word for cities, *shearim*, also means gates — and on the tenth of Teveth Nebuchadnezar came down on the city and closed round its gates. As for "Praise, praise Devorah," Rashi explains that it is said because the spirit of G-d had left her, since she had praised herself. Which belongs to this week too: the Temple lost its spirit because the people did not bless the Torah they studied. All Torah and all prophecy come from Him, and there is no room to praise yourself for it.

Sotah's fifteenth daf sets the Sotah's offering beside the metzora's, and notes that the metzora's purification is the more severe. The metzora's sin is *lashon hara* — which is weighed against all three of the great sins, and is another reason given for the Temple's fall. And he is sent out of the camp, and can only come back once he is clean, which is the exile that followed.

The generation is Peleg, named so because in his days the tower was built and the world's people were split and scattered into different lands. That is the same exile, and the same sentence as the metzora's, who was sent out for having split people apart with his mouth. The Babylonians made a point of taking most of the people out of the land and settling others in parts of it, and the division between Israel and the Babylonian diaspora held for centuries.

The journey is to a place named for a mouth: "They journeyed from Hazeroth and camped in Rithmah." Rithmah is also Kadesh Barnea, where the spies slandered the Land — the lesson of Miriam not having been learned — and what came of that, and of the people accepting it, was Tisha B'Av. Rashi derives the name from the slander: "What can He give you, and what can He add to you, you deceitful tongue? Sharpened arrows of a mighty man, with coals of brooms."

Slandering the Land was in the end slandering Him: they did not believe He could bring them into it. Last week was bad speech about people and rebellion against leaders; this week is bad speech about G-d and about the Land. And the Talmud teaches that whoever does not show gratitude to another person will end up not showing it to Hashem either.

102.title: Handling Reproof
body: "And Hannah answered and said: 'No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit; I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but I poured out my soul before the Lord.'"
That is the fast, in a sentence. Sorrow said out loud, nothing drunk, and the soul poured out instead.

The week's quality is that the Torah distances him from sin — which does not only mean that he does not sin. It also means that a person wrongly suspected of sinning is required to speak up. The Talmud learns that principle from this very verse.

Proverbs' fifteenth chapter is about how reproof is given and how it is taken. "A gentle reply turns away wrath, but a distressing word stirs up anger… A fool despises the discipline of his father, but he who keeps reproof will become cunning… A scorner does not like being reproved; he does not go to the wise… The ear that listens to reproof of life shall lodge among the wise. He who rejects discipline despises his life, but he who hearkens to reproof acquires sense. The fear of the Lord is the discipline of wisdom, and before honor there is humility." A fast day is largely about knowing how to take reproof and turn.

The tenth of Teveth is the yahrzeit of Rebbe Nosson of Breslev, Rebbe Nachman's main disciple, who published his works and carried the thing forward. Rebbe Nachman called him his Yehoshua, and Breslev chassidim say plainly that without Rebbe Nosson we would be lost. His life was faith and determination against very hard opposition: in trying to hold on to Rebbe Nachman he was opposed not only by other Chassidic leaders but by his parents, his in-laws, and his wife. He stayed with it, knew how to take opposition and reproof that was not deserved, and went on pouring out his soul.

The twelfth of Teveth is the yahrzeit of Rebbe Moshe of Peshevorsk, from whom that dynasty comes. This week belongs to the written Torah, and he was known for the Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot that he wrote — a man of great purity, and the author of Ohr Penei Moshe.

103.title: Jerusalem and Motherhood
body: "King Solomon made himself a palanquin of the trees of Lebanon. Its pillars he made of silver, its couch of gold, its curtain of purple, its interior inlaid with love, from the daughters of Jerusalem. Go out, O daughters of Zion, and gaze upon King Solomon, upon the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his nuptials and on the day of the joy of his heart."
Solomon in this book is always Him, and here the Jewish people are His mother. Rashi cites a Midrash: calling them His mother is the highest thing He says about His love for them.

And that image stands against what this week remembers. Jeremiah, on the siege: "Better off were the victims of the sword than the victims of hunger… The hands of compassionate women boiled their own children; they have become their food in the destruction of the daughter of my people."

In time to come, the tenth of Teveth will be a day of joy. These verses look like that time — full of the Temple and the Tabernacle and Jerusalem, with the day of his nuptials being the giving of the Torah and the day of the joy of his heart the Tabernacle's dedication.

Of the seventy souls the fifteenth is Kehath, who is Moshe and Aharon's grandfather and also their uncle, their mother Yocheved's brother. The Rebbe explains that Kehath comes from a word meaning to gather. His charge in the Tabernacle was the highest of all the Levites': carrying the Holy Ark and its vessels. And it was Kehath's camp that Korach belonged to, which ended in enormous destruction. The destruction belongs to this week and the highest task to the time when the Temple stands again and this day is a feast.

Shevuot's fifteenth daf is the sanctifying of the Temple's vessels, and the ritual of adding on to Jerusalem or to the Azarah — which is done with singing and with loaves of bread carried. Set that against the tenth of Teveth, when Jerusalem was not added to but closed in; when instead of singing there was mourning, and instead of bread, famine.

Jeremiah's fifteenth chapter takes the same two subjects, motherhood and Jerusalem, from the dark side: "She who bore seven has been cut off, her soul grieves, her sun sets when it is still day." And: "Woe is to me, my mother, that you bore me, a man of quarrel and a man of contention to the whole land."

104.title: Reviewing the Second Week of Teveth - Psalms 43-45; 42:11-12, 59:1-2; 89:16
body: The second week of Teveth in psalms: the forty-third, forty-fourth and forty-fifth, with the end of Psalm 42, the opening of Psalm 59, and a verse of Psalm 89.

Psalm 43 is short and asks for an escort. "Avenge me, O G-d, and champion my cause against an impious nation… For You are the G-d of my strength; why have You abandoned me?" Then the request that gives the psalm its shape: "Send Your light and Your truth, they will guide me; they will bring me to Your holy mountain and to your sanctuaries. Then I will come to the altar of G-d." And the question again, and the same answer: "Why are you downcast, my soul… Hope to G-d, for I will yet thank Him."

Psalm 44 is the hardest psalm in this stretch. It opens on what the fathers told: "You drove out nations with Your hand… For not by their sword did they inherit the land, and their own arm did not save them, but by Your right hand." Then it turns, and the turn is brutal: "Though You abandon and disgrace us… You deliver us like sheep to be devoured, and scatter us among the nations; You sell Your nation without gain, and do not set a high price upon them." And then, in the middle of that, the thing it refuses to give up: "all this has come upon us, yet we have not forgotten You, nor have we been false to Your covenant… Even when You crushed us in the place of serpents, and shrouded us in the shadow of death — did we forget the Name of our G-d, and extend our hands to a foreign G-d? Is it not so that G-d can examine this, for He knows the secrets of the heart." Then: "For it is for Your sake that we are killed all the time; we are regarded as sheep for the slaughter." And it ends shouting: "Arise! Why do You sleep, my Lord? Wake up!"

Psalm 45 is a wedding song, and it knows it: "My heart is astir with a noble theme; I say, 'My composition is for the king; my tongue is the pen of a skillful scribe.'" Then: "Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one — it is your majesty and splendor."

Psalm 42's last verses carry the reproach — "my oppressors have reproached me by saying to me all day long, 'Where is your G-d?'" — and Psalm 59 opens with Saul's men around the house: "Save me from my enemies, my G-d; strengthen me against those who rise up against me." Psalm 89's verse is the shofar: "Fortunate is the people that know the blasting of the shofar."

105.title: The Wild Goose Is Saying
body: The wild goose opens — seeing Israel busy with Torah — and the gathering sets the way through the wilderness against a palanquin.

"A voice cries out: Prepare in the wilderness the way for G-d" is framed by the shofar and the light: "Fortunate is the people that know the blasting of the shofar" / "O Lord, may they walk in the light of Your countenance." Then the straight path, and the daughters of Zion called out to look: "Make straight in the desert a path for our G-d" / "Go out, O daughters of Zion, and gaze upon King Solomon."

The people going down to the cities comes next, with the palanquin built around it: "Then the people of the Lord went down to the cities" / "King Solomon made himself a palanquin of the trees of Lebanon" / "Praise! Praise! Deborah" / "its pillars he made of silver, its couch of gold, its curtain of purple."

Then the interior inlaid with love, the trembling, and the crown: "its interior inlaid with love, from the daughters of Jerusalem" / "People heard, they trembled" / "upon the crown with which his mother crowned him."

The goose's second song arrives here, braided with Haazinu's growing fat — the two readings of *shemen* side by side: "And upon finding its food in the wilderness, it says" / "And Jeshurun became fat and rebelled" / "Cursed is the man who trusts in human beings" / "you grew fat, thick and rotund" / "Blessed is the man who trusts in G-d" / "Israel forsook the G-d Who made them" / "and He sent out arrows and He scattered them."

The last stretch is Hannah answering, with Saul's men at the door: "And Hannah answered and said: 'No, my lord'" / "I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit" / "with murder in my bones, my oppressors have reproached me" / "I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink" / "but I poured out my soul before Hashem."
It ends: "Save me from my enemies, my G-d" / "a shudder seized the inhabitants of Philistia" / "strengthen me against those who rise up against me" / "and G-d shall be his assurance."

106.title: To Use Adversity as a Way to Grow, Relying on G-d for Support
body: Week sixteen, and the ducks — plural, which matters — say: "Trust in G-d forever and ever, for G-d, the Eternal, is the strength of worlds." (Isaiah 26:4)

The Talmud calls Teveth the coldest month of the year, "when the body takes pleasure in the body." And Perek Shirah has ducks here rather than a duck. They breed fast and keep large families; they travel in groups and depend on each other to get through the cold.

Which is this month's own story. After the first Temple fell, very few were left — the Book of Jeremiah counts four thousand six hundred exiled to Babylon altogether. And in a fairly short time that community in Babylon became numerous, influential and rich.

The song is about His strength and also about His giving us the power to bring life. *Tzur* means strength and also Creator, or Craftsman; *Yotzer*, from the same root, is used of the One who "fashioned you from the womb." And the verse mixes the Names: the feminine one of *yud* and *hey*, the masculine *Tzur*, and between them the Name that holds both.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: three who eat at one table and speak no words of Torah have eaten of idolatrous sacrifices — "all tables are filled with vomit and filth, devoid of the Omnipresent." But three who eat at one table and do speak words of Torah have eaten at G-d's own table: "This is the table that is before G-d."

That belongs here because the Temple fell over how little Torah study was thought to be worth. And Rabbi Shimon, who knew the hidden part of the Torah better than anyone, is teaching how to serve Him with the body — which is the deeper reading of the body taking pleasure in the body. The Lubavitcher Rebbe explains that serving Him with the body, not only with mind and soul, reaches further: to His essence. An ordinary meal becomes the table of G-d. The same is true of marriage, which can be the holiest thing a person does or the most profane, depending entirely on the two people and what they intend.
The pairing is Gevurah shebeTiferet: recovering from the loss, and using discipline to get back to the balanced beauty of the Torah.
The ducks' own lesson is to lean on Him completely, the way you would lean on a rock.

107.title: Michaiah and the Oral Torah
body: "They provoked His zeal with alien worship; they made Him angry with abominable deeds." (Deuteronomy 32:16) Idolatry, which is what brought the first Temple down — and which is tied to Dan in particular, the tribe that first brought idol worship into the Land after the conquest, in the account of Pessel Micha near the end of Judges.

The verse can also be turned around. The zeal and the anger need not be His: they can be the people's, zealous and angry *for* Him. Zeal against idolatry was the Maccabees' defining mark, and kohanim as a class are known for zeal — and sometimes for being hot-headed with it.

The haftorah reads better the second way: "And the depths of the sea appeared; the foundations of the world were laid bare, by the rebuke of the Lord and the blast of the breath of His nostrils." (II Samuel 22:16) Rashi takes it to the splitting of the sea. The depths of the sea may be the Talmud; and the foundations of the world may be the Temple, which holds the Even Shtiah, the stone creation began from.
The quality is Mishnah, the Oral Torah — in a week still shaped by the tenth of Teveth, which came of Torah study not being held holy enough.

The prophet is Michaiah son of Imlah, and the Oral Torah is exactly his problem. It has to be handed on faithfully, and interpreted honestly. Sometimes men claim to speak for the tradition and are corrupting it. In his story four hundred prophets gave the king the answer he wanted, and one prophet saw what was actually there. Even false prophets can be moved by a spirit; the spirit can be false. He prophesied in the days of Ahab, a wicked king who nevertheless studied Torah — which is the same corruption of what study is for.

The Levitical city is Ayalon, where Joshua told the moon to stand still, and where he beat five Amorite kings. The Talmud reads the sun and moon as Moshe and Joshua and the passing on of the oral tradition: as Joshua took it from Moshe, the moon takes its light from the sun, having none of its own. Teveth is the only month with a festival at the new moon. And a moon that nearly disappears and then comes back to full is this month and this tribe exactly — as is Ayalon's own history, pushed out of Dan's hands by the Amorites, later the scene of Saul and Jonathan's victory, later held by Benjamin and Efraim, and in the end a border town that Rehoboam fortified.
107.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 16.

108.title: Overcoming Setbacks
body: "Then the chieftains of Edom were startled; as for the powerful men of Moab, trembling seized them." Startled, and trembling — and at the siege it was this people's turn to shudder.

The haftorah repeats the matter of the spirit leaving Devorah for praising herself: "Praise! Praise! Utter a song. Arise Barak, and capture your captives, son of Abinoam." And the captives taken may also be Jerusalem's own, carried off once the city fell.

Sotah's sixteenth daf is still the Sotah's offering, now the soil put into the water she drinks, with a good deal about the metzora alongside — which keeps to this month's subjects: exile, and not enough to eat or drink.

The generation is Reu, Peleg's son, born just after the world's people had been split up and scattered. And where his father's name means separation, Reu's is related to the words for shepherd and for friend. So the name looks like the ability to gather again and do well after a scattering — after that tower, and after Babylon.

The journey is to a bursting fruit: "They journeyed from Rithmah and camped in Rimmon Perez." Rimmon Perez means a pomegranate bursting open, and a pomegranate full of seeds stands for being fruitful and for keeping mitzvot. Last week was slander and the exile that comes with it. This week is regrouping, and getting back to being productive.

109.title: Bringing Oneself Close to Merit
body: "Count not thy handmaid for a wicked woman: for out of the abundance of my complaint and my vexation have I spoken hitherto." She asks Eli to judge her favourably rather than as a wicked woman. The word she uses, *Bli'al*, is also bound up with idolatry — and the sages learn from here that a person who prays the Amidah drunk is likened to one who worships idols. And she names her vexation, which is this month's own feeling.
The week's quality is that the Torah brings a person close to merit. Her speech is the illustration.

Proverbs' sixteenth chapter is about the same thing — a man's part and His part. "The preparations of the heart are man's, but the answer of the tongue is from the Lord. All ways of man are pure in his eyes, but the Lord counts the spirits… With loving-kindness and truth will iniquity be expiated… When the Lord accepts a person's ways, He will cause even his enemies to make peace with him. Better a little with righteousness than great revenues with injustice. A man's heart plans his way, but the Lord prepares his step."

Three yahrzeits this week, all of them tied to the Seer of Lublin. The sixteenth of Teveth is Rabbi Aryeh Leibish of Vishnitza, called Rebbe Leibish Charif, the sharp one, a very close disciple of the Seer. The seventeenth is Rabbi Fischel Shapira of Strickov, who was a disciple in turn of the Maggid of Mezritch, then of Rebbe Elimelech, then of the Seer — known for such humility that he was called *Olah Temimah*, the unblemished offering.

And the eighteenth is Rabbi Tzvi Elimelech Shapira of Dinov, author of the Bnei Yissachar, which is the basis for a great many of the insights in this work. He was Rebbe Elimelech's nephew, and a disciple of the Seer of Lublin and of Menachem Mendel of Rimanov.

110.title: Being Wife and Midwife
body: "Behold, you are fair, my beloved; behold, you are fair; your eyes are like doves, from within your kerchief; your hair is like a flock of goats that streamed down from Mount Gilead. Your teeth are like a flock of uniformly shaped ewes that came up from the washing, all of whom are perfect, and there is no bereavement among them. Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your speech is comely; your temple is like a split pomegranate from within your kerchief."

This week's verses and next week's — the first six of the fourth chapter — are the ones that use the body most openly as a figure for what this people is. Which belongs to the month in which the body takes pleasure in the body, meaning the essence of this people meeting His essence.

Of the seventy souls the sixteenth is Merari, whose family had the least prestigious and the heaviest job in the Tabernacle: carrying the beams, the crossbars, the pillars and the bases. *Merari* comes from *mar*, bitter — the same root as Miriam. The Rebbe's father explains that of Yocheved's three children, Miriam answers to Merari. These were the foundations the rest of it stood on, which is the quiet and necessary thing Miriam did as a midwife. Teveth is cold and in some ways bitter, and it is also strength, foundation, and the power to multiply.

Shevuot's sixteenth daf asks whether the holiness of the first Temple was temporary or permanent, and takes up the case of someone who becomes impure inside it, and the laws of bowing there. The fast of the tenth belongs to that Temple in particular.

Jeremiah's sixteenth chapter turns the month's other subject dark: "You shall take no wife, and you shall have no sons or daughters in this place." And: "Behold, I will cut off from this place in your presence and in your days a voice of mirth and a voice of gladness, a voice of a bridegroom, and a voice of a bride."

111.title: Reviewing the Third Week of Teveth - Psalms 46-48; 59:3-5; 89:17
body: The third week of Teveth in psalms: the forty-sixth, forty-seventh and forty-eighth, with three verses of Psalm 59 and one of Psalm 89. All three are headed as being about the Messianic era, when weapons are put down.

Psalm 46 is steadiness while everything else moves. "G-d is our refuge and strength, a help in distress, He is most accessible. Therefore, we will not be afraid when the earth is transformed, when mountains collapse in the heart of the seas." Then the city: "The river — its streams will bring joy to the city of G-d, the sacred dwelling of the Most High. G-d is in her midst, she will not falter." And the end of war, stated as an act: "To the end of the earth He causes wars to cease; He breaks the bow, snaps the spear, and burns the wagons in fire." Then the one-word command: "Stop waging war! And know that I am G-d." It closes on the refrain it used before: "The Lord of Hosts is with us; the G-d of Jacob is our stronghold forever."

Psalm 47 is the shofar psalm said before the blowing. "All you nations, clap hands; sound to G-d with a sound of jubilation… He chooses our heritage for us, the glory of Jacob whom He loves eternally. G-d ascends through teruah, the Lord — through the sound of the shofar." And at the end the nations are not beaten but gathered: "The most noble of the nations are gathered, the nation of the G-d of Abraham."
