Psalm 48 walks around a city. "The Lord is great and exceedingly acclaimed in the city of G-d, His holy mountain. Beautiful in landscape, the joy of the whole earth is Mount Zion." Kings came against her, "they saw and were astounded; they were terror-stricken, they hastened to flee. Trembling seized them there, pangs as of a woman in the throes of labor." And then the line this week's other books keep reaching for: "As we have heard, so have we seen." It ends with an instruction: "Walk around Zion, encircle her, count her towers. Consider well her ramparts, behold her lofty citadels, that you may recount it to a later generation."
Psalm 59's verses are the ambush: "For behold they lie in ambush for my soul, mighty ones gather against me — not because of my sin nor my transgression, O Lord."

112.title: The Ducks are Saying
body: The ducks open, and this gathering braids a description of beauty with an ambush.

"Trust in G-d forever and ever" arrives already surrounded by the washing and the perfect flock — "that came up from the washing" / "all of whom are perfect" — and then the rejoicing: "they rejoice in Your Name all day" / "for G-d, the Eternal, is the strength of worlds."

The teeth and the temple follow, with the righteousness between them: "Your teeth are like a flock of uniformly shaped ewes" / "and they are exalted through Your righteousness" / "your temple is like a split pomegranate from within your kerchief."

Then the zeal and the rebuke, and the protest of innocence laid right across them: "They provoked His zeal with alien worship" / "by the rebuke of the Lord and the blast of the breath of His nostrils" / "without iniquity on my part, they run and prepare" / "awaken towards me and see!" / "they made Him angry with abominable deeds" / "rescue me from evildoers, save me from men of bloodshed."

Channah's own protest comes in here, broken across the psalm's: "and my vexation have I spoken hitherto" / "not because of my sin nor my transgression, O Lord" / "count not thy handmaid for a wicked woman" / "for behold they lie in ambush for my soul" / "for out of the abundance of my complaint" / "mighty ones gather against me."
Then the chieftains of Edom are startled, with the scarlet thread beside them, and Moab's trembling, and the hair like a flock of goats, and the praise: "Praise! Praise! Utter a song."

It ends where it is fairest: "Behold, you are fair, my beloved; behold, you are fair" / "your eyes are like doves, from within your kerchief" / "Arise Barak, and capture your captives, son of Abinoam" / "and the depths of the sea appeared" / "that streamed down from Mount Gilead" / "the foundations of the world were laid bare" / "and there is no bereavement among them."

113.title: To Pay Attention to G-d’s Guidance and to Trust in Our Redemption
body: Week seventeen, the last of Teveth, and the bee-eater says: "I will whistle to them and gather them, for I have redeemed them, and they shall increase as they have before increased." (Zechariah 10:8) The increase is Dan again. The whistle is a shepherd's.

This week holds the yahrzeit of the Alter Rebbe, on the twenty-fourth of Teveth. He died largely of the flight from Napoleon. He had backed Russia in that war, because he judged that Napoleon's egalitarian promises would end in assimilation — and that spiritual persecution of that kind was more dangerous than the physical oppression of the Russian government, much as the Greeks had been more dangerous than other empires.

On the flight, the Alter Rebbe rode in the third carriage and his grandson Rabbi Nachum in the first, and at every crossroads they asked him which way. At one of them Rabbi Nachum misheard. When the mistake came to light, much later, "the Alter Rebbe sighed deeply and said: 'How good is it when a grandson follows in the path of his grandfather — and the opposite is true when a grandfather has to follow the path in which his grandson leads him.' … The mistake at the crossroads caused all kinds of troublesome detours, and soon after Alter Rebbe passed away in Piena."

The whistle, then, is the ways He uses to turn a lost Jew back. He is the shepherd and we are the flock. The Zohar calls Moses *Rayah Mehemnah*, a faithful shepherd and a shepherd of faith, and the leader of each generation is that generation's Moses. The point of following such advice is not to lose your way in the dark, which is exactly what happened in that story.

Seventeen is the numerical value of *tov*, good — and it is also the number of the seventeenth of Tammuz, which began the Temple's end. The Talmud ties the two kinds of loss together: the passing of tzadikim is likened to the burning of the Temple. The Lubavitcher Rebbe answers the difficulty the same way for both: this is a descent for the sake of an ascent, and the ascent is great enough to make the exile worth it, there being no other way to reach that rung. The passing of a tzadik opens a level nothing else reaches, and that is the only reason for it. So seventeen really is good, with the extent of the good hidden for now. It is also the value of *cheit*, sin, which is the one thing holding the redemption back — because of our sins we were exiled from our land.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Chanina the son of Chachina'i: "One who stays awake at night, or travels alone on the road, and turns his heart to idleness, has forfeited his life." The night is exile. In it you cannot be alone and occupied with nothing; you have to be gathered, listening for the whistle, and studying — or you lose the road.

Rebbe Nachman reads the same words the other way round. Travelling alone is making your own path in prayer and hitbodedut; *batalah*, idleness, he hears as *bitul*, self-nullification; and "forfeits his life," *mitchayev et nafsho*, he reads as making his soul such that the whole world is obliged to exist for it. Which is the condition of a generation's tzadik.

The pairing is Tiferet shebeTiferet. And the bee-eater's Hebrew name, *Rachamah*, has *rachamim* in it — mercy, which is tiferet's other name. Its lesson is to be sure He is with you and guiding you through the bad part, and also to be listening, so that when the call comes you do not miss it.

114.title: Obadiah and Minimized Business Activity
body: "They sacrificed to demons, which have no power, deities they did not know, new things that only recently came, which your forefathers did not fear." (Deuteronomy 32:17) Idolatry again, which is Teveth and is Dan.

And again the verse can be turned: would they sacrifice to demons? No. Their power was G-d; they did not know new ones. Which is worth stopping on, because the verse names what makes assimilation attractive. It is *new* — then as now, the Torah gets painted as out of date. And it comes "from close by." What pulls hardest in another culture is the part that most resembles our own. The Greeks and the Hellenized Jews came from close; what they championed, wisdom and humanism, was often very near Jewish ideals.

The haftorah goes with the positive reading: "He sent from on high and He took me; He drew me out of many waters." (II Samuel 22:17) And many waters, as Book 1 has it, is the struggle of making a living.

Which is the quality: *miut schorah*, minimised business activity. Money and the getting of it turn idolatrous very easily — it becomes the end, and we forget we wanted it in order to serve Him better and provide for a family. So business is to be conducted with *miut*, smallness and humility, with study and service still the main thing.

The prophet is Obadiah, who prophesied like Michaia in Ahab's days, when idolatry was everywhere. Ahab is the opposite of this quality: he took another man's field by force and had the owner killed, and for that he was sentenced from Heaven. Obadiah is the quality itself — he used his own money to keep a hundred prophets alive and hidden from Ahab and Jezebel, and that act earned him prophecy. His name says it: servant of G-d. He understood whose work he was actually doing.

His prophecy is that G-d loves Jacob and hates Esau, which is the message in a fight against assimilation. Much of what drew Jews to Roman culture and its offshoots was how like Judaism they looked. Esau is Jacob's brother, after all. And Jacob, meeting him, says: "My master knows that the children are tender, and the flocks and the cattle, which are raising their young, depend upon me, and if they overdrive them one day, all the flocks will die. Now, let my master go ahead before his servant, and I will move at my own slow pace." He did not want Esau near his family — and, reading the flocks as well as the children, he did not want his possessions exposed to Esau's appetite either.
The Levitical city is Gath-rimmon, the winepress of pomegranates: out in the world and in its dark, there is a great deal of good available, and a person can come back as full as that fruit.
114.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 17.

115.title: Avraham, Serug, and the Alter Rebbe
body: "All the inhabitants of Canaan melted. May dread and fright fall upon them." And the haftorah could not suit Dan better: "Then ruled a remnant among the mighty of the nations; the Lord dominated the strong for me." A remnant ruling over the mighty, which is being small and then not.

Sotah's seventeenth daf is the writing of the curses on the scroll that gets dissolved in the water, and how curses can be inferred from blessings — and how even in the words for man and woman there is *fire* waiting, if the Divine Presence does not dwell between the couple. Both halves belong to this month: blessings turned to curses, and two Temples left by the Presence and then burned.

The daf also tells how Avraham was rewarded for refusing the spoils of the king of Sodom. Which runs alongside the Alter Rebbe. Napoleon was offering Jews more money and more freedom, and he saw where it led. The king of Sodom had said, take the goods and I will take the souls — and Avraham would not. And where Avraham refused even the smallest personal thing, Napoleon went looking for the smallest personal thing belonging to the Alter Rebbe, who had set fire to his own house before leaving, so that nothing was found.

The generation is Serug, Reu's son, and his name is a further gathering: from *lesareg*, to interlace, to interweave. More than rejoining a flock — being woven in. Which is the Alter Rebbe's own innovation: that chassidim are one family, bound unbreakably. The Hayom Yom for the twenty-fourth of Teveth has it exactly. Asked what the Alter Rebbe meant by the "ways of Chassidus" and by "Chassidus," the Tzemach Tzedek answered: the ways of Chassidus are that all chassidim are to be like one family, with affection, as the Torah teaches. And Chassidus is vitality — to bring life and light into everything, to shed light even on what is undesirable, "to become aware of one's own evil exactly as it is, in order to correct it."

The journey is to bricks: "They journeyed from Rimmon Perez and camped in Libnah." Libnah is from *leveinim*, bricks, which belong to the labour in Egypt — where at the end they were not even given straw. In Torah Or, quoting the Zohar, the Alter Rebbe explains that that labour has a counterpart in study: *leveinim*, bricks, points at *libun hilchesa*, the clarifying of law, and *chomer*, mortar, at *kal vachomer*, one of the main rules of interpretation. The hard labour of exile can be exchanged for the labour of study. Last week was being fruitful; this week is studying properly — which is the thing this month remembers the lack of.

116.title: Going to Peace
body: "And Eli answered and said: Go in peace, and the God of Israel will grant your request which you have asked of Him."

The Hebrew is *Lechi L'Shalom*, which is *go to peace* rather than *go in peace* — and *Lech B'Shalom*, go in peace, is said only of those who have died. Rav Kook explains that nobody can be wished final peace in this world. This is a world of struggle, and Teveth more than most of it. The ultimate peace will come; in the meantime, expect an intense journey. The events around the Alter Rebbe's passing were exactly that.

The week's quality is that from such a person people enjoy counsel. Which is the verse: Eli's counsel is what finally lets Channah breathe, knowing the prayer will be answered. And the whole Book of Proverbs is counsel from the wise enjoyed; the seventeenth chapter is no different.

Besides the Alter Rebbe, the twenty-fourth of Teveth carries two more yahrzeits. Rabbi Shmuel Bornstein of Soccatchov, son of the Avnei Nezer, known for the Shem MiShmuel — and like the Alter Rebbe, both father and son were known for the revealed Torah and the law as much as for their Chassidic insight.

And Rabbi Moshe Mordechai Biderman, the sixth Lelover Rebbe, who was living in Israel when Jerusalem was liberated. Of all the Chassidic rebbes he spent the most time at the Kotel; he moved to Jerusalem to be near it, and his prayers there would take up most of the day.

117.title: Our Intimate Connection with G-d
body: "Your neck is like the Tower of David, built as a model; a thousand shields hanging on it, all the quivers of the mighty men. Your two breasts are like two fawns, the twins of a gazelle, who graze among the roses. Until the sun spreads and the shadows flee, I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense."

These are the verses that use the body most openly for what this people is. The two breasts belong to bearing and feeding, which is Teveth — and Rashi reads them as Moshe and Aharon, and as the two tablets, and explains how the laws on the first, between a person and G-d, answer to the laws on the second, between a person and a person.

Which is this week's own man as well. *Shneur* is *shnei or*, two lights, and he made good on the name: the light of Chassidus and the Torah's deep secrets, in the Tanya and the rest; and a light in the revealed Torah, in his Shulchan Aruch.
Of the seventy souls the seventeenth — not named outright — is Yocheved, the mother of Moshe and Aharon, who like Miriam did the quiet work of midwifing Jewish children.

Shevuot's seventeenth daf is about not taking your time leaving the Temple, and not taking the shortest way out, and entering the grounds improperly. Then it turns to how a man withdraws from a woman who becomes a niddah during intercourse. Both halves are this month's: sins about the Temple, and marriage.

Jeremiah's seventeenth chapter holds the wild goose's own verses from two weeks ago, and they are about multiplying from nothing: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm… He shall be like a lone tree in the plain… Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord; the Lord shall be his trust. For he shall be like a tree planted by the water, and by a rivulet spreads its roots, and will not see when heat comes, and its leaves shall be green, and in the year of drought will not be anxious, neither shall it cease from bearing fruit."
Trees, in the week before Rosh Chodesh Shevat.

118.title: Reviewing the Fourth Week of Teveth - Psalms 49-51; 59:6-8; 89:18
body: The fourth week of Teveth in psalms: the forty-ninth, fiftieth and fifty-first, with three verses of Psalm 59 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 49 is addressed to everybody and aimed at the rich. "Hear this, all you peoples… sons of common folk and sons of nobility, rich and poor alike." Then the question it answers: "Why am I afraid in times of trouble? Because the sins I trod upon surround me." And what money cannot do: "There are those who rely on their wealth, who boast of their great riches. Yet a man cannot redeem his brother, nor pay his ransom to G-d. The redemption of their soul is too costly, and forever unattainable." It watches men who know better do it anyway: "Though he sees that wise men die, that the fool and the senseless both perish, leaving their wealth to others — nevertheless, in their inner thoughts their houses will last forever."

Psalm 50 is G-d speaking, and what He says He does not want is the surprise. "Not for the lack of your sacrifices will I rebuke you, nor for the lack of your burnt offerings… I do not take oxen from your house, nor goats from your pens; for every beast of the forest is Mine, the cattle of a thousand mountains." And then: "Were I hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and everything in it is mine. Do I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Offer confession as a sacrifice to G-d, and fulfill your vows."

Psalm 51 is David after Nathan came to him, and it is the psalm to say over one's own sins. "Be gracious to me, O G-d, in keeping with Your kindness… Cleanse me thoroughly of my wrongdoing, and purify me of my sin. For I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is always before me. Against You alone have I sinned." Then: "You desire truth in the innermost parts; teach me the wisdom of concealed things. Purge me with hyssop and I shall be pure; cleanse me and I shall be whiter than snow. Let me hear tidings of joy and gladness; then the bones which You have shattered will rejoice." And the request that is this week's whole business: "Create in me a pure heart, O G-d, and renew within me an upright spirit. Do not cast me out of Your presence, and do not take Your Spirit of Holiness away from me."

Psalm 59's verses are a city circled by dogs: "They return toward evening, they howl like the dog and circle the city. Behold, they spew with their mouths, swords are in their lips, for they say, 'Who hears?'"

119.title: The Bee-Eater is Saying
body: The bee-eater opens, and this gathering sets being drawn out of the water against dogs circling a city.

"I will whistle to them and gather them" / "He sent from on high and He took me" / "the twins of a gazelle, who graze among the roses" / "He drew me out of many waters" / "and they shall increase as they have before increased."
Then the splendour, and the remnant ruling: "Indeed, You are the splendor of their might" / "the Lord dominated the strong for me" / "and in Your goodwill our glory is exalted."

The demons come next, with Canaan melting: "They sacrificed to demons, which have no power" / "all the inhabitants of Canaan melted" / "may dread and fright fall upon them" / "which your forefathers did not fear" / "then ruled a remnant among the mighty of the nations" / "deities they did not know, new things that only recently came."

And then the swords in the lips, and the quivers, and the waking: "swords are in their lips, for they say, 'Who hears?'" / "all the quivers of the mighty men" / "And You, Lord, G-d of Hosts, G-d of Israel" / "until the sun spreads and the shadows flee" / "wake up to remember all the nations" / "a thousand shields hanging on it" / "behold, they spew with their mouths" / "your two breasts are like two fawns" / "they howl like the dog and circle the city."

It ends with Eli's blessing laid between the mountain of myrrh and the request granted: "and to the hill of frankincense" / "And Eli answered and said: Go in peace" / "I will go to the mountain of myrrh" / "and the God of Israel will grant your request" / "for I have redeemed them" / "they return toward evening" / "your neck is like the Tower of David, built as a model" / "do not grant favor to any of the iniquitous traitors, Selah" / "which you have asked of Him."

120.title: To Live in Harmony with Nature in a Manner that is Above Nature
body: Week eighteen is Rosh Chodesh Shevat, and the grasshopper asks a question: "I lift my eyes up to the mountains, where shall my help come from?" (Psalms 121:1)

It is answered ten weeks back. The swift, the eighth creature, sings the verse that comes next: "My help comes from the Lord, Creator of Heaven and Earth." Eighteen and eight, question and answer — and eight is the number of what is beyond nature. The grasshopper's song tends to land in the weeks of Vaera or Bo, which are the plagues, locusts among them: help arriving from Him with nature set aside entirely.

Shevat is Tu B'Shvat, the New Year of the Trees, kept on the fifteenth — though the Mishnah has a dispute about whether it should be the first. Which is itself the month's subject: we keep the trees' new year in the middle of winter, and that is faith.

The tribe is Asher, and the word is *ta'anug*, pleasure or delight; the Sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe notes that *asher* itself means delight, from *ashruni*. Jacob blesses Asher that he will bring delicacies to the king. On Tu B'Shvat we drink wine and eat many kinds of fruit — and the delights of this month are intellectual too.

Shevat belongs to the Oral Torah. It was on Rosh Chodesh that Moses began going back over everything he had taught in forty years, which is the whole Book of Deuteronomy. The Chidushei HaRim says that every new Torah insight a person has comes to him in Shevat.

And passing on the Oral Torah needs one trait above all: humility. Without it a person cannot teach purely and plainly what he received from the one before him. Humility is Moses' own mark, the humblest of men and the first to hand it on. Which may be why in Perek Shirah the insects — the humblest creatures — are the ones singing through all four weeks of Shevat. As David said, "I am a worm and not a man."

Eighteen is *chai*, life, which is why gifts are given in multiples of it. Rosh Chodesh Shevat and Tu B'Shvat are a celebration of life in general, not only human life. And *chai* is also a thing's essence: the Ba'al Shem Tov and the Alter Rebbe were both born on Chai Elul, the eighteenth, the life and essence of Elul; Rebbe Nachman's yahrzeit is the eighteenth of Tishrei; Lag Ba'Omer is the eighteenth of Iyar. Eighteen is also the number of blessings in the Amidah, which is called simply *Tefilah* because it is prayer's essence — and prayer is the recognition that a Jew's life is not natural at all.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Nechunia the son of Hakanah: "One who accepts upon himself the yoke of Torah is exempted from the yoke of government duties and the yoke of worldly cares; but one who casts off the yoke of Torah is saddled with" both. Take up the Tree of Life, which is above the world, or be handed the world's obligations instead. Calling the Torah a yoke also says what acquiring it costs. Rabbi Mendel of Kotsk points out that plenty of sages had worldly work and even professions, and did not experience it as a yoke or a worry.

The pairing is Netzach shebeTiferet. A tree is a balance of root, trunk, branch and leaf, and only the balance keeps it up: no roots and it falls, too many branches and it falls, too few leaves and it cannot make enough to grow. In Shevat, mid-winter, it has to hold on. The same balance is wanted between the two yokes, and what it is differs from person to person and from one part of a life to another.

The grasshopper's lesson is that help comes from Him, provided we are willing to look up past our own small view. The Midrash reads the mountains as the patriarchs, and says it is largely for their deeds that we are saved — so look past the present situation, at the whole of what you are and where you came from.

121.title: Achia HaShiloni and "Minimized" World Activity
body: "You forgot the Mighty Rock Who bore you; you forgot the G-d Who delivered you." (Deuteronomy 32:18) Shevat is a month of nature, and the verse puts His relation to us as birth, which is the most natural figure there is. But Shevat is also what stands above nature, and the Oral Torah, and *ta'anug*, and *emunah* — keeping the trees' new year in the depths of winter.

And the verse can be read as a prayer instead: Rock, they are your children; forget completely our sins; G-d delivers you. The haftorah goes with that: "He delivered me from my mighty enemy; from them that hated me; for they were too powerful for me." (II Samuel 22:18) Help against odds, which is nature set aside.

The quality is *miut derech eretz*, minimised worldly activity — which is the same thing Pirkei Avot says this week from the other side. When a person's affairs are conducted small and humbly, His hand becomes much easier to see in them.

The prophet is Achiah HaShiloni, who may represent being above nature better than anyone: Maimonides records that he lived longer than any other prophet, and he taught both Eliyahu and the Ba'al Shem Tov. It was precisely because those two kept their worldly activity small that they merited having him revealed to them. And Achiah told the Ba'al Shem Tov that he had to reveal himself to the world — to be involved in it, but in the way of *miut*, smallness. The Ba'al Shem Tov himself spoke about being a genuinely good person with a simple connection to G-d: both *derech eretz*, being a mentsch, and caring for the *amei ha'aretz*, the simple folk.

The Levitical city is Mishal, which means a prayer, a request. Which is the grasshopper's question, and the eighteen blessings, and this month's faith and delight. Mishal also has the letters of *moshel*, to rule — and in prayer we accept who the Ruler is.
121.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 18.

122.title: Nahor and Ta'anug
body: "With the arm of Your greatness may they become as still as a stone, until Your people cross over, O Lord." Still as a stone — and entering Shevat we are reminded of the four levels in nature: *domem*, the silent or mineral; *tzomeach*, the growing; *chai*, the living; *medaber*, the speaking. Each week of this month touches one of them, and this week's verse gives us the stone.

The haftorah begins something that will run through Shevat and Adar: what each tribe did in the fight against Sisera. This week is Ephraim and Benjamin, whom Rashi reads as Joshua and Shaul, and how they fought Amalek. Joshua is the Oral Torah, which is Shevat; Shaul belongs to Purim and Adar. And though Amalek is Adar's business, Amalek is the opposite of *emunah* — *Amalek* has the same numerical value as *safek*, doubt. The war against Sisera was a test of faith that not all the tribes passed, and which tribe showed faith and which showed doubt is the thread from here to Adar.

Sotah's eighteenth daf continues with the writing of the curses, and its theme is that things done twice rather than once, or divided rather than whole, or for two people rather than one, are invalid. Nature is multiplicity — and all of it still comes from Him.

The generation is Nahor, Serug's son and Avraham's grandfather. He lived in Ur Kasdim, where Avraham was born, and he had a grandson also called Nahor — continuity through children, as in nature. The name comes from *nachar*, to blow the nose, to sneeze, to snort. Which connects to the breath blown into Adam's nose, and so to nature and the world's making. And sneezing is a physical pleasure, which is this month's quality. The Talmud says that sneezing during prayer is a good sign, since as one is relieved below, so above.

The journey is to being broken: "They journeyed from Libnah and camped in Rissah." Rissah means broken — and only through that brokenness and smallness can a person actually take the Torah in. Rabbi Jacobson notes that Rissah also means a stopped-up well in Arabic: to draw water from the Torah's well, you have to feel that small. Last week was studying properly; this week is being broken enough to receive what is taught.

123.title: Wisdom That Brings Others Enjoyment and Pleasure in Life
body: "And she said: May your bondswoman find favor in your eyes; and the woman went on her way and ate, and her face was not sad anymore."

That she *ate* looks like an idle detail and is not. It is the measure of how much she had been let go of. Her faith in what Eli said let her take pleasure in food again — *ta'anug*, which is this month.

The week's quality is that people enjoy wisdom from such a person. Eli's wisdom is what lets her be comforted and eat. The word used is *Tushiah*, which is rare in Tanach and can also be rendered resourcefulness. Even having first misread her entirely, he was quick enough, once she spoke, to see his mistake and bless her with a child. And the first verse of Proverbs' eighteenth chapter uses that same rare word: "He who is separated seeks lust; in all sound wisdom, he is exposed."

Two great yahrzeits. The second of Shevat is Reb Zusha of Anipoli, one of the Maggid of Mezritch's main disciples and the brother of Rebbe Elimelech of Lizhensk. The two of them travelled Eastern Europe bringing Torah and life to the communities there, and Rabbi Noach of Kobryn once heard that Chassidus took root only in the places those brothers had passed through. The stories about him are of miracles, of humility, and of how deeply he looked at himself.

And the fourth of Shevat is the Baba Sali, grandson of Rav Yaakov Abuchatzeira — among the most prominent of Sefardi holy men, with thousands of stories of open miracles, and a man whose love for Hashem, for this people and for the Torah was past measuring. He kept close relations with Torah sages of every kind, and had a particular affinity for Chassidic teaching and its leaders.

124.title: Nature as a Metaphor and the Setting for Our Relationship with G-d
body: "You are all fair, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you. With me from Lebanon, my bride, with me from Lebanon shall you come; you shall look from the peak of Amanah, from the peak of Senir and Hermon, from the lions' dens, from mountains of leopards. You have captivated my heart, my sister, my bride; you have captivated my heart with one of your eyes, with one link of your necklaces."

The middle verse is all nature: a forest, three peaks, lions, leopards. Rashi reads it as His being with us in exile and coming back out of it with us. And the peak of Amanah has the root of *emunah* in it.

Of the seventy souls the eighteenth is Judah, who of all the brothers stands most for the Oral Torah: Jacob sent him ahead to set up a yeshiva in Egypt before the family came down. He is this month's two qualities as well. He showed great faith facing the viceroy who turned out to be Joseph — and his pleasure-seeking, with Tamar, got him into trouble he was not afraid to own and turn from.

Shevuot's eighteenth daf continues on withdrawing from a niddah, where the point is avoiding pleasure, and on separating before the set period of impurity; then on whether a person must know what made him impure before he forgot that he was. It takes in forbidden foods, forbidden relations, and acts that show a lack of faith, like working on Shabbat or Yom Kippur.

Jeremiah's eighteenth chapter is G-d as the potter, which asks for faith that all of it comes from Him. "And at one instant I may speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant." And then: "Shall one abandon water flowing from rocks of the field that comes from the snow of Lebanon? Shall strange cold flowing water be abandoned?" In Shevat the sap begins to move while the cold is still on. Lebanon, whose trees went into the Temple, is in the Song's verses above too — and Levanon is often the Temple itself.

125.title: Reviewing the First Week of Shevat - Psalms 52-54; 59:9-11; 89:19
body: The first week of Shevat in psalms: the fifty-second, fifty-third and fifty-fourth, with three verses of Psalm 59 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 52 is about Doeg, who informed on David to Saul, and about a man who takes pride in harm. "Why do you boast with evil, O mighty one? G-d's kindness is all day long. Your tongue devises treachery; like a sharpened razor it works deceit. You love evil more than good, falsehood more than speaking righteousness." And then the answer: "G-d will likewise shatter you forever; He will excise and pluck you from" where you stand.

Psalm 53 is headed as speaking of when Titus pierced the curtain of the Holy of Holies with his sword and thought he had killed Him. It opens with the fool: "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no G-d!'" And the looking down: "G-d looked down from heaven upon mankind, to see if there was any man of intelligence who searches for G-d. But they all regressed together." Then the fright: "There they will be seized with fright, a fright such as never was." And the wish at the end: "O that out of Zion would come Israel's deliverance!"

Psalm 54 is from when the Ziphites told Saul that David was hiding with them, and it is short and direct. "O G-d, deliver me by Your Name, and vindicate me by Your might. G-d, hear my prayer, listen to the words of my mouth. For strangers have risen against me, and ruthless men have sought my soul; they are not mindful of G-d." Then the turn: "Behold, G-d is my helper; my Lord is with those who support my soul." And the close: "With a free-will offering I will sacrifice to You; I will offer thanks to Your Name, O Lord, for it is good. For He has saved me from every trouble."

Psalm 59's verses are the laughing: "But You, Lord, You laugh at them; You mock all nations. Because of his might, I wait for You, for G-d is my stronghold. The G-d of my kindness will anticipate my need."

126.title: Week 18: The Grasshopper is Saying (Book 7)
body: The grasshopper opens with its question, and the gathering answers it from four directions at once.
"I lift my eyes up to the mountains" / "where shall my help come from?" / "For our protectors turn to the Lord" / "and our king to the Holy One of Israel."

Then the peaks and the dens, with waiting laid under them: "You shall look from the peak of Amanah" / "from the peak of Senir and Hermon" / "from the lions' dens, from mountains of leopards" / "because of his might, I wait for You, for G-d is my stronghold" / "the G-d of my kindness will anticipate my need."

The stone comes next, with the crossing and the rescue: "With the arm of Your greatness may they become as still as a stone" / "until Your people cross over, O Lord" / "He delivered me from my mighty enemy" / "from them that hated me; for they were too powerful for me" / "But You, Lord, You laugh at them; You mock all nations."

Then the forgetting, braided with the tribes: "You forgot the Mighty Rock Who bore you" / "you forgot the G-d Who delivered you" / "Out of Ephraim, whose root was against Amalek" / "after you will be Benjamin with your abaters."

The captivating follows — "You have captivated my heart, my sister, my bride" / "you have captivated my heart with one of your eyes" / "with one link of your necklaces" — and then Channah asking for favour.

It ends with the fairness, Lebanon, and the face: "You are all fair, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you" / "with me from Lebanon, my bride, with me from Lebanon shall you come" / "and the woman went on her way and ate" / "and her face was not sad anymore."

127.title: To Feel that G-d is Close Even When He Seems Far Away
body: The locust is saying, "O G-d, You are my Lord; I will exalt You, I will praise Your Name; for You have done wondrous things; Your counsels of old are faithfulness and truth." (Isaiah 25:1) It blesses G-d for His wonders and for the true and loyal advice He gives from afar.

The nineteenth week holds Yud Shevat, the yahrzeit of the Sixth Rebbe of Lubavitch, Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneerson, and the date on which his successor, Rebbe Menachem Mendel Schneerson, became rebbe exactly one year later. Shevat is the transmission and development of the Oral Torah; the first to pass it on was Moses, who transmitted it to Joshua. Yud Shevat is the transmission of the Torah of Chassidut from the Sixth Rebbe to the Seventh.

The song holds the word etzot and the word emunah. Etza means advice, but etz means tree, and emunah means faith — and the month is both. In the middle of winter the trees are cold and leafless, and on Tu B'Shvat the Jewish people celebrate them anyway, trusting that they will blossom and yield fruit.

The song also reaches for three names at once. Hashem is the Name for how He is above nature and time, connected to Rachamim, mercy. Elohai, my Elohim, is G-d as He is expressed in nature, connected to gevurah, strength or discipline. Atah, You, is the way of calling out that shows closeness, and it also points to His essence far above any given name. So the locust sings of connecting to G-d above nature yet still within it, and of feeling distant from Him while being close to Him at the same time.

Rav Moshe Wolfsohn reads the Akeidah along the same lines. Ness means a test, but also to raise. The main test, the tenth and final one, was not the willingness to sacrifice his son — Abraham's first test was throwing himself into a furnace before G-d had even revealed Himself to him — but that Hashem seemed so far away: "Vaya'ar Et HaMakom Merachok," he saw the place from a distance, and Hamakom is itself one of Hashem's names. After years of closeness Abraham was stripped of his levels of greatness and had to serve like the simplest of Jews, with simple emunah, like the generation of Ikvessa d'Meshicha, the heels of Mashiach. He was rewarded, "Ekev Asher Shamatah beKoli," because you hearkened to My voice — and ekev also means heel. The verse of the week ends with the words "Merachok Emunah Amen."

Bati LeGani was the last ma'amar of the Previous Rebbe and the first of his successor, and the Rebbe went deeper into it for over forty years. It tells how the Shechinah rested and was revealed in the world at the beginning of creation, then became distanced and hidden through sins beginning with the eating of the Tree of Knowledge, then returned by degrees through the acts of tzadikim until the giving of the Torah at Mount Sinai — and it draws the parallel to the final redemption.

Nineteen is a number of increments. Shmoneh Esreh was increased from 18 to 19, and it is a ladder to G-d like the ladder in Jacob's dream, where the angels ascended and descended; with every blessing we climb a rung. Nineteen is also the gematria of Chavah, Eve, whom some commentaries call a loftier version of Adam.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Chalafta the son of Dosa of the village of Chanania, who counts the levels down: ten who sit and occupy themselves with Torah have the Divine Presence among them, and so do five, and three, and two, and even one. The combination is Hod shebeTiferet, grateful service within beauty and balance — and in the month of trees, gratitude is what makes faith easier to hold. The Kotzker Rebbe, as a child, was asked where G-d is. The expected answer was "everywhere." He said: "G-d is wherever you let Him in."

128.title: Jehu and "Minimized" Pleasure (Ta'anug)
body: The second week of Shevat. Haazinu keeps to the parent and the child: "And the Lord saw this and became angry, provoked by His sons and daughters." (Deuteronomy 32:19) Read in a positive light, the anger is not His at them — He saw the prayer and was insulted by the anger directed against His sons and daughters.

The Haftarah verse agrees: "They confronted me on the day of my calamity; but the Lord was a support to me." (II Samuel 22:19) The support comes from King David's emunah, which is one of the themes of Shevat, along with ta'anug, pleasure.

So the quality is minimized pleasure, miut ta'anug. The idea is not to be rid of pleasure but to take it with miut, smallness and humility — to enjoy the world's pleasure in the way that lifts the world and connects it back to its Creator.

The prophet is Jehu son of Hanani, who spoke out against the corruption of the kings of both Israel and Judah. In one of his few positive statements he praises Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, for exactly this quality — for having removed the idolatrous Ashera trees: "Nevertheless there are good things found in thee, in that thou hast put away the Asheroth out of the land, and hast set thy heart to seek G-d." (2 Chronicles 19:3) The trees were used for idol worship and to beautify the place where it was done; pleasing to the senses, and forbidden beside the altar. Maimonedes writes that one may not derive any pleasure or benefit from them at all.

The levitical city is Abdon, from eved, servant. It brings to mind the verse in Beshalach: "Vaya'aminu BaHashem ub'Moshe Avdo," and they believed in Hashem and in Moshe His servant. Abdon was also the name of one of the Judges, whose sons and grandsons rode on seventy donkeys. All of it is the yoke of Torah taken up willingly, and in this month, the Oral Torah.
128.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 19.

129.title: Terah and Nature
body: The Song of the Sea reaches the arrival: "until this nation that You have acquired crosses over. You shall bring them and plant them on the mount of Your heritage." Acquiring and inheriting are the themes of Yud Shevat, the Previous Rebbe's yahrzeit and the day the Rebbe took the leadership a year later. The verses also carry two of the elements — the plant kingdom in "and plant them," the mineral in the mountain.

The Haftarah sends the high officials down into the fighting: "out of Machir came down officers, and out of Zebulun they that handle the pen of the scribe." Machir is of the tribe of Menashe. That is the message of Yud Shevat and of Bati L'Gani, studied that day, where we are told to spend all the treasures and use everything at our disposal. Chassidic texts that only a select few could reach in manuscript — by the pen of the scribe — were now printed for everyone. The Rebbe's decision to accept was itself a coming down, into the wars of Hashem.

Daf Yud Tet of Sotah is her drinking the water and waving the mincha offering, with a discussion of when a woman can be forced to drink and whether the Name has already been erased. There too different elements in nature act on each other. And it runs parallel to the Chassidim urging the Rebbe to accept: he could not be forced into it.

The generation is Terah, son of Nahor, father of Avraham. He moved from Ur Kasdim to Charan on his way to the Land of Canaan and never arrived. Terah means delay, and he was delayed; it also means to breathe, from re'ach, smell. His father's name, Nahor, means sneezing or snorting. Breathing and smelling belong to pleasure and to nature, which are Shevat.

The journey is from Rissah to Kehelathah. Kehelathah means gathering, and it is the place of Korach's rebellion — where on Yud Shevat the emphasis is the exact opposite: a gathering to accept a new leader who was wholly devoted to the one before him. The personal journey is to be broken in order to receive the Torah, and then to gather with others and commit to the leader.

130.title: Wisdom, Understanding and Knowledge
body: Channah's nineteenth verse is the answer arriving quietly: "And they arose early in the morning, and prostrated themselves before the Lord: and they returned and came to their house, to Ramah, and Elkanah knew Hannah, his wife, and the Lord remembered her."

Shevat is pleasure, Ta'anug, and faith, Emunah, and the verse carries both. It speaks of marital relations, which the Torah often calls knowledge, Da'at — and Da'at is the connecting point between the male aspect of intellect, Chochmah, wisdom, and the female one, Binah, understanding. It is what lets Chochmah impregnate Binah. And it says that Hashem remembered Channah, that her Emunah was rewarded.

The quality of Pirkei Avot is that people enjoy understanding, Binah, from those who study Torah for its own sake. Channah in the verse is Binah. The whole Book of Proverbs is about enjoying understanding from those who have it, and chapter 19 keeps to it: "He who acquires sense loves his soul; he who guards understanding will eventually find good," and "Beat a scorner, and a simple man will gain cunning; reprove a man of understanding, and he will understand knowledge." Rashi reads that second one as a reference to the plagues in Egypt — which is the locust of this week in Book 1.

Besides the Previous Rebbe, the week holds the yahrzeits of two great tzadikim of Yemeni descent, both on the 10th of Shevat: Rabbi Shalom Shabazi, the leader of his generation, known as Mori, a tremendous scholar and the greatest of Yemenite poets, and Rabbi Shalom Sharabi, the Rashash, the father of all contemporary sephardic kabbalists.

Two rabbis from Chassidic dynasties have yahrzeits this week as well. Rabbi David Biederman of Lelov, on the 7th of Shevat, was one of the main disciples of the Seer of Lublin and the founder of the Lelover dynasty; he was known for his extraordinary ability to see every Jew in a positive light, and he taught Rebbe Yitzhak of Vorka, known for the same tremendous Ahavat Yisrael.

131.title: Spiritual Pleasure
body: The Song's verses this week are all fragrance and sweetness: "How fair is your love, my sister, [my] bride; how much better is your love than wine, and the fragrance of your oils than all spices!" Then: "Your lips drip flowing honey, O bride; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of Lebanon." And then the closing: "A locked up garden is my sister, [my] bride; a locked up spring, a sealed fountain." Nature again, and Ta'anug, pleasure.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the nineteenth is Shelah. Judah's first two sons are skipped because they died childless through their sins, and those brothers stand for pleasure engaged in wrongly. Shelah was meant to marry Tamar; he was still young, and Yehudah later looked for ways to keep her from him.

Daf Yud Tet of Shvuot is mostly the one who forgot both that he was impure and that he was in the Temple, and then the two main kinds of oath, both about food. The forgetting belongs to the Oral Law, which is this month's focus. The food belongs to Ta'anug.

Jeremiah's nineteenth chapter is the same pair gone wrong — eating and pleasure, completely corrupted. "Because they forsook Me and they estranged this place and burnt incense therein to other gods, which they had not known." "And they built the high places of Baal to burn their children with fire as burnt offerings to Baal, which I did not command, neither did I speak nor did it enter My mind." And the end of it: "And I will feed them the flesh of their sons and the flesh of their daughters, and each one will eat the flesh of his friend, in the siege and the straits."

132.title: Reviewing the Second Week of Shevat - Psalms 55-57; 59:12-14; 89:20
body: The second week of Shevat in psalms: the fifty-fifth, fifty-sixth and fifty-seventh, with three verses of Psalm 59 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 55 is from David escaping Jerusalem before the slanderers, Doeg and Achitofel, who had declared him deserving of death. He had counted Achitofel a friend and given him the utmost honour, and Achitofel breached their covenant. The wound is that it came from inside: "For it is not the enemy who taunts me-that I could bear; nor my foe who raises himself against me, that I could hide from him. But it is you, a man of my equal, my guide and my intimate. Together we took sweet counsel; we walked with the throng to the house of G-d." Before that is the wish to be gone: "If only I had wings like the dove! I would fly off and find rest." And the smooth words: "Smoother than butter are the words of his mouth, but war is in his heart; his words are softer than oil, yet they are curses." It ends where it can: "Cast your burden upon the Lord, and He will sustain you; He will never let the righteous man falter."

Psalm 56 is from mortal danger at the palace of Achish, brother of Goliath, when the Philistines seized him in Gath, and in that danger David accepts vows upon himself. "On the day I am afraid, I trust in You." And twice over: "in G-d I trust, I do not fear-what can [man of] flesh do to me?" Then the flask: "You have counted my wanderings; place my tears in Your flask-are they not in Your record?" And both hands of it: "When G-d deals strictly, I praise His word; when the Lord deals mercifully, I praise His word."

Psalm 57 is from hiding in the cave from Saul. Like Jacob facing Esau, David prayed that he neither be killed nor be forced to kill. "Favor me, O G-d, favor me, for in You my soul took refuge, and in the shadow of Your wings I will take refuge until the disaster passes." The lions: "My soul is in the midst of lions, I lie among fiery men; their teeth are spears and arrows, their tongue a sharp sword." The pit they dug: "they dug a pit before me, [but] they themselves fell into it." And then the waking: "My heart is steadfast, O G-d, my heart is steadfast; I will sing and chant praise. Awake, my soul! Awake, O harp and lyre! I shall awaken the dawn."

Psalm 59's verses ask for less than destruction, so that nothing is forgotten: "Do not kill them, lest my nation forget; drive them about with Your might and impoverish them, O our Shield, my Master." And Psalm 89's verse is the choosing: "I have granted aid to [David] the mighty one; I have exalted the one chosen from among the people."

133.title: Week 19: The Locust is Saying (Book 7)
body: The locust opens, and what it opens is a braid of the week's six books into one song.

The anger first, and the asking that it stop short: "At the sight of their accursed state and deterioration, [people] will recount" / "Consume them in wrath, consume them and they will be no more" / "And the Lord saw this and became angry" / "Provoked by His sons and daughters" / "Do not kill them, lest my nation forget" / "Drive them about with Your might and impoverish them."

Then the crossing and the planting: "Until this nation that You have acquired crosses over" / "You shall bring them and plant them on the mount of Your heritage" / "And they will know that G-d rules in Jacob, to the ends of the earth, Selah."

Then the morning in Ramah, and the support: "And they arose early in the morning, and prostrated themselves before the Lord" / "And they returned and came to their house, to Ramah" / "I will praise Your Name; for You have done wondrous things" / "They confronted me on the day of my calamity" / "But the Lord was a support to me."

Then the scribes and the remembering: "Out of Machir came down officers" / "And out of Zebulun they that handle the pen of the scribe" / "And Elkanah knew Hannah, his wife, and the Lord remembered her" / "Your counsels of old are faithfulness and truth."

And the end is the garden: "How fair is your love, my sister, [my] bride" / "How much better is your love than wine, and the fragrance of your oils than all spices!" / "Your lips drip flowing honey, O bride" / "Honey and milk are under your tongue" / "O G-d, You are my Lord; I will exalt You" / "And the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of Lebanon" / "A locked up garden is my sister, [my] bride" / "A locked up spring, a sealed fountain."

134.title: To Be Solid and Giving in Our Relationships
body: The spider is saying, "Praise Him with sounding cymbals! Praise Him with loud clashing cymbals!" (Psalms 150:5) It is the twentieth animal, and this is the week of Tu B'Shvat, the New Year of the Trees.

The spider mattered to King David, to whom Perek Shirah is attributed. A Midrash teaches that he once wondered why G-d had created it at all and could find no purpose for it. Later, fleeing from Saul, he entered a cave, and a spider spun an entire web across the entrance. Saul's men saw the web and reasoned that nobody could have been inside for long, so they went away without checking. The web saved his life and taught him that everything G-d creates has a glorious purpose. Perhaps that is why he kept the spider for Tu B'Shvat itself, the high point of Judaism's celebration of nature, and why its verse comes from the very last Psalm, where the praise comes to its culmination.

A web and a tree are built the same way. A tree takes a long time to grow and then bears fruit; a spider takes a long time to make its web, and its fruits are what the web catches. Both are examples of balance and resistance, both are delicate, and both stand up to very strong winds because they can absorb impact by giving a little instead of breaking.

Twenty is two complete units, so it intensifies the duality and the relationship that two already holds. It is also the age of full maturity, when a man may be enlisted for war and is expected to provide for his own sustenance, and from twenty onward we are held accountable in the Heavenly court.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Elazar of Bartota: give to Him what is His, for you and all that is yours is His, as King David said, "For everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we give to You." (I Chronicles 29:14) Fitting that David is the one quoted, in the week that is so much his. Tzedakah comes from the word for justice, and the Tanya explains that it is arguably the highest of all the mitzvoth: when we give away part of our livelihood we give away part of our own life. We fought hard for that money, and letting it go is the clearest admission that all of it was a gift to begin with — and that even after Hashem gives, it stays His, because He is the Supreme Owner of everything.

Rabbi Elazar's line belongs to Tu B'Shvat directly. The first fruits were brought as an offering to the Temple, and all fruit requires ma'aser, tithing; Tu B'Shvat is the day the obligation to tithe the fruit begins, which is why it is the Rosh Hashanah of the Trees. He grants the fruit, so at least a tenth of it goes back to Him, as at least a tenth of our income goes to tzedakah.

The same holds for passing on the Oral Torah. Whoever transmits it has to stay conscious that it comes from G-d, the Ultimate Teacher — both what came from a teacher and the new insight that looks like one's own. He grants knowledge for safekeeping and for the best use we can make of it, and there is a concept of tithing one's time to teach Torah too.

The combination is yesod shebetiferet, a foundation that has both beauty and balance, which is what a tree is. And from the spider: with total confidence and a loud, firm voice — like the smashing of cymbals — we can be a good influence on others, and help them see that nobody is alone.

135.title: Azariah and "Minimized" Sleep
body: Tu B'Shevat, and Haazinu's verse hides His face: "And He said, 'I will hide My face from them. I will see what their end will be, for they are a generation of changes [reversals]; they are not [recognizable] as My children whom I have reared.'" (Deuteronomy 32:20) Read positively, He hides His face from their sins and focuses on how they will be at their completion — a generation transformed by teshuvah, and His children after all, with faith in them.

The Haftarah says the same from the other side: "And He brought me forth into a wide place; He delivered me because He took delight in me." (II Samuel 22:20) Once we are taken out of our confines, our essence comes out, which is what He desires. Delight and desire are Ta'anug, and Ta'anug is Shevat. The Hebrew for "generation of changes" is Dor Ta'apuchot, which sounds like Tapuach, apple — and the theme underneath is emunah, which is also the ability to change for the better. To celebrate the New Year of the Trees in the middle of winter, knowing spring will come, is the whole message of the day.

So the quality is minimized sleep, miut sheinah. Sleep confines us; consciousness drops and so does the ability to serve. But sleep is also a moment of increased faith, because we trust that we will wake. That is Tu B'Shvat again: the tree's vitality is still dormant and the fruit is already there in potential. Better not to sleep — not to slacken — in serving Him; and in the hours when we are less attuned, to act with miut, smallness and humility, hoping to serve better soon.

The prophet is Azariah son of Oded, and his prophecy to King Asa is exactly this. "Hearken to me, Asa and all of Judah and Benjamin; the Lord is with you because you are with Him, and if you seek Him, He will be found by you, but if you forsake Him, He will forsake you." He describes the sleeping years — "there were many days for Israel without a true G-d and without an instructing priest, and without the Torah" — and then the waking: "And they returned to the Lord, the G-d of Israel, when they were in distress, and they sought Him, and He was found by them." And the charge: "But you be strong and let your hands not slacken, for there is reward for your work." Asa heard it, strengthened himself, removed the abominations from Judah and Benjamin and from the cities he had captured from Mount Ephraim, renewed the altar, and gathered the people.
The levitical city is Helkath, from chelek, part — which is the tithing of produce again, the thing this day begins.
135.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 20.

136.title: Avraham and Giving
body: The Song of the Sea names the house: "directed toward Your habitation, which You made, O Lord; the sanctuary, O Lord, [which] Your hands founded." Rashi explains "directed toward Your habitation" to mean that the Temple below stands directly opposite the Temple above. At that moment neither the Temple nor the Tabernacle had been built; they were there only in potential, a reflection of the one above. Which is Tu B'Shevat exactly — celebrated in midwinter, when the fruit is only there in potential.

The Haftorah brings Issachar: "And the princes of Issachar were with Deborah, as was Issachar with Barak; into the valley they rushed forth with their feet." Issachar was wholly given to learning Torah and passing it on, and so stands for the Oral Torah more than any other tribe, which is this month.

Daf Kaf of Sotah keeps on with the drinking and when she can refuse, and takes in teaching Torah to women, how the water tests her, what ink may be used, and how a woman's merit can hold back punishment. It also has a passage that looks down on withholding from pleasure improperly — and pleasure is the theme of the day.

The generation is Avraham, forefather of the Jewish people and father, Av, of many others, which is what his name means. At the time his name was changed, and even before that, he was still childless: his children too were there only in potential. He was known for his hospitality, feeding his guests all kinds of delicacies, and that was how he taught them about the One True G-d.

The connection is plainer still in the tamarisk. "And Avraham planted an eshel, a tamarisk tree… and there he called in the name of G-d, L-rd of the world," and then, "And Avraham lived in the land of the Philistines for an extended period" — and after those verses comes the binding of Yitzchak. Why does it matter that he planted a tree? The tamarisk is large and broad-branched, and he was living in a desert, so he planted it to shade wayfarers from the scorching sun. The Talmud widens eshel from one tree to an orchard, so that passersby could refresh themselves with fruit, and offers a second reading in which eshel is an inn: bread and meat, drink and lodging. The Midrash says he even gave his guests a court of law to settle any dispute among them. He did not stop at bread, salt and water — not the bare minimum but the things that bring pleasure: fruit, wine, delicacies, lodging, and a court for their troubles.

The journey is from Kehelathah to Mount Shepher. Rabbi Jacobson explains that Mount Shepher means beautiful mountain, and cites Targum Yonasan, which renders it mountain with beautiful fruit. The personal journey moves on from the gathering and the commitment to the leader, to the enjoyment and the beauty of both the natural and the spiritual fruit.

137.title: Hanging in There Through the Winter
body: Channah's twentieth verse is the birth: "And it was, when the time came about (lit. after the seasons and the days), after Hannah had conceived, that she bore a son, and she called his name Samuel, because (she said); 'I asked him of the Lord.'" Conception and birth run through this month. In Shevat the fruit is there in potential, and it still takes a turn of seasons and days before the tree bears it — and in the meantime there is the harshness of winter to get through.

The Pirkei Avot quality is that people enjoy power from those who study Torah for its own sake, Lishmah: "Mine are counsel and wisdom, I am understanding, mine is power." Gevurah is might, strength, discipline, and also judgment. In the story, Eli's blessing is what gives Channah the strength to bear a child, and the name Shmuel and the reason given for it say plainly that it all came from Hashem.

Proverbs 20 carries the same. "Fear of a king is like a lion's roar; he who provokes him forfeits his life." "A king sits upon a throne of judgment; all evil is spread out before him." "Who will say, 'I have cleansed my heart; I have become purified of my sin'?" And then: "'It is bad, it is bad,' says the buyer, but when he goes away, then he boasts." Rashi reads that last one as the pains and the rewards of Gevurah together — one who acquires Torah through poverty and the pains of hunger says woe is me for this trouble, and then goes away full of wisdom and boasts about the pain he suffered.

The week usually holds the yahrzeits of two Chassidic founders: Rabbi Mordechai of Lechovitch on the 13th of Shevat and Rav Yechiel Danziger of Alexander on the 14th. Rabbi Mordechai is one of the foremost figures in the Karlin dynasty, and Lechovitch later branched into Kobrin, Koidanov and Slonim. There are many stories about him and many recorded statements; he once gave this blessing: "Don't fool yourself, don't fool G-d, and don't fool people."

Rav Yechiel Danziger founded Alexander, which before the Holocaust was the second largest dynasty after Ger. He was a student of Rabbi Yitzchak Kalish of Vorka, and after Rabbi Yitzchak's son, Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Vorka, passed away, many of his disciples became Alexander Chassidim. Rav Yechiel's teachings are recorded in the group's primary text, Yismach Yisroel, written by his son.

Strikov continues Alexander. After Rav Yechiel's son, Rabbi Yisroel Yitzchok Danziger, passed away, the leadership was eventually transferred to Rav Elimelech Menachem Mendel Landau of Strikov, whose yahrzeit also often falls this week, on the 19th of Shevat; he only accepted it once his brother, Rabbi Tzvi Aharon, had passed away. Under him there were 150 Strikover houses of study throughout Poland; he founded Yeshivas Zechusa DeAvraham in Israel, and his Torah thoughts are published in Maggid Devarav L'Yaakov and Bayeshishim Chochmah. Also this week: Rav Yaakov Yehoshua Falk Katz, the Pnei Yehoshua, and Rabbi Aryeh Kaplan on the 14th of Shevat, Rav Yechezkel of Kuzmir, grandfather of the first Modzitzer Rebbe, on the 17th, and sometimes Rav Shmuel Weinberg of Slonim, the Divrei Shmuel, on the 19th.

138.title: Perez and Bursting Out of the Cold
body: This week the Song names the fruit outright. "Your arid fields are as a pomegranate orchard with sweet fruit, henna and spikenard." Then the whole list: "Spikenard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all frankincense trees, myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices." And then the water: "A garden fountain, a well of living waters and flowing streams from Lebanon." Nature and pleasure again, but fruit and trees by name, because this is the Rosh Hashanah of the trees.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the twentieth is Perez, whose name means to burst forth. His birth is told in some detail, and how he burst forth to become the firstborn — which is how the flowers and the fruit have to come out, after the trees have endured the cold.
Daf Kaf of Shvuot keeps on with the laws of oaths, most of them about eating and pleasure.

Jeremiah's twentieth chapter is the pain he endured, and its most striking part is where he speaks of the day of his birth. "Cursed be the day in which I was begotten; the day in which my mother bore me shall not be blessed." "That he did not put me to death from the womb, that my mother should be my grave and her womb a perpetual pregnancy. Why did I come forth out of the womb to see toil and grief, and my days end with shame?" Birth and conception again, from the other end of it.

139.title: Reviewing the Third Week of Shevat - Psalms 58-60; 59:15-17; 89:21
body: The third week of Shevat in psalms: the fifty-eighth, fifty-ninth and sixtieth, with three verses of Psalm 59 again and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 58 is David's anguish at Avner and the others who justified Saul's pursuit of him. It opens by asking the judges why they are silent: "Is it true that you are mute [instead of] speaking justice? [Instead of] judging men with fairness?" Then the venom: "Their venom is like the venom of a snake; like the deaf viper that closes its ear so as not to hear the voice of charmers, [even] the most skillful caster of spells." Then the asking: "O G-d, smash their teeth in their mouth." "Let them melt like water and disappear." "Like the snail that melts as it goes along." And the end of it: "And man will say, 'There is indeed reward for the righteous; indeed there is a G-d Who judges in the land.'"

Psalm 59 is the great miracle of the escape through a window, unnoticed by the guards at the door, with the prayers he offered then. "Rescue me from my enemies, my G-d; raise me above those who rise against me." The dogs: "They return toward evening, they howl like the dog and circle the city." The laughing: "But You, Lord, You laugh at them; You mock all nations." Then the asking for less than destruction, so nothing is forgotten: "Do not kill them, lest my nation forget." And the morning at the end: "As for me, I shall sing of Your might, and sing joyously of Your kindness toward morning, for You have been a stronghold to me, a refuge on the day of my distress."

Psalm 60 has a story behind it. Joab, David's general, came to Aram Naharayim for war and the people asked him: are you not from the children of Jacob? What of the pact he made with Laban? He did not know what to answer and put it to the Sanhedrin. The psalm is David's prayer for success in that war, and it starts from the breach: "O G-d, You forsook us, You have breached us! You grew furious-restore us! You made the earth quake, You split it apart-heal its fragments, for it totters!" Then the banner: "[Now] give those who fear You a banner to raise themselves, for the sake of truth, Selah." Then the dividing up of the land, Shechem and the Valley of Succot, Gilead and Menasseh, Ephraim and Judah, Moab and Edom and Philistia. And the close, which gives the fighting back to Him: "Grant us relief from the oppressor; futile is the salvation of man. With G-d we will do valiantly, and He will trample our oppressors."
Psalm 89's verse is the anointing: "I have found David, My servant; I have anointed him with My holy oil."

140.title: The Spider is Saying
body: The spider opens, and the week's six books come in around it.

The howling first, braided with the hiding: "And they will return toward evening" / "They will howl like the dog and circle the city" / "And He said, 'I will hide My face from them. I will see what their end will be'" / "They will wander about to eat" / "When they will not be sated they will groan" / "For they are a generation of reversals" / "They are not My children whom I have reared."

Then the singing toward morning, and the princes going down: "As for me, I shall sing of Your might" / "And sing joyously of Your kindness toward morning" / "And the princes of Issachar were with Deborah" / "As was Issachar with Barak."

Then the birth and the anointing together: "And it was, after the seasons and the days" / "After Hannah had conceived, that she bore a son" / "I have found David, My servant; I have anointed him with My holy oil" / "And she called his name Samuel" / "Because, 'I asked him of the Lord.'"

Then the house, with the refuge inside it: "Directed toward Your habitation" / "Which You made, O Lord" / "For You have been a stronghold to me" / "A refuge on the day of my distress" / "The sanctuary, O Lord, [Which] Your hands founded" / "And He brought me forth into a wide place."

And the end is the orchard and the cymbals: "Your arid fields are as a pomegranate orchard" / "With sweet fruit, henna and spikenard" / "Praise Him with sounding cymbals!" / "Into the valley they rushed forth with their feet" / "Spikenard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all frankincense trees" / "He delivered me because He took delight in me" / "Myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices" / "A garden fountain, a well of living waters and flowing streams from Lebanon" / "Praise Him with loud clashing cymbals!"

141.title: To Keep Things in Perspective
body: The fly, when Israel is not busying itself with Torah, is saying: "The voice said, 'Call out'. And he said, 'What shall I call out? All flesh is grass, and all its grace is as the flower of the field.' '…The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our Lord shall endure forever.'" And then: "I will create a new expression of the lips: Peace, peace for him who is far off and for him who is near, says G-d, and I will heal him." (Isaiah 40:6,8; 57:19) The song is a kind of dialogue — one voice says call out, and the second asks what there is to say.

This is the last week of Shevat, and it holds the yahrzeit of Rebbetzin Chaya Mushka, the Rebbe's wife, on the 22nd of Shevat. Just after Tu B'Shvat, with trees and nature still in view, the fly comes to remind us that nature and life itself, beautiful and pleasurable and meaningful as they are, are fleeting. They reflect the Creator; only the Creator, and those attached to Him, last.

Flies do not disturb the tzadikim. Perhaps that is why we only know what the fly sings when the Jews are not studying Torah: when we are truly engaged in it we are all tzadikim, no fly comes near, and so there is no way to hear the song.

The fly recalls the Shunammite woman, the Ishah Shunamit. She kept the great mitzvah of hachnasat orchim, hospitality, in the tradition inherited from Abraham, and prepared a room so the prophet Elisha could always stay with her and her husband. The Talmud and the Zohar explain how she knew his greatness: she never saw a fly land on his table. His table was like the altar of the Temple, where there were never flies, despite the constant meat and blood — so the story is about the sanctification of pleasure. She was childless and always satisfied with what she had; asked by the prophet whether she needed anything, she answered, "I dwell within my people." Her behaviour toward Elisha, the disciple of Elijah, is one of the prime biblical examples of humility, modesty, kindness and hospitality.

The same things show in the Rebbetzin's life. She had no children of her own and considered all her people, the Chassidim, to be her children. She was the Rebbe's best friend and most devout partner throughout his life, and she was known for her great kindness, hospitality and modesty, learned in the home of her father, Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, the Sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe.
Twenty-one is the sum of the first three letters of Hashem's name. It is also the square root of 441, the gematria of Emet, truth, which is G-d's seal.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Yaakov: one who walks along a road and studies, and interrupts his studying to say, "How beautiful is this tree!", "How beautiful is this ploughed field!" — the Torah considers it as if he had forfeited his life. That is the fly's song again. The eternal words of the Creator are not to be put down in order to enjoy something passing, or even to exalt His own Creation. The Maggid of Mezritch reads the teaching as being about someone who stops learning in order to reflect on how much he has learned.

This week completes the third cycle of seven, and the combination is Malchut shebeTiferet, kingship within beauty. Malchut is a female sefirah, and the truest feminine beauty is inner beauty: "Kol Kvudah Bat Melech Pnimah," all the glory of the princess is within. One of the last verses of Eshet Chayil, sung before Kiddush on Shabbat night, says the same — "charm is deceitful and beauty is vanity; a woman that is G-d-fearing, she is the one to be praised" — and those are among the last verses of Solomon's Book of Proverbs. King Solomon, who also wrote Ecclesiastes, knew what held permanent value and what was only vanity of vanities. The fly teaches the same lesson, and adds that healing always comes through Him, with no need of intermediaries.
The 22nd of Shevat is also the yahrzeit of Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Kotsk, who was known for cutting through people's flowery, egocentric behaviour and keeping entirely to the truth.

142.title: Jahaziel and "Minimized" Speech
body: The last week of Shevat. Haazinu answers provocation with provocation: "They have provoked My jealousy with a non G-d, provoked My anger with their vanities. Thus, I will provoke their jealousy with a non people, provoke their anger with a foolish nation." (Deuteronomy 32:21) Read positively, it turns around completely: they have been zealous for Me against a non-G-d and angered for Me against the vanities of the nations, so I will be zealous for them and angry for them in return.

The Haftarah verse says exactly that: "The Lord rewarded me according to my righteousness; According to the cleanness of my hands He recompensed me." (II Samuel 22:21) Zealotry, done rightly, comes out of the depths of faith, as it did in Pinchas and Eliyahu, and the promise is that we will be rewarded for our emunah. Vanities, meanwhile, are a focus on what is not essential — the same thing as "How beautiful is this tree."

So the quality is minimized conversation, miut sichah; idle talk is the standing example of vanity. Conversation distracts and runs on into consequences nobody intended, which is why the sages warn against too much of it, even with one's own wife. But purposeful conversation taken with miut, humility and smallness, is a very good quality. Prayer itself is called conversation — Isaac went to converse in the field — and Rebbe Nachman holds Hitbodedut, conversing with G-d, to be the highest of all levels. Conversation in a field suits this month well.

The prophet is Jahaziel the Levite, and his prophecy is this quality at work. "Hearken, all Judeans, inhabitants of Jerusalem, and King Jehoshaphat, so said the Lord to you: You shall not fear, neither shall you be dismayed because of this great multitude, for the war is not yours but G-d's." And then: "It is not for you to fight in this [war]; set yourselves, stand and see the salvation of the Lord with you, O Judah and Jerusalem; fear not and be not dismayed." The salvation that follows is full of humility, with singing and praise. When we do our part and then step back and let Hashem do the rest, incredible things happen. Sometimes the best thing is to be quiet, as at the splitting of the Sea of Reeds: "The Lord will fight for you, but you shall remain silent." (Exodus 14:14)

The levitical city is Rehob, which means street, from rahav, wide. The near word merchav, wide place, is in last week's Haftarah verse. Called to out of dire straits, He answers broadly, and that is the essence of emunah.
142.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 21.

143.title: Isaac and Emunah
body: The Song of the Sea's verses are first of all a declaration of faith, Emunah, which is this month: "The Lord will reign to all eternity; When Pharaoh's horses came with his chariots and his horsemen into the sea." They hold the elements too — Pharaoh and the horsemen are man, the horses are animal, and the sea is mineral, Domem.

The Haftorah turns to doubt: "(But) among the divisions of Reuben, (there were) great resolves of heart. Why do you sit between the borders." Great resolves and no resolve — that was Reuben's own difficulty. He knew he had to save Joseph and lacked the emunah to do it outright; he knew later that Benjamin had to be brought to Egypt, and again could not carry his father.

Daf Kaf Alef of Sotah keeps on with how the merit of Torah and mitzvoth can protect from punishment, and how a woman can earn merit from Torah — fitting in the week of the Rebbetzin's yahrzeit, the 22nd of Shevat.

The generation is Yitzchak, the second forefather, whose whole life, and above all his near sacrifice, was Emunah. His name comes from Tzchok, laughter: Yitzchak means he will laugh, which is faith in what has not happened yet, and also pleasure, Ta'anug.

The journey is from Mount Shepher to Haradah. Haradah means trembling, and it is tied to the fear the people felt after the plague that followed Korach's rebellion. Trembling also belongs to happiness: "Vegilu b'Readah," rejoice in trembling, and the Talmud says that where there is gilah, rejoicing, there must be trembling. The personal journey takes the beauty and the enjoyment of the last stop and gets ready for the trembling happiness of Adar.

144.title: Malchut (Kingship)
body: Channah's twenty-first verse is the yearly pilgrimage: "And the man, Elkanah and his entire household, went up to slaughter to the Lord, the sacrifice of the days and his vow." Household, Beitoh, usually means a man's wife — so the verse is there to set up what comes next, that Channah stays behind to nurse Shmuel and will only bring him to the Tabernacle, to live there, once he is weaned.

The Pirkei Avot quality is that the Torah grants him kingship, Malchut, which is a feminine sefirah and receives its energy from the others. The verse says the Torah gives kingship; it is left to us to know how to receive it. And Elkanah goes up out of gratitude.

Proverbs 21 opens on kingship and then turns to the weight a wife carries, here for the worse. "A king's heart is like rivulets of water in the Lord's hand; wherever He wishes, He turns it." "It is better to sit on the corner of a roof than with a quarrelsome wife and the house of a friend." "It is better to dwell in a desert land than [with] a quarrelsome and vexatious wife."

Besides Rebbetzin Chaya Mushka's yahrzeit on the 22nd of Shevat, the week holds Rebbe Menachem Mendel of Kotzk on the same day and Rebbe Yehoshua Rokeach, the Second Rebbe of Belz, son of the Sar Shalom, on the 23rd. The Kotzker was known for immense Torah knowledge reached very young and for an uncompromising pursuit of truth; his sharp, penetrating sayings cut through people's ego and fantasies. Among his students were the first two leaders of Ger, the largest Chassidic group in all of Poland. The 22nd of Shevat is also the yahrzeit of one of his closest disciples, Rabbi Yehuda Leib Eiger of Lublin, grandson of Rabbi Akiva Eiger, and the 21st of Shevat that of another, R. Yechiel Meir Lifschitz of Gostynin, Der Tilim Yid.

Rebbe Yehoshua Rokeach grew the Belz dynasty his father had begun into the largest in Galicia. He fought vigorously against the Haskalah, the Jewish secularist enlightenment movement. He was a tremendous Torah scholar, known also for common sense in his leadership; he moved his followers to study with great devotion and set up programs for newly married men to stay in Yeshiva. Sometimes this week also holds Rav David HaLevi Segal, author of the Turei Zahav, and Rabbi Mordechai Yosef Elazar Leiner, the Radziner Rebbe, both on the 26th of Shevat.

145.title: Celebrating "Sweet Fruit" in the Winter
body: The Song calls both winds and then sits down to eat. "Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out; let my beloved come to his garden and eat his sweet fruit." Then the answer: "I have come to my garden, my sister, [my] bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spice, I have eaten my sugar cane with my sugar, I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, friends; drink, yea, drink abundantly, beloved ones." The drinking abundantly may be looking ahead to Adar. And then the verse that is Shevat itself: "I sleep, but my heart is awake. Hark! My beloved is knocking: Open for me, my sister, my beloved, my dove, my perfect one, for my head is full of dew, my locks with the drops of the night."
