Still the middle of winter, but past Tu B'Shvat, and inside the trees the sap has begun to melt.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the twenty-first is Zerach, Perez's brother, whose name means sunrise. At the birth he was the first to put out his hand and the second to be born. Sunrise is like that too: it is the first moment the morning Shmoneh Esreh can be said, and where the day begins, though most people start praying much later. Shevat is the same — the first appearance of spring and the sun, with spring itself a long way off.
Daf Kaf Alef of Shvuot keeps on with the laws of oaths, most of them about eating.

Jeremiah's twenty-first chapter is full of nature — valleys, plains, fruit, a forest. "Behold I am against you, O dweller of the valley, rock of the plain, says the Lord, those who say, 'Who will encamp upon us, and who will come into our dwellings?'" And then: "And I will visit upon you according to the fruit of your deeds, says the Lord, and I will ignite a fire in her forest, and it will consume all her surroundings."

146.title: G-d is our Strength - Psalms 61-63; 59:18, 77:1-3; 89:22
body: G-d is our strength, in three psalms: the sixty-first, sixty-second and sixty-third, with one verse of Psalm 59, the opening of Psalm 77, and one verse of Psalm 89.

Psalm 61 David composed while fleeing from Saul, and all of it asks for long life — not to pursue the pleasures of the world but to serve G-d in awe, all his days. "From the end of the earth I call to You, when my heart is faint [with trouble]: Lead me upon the rock that surpasses me!" Then the shelter: "I will dwell in Your tent forever; I will take refuge in the shelter of Your wings, Selah." And the asking itself: "Add days to the days of the king; may his years equal those of every generation. May he sit always before G-d; appoint kindness and truth to preserve him."

Psalm 62 prays for the downfall of his enemies and tells his generation not to rest their faith in riches, because piling up wealth is futility. "To G-d alone does my soul hope; my salvation is from Him. He alone is my rock and salvation, my stronghold; I shall not falter greatly." The blessing that is a curse: "with their mouths they bless, and in their hearts they curse, Selah." The weighing: "Men are but vanity; people [but] transients. Were they to be raised upon the scale, they would be lighter than vanity." The warning: "Put not your trust in exploitation, nor place futile hope in robbery. If [corrupt] wealth flourishes, pay it no heed." And the close, one thing heard as two: "G-d spoke one thing, from which I perceived two: That strength belongs to G-d; and that Yours, my Lord, is kindness."

Psalm 63 is from hiding in the Judean desert, yearning toward the place of the Holy Ark like a man thirsty for water. "My soul thirsts for You, my flesh longs for You; [like one] in a desolate and dry land, without water, so [I thirst] to see You in the Sanctuary, to behold Your might and glory. For Your kindness is better than life; my lips shall praise You." Then the nights: "Indeed, I remember You upon my bed; during the watches of the night I meditate upon You." And the holding on: "My soul cleaved to You; Your right hand supported me."

Psalm 59's verse is the strength: "[You are] my strength, to You I will sing, for G-d is my stronghold, the G-d of my kindness." Psalm 77 begins in the night that will not close: "[I raise] my voice to G-d and cry out; [I raise] my voice to G-d and He will listen to me. On the day of my distress, I sought the Lord; my wound oozes at night and does not abate; my soul refuses to be comforted." And Psalm 89's verse answers it: "It is he whom My hand shall be prepared [to assist]; My arm, too, shall strengthen him."

147.title: The Fly is Saying
body: The fly opens — when Israel is not busying itself with Torah — and the week's books answer around it.

The sea and the provoking first: "When Pharaoh's horses came with his chariots" / "And his horsemen into the sea" / "They have provoked My jealousy with a non-G-d" / "Provoked My anger with their vanities" / "All flesh is grass, and all its grace is as the flower of the field" / "(But) among the divisions of Reuben, (there were) great resolves of heart."

Then the calling out, with the sitting still and the sleeping beside it: "The voice said, 'Call out'. And he said, 'What shall I call out?'" / "Why do you sit between the borders?" / "I sleep, but my heart is awake. Hark! My beloved is knocking" / "My perfect one, for my head is full of dew" / "My locks with the drops of the night" / "My wound oozes at night and does not abate" / "My soul refuses to be comforted."

Then what withers and what does not: "The grass withers, the flower fades" / "But the word of our Lord shall endure forever" / "The Lord will reign to all eternity" / "[You are] my strength, to You I will sing" / "The Lord rewarded me according to my righteousness" / "According to the cleanness of my hands He recompensed me."

Then the healing and the arm: "I will create a new expression of the lips: Peace, peace for him Who is far off and for him who is near, says G-d, and I will heal him" / "It is he whom My hand shall be prepared [to assist]" / "My arm, too, shall strengthen him."

And the end is the garden, with the pilgrimage and the crying out braided through it: "Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind" / "Blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out" / "And the man, Elkanah and his entire household, went up to slaughter to the Lord" / "Let my beloved come to his garden and eat his sweet fruit" / "For G-d is my stronghold, the G-d of my kindness" / "I have come to my garden, my sister, [my] bride" / "I have gathered my myrrh with my spice" / "[I raise] my voice to G-d and cry out" / "I have drunk my wine with my milk" / "On the day of my distress, I sought the Lord" / "Eat, friends; drink, yea, drink abundantly, beloved ones" / "Open for me, my sister, my beloved, my dove."

148.title: To Complement Each Other in Happiness
body: The Sea Monsters say: "Praise G-d from the land, the sea monsters and all the depths." (Psalms 148:7) This is the week of Rosh Chodesh Adar, whose sign is Pisces, so the water creatures are rightly the ones singing through the four weeks of this month. Adar is the month of Purim, and when it begins we increase in joy. The depths of the song are the deep and hidden miracles He did for us in it.

Adar belongs to the tribe of Naftali, and to the quality of being an emissary, a sheliach. Jacob's blessing calls Naftali an ayalah shlucha, a sent-off gazelle, and he was sent as a messenger more than once. Moses's blessing calls him seva ratzon, satisfied will — and ratzon, will, belongs to keter, the highest of the sefirot, which means crown. Naftali is the only tribe described as a feminine animal, and the crown fits, because the hero of this month is a woman sent on a mission to obtain a crown, Queen Esther. Like her, Naftali stands for self-sacrifice and humility: the tribe was known for its speed and alacrity, and its prince accepted being last to bring an offering at the inauguration of the Tabernacle. Being a sheliach takes enormous nullification before the one who sends you, and tremendous will to see the mission done.

The phrase "Ve'anochi Tola'at ve lo Ish," I am a worm and not a man, belongs here too: Velo Ish has the same numerical value as Sheliach. It comes from Psalm 22 — the same number as this week — whose opening verse holds ayelet hashachar, the gazelle of the morning. The sages teach that ayelet hashachar is the planet Venus, the last star to appear before morning, and Queen Esther, the last prophet to appear before the redemption. Adar is likewise the last month counting from Nissan, and the prince of Naftali was the last to bring his offering, wrapping up the work of Asher and of all the tribes before him. That is a sheliach's work, and ours: to finish what those before us began.

Adar is the only month often counted twice. Seven times every nineteen years there are two, Adar I and Adar II, and Adar II belongs to the tribe of Levi. The parallels are strong. Like Naftali, the Levites, and the kohanim above all, were known for alacrity and care in the mitzvot, and they served as emissaries for the whole people in the Temple, with tremendous self-sacrifice. There is one more link between Levi and the sea animals of this month: the animals in the sea did not perish in the Flood, and the tribe of Levi was never enslaved by the Egyptians.

So Adar runs on duality. Pisces is two fish facing opposite ways. The Purim story has not one hero but two, Esther and Mordechai. And this is the month of the half-shekel, a contribution to the Temple so that sacrifices could be brought for the whole public — half and not whole, because no Jew is complete alone, and each of us completes the other.

Twenty-two is the number of letters in the Hebrew alphabet. Hashem made the Torah and the world by combining them, so each letter completes the others too; and the Torah starts with beit, which is duality and relationship. The sea monsters hold the same thing. It seems strange that they should sing about praise on land, until you see that they know their own song is not enough by itself.

The other duality of the month is hidden and revealed. The miracle of Purim came through hidden means, and though His hand is more than apparent in the events, the actual name of G-d never appears in the Megillah. Even the name Megillat Esther says it: Megillah is of nigleh, revealed, and Esther of nistar, hidden. In the song, the depths are what is hidden and the land is what is revealed. The song also recalls Jacob's blessing to his two grandchildren, Ephraim and Menashe: "You will multiply like fish in the face of the land." Rabbi Yitzchak Ginsburgh notes that the gematria of Naftali equals the gematria of Ephraim and Menashe.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Dusta'i the son of Rabbi Yannai, in the name of Rabbi Meir: whoever forgets even a single word of this learning, the Torah considers it as if he had forfeited his life, from "Just be careful, and verily guard your soul, lest you forget the things that your eyes have seen." (Deuteronomy 4:9) But the verse continues, "and lest they be removed from your heart," so nobody forfeits his life for studies that proved too hard — only for deliberately putting them out of his heart. One of the main mitzvot of Adar is remembering what Amalek did and the command to destroy it; forgetting to destroy evil puts our own lives in danger.

The combination is chesed shebenetzach, kindness within victory. The week begins two months of victory and redemption, netzach, which carry Purim and Passover, and we mark the kindness He showed us by being more joyful than usual. The lesson from the sea monsters is that praising G-d by ourselves is not enough — we have to think of those who are distant, as they think of those on land.

149.title: Adar, Eliezer son of Dodavahu, and "Minimized" Laughter
body: Rosh Chodesh Adar, the month of Naftali and of ratzon, desire. Haazinu burns: "For a fire blazed in My wrath, and burned to the lowest depths. It consumed the land and its produce, setting aflame the foundations of mountains." (Deuteronomy 32:22) Read positively, the wrath is not against Israel but against the foolish nation that attacks it — Amalek. The Hebrew behind "lowest depths" is Sheol, which can also be read as Shaul, the first king, who failed to wipe Amalek out; the anger has burned since. In Adar we read Parashat Zachor and remember to destroy Amalek and everything it stands for. The Purim story sets Mordechai, a descendant of Shaul, against Haman, a descendant of Hagag, king of the Amalekites — and Mordechai wins, and Haman is killed along with his sons.

The Haftarah verse draws the same line twice: "For I have kept the ways of the Lord and have not wickedly departed from [the commandments of] my G-d." (II Samuel 22:22) The good half, "Shamarti Darchei," I have kept the ways, holds the letters of Mordechai. The second half, "Veloh Rashati," have not wickedly, points to Haman, who is called Haman HaRashah — and sounds like the name of Vashti, Achashverosh's wife before Esther.

The quality is minimized laughter, miut schok. Laughter can slide into frivolity and pull a person into the wrong circles. It is not bad in itself — it can open the mind, and there is even a custom, based on the Talmud, of beginning each lesson with a joke — but it has to be held with miut, smallness and humility. That holds for the whole month, when we are Marbim B'Simcha, and for Purim itself, when it is a mitzvah to get drunk and behave with schok; what has to stay is the intention.

The prophet is Eliezer son of Dodavahu, and his words to King Yehoshaphat are about exactly this care in company. Yehoshaphat was righteous, and at one point he associated himself with King Ahab. The prophet rebuked him and he was punished: the ships he had built with Ahab were broken and could not sail. That is the last event the Tanach records before his death.

The levitical city is Kedesh, also a city of refuge. Its name is from Kadosh, holy, and it is near the word Kiddush, the blessing over wine — which fits the drinking of this month, superficially frivolous and in fact tremendously holy, in some ways holier than Yom Kippur.
149.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 22.

150.title: Adar and Ratzon (Will, Desire)
body: Rosh Chodesh Adar. The Talmud says MisheNichnas Adar Marbim b'Simcha — when Adar enters, we increase in joy. The month belongs to Naftali, the Ayalah Shluchah, the swift gazelle sent out; when there are two Adars the second belongs to Levi, who served, and will serve again, as emissary for the whole people in the Temple.

The Song of the Sea is back in the water: "and the Lord brought the waters of the sea back upon them; and the children of Israel walked on dry land in the midst of the sea." Dry land in the midst of the sea is the same paradox as Jacob's blessing to Efraim and Menashe, that they would increase like fish over the land.

The Haftorah stays with Reuben's doubt: "to hear the bleatings of the flocks? At the divisions of Reuben, (there are) great searchings of heart." Resolve is ratzon, will, and this month is full of it. Naftali is s'vah ratzon, filled with will; Levi was known for determination and self-sacrifice; Reuben's conduct shows neither. Each tribe had a perfectly good excuse for staying out of the fight — they did not share a border with where it happened — and Devorah makes plain that more was expected of them.

The bleating is worth following. The Tanach has a later one, tied tightly to this month, and it belongs not to Reuven the firstborn but to Shaul the first king. Shaul was commanded to destroy Amalek completely. He did not act with enough Ratzon: he left Amalek's king alive, and the best of the flock. Amalek has the same numerical value as Safek, doubt, which is the opposite of Ratzon. When Shmuel came to reprimand him, Shaul said he had fulfilled the command, and Shmuel asked what, then, was this bleating of flocks he was hearing. The hesitation is the same as Reuven's, a divided heart — and as Reuven is replaced as firstborn, Shaul is replaced as king.

Daf Kaf Beit of Sotah keeps on with the acts that can look pious and end up destroying the world. One of its main discussions is of someone who rules when he is not capable of it, and does not rule when he is. Shaul again: he ruled where he should have obeyed, letting the king and some of the flock live, and did not take his own prominence seriously enough — small in the eyes of the people — and the destruction Amalek still causes came of it.

The generation is Jacob, whose name is from Ekev, heel. A heel treats someone else as the head, which is a messenger's position, and Purim belongs to the people as heel, Ya'akov, rather than head, Yisrael, and to the times of Yikveta d'Meshicha.

The journey is from Haradah to Makheloth. Makheloth means assembly, and in modern Hebrew a choir, a gathering to sing and play. Rabbi Jacobson suggests it may be where the people gathered to see the miracle of Aharon's staff. The personal journey takes last week's trembling happiness further, into unity and into gatherings of singing and dancing.

151.title: Dominion versus Kingship, Royalty
body: Channah's twenty-second verse is the staying behind: "But Hannah did not go up, for she said to her husband: 'Until the child is weaned, then I shall bring him, and he shall appear before the Lord, and abide there forever.'" The text is careful to say that she told her husband why, which shows her concern for him and a certain subservience — even though she has her way in the end. Adar is the month of Purim, where another woman, Queen Esther, convinces her husband, Achashverosh, to save her people and destroy Haman, who was effectively running the kingdom.

The Pirkei Avot quality is that the Torah grants dominion, Memshalah. It is not kingship, Malchut, because it does not need royalty: one can rule without being king, as Joseph did as viceroy and, LeHavdil, as Haman did. Memshalah is a more masculine power, sheer power and force, where Malchut is the more sublime feminine quality, connected to speech. Both are in the verse, and both are in this month.

Proverbs 22 is about power, mostly economic. "A name is chosen above great wealth; good favor over silver and gold." "A rich man and a poor man were visited upon; the Lord is the Maker of them all." "In the wake of humility comes fear of the Lord, riches, honor, and life." And then: "A rich man will rule over the poor, and a borrower is a slave to a lender." The word for rule there is Yimshol, the same root as Memshalah.

In a year with two months of Adar the yahrzeits are usually kept in the second, unless the person died in the first Adar of a year that also had two — so the descriptions wait for next month, when weeks 22 through 25 come round again.

152.title: Mordechai the Shepherd
body: The Song undresses and washes: "I have taken off my tunic; how can I put it on? I have bathed my feet; how can I soil them?" Taking off the head garment reads as letting go of the intellect, which belongs to this month, and turning to the feet. The Rebbe's Ma'amar Ve'Atah Tetzaveh speaks of Mordechai, the Moshe of the generation, as the head, and the Jewish people as the feet.

The next verse is almost the two most crucial verses of Megillat Esther: "My beloved stretched forth his hand from the hole, and my insides stirred because of him." Against it: "And it came to pass when the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, that she won favor in his eyes, and the king extended to Esther the golden scepter that was in his hand, and Esther approached and touched the end of the scepter."

Then the myrrh: "I arose to open for my beloved, and my hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers with flowing myrrh, upon the handles of the lock." Myrrh is Mor, and the Talmud says Mordechai is hinted in the Torah at the verse about pure myrrh, Mor Dror, which in Aramaic is Mara Dachia.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the twenty-second is Hezron. Hezron comes from chatzer, courtyard or enclosure — and to carry in a courtyard, two neighbours have to set up an eruv chatzeirot. Eruv shares its root with Arev, sweet. When Jews come together and their duality works for the good, there is sweetness, which is this month.

Daf Kaf Beit of Shvuot keeps on with oaths about eating, but its weight falls on the laws of speech, and on whether drinking counts as eating. Drinking is one of the main themes of Adar — drinking to the point of not knowing the difference between blessed is Mordechai and cursed is Haman. The daf opens its discussion of speech with someone who curses Hashem by mistake and must bring a sacrifice.

Jeremiah's twenty-second chapter is a people left leaderless and confused, with eating and drinking through it. "Shall you reign, for you compete with the cedar? Your father-did he not eat and drink and perform justice and righteousness? Then it was well with him." "All your shepherds shall be broken by the wind, and your lovers shall go into captivity." And the end: "O land, land, land, hearken to the word of the Lord."

153.title: Reviewing the First Week of Adar - Psalms 64-66; 77:4-6; 89:23
body: The first week of Adar in psalms: the sixty-fourth, sixty-fifth and sixty-sixth, with three verses of Psalm 77 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 64 the masters of homiletics read as Daniel in the lion's den — David foresaw it with divine inspiration and prayed for him, Daniel being a descendant of his. The tongues are the weapon: "who have sharpened their tongue like the sword, aimed their arrow-a bitter word-to shoot at the innocent from hidden places; suddenly they shoot at him, they are not afraid." The hiding: "They sought pretexts; [and when] they completed a diligent search, each man [kept the plot] inside, deep in the heart." And then it turns on them: "But G-d shot at them; [like] a sudden arrow were their blows. Their own tongues caused them to stumble."

Psalm 65 is praise that gives up on praising. "Silence is praise for You, O G-d [Who dwells in] Zion" — because who could recount His mighty acts? Then the rain, which is most of the psalm: "You remember the earth and water it, you enrich it abundantly [from] G-d's stream filled with water." "You saturate its furrows, gratifying its legions; with showers You soften it and bless its growth. You crown the year of Your goodness [with rain], and Your clouds drip abundance." And the fields answering: "The meadows don sheep, and the valleys cloak themselves with grain; they sound blasts, indeed they sing."

Psalm 66 is the praise we will offer when the exiles are gathered in. "Raise your voices in jubilation to G-d, all the earth!" "Go and see the works of G-d, awesome in His deeds toward mankind. He turned the sea into dry land, and they passed through the river on foot; we rejoiced in Him there." Then the testing: "For You tested us, O G-d; You refined us as one refining silver. You brought us into prison; You placed a chain upon our loins. You mounted men over our head; we went through fire and water, and You brought us out to abundance." And the end, which asks to be listened to: "Come listen, all you who fear G-d, and I will relate what He has done for my soul."

Psalm 77's verses are a man awake all night: "I remember G-d and I stir; I speak and my spirit becomes faint, forever. You held fast the awakenings of my eyes; I throb and I do not speak. I think of days of yore, ancient years." And Psalm 89's verse is the protection: "No enemy will exact from him, neither will an unjust person afflict him."

154.title: The Giant Sea Creatures Are Saying
body: The giant sea creatures open, and what they ask for is praise from the other element: "Praise G-d from the land, the giant sea creatures and all the depths."

Then the fire and the water, one after the other: "For a fire blazed in My wrath, and burned to the lowest depths" / "It consumed the land and its produce, setting aflame the foundations of mountains" / "And the Lord brought the waters of the sea back upon them" / "For I have kept the ways of the Lord and have not wickedly departed from my G-d" / "And the children of Israel walked on dry land in the midst of the sea."

Then the child left at home, and the forever in both: "But Hannah did not go up, for she said to her husband: Until the child is weaned, then I shall bring him" / "I remember G-d and I stir; I speak and my spirit becomes faint, forever" / "And he shall appear before the Lord, and abide there forever" / "No enemy will exact from him, neither will an unjust person afflict him."

Then the hand through the hole, with the washing and the bleating between: "My beloved stretched forth his hand from the hole, and my insides stirred because of him" / "I have taken off my tunic; how can I put it on?" / "To hear the bleatings of the flocks?" / "I have bathed my feet; how can I soil them?" / "At the divisions of Reuben, (there are) great searchings of heart."

And the end is the myrrh on the lock, and the sleeplessness beside it: "I arose to open for my beloved, and my hands dripped with myrrh" / "You held fast the awakenings of my eyes; I throb and I do not speak" / "And my fingers with flowing myrrh, upon the handles of the lock" / "I think of days of yore, ancient years."

155.title: To Be Happy Even Without Knowing Why Things Are the Way They Are
body: The Leviathan is saying, "Give thanks to G-d for He is good, His kindness endures forever." (Psalms 136:1) This week holds the seventh of Adar, the birthday and the yahrzeit of Moses, Moshe Rabbeinu, who is from the tribe of Levi — and the first three letters of Leviathan spell Levi.

So the Leviathan is Moses. Fish stand for tzadikim, and as the Leviathan is the biggest of all fish, Moses is the greatest of all tzadikim. There is a hidden version of the same thing in the name of his main disciple, Yehoshua Bin Nun: Nun means fish in Aramaic, and a student is considered like a son. The gematria of Nun is fifty, and Moses reached the fiftieth level of holiness when he passed away, which is implied in the name of his burial place, Mount Nevoh — read as Nun Boh, the Nun is in it. The last letter of Leviatan is Nun; exchange the Lamed, thirty, and the Yud, ten, for a Mem, forty, and the word becomes Mavet, death, and Nun — though we say that Moshe Rabbeinu never truly died.

The song itself is well known, repeated many times in Psalm 118: "Hodu l'Hashem Ki Tov Ki l'Olam Chasdoh." Ki Tov, for He is good, is exactly what the Torah says Yocheved saw in her newborn son — she saw Ki Tov, that he was good — which is why one of Moses's names is Tuviah, from Tov. Rashi explains that at his birth his mother saw the house fill with light, and our sages say that is the light which will only be revealed at the end of creation.

Twenty-three is the gematria of ziv, light, radiance. Rabbi Yitzchak Ginsburgh explains that ziv, unlike or, is light shining far from its source. The Leviathan is mysterious and unknown, and will only be fully revealed in the messianic era; what we understand of it now is negligible, no more than brightness coming from a long way off. We know from Psalm 104:26 and from Midrashim that G-d created it to play with, without knowing what that means, and we know it will be the food served to us in the final redemption.

Ziv is also a biblical name for Iyar. The Torah says it was in the month Ziv that Solomon began to build the Temple, and the Second Temple was begun in Iyar too. Iyar is when we count the omer, and Sefirat Ha'Omer comes from sapir, saphire: in Iyar we work to become radiant like saphire, proper vessels for Him to dwell in. Entering Adar, with Moses's birth and passing in it, we begin on our inner Temple. The Torah reading of this week usually concerns the building of the Tabernacle, and we are still collecting the half-shekel, which went to the Temple's upkeep.

Balance in the world required that the female Leviathan die, and the Leviathan sings about kindness anyway. It knows perfectly well that everything Hashem does is for the good. Moses too showed great kindness, leading the people out of Egypt to receive the Torah at Mount Sinai. And as the largest of the fish, the one closest to G-d, the Leviathan is not content to praise by itself: it commands others to do their part.

The last ma'amar the Rebbe reviewed and edited, Ve'Atah Tetzaveh, was delivered during Adar, and it is about the relationship between Moses and the rest of the people. Tetzaveh means to command, and also to tie or unite — the root of mitzvah. Tetzaveh is the one portion since Moses was introduced in which his name does not appear, said to be a hidden reference to his passing on the 7th of Adar, since the portion is read around then. The connection is so strong that when there are two Adars his yahrzeit is kept in the first, because that is when Tetzaveh is read, even though the main date for a yahrzeit is normally the second.

The Rebbe's stroke was on the 27th of Adar I. Two years later, on that same date in 5754, he suffered another, which led to his passing a few months later. Less than two months before the first one he gave an enigmatic talk about how his late father-in-law, the Previous Rebbe, had not been able to speak clearly in his last years — and said that we all had to take it on ourselves to increase Torah study and Chassidic gatherings to make up for that difficulty, and to do it with happiness. Two months later he was in the same condition.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Chanina the son of Dosa: whoever's fear of sin takes precedence over his wisdom, his wisdom endures, and whoever's wisdom takes precedence over his fear of sin, it does not. Moses showed fear of Hashem from their first meeting at the burning bush. Rabbi Chanina also says that one who is pleasing to his fellow men is pleasing to G-d, and one who is not, is not — which fits Moses too. The Talmud teaches that every day a heavenly voice says, "the entire world is sustained in merit of Chanina my son, yet for Chanina my son, one measure of carobs is enough from Friday to Friday."

The combination is gevurah shebenetzach, discipline and strength within determination and victory. Moses represents netzach, and his death is connected to gevurah. The lesson from the Leviathan is that everything G-d does is for the good, so He can be trusted entirely.

156.title: Hosea and Slowness to Anger (Erech Apayim)
body: The week of the seventh of Adar, Moshe's birth and his passing. Haazinu keeps on with the loss: "I will link evils upon them. I will use up My arrows on them." (Deuteronomy 32:23) Read positively, it is the gathering up of evil that was over them and the complete destruction of the arrows — Amalek among them — that had been used against the people. Rashi's commentary hints at this: it is the arrows that are diminished, not the Jews.

The Haftorah stays positive: "For all His ordinances were before me; and [as for] His statutes, I did not depart from it." (II Samuel 22:23) The word for before me is Lenegdi, which can also be read Lenegdai, toward those against me — so the commandments are a protection against the attackers.

The quality is slowness to anger, erech apayim, and it belongs to this week, because it was through Moshe's pleading for the people that G-d revealed this quality of His, one of the thirteen attributes of mercy. In that plea Moshe said that if G-d would not forgive them, "erase me from Your book" — and because of it his name does not appear in Tetzaveh, read in the week of his yahrzeit. And it was a relative lack of this attribute, at his own level, which we cannot fathom, that led him to castigate the people and strike the rock instead of speaking to it, and so kept him from entering the Land of Israel.
The prophet is Hosea, whose prophecies turn on G-d's unending mercy and slowness to anger, and His love for the people despite their sins.

The levitical city is Hamoth-Dor, the springs of Dor. Hamoth shares a root with Hamath, anger. Springs are heat contained: the springs of Tiberias are said to come from an opening in the gates of Gehinnom made at the time of the Flood — an opening that came out of anger and was then contained and put to good use. And Dar is from the word for home, a domesticated anger.
156.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 23.

157.title: Being an Emissary
body: Zayin Adar, Moshe Rabbeinu's birthday and yahrzeit. Just as Zayin Adar usually falls on Tetzaveh, where his name is left out, his name is left out of the verses after the Song of the Sea as well: "Miriam, the prophetess, Aaron's sister, took a timbrel in her hand, and all the women came out after her with timbrels and with dances. And Miriam called out to them, Sing to the Lord, for very exalted is He; a horse and its rider He cast into the sea." It is her turn to lead now, and she is called Aaron's sister, not Moshe's — a sheliach again, a shluchah in this case.

The Haftorah rebukes two more: "Gilead abides beyond the Jordan; and Dan, why does he gather into the ships?" There is a division inside Menashe here — Machir went to the war and Gilead stayed. Dan's choice looks worse still, because it is the reverse of the Sea of Reeds: there the people went into the sea and turned it into land and so beat their enemy, and here Dan leaves the land to take refuge in the sea. That is the opposite of a sheliach, who gives himself up for something larger.

Daf Kaf Gimmel of Sotah takes up when a Mincha offering is disqualified, and then mostly the differences between men and women in the laws of priesthood and sacrifices. The parallel is that there are things a woman can do in a man's place, as Miriam did, and others she cannot, or does differently.

The generation is Yehudah, leader of his brothers, the lion, the king of the tribes. His name comes from Hoda'ah, acknowledgement: his brothers acknowledge him and act according to his will, on his behalf, like shluchim. And Yehudah was himself an emissary for Jacob, sent to Egypt ahead of the others to found a Yeshiva, a dwelling place for Torah in exile.

The journey is from Makheloth to Tahath. Tahath means bottom, a low point, as Moshe's passing was. It also holds the chance of rising. Rabbi Simon Jacobson puts it this way: Tachath is also the depths we fall to when we leave Mak'heloth, forsaking unity; and we can turn Tachath into a place of peace, when each of us dwells beneath — tachath — our vine and fig tree. It belongs with the idea that Hashem made the world because He desired a Dira Ba'Tachtonim, a dwelling place in the lower realms. The personal journey is unity and joy in a place where the focus is on those around Moses rather than on Moses himself, and from there, making that dwelling place below out of a situation of spiritual lowliness — which is the story of Purim, and the sacrifices Esther made.

158.title: Coming to a Good Decision
body: Channah's twenty-third verse is her husband letting her decide: "And Elkanah her husband said to her: 'Do what seems good to you. Stay until you have weaned him, only, may the Lord fulfill His word.' And the woman stayed and nursed her son, until she weaned him."

Which word? Rashi gives two answers. By the simple reading: you asked of Him seed of righteous men, and Eli announced to you through divine inspiration that the God of Israel will grant your request — may the Lord fulfill His word. The Midrash Agadah gives another. Rabbi Nehemiah said in the name of Rabbi Samuel, the son of Rabbi Isaac, that every day a divine voice would resound through the world saying that a righteous man was destined to arise and his name would be Samuel; so every woman who bore a son named him Samuel, and as soon as they saw his deeds they said, this is not Samuel. When our Samuel was born and people saw his deeds, they said it seems that this one is the expected righteous man. That is what Elkanah was praying for. There is a clear parallel with Moshe Rabbeinu, the expected redeemer.

The Pirkei Avot quality is that the Torah grants jurisprudence, Chikur Din — investigating a matter in order to reach the right decision. In the verse, Elkanah hands the decision to Channah: do what seems good to you. It sits well with this week's combination, Gevurah shebeNetzach.

Proverbs 23 is jurisprudence, and keeps last week's rulership going. "If you sit down to dine with a ruler, you should understand well who is in front of you." "Bring your heart to discipline and your ears to words of knowledge." "Hear you, my son, and grow wise, and walk in the way of your heart."
As last week, in a year with two months of Adar the yahrzeits are usually kept in the second, so the descriptions wait for next month, when weeks 22 through 25 come round again.

159.title: When Hashem and our Leaders Are Hidden
body: The Song opens the door and finds nobody: "I opened for my beloved, but my beloved had hidden and was gone; my soul went out when he spoke; I sought him, but found him not; I called him, but he did not answer me." Then the beating: "The watchmen who patrol the city found me; they smote me and wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took my jewelry off me." And then the asking: "I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, what will you tell him? That I am lovesick."

Looking and not finding, calling and getting no answer, being smitten and wounded — all of it may be the loss of Moshe. The hiddenness is also Hester Panim, when His face is hidden, which is the Purim story. Rashi, on that third verse, refers directly to Mordechai's generation in the days of Haman, and how the people kept the Torah through all the suffering. That is the message of Adar. Our sages teach that Mordechai in his generation was like Moshe in his.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the twenty-third is Hamul, whose name looks to come from Chemlah, pity, mercy. Hamul would be one who is dealt with mercifully — as Moshe was at his birth.

Daf Kaf Gimmel of Shvuot keeps on with whether drinking belongs to eating, and much of it is about wine and intoxicating drink. It also takes up combining many oaths into one, and then an oath not to eat forbidden food. One of the great points of contention in the Purim story was eating at Achashverosh's meal.

Jeremiah's twenty-third chapter is a people left without a proper shepherd, and then Mashiach, who will be like Moshe: "Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will set up of David a righteous shoot, and he shall reign a king and prosper, and he shall perform judgment and righteousness in the land." The future redemption will be like the one from Egypt and larger: they shall no longer say, "As the Lord lives, Who brought up the children of Israel from the land of Egypt," but, "As the Lord lives, Who brought up and Who brought the seed of the house of Israel from the northland and from all the lands where I have driven them." And the prophet himself, drunk without wine: "Because of the prophets my heart is broken within me, my bones shake, I was like a drunken man and like a man whom wine has overcome, because of the Lord and because of His holy words."

160.title: Reviewing the Second Week of Adar - Psalms 67-69; 77:7-9; 89:24
body: The second week of Adar in psalms: the sixty-seventh, sixty-eighth and sixty-ninth, with three verses of Psalm 77 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 67 is known as an especially revered prayer. It speaks of the ingathering of the exiles and the wars of Gog and Magog, a time when the Lord will be One. "May G-d be gracious to us and bless us; may He make His countenance shine upon us forever, that Your way be known on earth, Your salvation among all nations." It is short and all of it is the nations joining in: "The nations will rejoice and sing for joy, for You will judge the peoples justly and guide the nations on earth forever."

Psalm 68 David composed about a future event — Sennacherib surrounding Jerusalem on Passover in the reign of Hezekiah — and about the good of the Messianic era. "Let G-d rise, let His enemies be scattered." Then the One who takes in whoever has nobody: "A father of orphans and judge of widows is G-d, in the abode of His holiness. G-d settles the solitary into a home, and frees those bound in shackles." Then Sinai: "the earth trembled, even the heavens dripped before the presence of G-d; this mountain of Sinai [trembled] before the presence of G-d, the G-d of Israel." The dove: "[you will be like] wings of a dove covered with silver, her pinions with brilliant gold." The chosen mountain: "Why do you prance, O mountains of peaks? This is the mountain G-d has desired as His dwelling." And the procession, with the tribes in it: "The singers began, then the musicians, in the midst of the maidens playing timbrels." "There Benjamin, the youngest, rules them; the princes of Judah stone them, [as do] the princes of Zebulun, and the princes of Naphtali."

Psalm 69 is a man going under. "Deliver me, O G-d, for the waters have reached until my soul! I have sunk in muddy depths without foothold; I have come into deep waters, and the current sweeps me away." The hatred without cause: "More numerous than the hairs on my head are those who hate me without reason." The loneliness of it: "I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother's sons, for the envy of Your House has consumed me." The mockery: "Those who sit by the gate speak of me, and [of me] are the songs of drunkards." Then the asking: "Rescue me from the mire, so that I not sink." "Do not hide Your face from Your servant, for I am in distress-hurry to answer me." The comfort that never came: "I longed for comfort, but there was none; for consolers, but I did not find. They put gall into my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink." And then the turn at the end: "I will praise the Name of G-d with song, I will extol Him with thanksgiving!" "For the Lord listens to the needy, and He does not despise His prisoners."

Psalm 77's verses are the night questions: "During the night I recall my music, I meditate with my heart, and my spirit searches: Is it for eternity that my Lord forsakes [me], nevermore to be appeased? Has His kindness ceased forever? Has He sealed the decree for all generations?" And Psalm 89's verse is the answer in force: "And I will crush his adversaries before him, and will strike down those who hate him." Crushing recalls the first lines of Tetzaveh, which speak of crushed, Catit, oil, and the striking down looks like Amalek. The Tikkun HaKlali verses belong to the loss of Moshe.

161.title: The Leviathan is Saying
body: The Leviathan opens on a door opened to nobody, and the week's books come in around it.

The hiding first, with the questions underneath: "I opened for my beloved" / "But my beloved had hidden and was gone" / "Is it for eternity that my Lord forsakes me?" / "Nevermore to be appeased?" / "Give thanks to the Lord, for He is good" / "For His kindness is eternal."

Then the sea, and the music recalled at night: "Sing to the Lord, for exalted is He" / "Horse and rider He cast into the sea" / "During the night I recall my music, I meditate with my heart and my spirit searches" / "My soul went out when he spoke, I sought him, but found him not" / "Has His kindness ceased forever?" / "Has He sealed the decree for all generations?"

Then the keeping of the ordinances, and the watchmen: "For all His ordinances were before me" / "And as for His statutes I did not depart from them" / "The watchmen who patrol the city found me" / "They smote me and wounded me" / "I will link evils upon them, I will use up my arrows on them" / "The watchmen of the walls took my jewelry off me" / "And I will crush his adversaries before him" / "And will strike down those who hate him" / "Only may the Lord fulfill His word."

Then the two who would not come, and the lovesickness: "Gilead abides beyond the Jordan" / "And Dan, why does he gather into ships?" / "I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, what will you tell him?" / "I called him, but he did not answer me."

And the end is the household and the timbrel: "And Elkanah, her husband said to her, Do what seems good to you" / "Stay until you have weaned him" / "For I am lovesick" / "Miriam, the prophetess, Aaron's sister, took a timbrel in her hand" / "And the woman stayed and nursed her son until she weaned him."

162.title: To Live Above Our Worldly Concerns
body: The fish are saying: "The voice of G-d is upon the waters, the G-d of glory thunders; G-d is upon many waters." (Psalms 29:3) This is the week of Purim, when we remember that Hashem is with us through everything, even if sometimes hidden. Purim is the salvation of the Persian exile, when Haman, with the King's support at first, sought to exterminate the whole people, and through Mordechai and Esther the decree was annulled and Haman, his sons and the enemies of the Jews were the ones killed.

The Zohar says that Yom Kippur, Yom haKippurim, is a day that is KePurim, like Purim — so Purim is higher. If on Yom Kippur we stand at the level of angels, then on Purim we must stand higher than angels, at the level of tzadikim; and fish, as last week, stand for tzadikim.

On Purim we drink many waters in order to come closer, trying to reach ad deloyadah, not knowing the difference between blessed be Mordechai and cursed be Haman. It is in many ways the experience of the four rabbis who entered the Pardes, where Rabbi Akiva said, "When you reach the stones of pure marble, do not say: 'Water, water.'" On Purim we see that there are no divisions on high, that all is One, and that there is no difference between what we take for good and what we take for evil. At those levels the desire to cleave to Him pulls like great waves, out of this world; the voice thunders as at Mount Sinai, and we want to nullify ourselves entirely — ratzo. To survive it we have to do as Rabbi Akiva did and enter in peace and return in peace, understanding that His desire is that we come back and make a dwelling place for Him here — shov.

The song says the voice, and He Himself, are above the waters. But the fish are not above the waters; they are inside them. Even they need emissaries in order to perceive Him fully. Shlichut runs all through the Purim story: Esther is Mordechai's emissary and he is hers, and their messages went through shluchim. So on Purim we give each other mishloach manot, from the word sheliach, preferably through a third person.

Many waters is in the Song of Songs too, where King Solomon writes that many waters cannot extinguish the love. The many waters are the difficulties and turbulences of making a living, which however great cannot put out a Jew's love for G-d.

The Hebrew for fish is dag. Rabbi Yitzchak Ginsburgh explains that fish are the rectification of worry, da'agah, especially about a livelihood. In the time of Nehemiah certain Jews desecrated the Sabbath by selling fish in the market of Jerusalem, not trusting Him for their living: the dag became da'ag, excessive concern. Fish are always aware of their dependence on water, which is more tangible than air — and so always aware of the Source of their existence.

Twenty-four is the twenty-four presents of the kohanim, of the tribe of Levi, and the priesthood was later divided into twenty-four watches. Caf and dalet spell kad, a jar: the famous kad of Chanukah, which held pure oil with the seal of the Kohen Gadol and lasted eight days instead of one. Even the impurity and turbulence of the Hellenistic period did not put out the people's love, and they came out of the struggle with the Greeks purer than before, with redoubled faith. Purim's link to the kohanim is strong too. Esther has to fast and enter the King's chamber to ask for her people's life, much as the Kohen Gadol on Yom Kippur. The Mishnah calls the Kohen Gadol a sheliach Hashem, and he also served as an emissary of the people; Esther was both at once. The kohen is also called malach Hashem, a messenger, literally an angel.

Purim carries two kinds of pairing. Mordechai, of the tribe of Benjamin, of King Shaul, and Haman, a descendant of Amalek, are polar opposites. Esther and Mordechai complete each other for the good, where Haman and Achashverosh completed each other for evil.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Dosa the son of Hurkinas: morning sleep, noontime wine, children's talk and sitting at the meeting places of the ignorant drive a person from the world. Every one of them is encouraged on Purim. There are two ways to reach ad deloyada, sleeping or drinking during the day. The Purim story turns on the words of children studying Torah, which is where the redemption came from. And on Purim we press our unity and make no distinction between rich and poor, in money or in Torah: mishloach manot, gifts to the poor, everyone at one feast. All of it takes us out of this world of illusion — olam, world, from he'elem, hidden — and into higher levels of reality.

The combination is tiferet shebenetzach, beauty and balance within persistence and determination, which is Esther and Mordechai exactly. The lesson from the fish is that material concerns must not eat into our trust in Him.

163.title: Amos and a "Good Heart"
body: The week of Purim. Haazinu's verse is as grim as they come: "They will sprout hair from famine, attacked by demons, excised by Meriri. I will incite the teeth of livestock upon them, with the venom of creatures that slither in the dust." (Deuteronomy 32:24) The simple positive reading turns it on Amalek. But the second half can be read positively of the Jewish people themselves. "Shen Behemoth Eshalach Bam Im Chamat Zochalei Afar" can be the mitzvoth of Purim: sleep, sheinah; eating a meal and providing one for the needy, behemoth, animals; messenger gifts, mishloach manot, eshalach bam; and drinking the venom of those who lie in the dust, chamat zochalei afar, the drunkards. Wine as venom is in Chabakuk: "Woe to him who gives his friend to drink, who adds Your venom and also makes him drunk in order to gaze upon their nakedness."

The Haftarah asks to be tamim, pure, here translated single-hearted: "And I was single-hearted toward Him, and I kept myself from my iniquity." (II Samuel 22:24) The whole difference between the Jewish people and Amalek comes down to this. Our sages explain that Amalek's essence is instilling doubt in Israel's faith — Amalek has the numerical value of Safek, doubt — and the way to win is to be tamim with G-d, to act with simplicity. That is also the test inside the mitzvah of drinking: when the mind is not fully in control and the truth of a personality comes out, is a person still devoted, and still clear of lewd and improper behaviour.

So the quality is a good heart, lev tov. Purim is all about the heart; the intellect is nullified with wine and the true emotions come out. Wine goes with the heart directly — wine gladdens the heart of the human being — and most explicitly at the start of the Megillah itself: "On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was good with wine, kitov lev bayayin." (Esther, 1:10)

The prophet is Amos, whose prophecy defines what a good heart is: "Seek good and not evil in order that you live, and so the Lord G-d of Hosts shall be with you, as you said. Hate evil and love good, and establish justice in the gate; perhaps the Lord G-d of Hosts will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph."

The levitical city is Kartan, apparently short for Kiriataim, two cities. Adar runs on duality, and the heart has its own: a good inclination and a bad one. On Purim both are meant to serve G-d, with the intellect out of the centre of the work.
163.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 24.

164.title: Peretz and the Power of Joy
body: Just after the Song of the Sea, there is no water. "Moses led Israel away from the Red Sea, and they went out into the desert of Shur; they walked for three days in the desert but did not find water. They came to Marah, but they could not drink water from Marah because it was bitter; therefore, it was named Marah." Our sages teach that water in the Torah always means Torah. Purim is the same situation — and the fast of Esther is three days without food or drink — with Hashem hidden and the people's lives embittered and threatened by Haman. Their answer was to reaffirm their belief and receive the Torah again.

The Haftorah turns to Asher, who also stayed out: "Asher dwelt at the shore of the seas, and by his breaches he abides." The word for his breaches is mifratzav, the root of Peretz, this week's generation. Rashi explains that Asher was worried about the parts of its land open to attack. Like the tribes before him, Asher's answer to the fight was to protect himself — and the whole idea of Adar is being willing to give yourself up for someone else.

Daf Kaf Dalet of Sotah is cases of women who do not drink, often for extenuating circumstances. Esther is the perfect example. The Midrash says she was married to Mordechai before Achashverosh, and even the plain reading is a problem because Achashverosh was not Jewish; it is hard to imagine greater extenuating circumstances than the days of the Purim miracle. She was in a certain way forced into the marriage, and her actions saved the entire people.

Peretz is one of the twin sons of Yehudah and Tamar. He burst out of the womb first and so took the firstborn's right, which had looked like going to his brother Zerach. Tamar's whole story has the theme Esther's has, and Yael's later in the Song of Devorah: that under extenuating circumstances acts which would otherwise deserve severe punishment are counted righteous. Peretz is from Lifrotz, to breach a fence or boundary, which can go either way — hence two sayings in our tradition: "Poretz Geder Yishchenu Nachash," one who breaks boundaries is bitten by a snake, and "Simchah Poretzet Geder," happiness breaks boundaries. Mashiach is also known as HaPoretz. That is the happiness of Purim and of the redemption, which turns darkness into light.

The journey is from Tahath to Tarah. Tarah is spelled like Terach, Avraham's father, and Terach comes from smell — and the Purim story has much to do with smell, which is very spiritual, and was the one element not used at Achashverosh's party. Rabbi Jacobson explains that Terach also means wild goat and old fool, which is the behaviour of Purim, brought onto the path of holiness. The personal journey moves from making a dwelling place below out of spiritual lowliness, to lifting our surroundings through holy foolish behaviour.

165.title: "When Wine Comes in Secrets Come Out"
body: Channah's twenty-fourth verse brings the child: "And she brought him with her when she had weaned him, with three bulls, and one ephah of meal, and an earthenware jug of wine, and she brought him to the house of the Lord, to Shiloh, and the child was young." The first word of what she brings is Parim, bulls, spelled the same as Purim. And there is a jug of wine in it.

The Pirkei Avot quality is that the Torah's secrets are revealed to him. The Talmud famously says "Nichnas Yayin Yotzeh Sod," when wine enters, secrets come out, which usually means something bad. On Purim it is good: when one drinks, the secrets of Torah are revealed.

Proverbs 24 is mostly about fighting evil, and it reads like the pair of phrases a person is meant to stop telling apart. "Do not envy men of evil; do not desire to be with them; for their heart thinks of plunder, and their lips speak of wrongdoing." "Wicked man, do not lurk by the dwelling of a righteous man; do not plunder his resting place. For a righteous man can fall seven times and rise, but the wicked shall stumble upon evil." "When your enemy falls, do not rejoice, and when he stumbles, let your heart not exult." And: "He who says to a wicked man, 'You are righteous'-peoples will curse him; nations will be wroth with him."

Its ending is another practice that is bad all year and good on this one day — sleeping in the daytime. "And I, myself, saw; I applied my heart; I saw and learned a lesson. Little sleep, little slumber, little clasping of the hands to lie down. Then your poverty will come strolling and your wants like an armed man." Which is Pirkei Avot for this week almost word for word: morning sleep, noontime wine, children's talk and sitting at the meeting places of the ignorant, drive a person from the world.
As before, in a year with two months of Adar the yahrzeits are usually kept in the second, so the descriptions wait for next month, when weeks 22 through 25 come round again.

166.title: the Intoxicating Power of Food and Drink
body: The Song is asked what is so special about him, and answers. "What is your beloved more than another beloved, O fairest of women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have so adjured us?" Then: "My beloved is white and ruddy, surrounded by myriads. His head is as the finest gold; his locks are curled, [they are as] black as a raven." The fairest of women is likely Queen Esther, chosen above all the women of the Persian Empire, and white and ruddy looks like the wine of Purim.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the twenty-fourth is Issachar, conceived on the night Rachel exchanged for the dudayim of Leah. The intoxicating nature of the dudayim runs parallel to the intensity of Purim, which also arrives through physical intoxication.

Daf Kaf Dalet of Shvuot keeps on with forbidden foods, and how one act of eating can break more than one law. One of the great points of contention in the Purim story was that the Jews ate at Achashverosh's festive meal.

Jeremiah's twenty-fourth chapter has duda'ey te'enim, translated pots of figs, literally dudayim of figs. "The Lord showed me two pots of figs, prepared before the Temple of the Lord after Nebuchadrezzar, king of Babylon, had exiled Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim king of Judah and the princes of Judah and the craftsmen and the sentries of the gates from Jerusalem and brought them to Babylon. One pot [contained] very good figs like the first ripe figs, and the other pot [contained] very bad figs that could not be eaten because they were so bad." Some could be eaten, some not at all — the very good and the very bad, which is Adar. The vision is about those who went willingly into exile in Babylon and those who stubbornly stayed in the Land of Israel. And its end sounds like Haazinu's verse for this week: "And I will send forth the sword, the famine, and the pestilence against them until they are consumed from upon the land that I gave them and their forefathers."

167.title: Reviewing the Third Week of Adar - Psalms 70-72; 77:10-12; 89:25
body: The third week of Adar in psalms: the seventieth, seventy-first and seventy-second, with three verses of Psalm 77 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 70 is short and urgent, a prayer that his enemies be shamed for shaming him and reveling in his troubles, and that the righteous then rejoice. "O G-d, [come] to rescue me; O Lord, hurry to my aid." "Let those who say, 'Aha! Aha!' be turned back in return for their shaming [me]." And the last line, which does not stop asking: "But I am poor and needy; hurry to me, O G-d! You are my help and deliverer; O G-d, do not delay!"

Psalm 71 is an old man's prayer, with his enemies declaring him deserving of death. It starts from the beginning of his life: "For You are my hope, O my Lord, G-d, my security since my youth. I have relied on You from the womb; You drew me from my mother's innards; my praise is of You always." Then the fear of the end: "Do not cast me aside in old age; do not forsake me when my strength fails; for my enemies say of me, and those who watch my soul conspire together, saying, 'G-d has forsaken him. Give chase and catch him, for there is no rescuer.'" He asks for time to finish the telling: "Even into old age and hoariness, O G-d, do not abandon me, until I tell of Your might to the generations, and of Your strength to all who are to come." And the reviving: "You, Who has shown me many and grievous troubles, You will revive me again; You will lift me again from the depths of the earth."

Psalm 72 David composed for Solomon, praying that he be granted the wisdom to provide justice for the poor. "O G-d, impart Your justice to the king, and Your righteousness to the son of the king. May he judge Your people with righteousness, Your poor with justice." The rain: "May [his words] descend like rain upon cut grass, like raindrops that water the earth." The reach: "And may he rule from sea to sea, and from the river until the ends of the earth." And what the kingship is for: "for he rescues the needy one who cries out, the poor one who has no one to help him. He pities the impoverished and needy, and saves the souls of the destitute. He redeems their soul from deception and violence, and their blood is precious in his eyes." It ends the second book of psalms: "Blessed is His glorious Name forever, and may the whole earth be filled with His glory, Amen and Amen. The prayers of David, son of Jesse, are concluded."

Psalm 77's verses keep asking through the night and then turn: "Has G-d forgotten mercy? Has He in anger restrained His compassion forever? I said, 'It is to terrify me that the right hand of the Most High changes.' I remember the deeds of Yah, when I remember Your wonders of long ago." And Psalm 89's verse answers: "Indeed, My faithfulness and My kindness shall be with him, and through My Name his glory shall be exalted."

168.title: The Fish Are Saying
body: The fish open on the voice above the water, and the week comes in around them.

The sea and the leaving of it first, with the terror in the middle: "The voice of G-d is upon the waters" / "Asher dwelt at the shore of the seas" / "Moses led Israel away from the Red Sea" / "And they went out into the desert of Shur" / "I said, 'It is to terrify me that the right hand of the Most High changes'" / "Has G-d forgotten mercy? Has He in anger restrained His compassion forever?" / "Indeed, My faithfulness and My kindness shall be with him" / "And I was single-hearted toward Him and I kept myself from my iniquity."

Then the bitter water, with the famine braided through it: "They came to Marah, but they could not drink water from Marah" / "Because it was bitter" / "Therefore, it was named Marah" / "They will sprout hair from famine" / "Attacked by demons, excised by Meriri" / "They walked for three days in the desert but did not find water" / "I will incite the teeth of livestock upon them" / "The G-d of glory thunders; G-d is upon many waters."
Then the glory and the remembering: "And through my name his glory shall be exalted" / "I remember the deeds of Yah" / "When I remember your wonders of long ago."

Then what was carried to Shiloh, and the venom beside it: "With three bulls, and one ephah of meal, and an earthenware jug of wine" / "With the venom of creatures that slither in the dust" / "My beloved is white and ruddy, surrounded by myriads" / "His head is as the finest gold" / "His locks are curled, black as a raven."

And the end is the child and the question: "And she brought him to the house of the Lord, to Shiloh" / "And the child was young" / "What is your beloved more than another beloved, O fairest of women?" / "What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have so adjured us?" / "And she brought him with her when she had weaned him" / "And by his breaches he abides."

169.title: To Have Self-Sacrifice in order to Fulfill Our Mission in Life
body: The frog is saying, "Blessed is the Name of the honor of His Kingdom for all eternity." (Talmud, Pesachim 56a) Its song is said every day, at least twice a day, because it is part of the Shemah — Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto L'Olam Va'ed — in which we accept His kingship and His commandments with great self-sacrifice.

This week is the yahrzeit of Rebbe Elimelech of Lizhensk, who exemplified exactly that. One of his main meditative techniques was to imagine throwing himself into a great pillar of fire to sanctify G-d's name, so that everything else he did that day would be done at the same level.

The frog appears in the introduction to Perek Shirah in a story of self-sacrifice. The second plague was frogs, and they jumped into the ovens of the Egyptians, giving up their lives without hesitation. That later inspired Chananya, Misha'el and Azariah, who refused to bow to an idol knowing they would be thrown into a burning furnace, and came out of it unscathed. The plague answered what the taskmasters had done: they worked the people so hard in the open sun that there was no time to eat or drink and they were left dehydrated. Frogs are water creatures whose bodies absorb moisture, and the Midrash teaches that during the plague a vast number of frogs sought out and absorbed all the moisture in Egypt, so the Egyptians felt dehydrated too. Water is a metaphor for Torah, and a sheliach's work is to find the Torah and the holy sparks of the Diaspora and absorb and elevate them, searching even in the driest places. We are all emissaries.

Perek Shirah explains that the frog, as an amphibian, does what no other animal does: it voluntarily serves as food for a land animal that feeds only on water animals. With water as Torah, the frog gives up its life to bring Torah to the animals on dry land. It tells King David that because of this, Hashem will make it whole, will complement it — each Jew completing the other, like the half-shekel of this month. And in Perek Shirah itself the frog joins land and sea again: it comes after the fish and before the sheep and goat, the link between the water animals of Adar and the land animals of Nissan.

The week of the frog always falls after Purim and close to the reading of Parah, which is about purifying a person from the greatest source of impurity, contact with the dead. The kohen who performs that purification sacrifices himself by becoming impure in the process, temporarily. Queen Esther does the same, making herself impure by marrying Achashverosh in order to save the whole people. Purim and Parah have very similar roots.

That double role — superficially negative, in fact extremely positive — is in Baruch Shem Kevod itself. The Talmud in Pessachim suggests the verse is somehow embarrassing to say out loud, which is why we say it quietly, and some authorities hold it to be a lower form of declaring His unity. But many famous commentaries teach the opposite: that it is far higher, said by the angels themselves, and we say it quietly only because it is too lofty for this world. The one day we say it openly is Yom Kippur, when we are all at the level of angels — and angels are emissaries.

There is a famous Midrash that the plague began as a single giant frog, and that when the Egyptians struck it, it multiplied into many smaller frogs, who split again, like the giant frog's emissaries. Rebbe Elimelech is known as a Rebbe of Rebbes, because the most prominent Polish Rebbes were his disciples or their disciples, all of them like emissaries continuing his legacy: the Chozeh of Lublin, who would thank G-d an hour a day for bringing down the soul of his Rebbe, the Ohev Yisrael, the Rimanover, the Maggid of Kozhnitz, and others. Rebbe Tzvi Elimelech of Dinov, the Bnei Issachar, was his nephew.

The frog also tells King David, "Every song I say contains three thousand parables." A parable brings an idea down so that others can reach it, so the frog has three thousand emissaries attached to its song. At his passing the Lubavitcher Rebbe had roughly three thousand emissaries, and there are roughly three thousand Chabad centres today. The number appears after the golden calf as well: Moses stood in the gate and said, "Whoever is for the Lord, [let him come] to me!", and all the sons of Levi gathered to him, and that day some three thousand men fell. The Levites acted with extreme self-sacrifice and did not consider brother or friend — right at the time, and perhaps still in need of a tikkun. The Chabad shluchim treat everyone as a brother and friend, and they too fall from a pure and holy way of living in order to reach people who need guidance. Three thousand halachot were also forgotten during the mourning for Moses, and perhaps the three thousand shluchim who study the Rebbe's words are a tikkun for that.

Roughly three thousand appears in Samson's story too. The house was full, all the lords of the Philistines were there, and on the roof about three thousand men and women watched his sport; and Samson said, "Let my soul die with the Philistines," and bent with his might, and the house fell, and the dead he killed at his death were more than he had killed in his lifetime. Like the kohen of the red heifer and like Esther, he was willing to sacrifice himself, spiritually and physically, to bring redemption. There is even a hint of Purim in it: the Hebrew for on the roof is "Al haGag," which in Aramaic would be "Agag" — and Haman descended from Agag, king of the Amalekites. At the end of the Purim story, besides Haman and his sons, 75,000 Amalekites are killed, which is twenty-five times three thousand.

Twenty-five belongs to Chanukah, which fell on the twenty-fifth of Kislev, and the word Chanukah itself means Chanu, they rested, and Kah, twenty-five. The twenty-fifth letter in the Torah is or, light. The Chashmonaim held the double role of kohanim and kings. And Rebbe Elimelech, whose name means G-d is my King, had a strong complementary bond with his saintly brother, the Tzadik Reb Zusya of Anipoli.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Elazar of Modi'in: one who profanes the kodashim, degrades the Festivals, humiliates his friend in public, abrogates the covenant of our father Abraham, or interprets the Torah contrary to its true intent, has no share in the World to Come, even with Torah knowledge and good deeds. Just after Purim we begin preparing for Passover — the Shulchan Aruch says to begin thirty days before — and the days of giving Maot Chitim, money so the poor can celebrate it properly. The five faults line up with those preparations. Profaning the holy is the Passover sacrifice, whose meat was sacred and had to be treated properly. Degrading the festivals is Passover itself, in its physical preparations, destroying the chametz, and its spiritual ones, clearing out egotism and inflated self-importance. Humiliating a neighbour publicly is why the charity goes out in advance, so that nobody has to beg in order to celebrate. The covenant of Abraham is circumcision: it was on Passover that the angels visited him and Sarah and he gave them matzot; all the men were circumcised just before the first Passover in Egypt, and Joshua had all the men circumcised again before entering Israel after the years in the desert, during which none were; and in the days of the Temple the uncircumcised could not eat the Passover sacrifice. Interpreting the Torah against its true meaning is the rulings people reach while cleaning: it is easy to ask whether Torah law does not simply require nullifying the chametz verbally, when the point is to hold to the letter and the spirit both, each at his own level.

The same list fits the time of Chanukah. The Greeks defiled the sacred objects of the Temple and opposed the sacred dates, Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh. The Hellenistic Jews had no shame and fought naked in gymnasiums, and many reversed their circumcision. Hellenistic Jews, Saducees and other cults sought to corrupt the true interpretations, and the Greeks tried to misrepresent the Torah's sacred nature and forced it to be translated into Greek.

The combination is netzach shebenetzach, victory within victory. This week is the midpoint, joining the victory of Adar to the victory of Nissan, and twenty-five is exactly midway through the Counting of the Omer. The lesson from the frog is to serve with great self-sacrifice, remembering how brief our stay here is.

170.title: Micah the Morashite and "Faith in the Sages"
body: The last week of Adar. Haazinu spares nobody: "From outside, the sword will bereave, and terror from within; young men and maidens, suckling babes with venerable elders." (Deuteronomy 32:25) That was Haman's decree exactly. Read positively, the verse turns the decree on its head and describes the destruction of Amalek, whom the people are commanded to wipe out entirely, women and elderly and babies included. Killing Agag, king of the Amalekites, Samuel says: "As thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women."

The Haftorah stays positive, and uses the word Leneged again, as in week 23: "And the Lord has recompensed me according to my righteousness; according to my cleanness before His eyes." (II Samuel 22:25) Leneged Einav, before His eyes, can also mean for the one against His eyes — because Amalek is not only against the Jewish people but against G-d Himself, a thorn in His eyes. Amalek is closely tied to keri, a source of impurity, so cleanness here may also mean fulfilling the command to destroy Amalek without question, correcting King Saul's mistake.

The quality is faith in the sages, emunat chachamim, and it is central to Purim, when the people trusted the actions of Mordechai and Esther. At first glance Mordechai could even be blamed for starting the persecution by not bowing to Haman. They did not blame him; they stood behind him and followed his directives. Haman saw them as an Am Mordechai, a nation of Mordechais.

The prophet is Micah the Morashite, and much of his prophecy is aimed at the heads of the people, its sages. "Hearken now, you heads of Jacob and officers of the house of Israel! Is it not incumbent upon you to know the judgment? Those who hate good and love evil-who rob their skin from upon them and their flesh from upon their bones." Then the prophets who mislead, "who bite with their teeth and herald peace, but concerning whomever does not give into their mouth, they prepare war." Then the darkness: "it shall be night for you because of the vision, and it shall be dark for you because of the divination, and the sun shall set on the prophets." And then himself: "But I am truly full of strength from the spirit of the Lord and justice and might, to tell Jacob his transgression and Israel his sin." The charge is bought justice: "Its heads judge for bribes, and its priests teach for a price; and its prophets divine for money, and they rely on the Lord, saying, 'Is not the Lord in our midst? No evil shall befall us.'" And the sentence: "Zion shall be plowed as a field; Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the Temple Mount like the high places of a forest." The hiddenness of Hashem runs through all of it, which is this month.

The link to emunat chachamim is plainer still in Jeremiah, where the elders of the land stand up and argue from Micah's case: Micah the Morashtite was prophesying in the days of Hezekiah the king of Judah and said that Zion shall be plowed for a field — did Hezekiah and all Judah put him to death? Did he not fear the Lord? And he entreated the Lord, and the Lord renounced the evil He had spoken. "But we are doing great harm to ourselves."

The levitical city is Jerusalem, because the Temple was also a city of refuge. For now half of it rests in Judah and half in Benjamin; in the future Jerusalem will have its own territory, separate from every tribe. This is the last week of the year for contributing the half-shekel toward the upkeep of the Temple there. And in the Megillah, when Achashverosh offers Esther up to half his kingdom, the sages learn that he meant up to Jerusalem.
170.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 25.

171.title: Hezron and Sweetening Bitter Judgments
body: The bitter water gets sweetened: "The people complained against Moses, saying, What shall we drink? So he cried out to the Lord, and the Lord instructed him concerning a piece of wood, which he cast into the water, and the water became sweet. There He gave them a statute and an ordinance, and there He tested them." Rebbe Elimelech of Lizhensk, whose yahrzeit is this week, teaches that this is the main service of the tzadik: to sweeten and cancel the bitter decrees against the Jewish people.

The Haftarah finishes its round of the tribes with the two who went: "Zebulun is a people that jeopardized their lives to die, as did Naphtali, upon the high places of the field." These two hold the whole spirit a sheliach needs; they are literally willing to give up their lives for the cause. Naphtali is the month of Adar, and Zebulun, in its partnership with Issachar, carries the month's other theme, duality.

Daf Kaf Heh of Sotah takes up what to do where a woman starts behaving immodestly in general, and whether a husband can cancel a warning — he can. Which is the same thing again: the tzadik's avodah, using self-sacrifice to cancel decrees against the people even when they are not behaving as they should.

The generation is Hezron, son of Perez, father of Caleb. Hezron comes from chatzer, courtyard or enclosure, a term discussed in halachah, especially in Eruvim, where two neighbours share one courtyard and have to set up an eruv chatzeirot in order to carry in it. Then both own the area together and it is no longer a separate domain for either. Eruv shares a root with Arev, sweet: when Jews come together and the duality works for the good, there is sweetness. Chatzer is also the courtyard of the Temple.

The journey is from Tarah to Mithkah, and Mithkah comes from matok, which also means sweet. The personal journey moves on from lifting our surroundings through holy foolish behaviour, to sweetening whatever bitterness we meet, our own or our people's.

172.title: "An Ever-Increasing Wellspring"
body: Channah's twenty-fifth verse is one line: "And when the bullock was slain, the child was brought to Eli." The last week of Adar is tied to bringing contributions to the Temple — by now the courts had the right to take the yearly half-shekel by force from anyone who had not brought it.

The Talmud teaches that this verse shows Shmuel's hidden greatness. Eli said, call a priest and let him come and kill the animal. Seeing them look for a priest, Samuel asked why: the shechitah may be performed by a layman. They brought him to Eli, who asked how he knew. He answered: Is it written, "The priest shall kill"? It is written, "The priests shall present the blood" — the office of the priest begins with receiving the blood, which shows that the slaughtering may be done by a layman. Eli said to him: you have spoken very well, but all the same you are guilty of giving a decision in the presence of your teacher.

Adar reveals what is secret. That is why the text we read on Purim is Megillat Esther, revealing, Legalot, what is hidden, Nistar — and here what is revealed is the hidden greatness of a little boy. Last week's quality was that the Torah's secrets are revealed to him; this week's is that he becomes as an ever-increasing wellspring. A wellspring is the same idea: it brings water, which is Torah, from the depths of the earth up to the surface. Ma'ayan is often associated with the hidden parts of Torah, like the teachings of the Baal Shem Tov. And Shmuel in that story is a living example of one.

Proverbs 25 opens on exactly this. "These too are Solomon's proverbs, which the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah, maintained. The honor of God is to conceal a matter, whereas the honor of kings is to search out a matter. The heaven for height, the earth for depth, and the honor of kings are unsearchable. Remove dross from silver, and a vessel emerges for the refiner."

The week holds the yahrzeits of Rebbe Elimelech of Lizhensk on the 21st of Adar and Rabbi Yitzchak Meir Alter, the Chiddushei HaRim, on the 23rd. Rebbe Elimelech was one of the main disciples of the Maggid of Mezritch and the Rebbe of Rebbes of the Jews of Poland and Galitzia, brother of Reb Zushia of Anipoli; many of his disciples became rebbes themselves, among them the Chozeh of Lublin, the Ohev Yisrael, Reb Menachem Mendel of Rimanov and the Maggid of Kozhnitz. He wrote the Noam Elimelech, one of the foundational texts of Polish Chassidism. Rabbi Yitzchak Meir Alter founded Ger, which became the largest of all Chassidic groups, in great part through his inspiring and caring leadership, and his Chiddushei HaRim is a Chassidic classic. Also this week: Rav Chanoch Henach of Alexander, who served as rebbe of Ger for some time after the Chidushei HaRim passed away, and Rabbi Nachum Mordechai of Chortkov, son of Rabbi Yisrael Friedman, both on the 18th of Adar, and Rabbi Meir Yechiel of Ostrovtze on the 19th.
