173.title: Learning Torah and Listening to the Leader of the Generation
body: The Song goes on describing him, and all of it is spice and precious material. "His eyes are like doves beside rivulets of water, bathing in milk, fitly set." "His jaws are like a bed of spice, growths of aromatic plants; his lips are [like] roses, dripping with flowing myrrh." "His hands are [like] wheels of gold, set with chrysolite; his abdomen is [as] a block of ivory, overlaid with sapphires." The myrrh the Talmud reads as Mordechai. Rashi explains that these verses are mainly about the study halls, and how there the mysteries of the Torah are clarified and uncovered. Our sages explain that it was the work of Mordechai and the Jews of that time to strengthen the public study of Torah which brought the redemption — and the month is Megillat Esther, uncovering, Legalot, the hidden, Nistar.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the twenty-fifth is Tola, later the name of one of the Judges, from the tribe of Issachar. Tola's sons are listed in Chronicles, and Rashi has a fascinating comment there: in the Pentateuch it is written "and Job," because Job was his name originally; but since they settled themselves to learn Torah, as it says of the sons of Issachar that they possessed understanding of the times, he merited to be called Jashub. Which belongs with Mordechai, the leader and judge in the time of Purim, and with that public study.

Daf Kaf Heh of Shvuot keeps on with the laws of oaths, and whether they can apply to the past as well as the future. Week 25 is the midway point of the Counting of the Omer of the weeks of the whole year.

Jeremiah's twenty-fifth chapter is about listening to the leader of the generation — here the king — and to the prophets and the words of Hashem, and much of it is drinking. "From the thirteenth year of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah, until this day, these twenty-three years the word of the Lord has come to me, and I spoke to you, arising early and speaking, but you did not hearken. And the Lord sent to you all His servants, the prophets, sending them early, but you did not hearken and you did not incline your ear[s] to listen." Then the cup: "Take this cup of the wine of fury from My hand, and you shall give it to all the nations to whom I send you, to drink. And they shall drink and reel to and fro and be like madmen because of the sword that I am sending among them." And it will not be refused: "Drink, become drunk, and vomit, fall and you shall not rise." "And it shall be, if they refuse to take the cup from your hand to drink, that you shall say to them: So said the Lord of Hosts: You shall surely drink."

174.title: Reviewing the Fourth Week of Adar - Psalms 73-75; 77:13-15; 89:26
body: The fourth week of Adar in psalms: the seventy-third, seventy-fourth and seventy-fifth, with three verses of Psalm 77 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 73 asks why the righteous suffer while the wicked prosper, and prays for an end to the long exile; read it, and you will find repose for your soul. It admits how close it came: "But as for me, my feet nearly strayed; in an instant my steps would have been swept aside. For I envied the revelers when I saw the tranquility of the wicked." Their ease: "They have no part in the toil of men, nor are they afflicted like other mortals; therefore they wear pride as a necklace." Their mouths: "They set their mouths against Heaven, while their tongues walk upon the earth." And the bitter thought: "Surely in vain have I purified my heart, and washed my hands in cleanliness; for I was afflicted all day, and my rebuke came each morning." He would not say it aloud: "Were I to say, 'I shall tell it like it is,' behold I would turn the generation of Your children to rebels." It only resolved in one place: "until I came to the sanctuaries of G-d, and perceived their end." Then the whole thing turns: "I was a boor and did not understand, like an animal was I with You. Yet I was always with You; You held my right hand." And the end of it: "Whom do I have in heaven [besides You]? And when I am with You I desire nothing on earth. My flesh and my heart yearn; G-d is the rock of my heart and my portion forever."

Psalm 74 mourns the synagogues and study halls that were burned — the Philistines destroyed the Tabernacle of Shiloh, Nebuchadnezzar the first Temple — and asks how long the exile can run. "Why, O G-d, have You abandoned us forever, does Your wrath fume against the sheep of Your pasture?" The burning: "They set Your Sanctuary on fire; they desecrated the Abode of Your Name to the ground. Their rulers thought together in their hearts; they burned all the meeting places of G-d in the land." And the worst of it, that nobody can say when it ends: "We have not seen our signs; there is no longer a prophet, and there is none among us who knows how long." Then it argues from His own power: "In Your might, You divided the sea; You shattered the heads of the sea-monsters on the waters. You crushed the heads of the Leviathan." "Yours is the day, the night is also Yours; You established the moon and the sun. You set all the boundaries of the earth; summer and winter-You created them." And the asking: "Do not give the soul of Your turtledove to the wild beast; do not forget the life of Your poor forever."

Psalm 75 says how great Israel is: on their holidays they do not take to frivolity but to song and praise and the study of the holiday's laws, and when they said at the giving of the Torah, "We will do and we will hear!", they let the world go on existing. It also warns those who indulge in worldly pleasures and credit their prosperity to themselves. "When I choose the appointed time, I will judge with fairness. When the earth and all its inhabitants were melting, I established its pillars forever." Then the warning: "Do not raise your pride heavenward, nor speak with an arrogant neck. For not from the east or the west, nor from the desert does greatness come. For G-d is Judge; He humbles one, and elevates the other." And a cup again: "For there is a cup [of punishment] in the hand of the Lord, with strong wine of full mixture; He pours from this, and all the wicked of the earth will drink, draining even its dregs."

Psalm 77's verses turn at last from asking to telling: "I meditate on all Your works, and speak of Your deeds. O G-d, Your way is in sanctity; what god is as great as G-d? You are the G-d Who works wonders; You make Your might known among the nations." And Psalm 89's verse sets the hand on the water: "I will set his hand upon the sea, his right hand upon the rivers."

175.title: The Frog Is Saying
body: The frog opens, and the two tribes who risked their lives open with it.

The jeopardy and the blessing first: "Zebulun is a people that jeopardized their lives to die" / "As did Naphtali, upon the high places of the field" / "Blessed is the Name of the honor of His Kingdom for all eternity."

Then the thirst, and the hand set on the water: "The people complained against Moses, saying, What shall we drink?" / "I will set his hand upon the sea, his right hand upon the rivers" / "His eyes are like doves beside rivulets of water, bathing in milk, fitly set."

Then the statute and the piece of wood: "There He gave them a statute and an ordinance, and there He tested them" / "So he cried out to the Lord, and the Lord instructed him" / "Concerning a piece of wood, which he cast into the water, and the water became sweet" / "I meditate on all Your works, and speak of Your deeds."

Then the spices and the gold, with the wonders between them: "His jaws are like a bed of spice, growths of aromatic plants" / "His lips are [like] roses, dripping with flowing myrrh" / "You are the G-d Who works wonders; You make Your might known among the nations" / "His hands are [like] wheels of gold, set with chrysolite" / "His abdomen is [as] a block of ivory, overlaid with sapphires."

And the end is the recompense and the sword, with the child carried in: "And the Lord has recompensed me according to my righteousness" / "According to my cleanness before His eyes" / "O G-d, Your way is in sanctity; what god is as great as G-d?" / "From outside, the sword will bereave, and terror from within" / "And when the bullock was slain, the child was brought to Eli" / "Young men and maidens, suckling babes with venerable elders."

176.title: To Be Humble and Let G-d Guide Us
body: The sheep and goat are saying: "Who is like You among the might ones, G-d, who is like You, mighty in holiness, awesome in praise, worker of wonders." (Exodus 15:11) The small pure domestic animal is the sheep — Nissan's sign is Aries — and the goat as well. Rosh Chodesh Nissan is the inauguration of the Mishkan, where sacrifices of pure kosher animals like these were brought, and Nissan is the month of redemption and miracles.

Shepherd and flock is one of the great metaphors for G-d and the Jewish people. He is far above our understanding, as a shepherd is entirely beyond the understanding of his flock; and like sheep we have complete humility and faith that our Shepherd leads us the right way, even with foxes and lions along it.

The goat stands for the Jewish people in Chad Gadya, sung on Passover night. The name means One Goat, and it sounds close to Haggadah, the text read at the Seder. Chad Gadya is like Perek Shirah in being full of animals and natural elements, but there the animals are the exiles and the nations that conquered the Land of Israel: the cat that eats the goat is the Assyrians, the dog that eats the cat is Babylon, the stick is Persia, the fire is Macedonia, the water is Rome, the ox is the Saracens, the slaughterer is the crusaders, and the Angel of Death is the Turks. At the end G-d saves us from all of them and brings us back to our Land.

The two zuzim the goat was bought for are said to be the two tablets of the Ten Commandments given at Mount Sinai, and also look like the two Temples that were destroyed and their people exiled. Zuz means to move, to change places; the Third Temple will not move. Each animal that sings during Nissan carries an exile and a redemption from it. Sheep were gods to the Egyptians, our first exile, and the goat, Seir, points to Esau, our last. We were redeemed from Egypt in this month, and in this month we will be redeemed again.

The Torah says plainly that Nissan is the head of all months, Rosh Chodashim, so it belongs to Judah, the leader of his brothers, from whom King David comes. Every legitimate king, Mashiach included, descends from David and so from Judah. Yehudah comes from hoda'ah, acknowledgement, the root of Modeh, as in the Modeh Ani we say on waking, acknowledging Him as King and thanking Him for returning the soul. The tribe is marked by self-sacrifice, acknowledgement and thankfulness.

Because the Egyptians idolized sheep, it is fitting that the sheep is the one to proclaim His absolute greatness. The sheep is the animal of the Passover sacrifice, which showed the Egyptians that G-d is far greater than any other god. On Shabat HaGadol, just before Passover, we mark the miracle that the Egyptians did not turn on the Jewish people when they tied sheep to their bedposts and told them they were about to sacrifice their gods. And since Nissan is the month of Passover, it is right that the song comes from the Song of the Sea, sung after the splitting of the Sea of Reeds.
Twenty-six is the gematria of Hashem. It is also twice thirteen, which is the gematria of echad, one, and of ahavah, love.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Yishmael: be yielding to a leader, affable to the black-haired, and receive every man with joy. Among the kohanim Rabbi Yishmael was the head, the Kohen Gadol, and besides his closeness to Hashem he had, as Aaron had before him, a great love for every member of the people whatever their status. And the verse fits Nissan, the head of the months.

The combination is hod shebenetzach. With humility and gratitude, self-sacrifice and acknowledgement, we reach the miraculous victory of this month. The sheep and the goat teach that all our work on ourselves rests on the belief that only Hashem can truly redeem us.

177.title: Amotz and Destroying our Arrogance
body: Rosh Chodesh Nissan, the month of Judah, the leader of the brothers, from whom King David and all his royal descendants come. Haazinu's verse is the last that speaks directly of destruction, and this time it is total: "I said that I would make an end of them, eradicate their remembrance from mankind." (Deuteronomy 32:26) Which confirms that the grim verses before it were about Amalek, since it is Amalek that will be utterly destroyed, not the Jewish people. Adar carries that destruction most, but Nissan has it too: Passover is marked by burning all the chametz. Spiritually chametz is the ego, and Amalek's impurity is bound up with an inflated ego. As Rabbi Shalom Arush explains, the kelipah of Amalek is haughtiness and a lack of gratitude. Haman had so much and said all of it was meaningless because one man, Mordechai, would not bow to him.

The Haftorah stays kind: "With a kind one, You show Yourself kind. With an upright mighty man, You show Yourself upright." (II Samuel 22:26) Rid of ego and personal wants, acting with temimut, purity, and keeping our attention on what He wants, we are answered in the same vein. The verse also carries hoda'ah, acknowledgement, which is the root of Judah's name — Judah courageously recognised Tamar's righteousness. Hoda'ah is also thanks: when we are grateful, He gives us more to be grateful for. And we should be grateful for everything, even what looks bad to us, because everything He does is for the good.
So the quality is acceptance of suffering, kabalat hayissurim, which is the ultimate sign of gratefulness and humility.

The prophet is Amotz, father of Isaiah. The Talmud teaches that Amotz was the brother of Amatziah, son of King Joash. He watched his brother fall. Amatziah began his reign well, obeying the prophet and winning militarily; then, having taken spoils from Edom, he began to worship their idols. G-d sent Amotz to question him, and Amatziah dismissed the prophet with tremendous arrogance — an arrogance the King of Israel, Joash, also pointed out before defeating him in battle. His downfall came of keeping the spoils of Edom and not cleansing them of idolatry, which is the burning of chametz exactly. Amotz did not press him: "So the prophet desisted, but he said, 'I know that G-d has made a plan to destroy you, for you have done this thing, and you have not heeded my counsel.'" He accepted that the suffering coming was G-d's will, and came of his brother's arrogance.

The levitical city is Hebron, also called Kiryat Arbah, and also a city of refuge. Kiryat Arbah means City of Four — the four couples buried there, Adam and Eve, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebeccah, Jacob and Leah, and also the four giants who lived there. Four is a theme of Passover too: four glasses of wine, four kinds of sons in the Hagaddah.

The four giants look like the four main exiles. Sheshai is Babylonia: the Jastrow dictionary calls Sheshai a surname for Babylonia, and it spells Bavel in the transposition known as Atbash; the Midrash says he was named for being made of marble, Shaish, which suits Nebuchadnezzar and the statues made in his honour. Achiman is Persia, his name a contraction of Achashverosh and Haman. Talmai is Greece, whose leader in that exile was Talmai, Ptolomy in English. The fourth is named only as the father of the other three, which is Edom, the father of the exiles, the longest and harshest by far.

Giants stand for arrogance, and the forefathers buried in Hebron for humility. Abraham said to G-d, "I am but dust and ashes" — and when we nullify the chametz we declare it like the dust of the earth.

The four giants also line up with the four couples. Sheshai and Bavel recall the Tower of Babel, whose generation and whose leader Nimrod Avraham confronted directly; Avraham is also known for destroying his father's statues. Achiman and Persia, and the Purim story, are marked by extreme self-sacrifice, which is Isaac and the Akeidah; and the Torah notes how Isaac and Rebecca prayed together for a child, and how much of what followed was settled by Rebecca's actions, like the blessing of Jacob over Eisau. Talmai and Greece were an affront to the Torah, its Divine origin and its way of life, and Torah is above all Jacob's: Jacob, Ish Tam, a wholesome and straightforward man, stands against the godless sophistication of the Greeks. The father of the giants is Rome, and it involves all of humanity — Pax Romana reached the whole world, and in many ways we are still under it. Edom is Eisav, who was red, like Mars and his military prowess. Adam and Eve are all of humanity, and Adam is also an acronym of three: Adam himself, David, and Mashiach. David was red too, a kosher version of Eisav and of the potential Eisav missed so badly. Mashiach son of David will redeem the whole world, fix the curse of the snake, and bring it back to the fullness it had in the Garden of Eden.
177.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 26.

178.title: Connecting to the "Head"
body: Rosh Chodesh Nissan is the head of the month that is the head of all the months. Nissan is king of the months as Judah, its tribe, was leader of all the tribes.

Beshalach gives the condition and the healing: "If you hearken to the voice of the Lord, your G-d, and you do what is proper in His eyes, and you listen closely to His commandments and observe all His statutes, all the sicknesses that I have visited upon Egypt I will not visit upon you, for I, the Lord, heal you." And then the camp: "They came to Elim, and there were twelve water fountains and seventy palms, and they encamped there by the water." The twelve fountains are the tribes and the seventy palms the seventy elders, and perhaps also the seventy general souls that went down to Egypt and the seventy nations. A true leader, the head of the people, has to be connected to all of them. The portion is faith in Hashem and the exodus — do our part, and He does His — and He is named as our Healer.
The Haftorah turns to kings: "The kings came and fought; then fought the kings of Canaan."

Daf Kaf Vav of Sotah returns to women who do not drink but dwells more on those who must, and its cases are not only unusual but often at an unusually low spiritual level: possible social outcasts, the Mamzer, converts. And in the middle of all that, a ray of hope. The verse "She will be vindicated, and bear seed" teaches that if she used to give birth in pain she will give birth easily; if she used to bear daughters she will bear sons; if she used to bear short babies she will bear tall ones; if she bore babies with a dark complexion she will bear babies with a light complexion. Which is the story of Judah and Mashiach. Out of Lot's daughter and her father comes Moab, a Mamzer; out of Judah and Tamar, who faced the death penalty and was vindicated; and later out of the persistent efforts of a convert, Ruth, who was vindicated too — comes King David, and Mashiach.

The generation is Ram, son of Hezron, father of Aminadav, who fathered Nachshon and Elisheva, Aharon's wife. Ram is also Calev's brother, and Calev is Miriam's husband, so he stands close to Moshe and the exodus. His name says it too: Ram means mighty, exalted, and the Jews left Egypt with a Yad Ramah, an exalted arm — and His arm runs all through Beshalach. As a side note, Ram in English is this week's Perek Shirah animal, and Nissan's sign is Aries.

The journey is from Mithkah to Chashmonah. Mithkah comes from matok, sweet. Chashmonah goes with the Chashmonaim and Chanukah: this week is the inauguration of the Mishkan as Chanukah is the inauguration of the Temple, and some note that Chashmonah is the 25th place journeyed to, as Chanukah is the 25th of Kislev and the name itself is Chanu-Kah, they rested on the 25th. Rabbi Simon Jacobson explains that Chashmonah means ambassador, and may also point to leadership; the Chashmonaim became kings. In the first days of Nissan the Nasi of each tribe brought sacrifices for the inauguration. The personal journey moves on from sweetening bitterness to rededicating ourselves, leading, staying connected to our leaders, and starting again in this second half of the year.

179.title: The Big Picture
body: Channah's twenty-sixth verse is a request whose content is not stated: "And she said, 'Please, my lord! As surely as your soul lives, my lord, I am the woman who was standing here with you, to pray to the Lord.'" Rashi fills it in: take care of him, that he become your disciple — and according to the Midrash of our sages, do not punish him with death. Last week Shmuel had shown great insight and in doing so had given a ruling in front of his master, which is punishable by death, and the more grievous because Eli was the Judge and head of the whole people. So she asks Eli both to take the boy on and to forgive him.

The Pirkei Avot quality is that he becomes an unceasing river. Shmuel's insight into one area of law belongs to the ever-increasing wellspring of last week, the ability to find new rulings by concentrating on chosen parts of the text. An unceasing river is the other thing: comprehensive knowledge of the whole Torah. That is what Channah is asking Eli to teach him.

Proverbs 26 is mostly about the actions of fools, and also the lazy, the quarrelsome, the deceptive and the wicked. What runs through it is that an act which might be righteous in itself becomes ridiculous in the wrong context — honouring fools, or fearing some danger purely as an excuse not to get out of bed. A person needs the big picture in order to act rightly.

The week holds the yahrzeits of Rav Yitzchak Abuchatzera, the Baba Chaki, on the 25th of Adar, and Rabbi Shlomo Hakohen Rabinowicz, the Tiferes Shlomo, founding Rebbe of Radomsk, on the 29th. The Baba Chaki was the Baba Sali's brother, and like him was known for great holiness and saintly conduct; like him he moved from Morocco to Israel, and he became chief rabbi of Ramla-Lod. Rabbi Shlomo Hakohen Rabinowicz was called the Tiferes Shelomo after the Chassidic masterpiece he wrote, and founded Radomsk in 1843. When Rabbi Moshe Biderman of Lelov made aliyah in 1850 he told his followers to become Chassidim of the Tiferes Shelomo, and the court grew to thousands upon thousands. Besides his scholarship and his speaking, the Radomsker Rebbe was known for a beautiful voice and for composing new nigunim. Also this week: Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Visiva, son of Rabbi Yisroel Hager of Vizhnitz, on the 25th of Adar, and Rabbi Elimelech of Grodzensk, author of Divrei Elimelech and Imrei Elimelech and father of the Piazeczna Rebbe, on the 1st of Nissan. Rosh Chodesh Nissan is also the birthday of Rebbe Nachman of Breslov.

180.title: The Importance of Speech
body: The Song finishes the description and then loses him again. "His legs are [as] pillars of marble, founded upon sockets of fine gold, his appearance is like the Lebanon, chosen as the cedars." "His palate is sweet, and he is altogether desirable; this is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem." And then the daughters ask: "Where has your beloved gone, O fairest of women? Where has your beloved turned, that we may seek him with you?"

All of it is the mouth, which is the chief symbol of Passover. Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev says that Pesach is Peh Sach, a mouth converses, because it is a special mitzvah at the Seder to recount and turn over the miracles of our liberation as much as possible. The Megaleh Amukos says Pharaoh is Peh Rah, an evil mouth. Rashi reads the verses the same way: his appearance is like the Lebanon means that one who reflects and ponders over His words finds blossoms and sprouts in them, like a forest in bloom — so are the words of Torah, and whoever meditates over them constantly finds new explanations in them. And his palate is sweet means his words are pleasant.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the twenty-sixth is Puvvah, whose name also looks to come from Peh, mouth, and so from Pessach. It is near the name Puah, spelled with an Ayin rather than an Aleph, which belongs to Miriam at the very start of the Exodus story: Puah comes from a root that implies a particular gift of speech, and Rashi comments that she could soothe a crying baby to sleep with her special way of talking. Puvvah is also the name of Tola's father, the Judge from the tribe of Issachar.
The daf of Shvuot this week keeps on with oaths, and above all whether an oath has to be spoken. Peh Sach again.

Jeremiah's twenty-sixth chapter presses the same point from the other end — not the mouth but the ear. "And the priests and the prophets said to the princes and to all the people, saying, 'This man is liable to death, for he prophesied concerning this city, as you have heard with your ears.'" "And Jeremiah said to all the princes and to all the people saying, 'The Lord sent me to prophesy concerning this house and concerning this city all the words that you have heard.'" And the warning: "But you should know that if you put me to death, that you are bringing innocent blood upon yourselves and upon this city and upon its inhabitants, for indeed God sent me concerning you, to speak into your ears all these words."

181.title: Reviewing the Week of Rosh Chodesh Nissan - Psalms 76-78; 77:16-18; 89:27
body: The week of Rosh Chodesh Nissan in psalms: the seventy-sixth, seventy-seventh and seventy-eighth, with three verses of Psalm 77 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 76 holds the prophecy of the vast army of Sennacherib seized by a deep slumber that left the soldiers' hands powerless to raise their weapons, so that they all fell in battle. "G-d is known in Judah, His Name is great in Israel." The sleep: "The stout-hearted were without sense, they slept their sleep, and all the warriors were unable to find their strength. At Your rebuke, O G-d of Jacob, chariot and horse were stunned." Then the stillness: "From heaven You let the verdict be heard; the earth feared and was still, when G-d rose to pass judgment, to save all the humble of the earth forever."

Psalm 77 is here whole, and it is the psalm whose verses have been arriving three at a time for weeks. It begins in the night that will not end — "my wound oozes at night and does not abate; my soul refuses to be consoled" — and asks everything it can: "Is it for eternity that my Lord forsakes [me], nevermore to be appeased? Has His kindness ceased forever? Has G-d forgotten mercy?" Then it turns on remembering: "I remember the deeds of Yah, when I remember Your wonders of long ago." And then the sea answers it: "You redeemed Your people with a mighty arm, the children of Jacob and Joseph, Selah. The waters saw You, O G-d, the waters saw You and trembled; even the deep shuddered." "Your way was through the sea, Your path through the mighty waters; and Your footsteps were not known." And the last line is the whole answer in one image: "You led Your people like a flock, by the hand of Moses and Aaron."

Psalm 78 recounts every miracle from the exodus to David becoming king, and it is built as a thing to hand on: "Listen, my people, to my teaching; incline your ear to the words of my mouth. I will open my mouth with a parable, I will utter riddles of long ago; that which we have heard and know [to be true], and that our fathers have told us. We will not withhold from their children, telling the final generation the praises of the Lord." The point of telling is that the next generation not be like the last: "And they shall not be like their fathers, a wayward and rebellious generation, a generation that did not set its heart straight." Then the sea and the rock: "He split the sea and brought them across; He erected the waters like a wall." "He split rocks in the wilderness, and gave them to drink as if from the abundant depths." Then the asking for meat: "They spoke against G-d; they said, 'Can G-d set a table in the wilderness? True, He hit the rock and waters flowed, streams gushed forth; but can He also give bread?'" And the answer that was already there: "He had rained upon them manna to eat, and given them grain of heaven. Man ate the bread of angels." Then the long account of forgetting and being forgiven: "Yet He is compassionate, pardons iniquity, and does not destroy; time and again He turns away His anger." "He remembered that they were but flesh, a spirit that leaves and does not return." Then the plagues told backwards into memory — the rivers turned to blood, the frogs, the grasshopper and the locust, the hail, the firstborn — and the shepherding out: "He drove His nation like sheep, and guided them like a flock in the desert." Then Shilo abandoned, and the waking: "And the Lord awoke like one who had been asleep, like a warrior shouting [to sober himself] from wine." And the end is the choosing: "He chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion which He loves." "And He chose David His servant, and took him from the sheep corrals. From following the nursing ewes, He brought Him to shepherd His nation Jacob, Israel His inheritance. And he tended them with the integrity of his heart, and led them with the skill of his hands."

The Tikkun HaKlali verses are the sea again — "the waters perceived You, they trembled, even the deeps quaked" — and Psalm 89's verse is the name he will call Him by: "He will call to Me, 'You are my Father, my G-d, and the Rock of my salvation.'"

182.title: The Lamb Is Saying
body: The lamb opens on who is like Him, and the week's books come in around it.

The holiness and the redeeming arm first, with the kings: "Who is like You among the might ones, G-d" / "Who is like You, mighty in holiness" / "You redeemed Your people with Your arm" / "The sons of Jacob and Joseph forever" / "The kings came and fought" / "Then fought the kings of Canaan."

Then the end of Amalek and the healing: "I said that I would make an end of them" / "Eradicate their remembrance from mankind" / "All the sicknesses that I have visited upon Egypt I will not visit upon you, for I, the Lord, heal you" / "With a kind one, You show Yourself kind" / "With the upright, mighty, You show Yourself upright."

Then the hearkening, and the cedars: "And he said, if you hearken to the voice of the Lord, Your G-d" / "And you do what is proper in His eyes" / "His appearance is like the Lebanon" / "Chosen as the cedars" / "O daughters of Jerusalem."

Then the waters trembling, and the marble pillars: "They trembled, even the deeps quaked" / "They poured forth thick waters" / "His legs are [as] pillars of marble" / "Founded upon sockets of fine gold" / "The skies let out a voice" / "Even your arrows went abroad."

Then the fountains and the palms, with the woman who stood there praying: "Water fountains and seventy palms" / "And they encamped there by the water" / "The waters perceived You, O G-d" / "The waters perceived You" / "And she said, 'Please, my lord! As surely as your soul lives, my lord'" / "And you listen closely to His commandments" / "And observe all His statutes" / "They came to Elim, and there were twelve."

And the end is the asking and the answering: "Where has your beloved gone, O fairest of women" / "Where has your beloved turned" / "I am the woman who was standing here with you, to pray to the Lord" / "His palate is sweet, and he is altogether desirable" / "This is my beloved, and this is my friend" / "He will call to Me, You are my Father, My G-d, and the Rock of my salvation" / "Awesome in praise, worker of wonders" / "That we may seek him with you."

183.title: To Purify Ourselves in order to Change
body: The cow is saying, "Rejoice to the Lord over our strength, trumpet to the Lord of Jacob!" (Psalms 81:2) The large pure domestic animal is the cow, and the week stands closer still to Passover.

The Jewish people are called both Israel and Jacob, and Jacob is the name used when we are in the more fragile, humble state. Feeling weak, we have to lean harder on Hashem as the source of our strength. This is also the week of the Rebbe Rashab's yahrzeit, on the 2nd of Nissan — and his leadership fell in a tumultuous time, with the people in a particularly fragile state, facing the harsh anti-religious oppression of the Bolsheviks in Russia.

The cow carries the spiritual exile and impurity of Egypt, in the golden calf. It also carries the purification of the Parah Adumah, the Red Heifer, which had to be entirely red, pure and whole, tamim. Its ashes purified the highest form of impurity, contact with the dead, and every Jew who found himself impure had to go through that in order to bring the Passover offering this month — which is why we read Parashat Parah in the weeks before the holiday. The Rebbe Rashab is a tremendous example of purity himself: he established the Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva system, whose students were known as tmimim, the pure and wholesome ones, and his last ma'amar was about the final destruction of Amalek and the husks of impurity, the kelipah.
Twenty-seven is kaf and zayin, which spell zach, pure. Preparing for Passover, we have to purify ourselves in body and in spirit, returning to G-d and waiting eagerly for His redemption.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Akiva, who first says how to keep that purity: jesting and frivolity accustom a person to promiscuity, and tradition is a safety fence to Torah, tithing a safety fence to wealth, vows a safety fence for abstinence, and a safety fence for wisdom is silence. Then the loves. Beloved is man, for he was created in the image of G-d, and it is a sign of still greater love that he was told so. Beloved are Israel, for they are called children of G-d, and it is a greater love that they were told so. Beloved are Israel, for they were given a precious article, and greater still that they were told so. All is foreseen, and freedom of choice is granted. And then the open shop: everything is placed in pledge, and a net is spread over all the living; the store is open, the storekeeper extends credit, the account-book lies open, the hand writes, and all who wish to borrow may come and borrow; the collection-officers make their rounds every day and exact payment from a man, with his knowledge and without it; their case is well founded, the judgment is a judgment of truth, and ultimately all is prepared for the feast. In Nissan too, everything is prepared for the feast.

Rabbi Akiva elsewhere says how praiseworthy the Jewish people are, whose purification comes directly from our Father in Heaven. And nobody suits this month better: he is one of the greatest examples of complete humility and self-sacrifice. He began to study Torah at the age of 40, sitting silently and humbly beside small children — and became one of the greatest Torah scholars of all time. His name shares a root with Jacob; both come from eikev, heel, where Israel holds the same letters as Li Rosh, mine is the head. The head is the highest part of the body and the heel the lowest.

The combination is yesod shebenetzach, foundation within determination and victory, which is perhaps the most prominent feature of Jewish education through the long exile. The lesson from the cow is that in the work of our tikkun — the very reason we came into the world — G-d is the source of our strength. The cow sings about Jacob, who worked all his life against the obstacles set in front of him, and only after much perseverance became Israel. Each of us changes and advances too, even without noticing, and He is beside us through it.

184.title: Eliyahu and Knowing One's Place
body: The second week of Nissan. Haazinu names what delays the end: "Were it not that the enemy's wrath was heaped up, lest their adversaries distort; lest they claim, 'Our hand was triumphant! The Lord did none of this!'" (Deuteronomy 32:27) Read as the destruction of Amalek, the reason it has taken so long is haughtiness — an inflated ego that distorts reality. Something of that was seen after the Six-Day War, when the miraculous victory led to uncalled-for exuberance and distortion, and from there to the debacle of the Yom Kippur War.

The Haftorah says it from the other side: "With a pure one, You show Yourself pure; But with a perverse one, You deal crookedly." (II Samuel 22:27) In the days before Passover we try our utmost to purify ourselves, above all of ego.

So the quality is he who knows his place, Hamakir Et Mekomoh, which may be the best description of humility there is. Being humble is not thinking oneself meaningless; it is knowing one's place — one's responsibility and task in life. And Makom, place, is one of the names of G-d, so Hamakir et Mekomoh can also mean he who knows his G-d. That is the message of Passover. Pharaoh, the ultimate overgrown ego, refused at first to release the people because he said he did not know G-d. Moshe, the most humble of men, knew Him better than any other mortal.

The prophet is Eliyahu, who was humble and still did not hesitate to speak against the King of Israel and to rebuke all of Israel for hesitating to serve G-d alone. He knew his place: asked, "Why are you here, Eliyahu?", he answered, "I have acted with great zeal for Hashem, G-d of Legions." He is also one of the best examples of one who knows his G-d — every Shabbat we read his description and exaltation of G-d's attributes, Patach Eliyahu — and he has a major part in the Passover Seder.

The levitical city is Libnah, also a city of refuge, from Lavan, white. It may point to the purification before Pessach, and to Libun, one of the koshering processes, in which metal is heated until it is white hot. Lavan is also one of the main enemies of the Jewish people: the Seder's recounting begins "Arami Oved Avi," an Aramean tried to destroy my father, which is Lavan, who tried to destroy Jacob.
184.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 27.

185.title: Amminadab, Emunah & Self-Sacrifice
body: This week holds the yahrzeit of Rabbi Shalom DovBer of Lubavitch, the Rebbe Rashab, and the Torah portion goes fully into Parashat HaMan — the training of a people to have faith and not complain. "They journeyed from Elim, and the entire community of the children of Israel came to the desert of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after their departure from the land of Egypt. The entire community of the children of Israel complained against Moses and against Aaron in the desert." The phrase "the entire community" comes twice, and against the complaining it says that the lack of emunah in that generation was widespread and would take serious work. The commentaries note that it was at this place that their food supplies ran out, and that was the source of the complaint.

The Haftorah's verse is the exact opposite of worrying about supplies: "in Taanach by the waters of Megiddo; they took no gain of money." The Canaanite kings took no money to come and attack. If our enemies will disregard their finances like that, how much more should we, who know where our sustenance comes from.

Daf Kaf Zayin of Sotah takes up a woman of ill repute, some cases of women who do not drink, and the punishment of the male adulterer, and ends with laws taught when Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah became the Nassi, and with how the Song of the Sea was sung between Moshe and the Children of Israel. Both of those belong to Judah and to this month: the Nassi had to be of the tribe of Judah, as an extension of the Davidic dynasty, and Rabbi Elazar's appointment is one of the crucial focus points of the Passover Hagadah. In these days we also read the Nassi for each day, connecting to the head of each tribe. And the Song of the Sea is the Exodus itself.

The generation is Aminadav, son of Ram, father of Nachshon and of Elisheva, Aharon's wife; Miriam was married to his uncle, Calev. There is a well-known Midrash that it was Nachshon's action which split the Sea of Reeds. Aminadav may be the main link between the line of Judah and the family of Moses, and so between the redemption from Egypt and the Messianic one. His name means offering of my people, and Nedavah is a voluntary offering, as the gift of inauguration was. The Rebbe Rashab was a Nasi too, one who offered himself with great Mesirat Nefesh on behalf of his people.

The journey is from Chashmonah to Moseroth, the place of Aaron's passing. Aaron was the Nassi of the tribe of Levi, and we read of his lighting of the Menorah as part of the inauguration; he is the fifth Shepherd, as the Rebbe Rashab was the Fifth Rebbe of Lubavitch. Rabbi Jacobson explains that Moseroth comes from musar, advice and chastisement about conduct — and cleaning for Passover is also a cleaning of ego, which takes the ability to accept criticism. Moseroth is near Mesirat Nefesh, self-sacrifice, and near Masoret, tradition, and much of Passover is the keeping of family custom. The personal journey moves on from rededication and leadership to self-sacrifice and emunah, clearing out the ego before the holiday.

186.title: He Becomes Modest
body: Channah's verse this week is the whole of her answer: "For this child did I pray, and the Lord granted me my request, which I asked of Him." The Talmud teaches that Eli the Kohen Gadol was willing to punish Shmuel and to pray that G-d give Channah a child even better than him. She would not have it: this was her child, the one she had prayed for — and by the next verse he is no longer hers but Hashem's.

That is Nissan and the redemption from Egypt exactly. The Jews of that time were far from perfect, and they were the children of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, whom He had promised to bring out; deeper than that, they were His children, and He redeemed them whatever their condition. Later, after the golden calf, He offers Moshe to destroy the people and build a nation out of him, and Moshe answers that if He did such a thing, "erase me from Your Book."

The Pirkei Avot quality is that he becomes modest. One side of modesty is not asking Hashem for personal greatness. Channah did not want a greater child than Shmuel; she was happy with her portion. Proverbs 27 opens on the same thing: "Do not boast for tomorrow, for you do not know what the day will bear. May a stranger praise you and not your mouth, an alien and not your lips."

Besides the Rebbe Rashab on the 2nd of Nissan, the week holds Rabbi Yochanan Twersky, the first Rebbe of Rachmastivka, on the 4th, and Rabbi Avraham Yehoshua Heschel, the Ohev Yisrael, Rebbe of Apt, on the 5th. The Rebbe Rashab was known for the love and care he gave his only son, Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak, the Rebbe Rayatz, above all in his education; he said that it is an absolute duty for every person to spend half an hour every day thinking about the education of his children, and to do everything in his power, and beyond his power, to inspire them to follow the path along which they are being guided.

Rabbi Yochanan Twersky was known for great humility. His father, Rav Mordechai Twersky, the Maggid of Chernobyl, said his son had the soul of Rabbi Yochanan Ben Zakkai; he was the last of eight brothers, each of whom became a rebbe. One story tells it best. When the Maggid of Chernobyl was niftar, his sons gathered to divide his spiritual inheritance — one took his kind heart, another his sharp mind, and so on. Reb Yochanan wanted his father's gornisht, his nothingness, his deep humility. But his brother, Harav Moshe of Koristchov, took the gornisht, so Reb Yochanan was left with gor gornisht, absolutely nothing, and he was pleased.

Rabbi Avraham Yehoshua Heschel was one of the close disciples of Rebbe Elimelech of Lizhensk, and was called the Ohev Yisrael, Lover of Israel, for his great love of his fellow Jew. A very similar inheritance story is told of his teacher: before he died, Rebbe Elimelech bequeathed the sight of his eyes to the Chozeh of Lublin, the spirit of his heart to the Kozhnitzer Maggid, the soul of his mind to Rebbe Menachem Mendel of Riminov, and the power of speech to Rebbe Avraham Yehoshua Heshel of Apt. Also this week: Rabbi Yaakov Yosef, son of Rabbi David Twersky, the Skverer Rebbe, on the 2nd of Nissan; Rabbi Tzvi Elimelech Shapira of Bluzhov, son of Rabbi David of Dinov, the Tzvi LaTzadik, and Rabbi Moshe son of Shlomo Rokeach, the Kiev-Zlotchover Rebbe, both on the 5th; and Rabbi Mordechai of Neshchiz, disciple of R. Yechiel Michel of Zlotchov, on the 8th.

187.title: Faith in the Shepherd
body: The Song puts him in the garden, grazing. "My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the spice beds, to graze in the gardens and to gather roses." Then the line that holds both sides: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine, who grazes among the roses." And then the praise: "You are fair, my beloved, as Tirzah, comely as Jerusalem, awesome as the bannered legions." Hashem as Shepherd, which is what these weeks of Nissan are about — a faithful flock and its Shepherd — and the month is Aries, the ram.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the twenty-seventh is Iob, whose name recalls Job without the aleph. Job is tied closely to the events before the redemption: the Midrash teaches that he was one of Pharaoh's three top advisors when the decision was made to throw the Jewish boys into the Nile. And Job is a standing symbol of the need for faith and humility.
Daf Caf Zayim of Shvuot takes up oaths about a mitzvah, and two oaths made over the same loaf of bread — which is the house being prepared for Passover.

Jeremiah's twenty-seventh chapter has behemot, domesticated animals, and chayot, wild ones, and several Passover phrases: an outstretched arm, and G-d's servant — a term usually kept for Moses — given here to Nebuchadnezzar. "I made the earth, the man and the beast that are upon the face of the earth, with My great strength and with My outstretched arm, and I gave it to him that pleased Me. And now, I have given these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, My servant, and even the beasts of the field I have given to him to serve him." The chapter also carries the yoke of Babylonian oppression and the rest of what that exile did. In Nissan we live through the exiles again, and the redemption from each of them.

188.title: Reviewing the Second week of Nissan - Psalms 79-81; 77:19-21; 89:28
body: The second week of Nissan in psalms: the seventy-ninth, eightieth and eighty-first, with three verses of Psalm 77 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 79 is Asaph thanking G-d for sparing the people and turning His wrath on the wood and stones of the Temple, and weeping bitterly all the same: the place where the High Priest alone could enter, and only on Yom Kippur, is now so desolate that foxes stroll through it. "O G-d, nations have entered Your inheritance, they defiled Your Holy Sanctuary; they turned Jerusalem into heaps of rubble." The unburied: "They spilled their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there is no one to bury [them]." The asking: "Do not recall our former sins; let Your mercies come swiftly towards us, for we have fallen very low." And the prisoners: "Let the groan of the prisoner come before You; liberate those condemned to death, as befits the greatness of Your strength." It ends with what the flock can still do: "And we, Your people, the flock of Your pasture, will thank You forever."

Psalm 80 asks Him to come near as He did long ago. "Listen, O Shepherd of Israel, Who leads Joseph like sheep. Appear, You Who is enthroned upon the cherubim." Its refrain comes three times: "Return us, O G-d; cause Your countenance to shine, that we may be saved." Then the vine, which is the whole middle of it: "You brought a vine out of Egypt; You drove out nations and planted it. You cleared space before it; it took root and filled the land. Mountains were covered by its shade, and its branches became mighty cedars." And then the breach: "Why did You breach its fences, so that every passerby plucked its fruit? The boars of the forest ravage it, and the creepers of the field feed upon it." And the asking to look: "O G-d of Hosts, please return! Look down from heaven and see, and be mindful of this vine."

Psalm 81 was chanted in the Holy Temple on Rosh Hashanah, a day of many miracles for Israel, and it opens with this week's song: "Sing joyously to G-d, our strength; sound the shofar to the G-d of Jacob. Raise your voice in song, sound the drum, the pleasant harp, and the lyre. Blow the shofar on the New Month, on the designated day of our Holy Day." Then Egypt: "He ordained it as a precept for Joseph when he went forth over the land of Egypt; I heard a language which I did not know. I have taken his shoulder from the burden; his hands were removed from the pot." Then the answer out of hiding: "In distress you called and I delivered you; [you called] in secret, and I answered you with thunderous wonders; I tested you at the waters of Merivah, Selah." Then the opening of the mouth: "I am the Lord your G-d who brought you up from the land of Egypt; open wide your mouth, [state all your desires,] and I shall grant them." And then the grief of it: "But My people did not heed My voice; Israel did not want [to listen to] Me." "If only My people would listen to Me, if Israel would only walk in My ways, then I would quickly subdue their enemies." And the last line, which is what was on offer: "I would feed him with the finest of wheat, and sate you with honey from the rock."

Psalm 77's verses are the thunder and the path through the sea, ending "You led Your people like a flock, by the hand of Moses and Aaron." And Psalm 89's verse is the rank: "I will also make him [My] firstborn, supreme over the kings of the earth."

189.title: The Cow Is Saying
body: The cow opens, and the week braids the garden into the desert.

The grazing and the journey first: "My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the spice beds" / "To graze in the gardens and to gather roses" / "And the entire community of the children of Israel" / "Came to the desert of Scin, which is between Elim and Sinai" / "You led Your people like a flock" / "By the hand of Moses and Aaron."

Then the date, and the complaining: "On the fifteenth day of the second month" / "After their departure from the land of Egypt" / "The entire community of the children of Israel" / "Complained against Moses and against Aaron in the desert" / "The sound of Your thunder was in the rolling wind" / "Lightning lit up the world; the earth trembled and quaked."

Then measure for measure, and the enemy's boast: "With a pure one, You show Yourself pure" / "But with a perverse one, You deal crookedly" / "Were it not that the enemy's wrath was heaped up" / "Lest their adversaries distort" / "Your way was through the sea" / "Your path through the mighty waters" / "And Your footsteps were not known."

Then the kings who took nothing: "In Taanach by the waters of Megiddo" / "They journeyed from Elim" / "They took no gain of money" / "Lest they claim, 'Our hand was triumphant! The Lord did none of this!'"

And the end is the trumpet and the child prayed for: "Rejoice to the Lord of our strength" / "Trumpet to the Lord of Jacob!" / "I will also make him [My] firstborn" / "Supreme over the kings of the earth" / "For this child did I pray" / "I am my beloved's" / "And my beloved is mine" / "Who grazes among the roses" / "You are fair, my beloved, as Tirzah" / "Comely as Jerusalem, awesome as the bannered legions" / "And the Lord granted me my request" / "Which I asked of Him."

190.title: To Recognize our Limits in order to Free Ourselves from Them
body: The pig and rabbit are saying: "G-d is good to the good, and to the straight-hearted." (Psalms 128:2) The small impure domestic animal is read by some as the pig and by others as the rabbit. This week carries the first night of Passover, the yahrzeit of the Third Lubavitcher Rebbe, Menachem Mendel, the Tzemach Tzedek, and the birthday of the Seventh Rebbe, who carries the Third's name, his ancestor by direct patrilineal descent.

The sages consider the pig a hypocrite: it displays the external mark of a kosher animal, split hooves, while its intestines make it non-kosher. The rabbit and its kind — the hare, the hyrax — are the exact reverse: no split hooves, and the intestines of a kosher animal. Inside they are upright of heart, and their outward actions are plainly not. Besides the pig and the camel, the hyrax and the hare are the only animals the Torah names explicitly as not kosher. The Midrash in Vaikra Rabbah explains that the hyrax is the Persian exile and the hare the Greek one; the pig is the Roman exile, which belongs to Esau and his descendants, and that is the exile we are in now. Their song is about the final redemption, when even the pig will be upright of heart and all of them will be kosher.

The Tzemach Tzedek and the Rebbe carry the message of Passover, which is redemption; Tzemach Tzedek is one of the names of Mashiach, as Menachem is. As the animals show, redemption has an inner side and an outer one. Inwardly, both of them brought important new concepts into Chassidic thought and were at last able to publish and spread the works of the Rebbes before them. Outwardly, both were extremely successful in action: the Tzemach Tzedek set up agricultural settlements that saved many Jews from dire poverty and rescued thousands upon thousands of children forced to enlist in the Russian army, and the Rebbe established Jewish centres all over the world and helped save thousands of Jews trapped behind the iron curtain of the Soviet Union.

Twenty-eight is twice fourteen, yad, the strong and outstretched arm that took us out of Egypt — here doubled, two outstretched arms. On Passover we celebrate that He saved us then while believing fully that He will save us again, more miraculously than in Egypt. Twenty-eight is also kaf and chet, which spell koach, strength — and koach also means potential, what has not yet been revealed. The pig looks as though it has the possibility of being kosher, and it is not, at least not yet. It stands for Esau, who had enormous potential; that potential made Isaac believe he would prove worthy of the firstborn's blessings. Like the pig, Esau would play the tzadik before his father, so much so that the Midrash relates he would ask Isaac how to tithe salt and straw — neither of which needs tithing, so that the question made him look ready to go beyond the letter of the law. The Rebbe explains that salt is an example of potential: on its own it is only salt, and with other food it brings out flavour and even keeps it from spoiling.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Eliezer the son of Azariah, and the rabbinical discussion in the Haggadah begins with his remarks. If there is no Torah, there is no common decency, and if there is no common decency, there is no Torah. If there is no wisdom, there is no fear of G-d, and without fear of G-d there is no wisdom. Without applied knowledge there is no analytical knowledge, and the reverse. If there is no flour, there is no Torah, and if there is no Torah, there is no flour. Then the trees: one whose wisdom is greater than his deeds is a tree with many branches and few roots, which a storm uproots and turns on its face — "He shall be as a lone tree in a wasteland" — and one whose deeds are greater than his wisdom is a tree with many roots and few branches, which all the storms in the world cannot budge: "He shall be as a tree planted upon water, who spreads his roots by the river; who fears not when comes heat, whose leaf is ever lush."

That is the inner and outer kosher again. Knowledge needs action and action needs knowledge, and Rabbi Elazar makes clear that action comes first — which the Rebbe stressed too: HaMa'aseh Hu HaIkar. The flour may also be the matzah, and the custom of providing flour to the poor, Maot Chitim, wheat money, so they can celebrate properly. And preparing for the holiday means ridding ourselves of chametz, the leavened bread outside and the inflated ego within.

This week completes another cycle of seven, and the combination is malchut shebenetzach. At the Seder we live victory, humility and redemption openly, in this physical world. From the pig and the rabbit we learn to want a life of complete integrity, and a complete redemption.

191.title: Elisha and Being Happy with One's Lot
body: The week of the first day of Passover. Haazinu: "For they are a nation devoid of counsel, and they have no understanding." (Deuteronomy 32:28) Read another way entirely: once this people — Amalek — is no more, there is counsel, and when they are nothing, there is understanding. Amalek is arrogance, and destroying it, burning the chametz of our inflated ego, is where wisdom comes from; Chochmah stands for Koach Mah, the strength of being "what," nothing. And read a third way: when the Jewish people make themselves like nothing, there is counsel and understanding.
The Haftarah agrees: "And the humble people You do deliver; But Your eyes are upon the haughty [in order] to humble them." (II Samuel 22:28)
So the quality is another of humility's basics: he who is happy with his lot, HaSameach Be'Chelkoh.

The prophet is Elisha, Eliyahu's disciple and successor, who showed it in accepting that place — and who later received a very special portion indeed, twice the spirit of Eliyahu. One of the greatest examples of being happy with one's lot is in his own story. Asking the Shunamite woman whether she needed anything, so that he could repay the great hospitality she and her husband gave him, he got this answer: "I dwell among my people." She asked for nothing, and she had no children at the time.
The levitical city is Eshtemoa, whose name seems to mean making oneself heard — which is the Seder, and the importance of speaking abundantly about the miracle.
191.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 28.

192.title: Nachshon and Help from Above
body: This week holds the first day of Passover, and the portion holds the people at their most desperate, forgetting every miracle they had just seen: "The children of Israel said to them, If only we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat by pots of meat, when we ate bread to our fill! For you have brought us out into this desert, to starve this entire congregation to death." And then the Mannah: "Behold! I am going to rain down for you bread from heaven, and the people shall go out and gather what is needed for the day, so that I can test them, whether or not they will follow My teaching." On Seder night one of the primary mitzvot is to eat matzah, the bread of faith and of healing, which runs parallel to the Mannah.

The Haftorah fights from the same direction: "From heaven they fought; the stars from their courses fought against Sisera." The Mannah came from heaven, and so did the whole salvation in Egypt. On Passover the initiative came from above to below — Ita'aruta d'Leilah, arousal from Above, and then Ita'aruta d'Letatah, arousal from below. The plagues and the splitting of the sea did not follow from any first effort of ours.

Daf Kaf Cheit of Sotah goes on to how the water also checks and punishes the male adulterer, who stays forbidden to her as her husband does, and how she becomes forbidden to eat Terumah. The punishment of the adulterer is open heavenly intervention: he was nowhere near the drinking, and it reached him exactly as it reached her. And the terumah runs parallel to the mannah, the matzah and above all the Passover offering — holy food, given to the kohanim by Divine decree, which could only be eaten in a state of purity.

The generation is Nachshon, the first Nassi of the tribe of Judah, who brought the first offering for the inauguration of the Mishkan, read on each of the first days of Nissan. He is best known for the splitting of the sea: diving in before it split is the very essence of faith. His name holds Nachash, snake, which has the same gematria as Mashiach, who will uproot the evil of the primordial snake, the yetzer harah — a clearer link still between the redemption from Egypt and the one to come.

The journey is from Moseroth to Benei Jaakan. Rabbi Jacobson writes that Benay Yaakan literally means the sons of Yaakan, grandson of Seir, and is also translated as wells of distress, a place that is narrow, confined and tight. On Passover we live through the distress and narrowness of the Egyptian exile as well as the redemption from it. The personal journey moves from purifying our conduct before the holiday to feeling both the narrowness and the freedom of the first exile and the last. This week faces Seir, literally goat, another name of Eisav, who is our last exile, and evil in general, and that primordial snake.

193.title: Being Patient and "Long" of Spirit
body: Channah's twenty-eighth verse hands him over: "And I also have lent him to the Lord; all the days which he will be alive, he is borrowed by the Lord." And he prostrated himself there to the Lord — Samuel, though some say Elkanah. On Passover we give ourselves over too, nullifying the ego entirely, and in the time of the Temple we went there and prostrated ourselves. The Passover story is leaving one domain, slavery in Egypt, and entering another, service of G-d: He took Goy MiKerev Goy, a nation from the innards of another nation.

The Pirkei Avot quality is that the Torah makes him patient — Erech Ruach, more literally long-spirited. It looks toward Mashiach, as we read in the Haftorah of the last day of Pessach: "And the spirit of G-d shall rest upon him.... And he will be permeated with the spirit of the fear of the L-rd." Menachem and Tzemach Tzedek are both names of Mashiach.

The Midrash Shmuel says Channah's own words were divinely inspired with Ruach HaKodesh without her knowing it: "For as long as he lives he is lent [sha'ul] to the Lord" — because as long as Samuel lived, so did Saul. That G-d let Shaul live on despite his grave sins is itself an example of His patience.

Proverbs 28 holds the same patience in a single verse: "Because of the sin of a land, its princes are many, but because of an understanding, knowledgeable man, so will [its retribution] be delayed" — Ya'arich, from Erech.

Besides the Tzemach Tzedek, the week holds at least three other great yahrzeits, major figures in both the Sefardi and Ashkenazi worlds, and like him authorities in the revealed and the hidden Torah both; all three lived in Tzfat. The 11th of Nissan is the yahrzeit of Rabbi Yeshayahu HaLevi Horowitz, the Shnei Luchot HaBrit, the Shlah. He was chief rabbi of Cracow, Frankfort and then Prague, later moved to Israel and became chief rabbi of Jerusalem, lived his last years in Tzfat, and is buried near Maimonedes' grave in Tiberias. His major work is a foundational kabbalistic text, a basis for many Chassidic works including the Tanya. The 13th of Nissan is the yahrzeit of Rabbi Yosef Karo and of Rabbi Moshe Alsheich. Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote the Shulchan Aruch, the basic text of Jewish law, still in use today; he was chief rabbi of Tzfat, and also wrote the Beit Yosef and the Maggid Meisharim, which records his conversations with an angel. Rabbi Moshe Alsheich was his student and a member of the Beit Din of Tzfat, and his interpretations and discourses on the Torah are widely used to this day. Also this week: R' Chaim Meir ben R' Yisroel Hager of Vizhnitz, the Imrei Chaim, on the 9th of Nissan, and Rabbi Asher Yeshaya of Ropshitz, son-in-law and successor of Rabbi Naftali of Ropshitz, on the 14th.

194.title: Shimron and the "Night of Vigil" (Leil Shimurim)
body: This week the Song speaks from His side. "Turn away your eyes from me, for they have made me haughty; your hair is like a flock of goats that streamed down from Gilead." "Your teeth are like a flock of ewes that came up from the washing, all of which are perfect and there is no bereavement among them." "Your temple is like a split pomegranate from beneath your kerchief." Domesticated animals again, the goat and the ewe, and a warning off haughtiness, which is the essential work of Passover: out with the chametz, in with the matzah.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the twenty-eighth is Shimron, whose name has Shomer in it, to keep, to guard. Matzah has to be Shmurah, guarded: "You shall guard the matzot." They are guarded so they cannot become chametz, or they may not be eaten. The main mitzvah of eating matzah falls on the first night, and that night is called Leil Shimurim, a night when we feel Him watching over us so strongly that it is even common custom to leave the doors unlocked.
Daf Kaf Chet of Shvuot keeps on with oaths made over a loaf of bread, and what happens if the bread is eaten — bread again, in the week when it is not eaten.

Jeremiah's twenty-eighth chapter has the yoke of the Babylonian exile, the kind a domesticated animal carries, and then the clearest case of a man so full of spiritual chametz that he believes his own false prophecies, against Jeremiah, who keeps his humility throughout. "And Hananiah the prophet took the bar off the neck of Jeremiah the prophet and broke it." "Go and say to Hananiah, saying: So said the Lord: Bars of wood have you broken, and you shall make in their stead bars of iron." "And Jeremiah the prophet said to Hananiah the prophet: The Lord did not send you, and you assured this people with a lie. Therefore, so said the Lord: Behold I send you off the face of the earth; this year you shall die, for you have spoken perversion against the Lord." And then: "And Hananiah the prophet died in that year, in the seventh month." Nissan is the seventh month counting from Rosh Hashanah.

195.title: Reviewing the Third Week of Nissan - Psalms 82-84; 90:1-4; 89:29
body: The third week of Nissan in psalms: the eighty-second, eighty-third and eighty-fourth, with the opening of Psalm 90 and one verse of Psalm 89.

Psalm 82 admonishes judges who feign ignorance of the law, dealing unjustly with the pauper and the orphan while coddling the rich and pocketing their bribes. "G-d stands in the council of judges; among the judges He renders judgment: How long will you judge wickedly, ever showing partiality toward the evildoers? Render justice to the needy and the orphan; deal righteously with the poor and the destitute." What their blindness costs: "But they do not know, nor do they understand; they go about in darkness, [therefore] all the foundations of the earth tremble." And what they are: "I said that you are angels, supernal beings, all of you; but you will die as mortals, you will fall like any prince."

Psalm 83 is a prayer about the wars against Israel in the days of Jehoshaphat, when the nations plotted against them. "O G-d, do not be silent; do not be quiet and do not be still, O G-d." The plot in their own words: "Come, let us sever them from nationhood, and the name of Israel will be remembered no more." Then the roll of them, conspiring with one heart: the tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagrites, Geval and Ammon, and Amalek, Philistia with the inhabitants of Tyre, and Assyria joined with them. Then the precedents: "Do to them as to Midian; as to Sisera and Yavin at the brook of Kishon." And the asking: "My G-d, make them like whirling chaff, like straw before the wind." It ends not in destruction but in recognition: "Fill their faces with shame, and they will seek Your Name, O Lord." "And they will know that You, Whose Name is the Lord, are alone, Most High over all the earth."

Psalm 84 mourns the destruction of the Temple from the depths of the heart and speaks of all the blessings that come with its restoration; fortunate is the one who trusts it will be rebuilt and does not despair in this long exile. "How beloved are Your dwellings, O Lord of Hosts! My soul yearns, indeed it pines, for the courtyards of the Lord." The bird in the ruin: "Even the bird has found a home, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she lays her young on the [ruins of] Your altars." The road there: "Fortunate is the man whose strength is in You; the paths [to the Temple] are in his heart. For those who pass through the Valley of Thorns, He places wellsprings; their guide will be cloaked in blessings. They go from strength to strength; they will appear before G-d in Zion." And the weighing: "For better one day in Your courtyards than a thousand [elsewhere]. I would rather stand at the threshold of the house of my G-d, than dwell [in comfort] in the tents of wickedness."

Psalm 90 begins here, and it is Moses's own: "A prayer of Moses, the man of G-d. O Lord, You have been our dwelling place throughout all generations. Before the mountains were born, and You brought forth the earth and the inhabited world, and from everlasting to everlasting, You are G-d. You bring man to the crushing point, and You say, 'Return, O sons of men.' For a thousand years are in Your eyes like yesterday, which passed, and a watch in the night." And Psalm 89's verse holds: "I will forever keep My kindness for him, and My covenant will remain true to him."

196.title: The Pig Is Saying
body: The pig opens, and the week sets the haughty next to the humble.

The eyes and the counsel first: "Turn away your eyes from me, for they have made me haughty" / "For they are a nation devoid of counsel and they have no understanding" / "G-d is good to those that are good, as well as to the straight-hearted" / "And the humble people You do deliver; but Your eyes are upon the haughty to humble them."

Then the pots of meat, and the crushing point: "The children of Israel said to them, If only we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt" / "When we sat by pots of meat, when we ate bread to our fill!" / "For you have brought us out into this desert, to starve this entire congregation to death" / "You bring man to the crushing point and You say, 'Return, O sons of men.'"

Then the flocks, and the dwelling place: "Your hair is like a flock of goats that streamed down from Gilead" / "Your teeth are like a flock of ewes that came up from the washing" / "All of which are perfect and there is no bereavement among them" / "A prayer of Moses, the man of G-d. O Lord, You have been our dwelling place throughout all generations."

Then the child lent, and what was there before the mountains: "And I also have lent him to the Lord; all the days which he will be alive, he is borrowed by the Lord" / "Before the mountains were born, and You brought forth the earth and the inhabited world" / "And from everlasting to everlasting, You are G-d."

And the end is the bread from heaven and the stars: "Behold! I am going to rain down for you bread from heaven" / "From heaven they fought; the stars" / "From their courses fought against Sisera" / "I will forever keep My kindness for him, and My covenant will remain true to him" / "Your temple is like a split pomegranate from beneath your kerchief" / "For a thousand years are in Your eyes like yesterday, which passed, and a watch in the night" / "And the people shall go out and gather what is needed for the day" / "So that I can test them, whether or not they will follow My teaching" / "And he prostrated himself there to the Lord."

197.title: After the Initial Inspiration, To Get to Work
body: The beast of burden is saying, "When you eat the fruit of your labors, happy are you and good is your lot." (Psalms 128:2) The large impure domestic animal, which Rabbi Slifkin translates simply as the beast of burden, and the week is Passover.

On Passover we feel the influx of blessing and redemption come in. And from the second day onward we begin counting the omer and working on ourselves, so that by Shavuot we will have earned the Torah, at least in part by the work of our own hands.

The animal looks to be Yishmael and his descendants. This son of Abraham was known for his great capacity for prayer and for trusting in G-d's blessings and salvation, and he did receive great blessings — though part of them showed how much of his way of living still needed improving: the angel tells Hagar that his hand would be on everyone. Later in life he repents, returns to G-d, and has a good relationship with Isaac, and in messianic times the two will live together in peace. Our sages read the verse as a double blessing: praiseworthy in this world, and good for you in the world to come. There is a Chassidic custom, instituted by the Ba'al Shem Tov, of making a meal on the eighth day of Passover called Moshiach Seudah, in honour of Mashiach and the world to come.

Twenty-nine goes with the cycle of the moon, 29.5 days, on which the Jewish month is based; Muslims, who consider themselves descendants of Yishmael, follow a purely lunar calendar. It is also the number of days in a woman's cycle.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Eliezer the son of Chisma: the laws of kinin, bird offerings, and the laws of menstrual periods — these are the meat of Halachah, while the calculations of solar seasons and gematria are the condiments of wisdom. On Passover we eat no chametz, which spiritually is setting aside everything that inflates us and takes from our essence; and on Passover He connects to us personally, as our Redeemer rather than as Creator of the Universe. The teaching says something like that: He does not want us lost in grandiose and esoteric subjects like astronomy and gematria, but also in the details of serving Him in how we behave from day to day. Both sets of laws are exactly about daily conduct, and both are fundamental — to the relationship between G-d and the Jewish people, and between husband and wife, which is itself a metaphor for the first, as Solomon's Song of Songs has it. Bird offerings belong to our coming closer: korban is from karov, close, and in the absence of sacrifices, prayer and study stand in their place. And the laws of the cycle are what make wives permissible to their husbands.

The combination is chesed shebehod: this week we work on ourselves in order to receive and appreciate the blessings of the holiday properly. What the beast of burden teaches is that He helps us and travels with us, and still we should not want our spiritual growth spoon-fed. Everything comes from Him, and we have to do the work.

198.title: Jonah, Gechazi, and Placing a Fence Around One's Words
body: Passover, days two through eight. Haazinu asks for reflection: "If [only] they were wise and would understand this; they would reflect upon their fate." (Deuteronomy 32:29) The word for fate is Acharitam, literally their end. Much of Pessach is reflecting not only on the redemption from Egypt but on using it to think about the final one — Acharit k'Reshit, as we say in our prayers. In the Diaspora the eighth day is kept, and in Hebrew it is not called Shmini, Eighth, but Acharon shel Pessach, the Last Day of Passover. On it the Ba'al Shem Tov instituted the Moshiach Seudah, a meal in honour of the messianic redemption, and the Rebbe Rashab instituted that four cups of wine be drunk at it, as at the Seder.

The Haftorah is light in the dark: "For You are my lamp, O' Lord; And the Lord does light my darkness." (II Samuel 22:29) We are still in the darkness of exile, and connecting to Him and to the final redemption brings light into it — as in the first redemption, when Egypt was plagued with darkness and the Jewish people still had light.
The quality is he who makes a fence around his words. During Pessach, and above all at the seder, we have to be very careful with words. Pessach stands for Peh Sach, the mouth talks.

The prophet is Jonah ben Amittai, of Jonah and the Whale, who was a disciple of Eliyahu and Elisha. He is this quality itself: he would not speak to the Assyrians, so as not to help those he foresaw would harm the Jewish people, and even on a storm-tossed ship about to sink because of his refusal he still would not speak. He belongs to the final redemption too — the Vilna Gaon explains that he is a prototype for Mashiach ben Yosef — and to the first, since the King of Nineveh is said to be Pharaoh himself.

Another student of Elisha who could well have been the twenty-ninth prophet is Gechazi, but the Tanach and the Oral tradition record enough mistakes of his that he likely missed it. Because he does not make a fence around his words, Gechazi becomes a Metzorah. Looked at closely, though, he held a spark of Mashiach ben David, and his intentions were most likely good; it was the actions that were wrong for the time and place. Our sages teach that he and his sons were the Metzora'im by the gates of Aram who ended up saving the Jews of their day — and Mashiach himself is described in the Talmud as a Metzorah by the gates of Rome.

The levitical city for the week of Passover is Juttah, spelled like Yatteh, to turn, incline, or stretch out one's hand. It is the word in this passage: "Now the Egyptians are men and not G-d, and their horses are flesh and not spirit, and the Lord shall turn His hand, and the helper shall stumble and the helped one shall fall, and together all of them shall perish." Rashi: the Holy One, blessed be He, supports everything with His hand, and when He turns it they fall, like one who holds something and tips his hand so that it drops. Jonathan renders it: shall raise the blow of His might. Which suits the week that holds the 7th day of Passover, when the Egyptian horses and their riders were thrown into the sea, and when He took us out with a strong hand and an outstretched arm — Yad Chazakah v'haZroah Netuyah, the same root as Yuttah.
198.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 29.

199.title: Salmah and Leaving Our Own "Egypts"
body: Beshalach keeps on with the Mannah and ends in knowing: "And it shall be on the sixth day that when they prepare what they will bring, it will be double of what they gather every day. [Thereupon,] Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel, [In the] evening, you shall know that the Lord brought you out of the land of Egypt." The mannah is a great reinforcement of emunah, which is the heart of Passover. The Talmud also draws an important principle of law from that verse — preparing for a holiday. "When they prepare what they will bring" is understood to mean having in mind beforehand what one will use, physically and spiritually, during the holiday; and that a holiday cannot prepare for an ordinary day or even for the Sabbath, and the Sabbath cannot prepare for an ordinary day or a holiday.

The Haftorah sweeps them away: "The brook Kishon swept them away, that ancient brook, the brook Kishon." That is the splitting of the Sea of Reeds, kept this week, where the Egyptians were swept away; Rashi states that the Kishon had been a guarantor for the Sea of Reeds.

Daf Kaf Tet of Sotah goes further into her being forbidden to eat Terumah, and into other purity laws of Terumah and of sacrifices generally. Passover was a time when the laws of purity were particularly strict, because the Passover sacrifice had to be brought and eaten in purity — and we are strict about what we eat on it still, many keeping to nothing but food from their own kitchen.

The generation is Salmah, son of Nachshon and father of Boaz. Salmah means a garment, and he is also called Salmon, a small garment, since "on" is a suffix of smallness — which makes Nachshon a small snake. Psalm 104 says "Oteh Ohr Ka'Salmah," He enwraps Himself with light as a garment, which is part of the preparatory prayers before donning the Talit. The Alter Rebbe explains in Tanya that the Torah is the intermediary which bridges the infinite and the finite, the light and the garment. Salmah stands between in just that way: between Nachshon and the generation of the exodus, and Boaz, who marries Ruth and sets up the birth of King David.
