Salmah also comes from Sulam, ladder, and the Midrash builds on it: because until him they formed a ladder of princes, and from him onwards a ladder of kings. Passover is an intermediary stage too, the Holiday of Spring, a first step toward freedom and the start of the summer months.

The journey is from Benei Jaakan to Hor hagidgad, a hole or crevice of Gidgad. On the Arizal's writings, Rabbi Jacobson explains that Hor HaGidgad has to do with the intellect, the head and its crevices. It also looks related to the Mannah, which was called zerah gad, a seed of gad. The Talmud translates gad several ways, one of them that it would be magid, that it would tell, resolving doubts; another that it comes from Haggadah, the stories of the Talmud, which draw the heart of the listener as the Mannah did. And to receive the Mannah we have to make a vessel for it, a crevice inside ourselves. The personal journey moves from the narrowness and the freedom of the exiles to opening our hearts — to the gift of the mannah, and the gift of emunah.

200.title: Forgiving of (Personal) Insults
body: Channah's song begins: "My heart has rejoiced through the Lord; My horn has been raised by the Lord. My mouth is opened wide against my enemies, For I have rejoiced in Your salvation." Passover is also a great rejoicing, thanking Him for salvation in the face of our enemies.

The Pirkei Avot quality is that the Torah makes him forgiving of insults — which looks hard to square with that verse. Channah makes a point of her victory over her enemies, and Rashi comments that she meant none other than her husband's other wife, Peninah, who had insulted her constantly for having no children. We also learn that Peninah paid a heavy price for those insults, and eventually lost all her children. So how do the two go together?

One answer is that she never names Peninah, which shows she was not bitter and had forgiven her rival. That is a difficult answer, since she still calls her an enemy even after Shmuel is born. A deeper one is inside Pirkei Avot itself. The Hebrew for insult here is Elbonoh, and the word appears again in the next section, which is the only thing linking the two: "Said Rabbi Joshua the son of Levi: Every day, an echo resounds from Mount Horeb proclaiming and saying: 'Woe is to the creatures for their insult to the Torah.'" A sage is obliged to protect the honour of the Torah and of those who study it; he may forgive insults to himself, and he cannot forgive insults to the Torah and to Hashem. Rabbi Levi states that Peninah's intentions were pure, that she only wanted Channah to pray more fiercely. Even so, to insult a woman as righteous as Channah, wife of one of the leaders of the generation, constantly, went past personal animosity. It was an affront to the Torah itself.

The same shape is in our redemption. The punishments the Egyptians received were not simply a quid pro quo for what they did to the Jews: Pharaoh's not knowing and not acknowledging Hashem was an affront to the Torah, though the Torah had not yet been given. And the Jews are told to avenge Midian not out of vengefulness but because what the Midianites did, using their own daughters to entice the Jews, was an affront to Torah.

Proverbs this week holds both halves. On calming things: "Scornful men inflame a city, but the wise turn away wrath." "When a wise man contends with a foolish man, whether he is angry or he laughs, he will have no contentment." "A fool lets out all his wind, but afterwards a wise man will quiet it." And on what falls on those who insult the Torah: "When the wicked attain greatness, transgression increases, and the righteous will see their downfall." "Without vision the people become unrestrained, but he who keeps the Torah is fortunate."

The week holds the yahrzeits of two well-known early founders of the Chassidic movement, both known for a profound love of their fellow Jews: Rabbi Aharon the Great of Karlin on the 19th of Nissan and Rabbi Yitzchak Kalish of Vorka on the 22nd. Rabbi Aharon was a close disciple of the Maggid of Mezritch, and Karlin was so large and prominent a group in Lithuania that at one point Chassidim in general were called Karliners; he is remembered for the ecstatic and unrestrained fervor of his prayer, for his solicitude for the needy, and for the moral teachings of his Azharos, Warnings. Rabbi Yitzchak Kalish founded the Vorki dynasty in Poland; travelling with his teacher, R. David of Lelov, he became a disciple of R. Yaakov Yitzchak, the Seer of Lublin, and of R. Simchah Bunem of Pshischah, and some of his teachings and stories about him appear in Ohel Yitzchak and Hutzak Chein. His son R. Yaakov David founded Amshinov, and his son R. Menachem Mendel continued Vorki. Also this week: Rabbi Yitzchak Twerski, first Rebbe of Skver, and Rabbi Meir Abuchatzeira, the Baba Meir, son of the Baba Sali, both on the 17th of Nissan, and Rabbi Yosef Dov Soloveitchik, the Rav, on the 18th.

201.title: Feeling Chosen (Our Special Bond with G-d)
body: The Song counts the others and then sets her apart. "There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and innumerable maidens. My dove, my perfect one, is but one; she is one to her mother, she is the pure one of she who bore her; daughters saw her and praised her, queens and concubines, and they lauded her." And then: "Who is this who looks forth like the dawn, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, awesome as the bannered legions?" It was on Passover that the Jews were truly born as a nation, and on the Seventh Day, when the Sea of Reeds split, that the distinction became clearest and the other nations most afraid.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the twenty-ninth is Zebulun, whose name comes from Yizbeleni in Leah's prophecy, which means he will make his chief dwelling with me. Which is the Song's words again. Passover is also the first step toward the Mishkan: the whole purpose of leaving Egypt is to serve Hashem and to have His dwelling among the people.

The daf of Shvuot this week takes up the sacrifices brought for breaking a two-part oath, about not eating figs and grapes, and the laws of vain oaths, and imposing an oath on someone else, with oaths over a loaf of bread again. A vain oath is one that contradicts what people know to be true, something impossible, like camels flying or a serpent the size of an olive press; or one that contradicts a previous oath, as in "I swear that I will eat this loaf, I swear that I will not eat it." The Splitting of the Sea contradicted everything everyone knew to be true, and the nature of the Sea, and apparently even the oath that the waters of Noah would never again pass over the earth. Moshe imposes an action on the Sea of Reeds all the same, to fulfil Hashem's oath to Abraham and the people's oath to Joseph about burying his bones in Israel. The Midrash Tehillim teaches that the sea only split when it saw Joseph's casket.

Jeremiah's twenty-ninth chapter is redemption from exile in the form of an oath, which was indeed fulfilled, and a special bond — seeking Him and finding Him. "For at the completion of seventy years of Babylon I will remember you, and I will fulfill My good word toward you, to restore you to this place. For I know the thoughts that I think about you, says the Lord, thoughts of peace and not of evil, to give you a future and a hope. And you shall call Me and go and pray to Me, and I will hearken to you. And you will seek Me and find [Me] for you will seek Me with all your heart." And the other side, for those who do not go to Babylon: "I will make them as the loathsome figs, which cannot be eaten because they are so bad."

202.title: Reviewing the Fourth Week of Nissan - Psalms 85-87; 90:5-7; 89:30
body: The fourth week of Nissan in psalms: the eighty-fifth, eighty-sixth and eighty-seventh, with three verses of Psalm 90 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 85 laments the long and bitter exile and asks why this one runs longer than the ones before, imploring Him to fulfil His promise quickly; every individual should say it when in distress. It begins with what He has already done: "O Lord, You favored Your land; You returned the captives of Jacob. You forgave the iniquity of Your people, and covered all their sin forever." Then the asking: "Return us, O G-d of our salvation, and annul Your anger toward us. Will You forever be angry with us?" Then the listening: "I hear what the Almighty Lord will say; for He speaks peace to His nation and to His pious ones, and they will not return to folly." And then the four of them meeting: "Kindness and truth have met; righteousness and peace have kissed. Truth will sprout from the earth, and righteousness will peer from heaven."

Psalm 86 is David's troubles and his enemies Doeg and Achitophel, with much praise through it; this one too is for any individual in distress. "Lord, turn Your ear, answer me, for I am poor and needy." "For You, my Lord, are good and forgiving, and exceedingly kind to all who call upon You." Then the nations: "All the nations that You have made will come and bow down before You, my Lord, and give honor to Your Name, for You are great and perform wonders, You alone, O G-d." Then the asking for one heart: "Lord, teach me Your way that I may walk in Your truth; unify my heart to fear Your Name." And the saving already done: "For Your kindness to me has been great; You have saved my soul from the depth of the grave."

Psalm 87 was composed to be sung in the Holy Temple, and praises the glory of Jerusalem, a city that produces many great scholars, eminent personalities and people of good deeds, and speaks of the good of the Messianic era. "The Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwelling places of Jacob. Glorious things are spoken of you, eternal city of G-d." Then the register, which is the whole point of it: "I will remind Rahav Egypt and Babylon concerning My beloved; Philistia and Tyre as well as Ethiopia, 'This one was born there.' And to Zion will be said, 'This person and that was born there'; and He, the Most High, will establish it." And the last line: "Singers as well as dancers [will sing your praise and say], 'All my inner thoughts are of you.'"

Psalm 90's verses are how fast it goes: "You carry them away as a flood; they are like a sleep; in the morning, like grass it passes away. In the morning, it blossoms and passes away; in the evening, it is cut off and withers." And Psalm 89's verse answers with what does not: "And I shall make his seed endure forever, and his throne as the days of the heavens."

203.title: The Beast of Burden is Saying
body: The beast of burden opens, and the week puts the fruit of our own labour beside the grass that withers.

The mouth opened wide, and the evening: "My mouth is opened wide against my enemies" / "For I have rejoiced in Your salvation" / "[In the] evening, you shall know that the Lord brought you out of the land of Egypt" / "That when they prepare what they will bring" / "It will be double of what they gather every day" / "When you eat the fruit of your labors" / "Happy are you and good is your lot."

Then the praising daughters, and the throne: "Daughters saw her and praised her" / "Queens and concubines, and they lauded her" / "And I shall make his seed endure forever" / "And his throne as the days of the heavens" / "And Hannah prayed and said."

Then the one who looks forth like the dawn, and the lamp: "Who is this who looks forth like the dawn" / "Fair as the moon, clear as the sun" / "Awesome as the bannered legions?" / "For You are my lamp, Oh Lord" / "And the Lord does light my darkness."

Then the grass, with the counting of queens through it: "In the morning, like grass it passes away" / "In the morning, it blossoms and passes away" / "Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel" / "There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and innumerable maidens" / "If [only] they were wise and would understand this" / "They would reflect upon their fate" / "For we perish from Your wrath" / "And from Your anger we are dismayed."

And the end is the brook and the one dove: "And it shall be on the sixth day" / "In the evening, it is cut off and withers" / "You carry them away as a flood" / "They are like a sleep" / "The brook Kishon swept them away" / "That ancient brook, the brook Kishon" / "My dove, my perfect one, is but one, she is one to her mother" / "She is the pure one of she who bore her" / "My heart has rejoiced through the Lord" / "My horn has been raised by the Lord."

204.title: To Know that the World Needs More Love and Respect
body: The camel is saying, "G-d shall roar from upon high and cause His voice to sound forth from His holy place, His shout echoes profoundly over His dwelling place." (Jeremiah 25:30) This is the last week of Nissan and the week of Yom HaShoah, Holocaust Remembrance Day.

The verse is Hashem lamenting the destruction of the Temple. Since it fell, the Jewish people have had to survive a very long time without their basic source of spiritual sustenance, as a camel survives long stretches without water. Nissan is the month of redemption, from Egypt and in the future both — and even on Passover there is an egg on the Seder plate as a sign of mourning, because the final redemption has not come. This week also holds the yahrzeit of Yehoshua Bin Nun, on the 26th of the month.

By the same Midrash cited in week twenty-eight, the camel is the Babylonian exile, when the First Temple was destroyed. Like the beast of burden, it also looks to point to Yishmael. Finishing Nissan, we live through all the exiles and all the redemptions, hoping soon for the one that takes us out of this exile.

Thirty intensifies the balance of three, and it is the numerical value of Yehudah, whose tribe this month belongs to. Pirkei Avot teaches that thirty is the age of koach, strength and potential, when a person is at the height of physical and intellectual capacity; it was at thirty that the kohanim began serving in the Temple. That strength belongs to Judah and to King David, who, unlike Esau, acknowledged their mistakes and repented of them, and so could use all their capacity for good.

Pirkei Avot gives Ben Zoma. Who is wise? One who learns from every man. Who is strong? One who overpowers his inclinations. Who is rich? One who is satisfied with his lot. Who is honorable? One who honors his fellows. All of it bears on the tragedy of the Counting of the Omer: the 24,000 disciples of Rabbi Akiva died because of how hard they found it to respect, accept and learn from each other's readings of their master's teachings. The destruction of the Temple and the exile we are still in, the Holocaust inside it, came of sinat chinam, baseless hatred; we will be redeemed from this last exile through ahavat chinam, baseless love for each person.

The teaching also fits Yehoshua Bin Nun. He was Moses's closest disciple and successor and could still meet anyone: on the verse describing Joshua as "a man in whom there is spirit," Sifrei explains that he was able to meet the spirit of every man. And the second question fits him too. The Rebbe once said of his yahrzeit that on this day assistance from heaven is granted to become a conqueror, like Yehoshua Bin Nun, the most prominent of the conquerors. This week we prepare for the conquests of Iyar.

The combination is gevurah shebehod. The Counting of the Omer, especially once Passover and Nissan are over, is a stretch of service that can be hard, and takes strength and discipline to overcome the evil inclination. And the camel reminds us what we are here for: to make a dwelling place for G-d in this world, beginning with a sacred space for Him inside ourselves.

205.title: Isaiah and Giving All the Credit to G-d
body: The last week of Nissan, with Yom HaShoah and the yahrzeit of Yehoshua in it. Haazinu counts the odds: "How can one [person] pursue a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight, unless their [Mighty] Rock has sold them out, and the Lord has given them over?" (Deuteronomy 32:30) Far-fetched as it sounds, that happened in the Holocaust. It also ran the other way in Yehoshua's conquest of the Land of Israel, when the Jews pursued nations far larger than they were — as in the War of Independence and the Six-Day War.

The Haftorah is the same arithmetic read positively: "For by You I run upon a troop; By my G-d I scale a wall." (II Samuel 22:30) King David runs at a whole troop alone and scales a wall, and the verse says who it is by.
So the quality is humility again: he claims no credit for his achievements, Einoh Machazik Tovah L'atzmo. The credit goes to G-d, as that verse says.

The prophet is Isaiah — Nissan begins with Amotz and ends with his son. His behaviour is this quality. Having one of the most vivid and intimate visions of G-d and the Divine Chariot, he does not think of himself and how great he must be to have merited it. The opposite: "Woe is me, for I am lost, because a man of unclean lips am I, and in the midst of people of unclean lips do I dwell; for the King, the L-rd of Hosts, have mine eyes seen." His prophecy holds many admonitions and many consolations, and the optimism always rests on G-d granting the success, once we return to Him. Joshua was very humble too, and took no credit; he always saw himself as Moshe's follower and disciple.

The levitical city is Beth-shemesh, the house of the sun. It was Yehoshua who told the sun to stand still: "Sun, stand still upon Gibeon, and Moon in the valley of Ajalon." "And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies." A city of the sun for his yahrzeit is striking, since our sages compare Moshe to the sun and Yehoshua to the moon — and perhaps that is the point, that he saw himself not as a separate thing but as being of the house of Moshe, the student who never left the tent. Beth-shemesh figures elsewhere in the Tanach too: it is the birthplace of Shimshon, whose name is also from Shemesh, and who stands more than any other leader for a supernatural strength that comes from G-d.
205.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 30.

206.title: Destruction and Conquest
body: Beshalach: "And [in the] morning, you shall see the glory of the Lord when He hears your complaints against the Lord but [of] what [significance] are we, that you make [the people] complain against us? And Moses said, When the Lord gives you in the evening meat to eat and bread in the morning [with which] to become sated, when the Lord hears your complaints, which you are making [the people] complain against Him, but [of] what [significance] are we? Not against us are your complaints, but against the Lord." He hears the complaints, and Moshe counts himself and Aharon as nothing — Nachnu Mah. Yehoshua shared that. What the Jewish people went through in the Holocaust cannot be described; and He hears our complaints.

The Haftorah treads: "tread down, O my soul, (their) strength. Then were pounded the heels of the horses." It could be read as Jewish suffering, the soul and the strength of a people trodden down into such horror. As Rashi explains, the simple meaning is that we trod with our feet on the strength of our enemies, as Joshua put his feet on the neck of the Canaanite kings. The horse is a symbol of strength, and next week's animal; and horses pounding recalls the horse and its rider thrown into the sea.

Daf Lamed of Sotah goes further into purity laws of terumah and sacrifices, and ends on how the Song of the Sea was sung — in detail, and how even babies and unborn fetuses sang it too. Part of what makes the Holocaust so terrible is that it reached infants, babies and the unborn. And so the month of Nissan ends back at the splitting of the sea.

The generation is Boaz, son of Salmah, husband of Ruth, and the leader of the people in his day. Boaz holds the word oz, strength — Yehoshua's strength, perhaps, and the rescue that came to Ruth after all the death she had seen.

The journey is from Hor hagidgad to Jotbathah, which means calm, peace and tranquility. The personal journey moves from opening our hearts to the mannah and to emunah, to the peace that comes with complete faith — and perhaps to the relative tranquility of returning to our homeland, marked next week on Yom Ha'Atzmaut.

207.title: Yehoshuah and Being Uplifted by the Torah
body: Channah's second verse: "There is none as holy as the Lord, For there is none besides You; And there is no rock like our God." Rashi cites the Talmud: there is no artisan, Tzayar, like our G-d, who makes a form within a form. In pregnancy He shapes and gives life to each of us. Yehoshua was formed by Hashem through Moshe in the same way, and is called the son of Nun, which is a reference to Moshe himself — a person's teacher is like the one who bore him. The Talmud goes on: read not "There is none bilteka" but "There is none lebalotheka," none to consume You. The nature of flesh and blood is to be outlived by its works, and the Holy One, blessed be He, outlives His works. Which reads differently in the week of Yom HaShoah, when so many were so brutally consumed.

The Pirkei Avot quality is that the Torah uplifts him. Few have been as uplifted as Channah at the birth of her child, and the verse shows it. It is true of Yehoshua too: he was not inherently cleverer than everyone else, and he worked on himself until he was chosen as Moshe's successor for his dedication to the Torah. And it is the Torah that lifted so many communities after the loss of the Holocaust.

Proverbs this week opens in exactly that posture of humility before what is transmitted: "For I am more boorish than any man, neither do I have man's understanding. Neither have I learned wisdom, nor do I know the knowledge of the holy ones. Who ascended to heaven and descended? Who gathered wind in his fists? Who wrapped the waters in a garment? Who established all the ends of the earth? What is his name and what is the name of his son, if you know? Every word of God is refined; He is a shield for all who take refuge in Him. Do not add to His words, lest He prove to you, and you be found a liar."

Then it turns to a generation gone wrong. "Distance falsehood and the lying word from me; give me neither poverty nor wealth; provide me my allotted bread." "A generation that curses its father and does not bless its mother. A generation that is pure in its eyes, but is not cleansed of its filth. A generation-how lofty are its eyes! And its eyelids are raised. A generation whose teeth are [like] swords, and its molars are [like] knives, to devour the poor of the land and the needy of men." And the things that are never full: "The grave, the confined womb, and the earth, which is not sated with water, and fire, which does not say, 'Enough!'"

The week holds the yahrzeits of the founders of two important dynasties. Rabbi Chaim Halberstam of Sanz, on the 25th of Nissan, was the first Rebbe of Sanz-Klausenberg, famous for extraordinary dedication to the mitzvah of tzedaka and as a renowned Torah scholar; his voluminous and wide-ranging writings were published as the Divrei Chaim, and his eldest son founded the Sanzer synagogue in Tsfat. Bobov and Klausenberg descend from him. Rabbi Moshe Pallier of Kobrin, on the 29th of Nissan, was a close follower of R. Mordechai of Lechovitch and then of his son R. Noach, and in 1833 became the first Rebbe of Kobrin, with thousands of chassidim, many of whom later moved to Eretz Yisroel; his teachings are collected in Imros Taharos. Also this week: Rabbi Nachman of Tulchin, student of Rabbi Nosson of Breslov, and Rabbi Moshe Teitelbaum, the Satmar Rebbe, both on the 26th of Nissan, Rabbi Aharon HaKohen Rosenfeld, the Pinsk-Karliner Rebbe, on the 28th, and Rabbi Mordechai Shalom Yosef Friedman, the Sadigerer Rebbe, on the 29th.

208.title: Sered, Nets and Chains
body: The Song goes down to the nut garden: "I went down to the nut garden to see the green plants of the valley, to see whether the vine had blossomed, the pomegranates were in bloom. I did not know; my soul made me chariots for a princely people." And then the calling back: "Return, return, O Shulammite; return, return, and let us gaze upon you." "What will you see for the Shulammite, as in the dance of the two camps?"

Rashi reads the garden largely as Torah scholarship and the keeping of the commandments, and mentions teachers of the Mishnah by name — the Oral Torah passed from Moshe to Yehoshua, and from Yehoshua to the elders and the generations after. He brings a second reading of the nut too: just as a nut that falls into the mud does not have its interior sullied, so are the Israelites exiled among the nations and smitten with many blows, and their deeds are not sullied. Which fits this week.

The next verse he reads as exile, the Roman one we are still in, where the Holocaust happened. On "I did not know," Rashi has the congregation of Israel lamenting: I did not know to beware of sin, that I should keep my honour and my greatness, and I erred in the matter of groundless hatred and controversy, which intensified in the reign of the Hasmonean kings, Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, until one of them brought the kingdom of Rome and received the kingship from their hand and became their vassal — and since then, my soul made me to be chariots, that the nobility of other nations ride upon me. The Second Temple fell to baseless hatred, and not learning the lesson of it is what has kept us in exile.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the thirtieth is Sered. A Sarad is a netmaker or a maker of chains. Yehoshua would catch and hold every word of Moshe as a netmaker catches fish — and Yehoshua Bin Nun literally means Joshua the son of a fish, which is Moshe himself. Chains suit the week too, for the captivity endured in the Holocaust.

Daf Lamed of Shvuot begins a new chapter on the oath taken by a witness in court: whom it applies to, the rules against favouring one party over another, and distancing oneself from falsehood. Much of it fits Yehoshua. There is also an emphasis on the people as a whole, with verses on Am — "B'Tzedek Tishpot Amisecha." Yom HaShoah marks a time full of falsehood, and a time when all Jews were persecuted together, whatever their religiosity or nationality.

Jeremiah's thirtieth chapter is destruction and calamity again, and Rashi notes that it is not only the Temple and the Babylonian exile but also Gog and Magog. It speaks of pain like birth pangs, as in the pangs before the Messianic era, Chevlei Mashiach, which many believe the Holocaust to be. "A sound of quaking we have heard, fear, and there is no peace." "Ask now and see whether a male gives birth. Why have I seen every man [with] his hands on his loins like a woman in confinement, and every face has turned to pallor?" "Ho! For that day is great, with none like it, and it is a time of distress for Jacob, through which he shall be saved." And unlike the chapters before it, this one has a silver lining, that this people will not be finished: "For I am with you, says the Lord, to save you, for I will make an end of all the nations where I dispersed you, but of you I will not make an end, but I will chasten you in measure, and I will not completely destroy you." The wound stays open all the same: "No one deems your wound to be healed, you have no healing medicines. All your lovers have forgotten you, they do not seek you."

209.title: Reviewing the Fifth Week of Nissan - Psalms 88-90; 90:8-10; 89:31
body: The fifth week of Nissan in psalms: the eighty-eighth, eighty-ninth and ninetieth, with three verses of Psalm 90 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 88 weeps bitterly over the maladies and the suffering Israel endures in exile, and describes them in detail. It is the darkest of them. "For my soul is sated with affliction, and my life has reached the grave. I was reckoned with those who go down to the pit, I was like a man without strength." The abandonment: "You have put me into the lowest pit, into the darkest places, into the depths. Your wrath has weighed heavily upon me, and all the waves [of Your fury] have constantly afflicted me. You have estranged my friends from me, You have made me abhorrent to them; I am imprisoned and unable to leave." Then the argument that there is no praise from the grave: "Do You perform wonders for the deceased? Do the dead stand to offer You praise? Selah. Is Your kindness recounted in the grave, your faithfulness in the place of perdition?" And still the praying: "But, I, to You, O Lord, I cry; each morning my prayer comes before You." It ends where it began: "You have estranged from me beloved and friend; I have been rejected by my intimates."

Psalm 89 is here whole — the psalm whose verses have come one a week all year. It is the kingship of the House of David, and the lament over its long fall. "I will sing of the Lord's kindness forever; to all generations I will make known Your faithfulness with my mouth. For I have said, 'The world is built with kindness.'" Then the covenant itself: "I have made a covenant with My chosen one; I have sworn to David, My servant: 'I will establish Your descendants forever; I will build your throne for all generations.'" Then the sea and the foundations: "You rule the vastness of the sea; when its waves surge, You still them." "Righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne; kindness and truth go before Your countenance." Then, one after another, every verse that has been arriving singly for weeks: the aid granted to David, the anointing with holy oil, the arm that strengthens him, the adversaries crushed, the hand set upon the sea, the calling out "You are my Father," the firstborn supreme over the kings of the earth. And then the condition and the promise that outlasts it: "If his children forsake My Torah and do not walk in My ordinances... then I will punish their transgression with the rod and their misdeeds with plagues. Yet I shall not take away My kindness from him, nor betray My faithfulness. I will not abrogate My covenant, nor change that which has issued from My lips." Then the turn, and it is severe: "Yet You have forsaken and abhorred; You became enraged at Your anointed. You annulled the covenant with Your servant; You have profaned his crown [by casting it] to the ground. You shattered all his fences; You turned all his strongholds into ruin." And the asking: "How long, O Lord, will You conceal Yourself-forever?" "Where are Your former deeds of kindness, my Lord, which You swore to David in Your faithfulness?" And then the last line, which is how the third book of psalms ends: "Blessed is the Lord forever, Amen and Amen."

Psalm 90 is Moses's prayer, which David found in this form by a tradition attributing it to him, and brought into the Tehillim; the Midrash attributes the next eleven to Moses as well. It is the brevity of a human life, and it moves a person to repent and to drop his pride. "My Lord, You have been a shelter for us in every generation. Before the mountains came into being, before You created the earth and the world-for ever and ever You are Almighty G-d." The measure: "Indeed, a thousand years are in Your eyes like yesterday that has passed, like a watch of the night." The grass: "In the morning it thrives and sprouts anew; in the evening it withers and dries." The count: "The days of our lives number seventy years, and if in great vigor, eighty years; most of them are but travail and futility, passing quickly and flying away." And then the one request that follows from all of it: "Teach us, then, to reckon our days, that we may acquire a wise heart." Then: "Satiate us in the morning with Your kindness, then we shall sing and rejoice throughout our days. Give us joy corresponding to the days You afflicted us, the years we have seen adversity." And the last line, twice over: "May the pleasantness of the Lord our G-d be upon us; establish for us the work of our hands; establish the work of our hands."

210.title: The Camel is Saying
body: The camel opens, and the week sets the treading down beside the nut garden.

The treading and the garden first: "Tread down, O my soul strength" / "Then were pounded the heels of the horses" / "I went down to the nut garden" / "To see the green plants of the valley" / "To see whether the vine had blossomed" / "The pomegranates were in bloom."

Then the condition and the hidden sins: "If his children forsake My Torah" / "And do not walk in My ordinances" / "You have set our wrongdoings before You" / "Our hidden sins before the light of Your countenance" / "For all our days have vanished in Your wrath" / "We cause our years to pass like a fleeting sound."

Then what significance are we, with the thousand and the ten thousand: "But [of] what [significance] are we, that you make complain against us?" / "When the Lord hears your complaints, which you are making complain against Him" / "How can one pursue a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight" / "Unless their Rock has sold them out, and the Lord has given them over?" / "There is none as holy as the Lord, for there is none besides You" / "And there is no rock like our God."

Then the meat and the bread, with the count of our years: "But [of] what [significance] are we?" / "And Moses said, Not against us are your complaints, but against the Lord" / "When the Lord gives you in the evening meat to eat" / "And bread in the morning to become sated" / "The days of our lives number seventy years, and if in great vigor, eighty years" / "Most of them are but travail and futility" / "Passing quickly and flying away."

And the end is the glory and the roar, and the calling back: "And [in the] morning, you shall see the glory of the Lord" / "When He hears your complaints against the Lord" / "G-d shall roar from upon high and cause His voice to sound" / "From His holy place, His shout echoes profoundly over His dwelling place" / "Return, return, O Shulammite" / "Return, return, and let us gaze upon you" / "What will you see for the Shulammite, as in the dance of the two camps?" / "I did not know; my soul made me chariots for a princely people" / "For by You I run upon a troop" / "By my G-d I scale a wall."

211.title: To Be Proud of Our Humble Connection with G-d
body: The horse is saying, "Behold, as the eyes of the servants to the hand of their master, as the eyes of the maidservant to the hand of her mistress, so are our eyes to G-d our Lord until He will favor us." (Psalms 123:2) This is the week of Rosh Chodesh Iyar, of the day of remembrance for the fallen soldiers of Israel and the victims of terror, and of the fifth of Iyar, the miraculous victory of the War of Independence.

From beginning to end of this month we are counting the omer. Iyar is also a month of healing, and its letters alef, yud and reish are an acronym of "Ani Hashem Rofecha," I am G-d your Healer. The month belongs to the tribe of Issachar, whom the Torah calls a strong-boned donkey — close to a horse — taking on the yoke of Torah study. Issachar and Zevulun had their partnership, Zevulun in commerce and supporting Issachar's full dedication to Torah; that dedication is Rabbi Shimon Bar Yochai, whose yahrzeit falls this month, and of whom it is said Toratoh Emunatoh, that his Torah study was his profession.

The horse belongs to the fifth of Iyar directly, because in ancient times the horse is military might. The Song of the Sea has G-d throwing horse and rider into the sea — which is the song of the ox, later this month. And for all that power, the horse sings of looking constantly to Hashem for mercy. In the War of Independence the people fought mightily and heroically, like horses, and the victory was only possible because it was miraculous, a product of His great mercy. A horse follows its rider loyally; like the horse, the Jewish people waited a very long time and suffered greatly until He showed favour and made it possible to live in our Holy Land again.

The song is also how a person who is ill or injured prays for healing, which belongs to the day of remembrance and to the fifth of Iyar both. The miracle of the War of Independence came shortly after the Holocaust, when the people as a whole was like a sick person in urgent need.

Thirty-one has the same numerals as thirteen, the thirteen attributes of mercy. It is also the number of kings the Tanach lists as defeated at the end of Joshua's conquest of the Land. And it is lamed and alef, which spell E-l, one of the names of G-d — a name of infinite power and also of infinite mercy. The word el appears many times in the horse's song.

Pirkei Avot gives Ben Azzai: run to pursue a minor mitzvah, and flee from a transgression, for a mitzvah brings another mitzvah and a transgression brings another transgression; the reward of a mitzvah is a mitzvah, and the reward of a transgression is a transgression. As one mitzvah draws the next, healing of body and spirit also comes slowly, a step at a time, like the Counting of the Omer. He also says: do not scorn any man, and do not discount any thing, for there is no man who has not his hour, and no thing that has not its place. Which is Yom Ha'Atzma'ut as much as the horse is — the Jewish people and the Land of Israel finally had their hour.

The combination is tiferet shebehod. With patience and balance, step by step, we serve Him and climb. The horse's example is to understand that for all our strength we are nothing more, and nothing less, than servants of G-d — to be proud of that humble connection, and to know that the journey may be slow and the arrival is certain.

212.title: Yoel and the Rock of Israel
body: Rosh Chodesh Iyar, and Yom Ha'Atzma'ut. Iyar belongs to Issachar, known for complete dedication to the study of Torah. Haazinu: "For their rock is not like our [Mighty] Rock. Nevertheless, our enemies sit in judgment." (Deuteronomy 32:31) The best description of that Tzur is probably King David's in this week's Haftorah verse: "[He is] the G-d Whose way is perfect; The word of the Lord is tried; He is a shield unto all them that trust (take refuge) in him." (II Samuel 22:31) Both verses describe His protection through Israel's difficult struggle for independence, against overwhelming odds, while the rest of the world simply sat in judgment — a hypocritical judgment that continues to this day.

The quality is beloved, Ahuv. Rabbi Meir uses the same word of those who study Torah for its own sake, Lishmah, as Issachar did. The victory kept on Yom Ha'Atzma'ut is itself a sign of how beloved we are, and that feeling came shortly after the Holocaust, when so many felt abandoned.

The prophet is Yoel, whose prophecy runs the same way: destruction and then the modern miracles. He describes the plague of locusts that devastated the Land of Israel, and after the Jews repent they are promised much grain, wine and oil.
The levitical city is Kishion, from kasheh, difficult, tough — which is Issachar, the strong-boned donkey, and which is how the Jews fought and won the War of Independence.
212.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 31.

213.title: Obed and Working Hard
body: Rosh Chodesh Iyar, Yom HaZikaron and Yom Ha'Atzmaut. Iyar is healing — Ani Hashem Rofecha — and the month of Issachar.

Beshalach: "And Moses said to Aaron, Say to the entire community of the children of Israel, Draw near before the Lord, for He has heard your complaints. And it came to pass when Aaron spoke to the entire community of the children of Israel, that they turned toward the desert, and behold! the glory of the Lord appeared in the cloud." Which is the horse's song: our eyes are a servant's eyes on his Master until He shows mercy. He saw everything we went through, heard the complaints, and brought us back to our Land.

The Haftorah has the horse in it too: "by reason of the prancings, the prancings of their mighty ones. 'Curse you Meroz,' said the messenger of the Lord, 'curse you bitterly (you) inhabitants thereof.'" Meroz and its people failed to help in the war.

Daf Lamed Alef of Sotah takes up serving G-d out of love and out of fear, and how many witnesses are needed to testify to her seclusion. Love and fear is the horse again. The War of Independence certainly had aspects of serving out of fear that had not been there before; it had an Ein Brera about it, no other way out, which belongs to the destruction of the Holocaust. The daf also names Iyov, Job, who suffered so much and served out of love, and whose fortunes were turned back in the end, his family, health and wealth restored.

The generation is Obed, son of Boaz and father of Yishai. Obed means worker, and is near eved, servant — the horse's song again. He could also point to the Jewish army and the pioneering, hardworking generation of Israel's independence.

The journey is from Jotbathah to Abronah, which is a river crossing, a ford. Arguably the most important crossing in history is the Jordan, to conquer the Land of Israel; another is the Jabok, when Yaakov faced Eisav. The very word Hebrew comes from crossing — Abraham was known as ha'Ivri. So a crossing is also establishing, or re-establishing, our identity in our own eyes and in other people's. The personal journey moves from the peace that comes with complete faith and with living in our homeland to re-establishing that identity in connection with the land, in the pioneers' phrase: livnot v'lehibanot, to build and to be built.

214.title: Accepting Greatness with Humility
body: Channah's third verse warns off pride: "Do not increasingly speak haughtily; Let not arrogance come out of your mouth, For the Lord is a God of thoughts, And to Him are deeds counted." Which is the horse again, looking to Hashem like a servant for all its strength. Israel's victory in the War of Independence came of His great mercy and is no reason for haughtiness.

The Pirkei Avot quality is that the Torah raises him above all creations. Even while it says that one who studies for its own sake is raised above everything, the word used is creations, Ma'assim, rather than things or people — which keeps the proportion right, since even the highest being is a minute creation beside the Creator. This is the very last of the qualities, the culmination of all the others.

Proverbs 31 begins with a king raised above everyone and chastised all the same by the one who gave him life: "The words of Lemuel the king; a prophecy that his mother chastised him; What, my son, and what, the son of my womb, and what, the son of my vows?" It is the last chapter of the book, and it closes with Eshet Chayil, an ode to the Torah itself.

The week holds many yahrzeits, among them two prominent students of the Maggid of Mezritch. Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk, on the 1st of Iyar, was an elder disciple of the Magid and one of the earliest Chasidic rebbes; he led the first modern aliyah to Israel, in 1777, where he and three hundred Chasidim and others settled in Tsefat, and after a few years they moved to Tiberias, where he is buried in the students of the Baal Shem Tov section of the Old Cemetery. His works include Pri HaAretz and Likutei Amarim. Rabbi Shmuel Shmelke HaLevi Horowitz of Nikolsburg, on the 2nd of Iyar, was a major disciple of the Maggid along with his younger brother Rabbi Pinchas, who became the Rabbi of Frankfort; many of the leading rebbes in Poland and Galitzia were originally his disciples, and among his books are Divrei Shmuel and Nazir HaShem. Also this week: Rabbi Chaim Vital, principal student of the Arizal, on the 30th of Nissan; Rabbi Yaakov Beirav, Chief Rabbi of Tzfat, and Rabbi Avraham of Slonim-Baranovich, the Beis Avrohom, on the 1st of Iyar; Rabbi Shmuel Eliyahu, son of Rabbi Shaul Yedidya Elazer Taub, the Modzhitzer Rebbe, on the 4th; Rabbi Chaim Meir Yechiel Shapira of Mogelnitz on the 5th; and Rabbi Yaakov Chaim Perlow, the Stoliner Rebbe, and Rabbi Yosef Meir Weiss on the 6th.

215.title: Strong and Praiseworthy
body: This week the Song's verses are all praise paid by the other nations, and a wish to cleave to the Jews. "How fair are your feet in sandals, O daughter of nobles! The curves of your thighs are like jewels, the handiwork of a craftsman." "Your navel is [like] a round basin, where no mixed wine is lacking; your belly is [like] a stack of wheat, fenced in with roses." "Your two breasts are like two fawns, the twins of a gazelle." That reads as rare and out of place, and it is exactly what happened after Yom Ha'Atzma'ut: for the first time in a long while, the Jews were widely admired, from 1948 onward. Rashi notes that where the Jewish people praise G-d from the top down, beginning at the head, the nations' praises of the Jewish people run from the bottom up, beginning at the feet — and the first praise after the War of Independence was for deeds and military might, which belong to the feet. The twins of a gazelle may be Iyar too: Yissachar and Zebulun, whose partnership was like twins.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the thirty-first is Elon, which means oak tree — majestic, large, strong, enduring. Elon Moreh is another name for Shechem, the first place Avraham visited, and Yaakov, and Yehoshua on entering the Land; and in modern times the first settlement established in Judea and Samaria after the Six Day War was Elon Moreh. Shechem is the gateway to the Land of Israel.

Daf Lamed Alef of Shvuot keeps on with the oath of a witness in court and with staying clear of falsehood, and takes up who is excluded from liability for a court oath, and mistakes made by accident or on purpose, Shogeg uMezid. The return to the Land is often discussed in Jewish law through the three oaths made during exile, one of them not to return by force. There is much debate over whether returning violated it, and if so whether, in the circumstances, anyone could be liable for it. Almost all opinions hold that it was not a violation.

Jeremiah's thirty-first chapter says it openly — a return, to build and be built. "Yet again will I rebuild you, then you shall be built, O virgin of Israel; yet again shall you be adorned with your tabrets, and you shall go out with the dances of those who make merry. Yet again shall you plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria." The call: "Rise! Let us go up to Zion, to the Lord, our God." The gathering, and who is in it: "Behold I bring them from the north country and gather them from the uttermost ends of the earth, the blind and the lame amongst them, the woman with child and she who travails with child all together; a great company shall they return there. With weeping will they come, and with supplications will I lead them, along brooks of water will I make them go, on a straight road upon which they will not stumble." The shepherd: "He Who scattered Israel will gather them together and watch them as a shepherd his flock." The turning: "I will turn their mourning into joy and will comfort them and make them rejoice from their sorrow." And then Rachel, and the answer to her: "A voice is heard on high, lamentation, bitter weeping, Rachel weeping for her children, she refuses to be comforted for her children for they are not. So says the Lord: Refrain your voice from weeping and your eyes from tears, for there is reward for your work, says the Lord, and they shall come back from the land of the enemy. And there is hope for your future, says the Lord, and the children shall return to their own border."

216.title: Reviewing the First Week of Iyar - Psalms 91-93; 90:11-13; 89:32
body: The first week of Iyar in psalms: the ninety-first, ninety-second and ninety-third, with three verses of Psalm 90 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 91 moves people to seek shelter under the wings of the Divine Presence. It also speaks of the four seasons of the year and their respective ministering powers, telling those who safeguard their souls to avoid them. "You who dwells in the shelter of the Most High, who abides in the shadow of the Omnipotent: I say of the Lord who is my refuge and my stronghold, my G-d in whom I trust, that He will save you from the ensnaring trap, from the destructive pestilence. He will cover you with His pinions and you will find refuge under His wings; His truth is a shield and an armor." Then the four times of danger: "You will not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow that flies by day; the pestilence that prowls in the darkness, nor the destruction that ravages at noon." Then the arithmetic of it: "A thousand may fall at your [left] side, and ten thousand at your right, but it shall not reach you." Then the angels: "For He will instruct His angels in your behalf, to guard you in all your ways. They will carry you in their hands, lest you injure your foot upon a rock. You will tread upon the lion and the viper." And the promise at the end: "When he calls on Me, I will answer him; I am with him in distress. I will deliver him and honor him. I will satiate him with long life, and show him My deliverance."

Psalm 92 the Levites sang every Shabbat in the Holy Temple; it speaks of the World to Come and comforts those crushed by suffering. "It is good to praise the Lord, and to sing to Your Name, O Most High; to proclaim Your kindness in the morning, and Your faithfulness in the nights." The thing a fool cannot see: "When the wicked thrive like grass, and all evildoers flourish-it is in order that they may be destroyed forever." And the tree that answers the grass: "The righteous will flourish like a palm tree, grow tall like a cedar in Lebanon. Planted in the House of the Lord, they shall blossom in the courtyards of our G-d. They shall be fruitful even in old age; they shall be full of sap and freshness- to declare that the Lord is just; He is my Strength, and there is no injustice in Him."

Psalm 93 is the Messianic era, when He will don grandeur and leave no room for a man to boast before Him as Nebuchadnezzar, Pharaoh and Sennacherib did. "The Lord is King; He has garbed Himself with grandeur; the Lord has robed Himself, He has girded Himself with strength; He has also established the world firmly that it shall not falter. Your throne stands firm from of old; You have existed forever." Then the rivers: "The rivers have raised, O Lord, the rivers have raised their voice; the rivers raise their raging waves. More than the sound of many waters, than the mighty breakers of the sea, is the Lord mighty on High."

Psalm 90's verses ask for the measure of a day: "Who can know the intensity of Your anger? Your wrath is commensurate with one's fear of You. Teach us, then, to reckon our days, that we may acquire a wise heart. Relent, O Lord; how long [will Your anger last]? Have compassion upon Your servants." And Psalm 89's verse continues last week's condition: "if they profane My statutes and do not observe My commandments."

217.title: The Horse is Saying
body: The horse opens, and the week sets the prancing of the mighty against the eyes of a servant.

The statutes and the prancings first: "If they profane My statutes and do not observe My commandments" / "By reason of the prancings" / "The prancings of their mighty ones" / "Do not increasingly speak haughtily" / "Let not arrogance come out of your mouth" / "[He is] the G-d Whose way is perfect" / "The word of the Lord is tried."

Then the shield, with the asking how long: "Your wrath is commensurate with one's fear of You" / "He is a shield unto all them that trust in Him" / "Relent, O Lord; how long? Have compassion upon Your servants" / "Who can know the intensity of Your anger?"

Then the servant's eyes, and the reckoning of days: "Behold, as the eyes of the servants to the hand of their master" / "So are our eyes to G-d our Lord until He will favor us" / "And Moses said to Aaron, Say to the entire community of the children of Israel" / "Teach us, then, to reckon our days" / "That we may acquire a wise heart."

Then the glory in the cloud, and the praises from the feet up: "And it came to pass when Aaron spoke to the entire community of the children of Israel" / "That they turned toward the desert, and behold! The glory of the Lord appeared in the cloud" / "How fair are your feet in sandals, O daughter of nobles!" / "As the eyes of the maidservant to the hand of her mistress" / "The curves of your thighs are like jewels, the handiwork of a craftsman" / "Your navel is a round basin, where no mixed wine is lacking" / "Your belly is [like] a stack of wheat, fenced in with roses" / "Your two breasts are like two fawns, the twins of a gazelle."

And the end is the curse on Meroz and the two rocks: "'Curse you Meroz,' said the messenger of the Lord" / "'Curse you bitterly inhabitants thereof'" / "For the Lord is a G-d of thoughts, and to Him are deeds counted" / "For their rock is not like our Rock" / "Nevertheless, our enemies sit in judgment" / "Draw near before the Lord, for He has heard your complaints."

218.title: To Recognize Deep in Our Heart How Small We Are, How Great G-d Is
body: The mule is saying, "All the kings of earth shall acknowledge You, G-d, for they have heard the sayings of Your mouth." (Psalms 138:4) The second week of Iyar, still joined to the miracles of Israel's independence — it was then that the right of the Jewish people to the Land of Israel was clearly recognised by the leaders of the world and the United Nations. A verse of the Psalms says, "Do not be like the horse or like the mule, without understanding." It took the nations a long time to understand that right, and for that brief moment in history the world did recognise it.

There is a contrast between this week's animal and next week's. The mule belongs to the gentile prophet Bilaam, whose mule spoke to him; the donkey belongs to Abraham, and to Moshe and Mashiach. The two lives run in parallel. Pirkei Avot teaches that Abraham and Bilaam are polar opposites: Abraham humble and the greatest source of blessing, Bilaam arrogant and the greatest source of curse. Rashi compares Abraham rising early to saddle his donkey, to go and sacrifice Isaac, with Bilaam rising early to saddle his mule, to meet Balak, bring sacrifices and try to curse the Jewish people. Abraham and his descendants were promised the Land; Balak and Bilaam did everything in their power to take it from them. In the end Bilaam was forced not only to recognise the glory of Israel but to praise it and bless it tremendously, and both he and Balak were later defeated by the conquering Israelites.

Iyar belongs to Issachar, whom the Torah calls a strong-boned donkey, and a mule is a donkey bred with a horse. The mule also carries this month's theme of deficiency and the need for healing: it cannot procreate.

Thirty-two is the thirty-two paths of wisdom, chochmah, named in Kabbalah. There are three opinions about Bilaam's connection to Laban: that Bilaam was Laban himself, or his son, or his grandson. Laban's name, Lamed Beit Nun, holds the thirty-two paths of wisdom, lamed beit, and the fifty gates of understanding, nun. Had Laban nullified himself before Yaakov, the tzadik of the generation, the evil in him would have been nullified and all those levels revealed in him.

Thirty-two is also lamed and beit, which spell lev, heart. Sometimes we understand something with the intellect and still cannot get the heart to understand it. For all the heart's stubbornness, in the end we will all acknowledge Hashem, as the mule's song says plainly. One way to hurry it is the saying of our sages the Lubavitcher Rebbe often quoted: words that come from the heart enter the heart. Lev is not only the physical organ; the heart of a thing is its essence. The Torah, which is the essence of Hashem, ends with lamed and begins with beit, which spells lev. The Land of Israel is the heart of our people, and Jerusalem is the heart of our heart. And in the episode of the spies, the only one besides Joshua who stood firmly for our ability to conquer the Land was called Kalev — the name itself shows his connection to our heart.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Levitas of Yavneh, who turns to the other side of the heart, the yetzer harah: be very, very humble, for the hope of mortal man is worms. The word he uses for man is enosh, the lowest of all the names for a human being: if we keep to our physical side, our only hope is to be food for worms. Attend to the soul instead, the divine part of us, and we will know how to use our hearts, and will be able to love our neighbour as ourselves. That is also the lesson of chapter 32, the lev of the Tanya. And it is close to the phrase Abraham is most famous for: "I am like dust and ashes" — dust, because man comes from dust and returns to it, and ashes, because Abraham and Sarah were sterile and could have no children, like the mule. And G-d is capable of anything: children for Abraham and Sarah, speech for a mule, the kings of the nations recognising His words, and Bilaam blessing Israel.

The combination is netzach shebehod. It takes great persistence to reach our own hearts. The mule is persistence and stubbornness itself. This week is also the yahrzeit of Eli the High Priest, on the 10th of Iyar: besides being Kohen Gadol he was leader of the generation, so he held both of these sefirot together — as Samuel, his disciple, also represents both, since the Book of Psalms equates him to Moses and to Aaron. Eli's death, falling backwards and breaking his neck on hearing the fate of the Mishkan, is close to next week's animal: the Torah commands that an owner who does not intend to redeem a firstborn donkey with a sacrifice must break the donkey's neck, and in Kabbalah the neck is the part of the body most associated with the Holy Temple and the Mishkan. The other animal with a commandment about breaking a neck is a female calf, in the case of an unexplained murder — and the mule is close to the donkey and female like the calf.

The lesson from the mule is that even kings, the rich and the powerful, must understand that they are completely subject to Hashem, who controls everyone without distinction. If anything a king is more subject than anyone, as Proverbs says: "A king's heart is like rivulets of water in the Lord's hand; wherever He wishes, He turns it."

219.title: Nahum and Light that Comes from Darkness
body: The second week of Iyar. Haazinu: "For their vine is of the vine of Sodom, and of the field of Gemorrah; their grapes are grapes of rosh, and they have bitter clusters." (Deuteronomy 32:32) Read of the Jewish people, their actions paralleled Sodom and Gemorrah and deserved great punishment. It can as easily be read of their enemies, following the verse just before it. And it can be read as the victory they won, which came out of enduring the suffering and the fermentation of Sodom, and the fields — the concentration camps — of Gemorrah: the strength came out of the bitterness. Rashi notes that the second half of the verse, and the next one, concern the suffering the Jews endured.

The Haftorah keeps to the positive: "For who is G-d, save the Lord? And who is a rock, save our G-d?" (II Samuel 22:32) He alone is G-d, and He alone is the Tzur. This week is bound to the one before it, Yom Ha'Atzma'ut, and to the one before that, Yom HaShoah.

The quality is loving G-d, ohev et HaMakom — and why that name for Him here? Perhaps because this week belongs to the Land of Israel, and it is in that place that we experience Him as fully as possible, as Yaakov did at Beit-El.

The prophet is Nahum, whose message is also that after great suffering He has redeemed the people and the Land, and so we show Him appreciation and love: "Behold on the mountains the feet of a herald announcing peace. O Judah, keep your feasts, pay your vows-for the wicked one shall no longer continue to pass through you; he has been completely cut off." And then: "Watch the way! Strengthen your loins! Fortify your power mightily. For the Lord has restored the pride of Jacob as the pride of Israel."

The levitical city is Dobrath, which means gathering a flock together — a perfect name for the week that marks the flock of the People of Israel gathered back to its Land. More fitting still, Dobrath is the name of a well-known kibbutz established in 1946, against much struggle and Arab opposition.
219.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 32.

220.title: Battling for the Land, Laying the Foundations
body: Like last week, this one is tied to Yom Ha'Atzmaut and the Land. Beshalach: "The Lord spoke to Moses, saying, I have heard the complaints of the children of Israel. Speak to them, saying, In the afternoon you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be sated with bread, and you shall know that I am the Lord, your G-d." He heard the complaints, and answered them mercifully and miraculously.

The Haftorah names again those who did not come: "because they came not to the aid of the Lord, to the aid of the Lord against the mighty." Why would He need aid in battle? Rashi states that those who aid Israel are as if they aid the Divine Presence. In 1948 the nations of the world did not come to Israel's aid. The Jewish people faced tremendous odds and came through by Divine mercy.

Daf Lamed Beit of Sotah takes up invalid witnesses, and the statements that must be said in Hebrew to be valid, and the blessings and curses said at Mount Grizim and Mount Eival when the people entered the Land. Entering the Land is this week; and the Hebrew may point to the renewal of the everyday use of the language.

The generation is Yishai, son of Obed and father of King David, and he was great in many ways. He is one of the eight princes of man in Micha according to Sukkah. He went out at the head of a multitude of followers and returned with a multitude, and he taught Torah to a multitude. He inspired David to fight Goliath. Four people died solely because of the serpent's advice to Eve, having never sinned, and Ishai was one of them. The Sages said that Ishai lived more than 400 years. He is identified as Beis haLachmi, usually rendered as from Beis Lechem, Bethlehem. Radak quotes a Midrashic reading of that term: after David killed Goliath, King Saul asked who David was, which is puzzling since he already knew — so some read the question as whether he was the scion of a powerful line, and David answered that he was a son of Yishai Beis haLachmi, meaning a man of war, from Milchamah.

This is week 32, whose gematria is lev, heart. Yishai, spelled yud, shin, yud, has the gematria of 320, ten times Lev. His name reads as Yesh Yud, there is Yud, perhaps the 32 paths of Chochmah, which are also Lev. Yishai laid the foundations for his son David to be king, as the pioneering generation that made the return possible laid the foundations for a redemption still to come. And like Israel's pioneers, he was a man of war.

The journey is from Abronah to Etzion geber, which means the crow of the rooster, and may also mean the wisdom of the rooster. The personal journey moves from re-establishing our identity with the land to the spiritual awakening of Lag Ba'omer, when we open ourselves to the inner wisdom of the Kabbalah.

221.title: Ups and Downs
body: Channah's fourth verse turns everything over: "The bows of the mighty are broken; And those who stumbled, are girded with strength." Which is an accurate description of what happened in 1948.

From here Pirkei Avot stops describing those who study Torah for its own sake and takes up verses on the greatness of the Torah itself, which gives life to its observers in this world and in the World To Come: "For they are life to he who finds them, and a healing to all his flesh." The first verse is life and the healing of flesh. At independence the Jewish people were broken, and somehow gathered strength and found life and healing. The same can be said of Channah.

And the readings move from Proverbs to Ecclesiastes. Its first chapter is the world going round in circles, with its ups and downs: the wicked may be on top for a time, and they fall in the end, and life and endurance go to those who stay humble. "The words of Koheleth son of David, king in Jerusalem." Rashi reads the opening that way — the sun rises, all the rivers run into the sea — and says he calls the wicked the sun, the moon and the sea, which have no reward; so it was taught in Sifrei, that the section deals with the wicked and compares them to the rising of the sun, which ultimately sets. Then: "A generation goes and a generation comes, but the earth endures forever." Rashi: however much a wicked man toils and labours to oppress and to rob, he does not outlive his works, for the generation goes and another comes and takes it all from his sons. And who are the ones who endure? The humble and low, who bring themselves down to the earth, as it says, "But the humble shall inherit the earth." And the Midrash Tanhuma states that all the righteous of Israel are called earth, as it is said, "for you shall be a desirable land." Then: "It goes to the south and goes around to the north; the will goes around and around, and the will returns to its circuits." Rashi again: however much the sun of the wicked rises, it will set; however much power they gain, they return to the place of filth they came from.

The week holds many yahrzeits, among them the founders of two prominent Chassidic lines. Rabbi Yitzchak Isaac Yehuda Yechiel Safrin ben Alexander Sender of Komarno, on the 10th of Iyar, was one of the most prolific and respected expounders of the Kabbalah teachings of the Baal Shem Tov. He insisted that every Jew should study the Zohar and the Writings of the Arizal, and emphasised the importance of Kabbalistic meditation. A close disciple of Rebbe Tzvi Hersh from Zhiditchov — Komarno is considered a branch of Zhiditchov — he was a hidden ascetic for many years, and only later, as Rebbe of thousands of chasidim, became known for his genius, piety and ability to work wonders. He wrote volumes on Jewish mysticism and on Mishnah and law; his commentaries include Heichal HaBrachah on the Torah, Otzar HaChaim on the commandments, and Zohar Chai on the Zohar.

Rabbi Naftali of Ropshitz, on the 11th of Iyar, was born on the same day the Besht passed away, and became rebbe to many thousands. Deciding to join the chassidic movement, he chose Rabbi Elimelech of Lizensk as his mentor, and then became a dedicated chasid of the three patriarchs: the Chozeh of Lublin, the Maggid of Koznitz, and Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Rymanov. During the Napoleonic wars the Tzaddikim were divided over Napoleon. Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Rymanov strongly supported him and held that the wars were Gog and Magog, a prelude to the Messiah; his disciple Rabbi Naftali, and Rabbi Shneur Zalman, the Baal HaTanya, were strongly opposed, sensing that a victory would bring changes that would threaten the community's way of life. After those three passed away he settled in Ropshitz, which became the focal point for thousands of chassidim. Ropshitz chassidut is known for its captivating niggunim, melodies of ecstasy and of yearning for nearness to G-d. He is a crucial figure in the development of Galician Chassidut, and many minhagei Ropshitz are followed in Galicia. He was known for profound wisdom, a sharp sense of humour and musical gifts, and was a master of kabbalistic interpretation; his demeanour, sermons and witticisms hid a depth that only his closest students could reach, foremost among them Rabbi Chaim of Tzanz. Some of his teachings are in Zera Kodesh, Ayalah Sheluchah and Imrei Shefer, and many stories about him are in Ohel Naftoli.

Also this week: Rabbi Yerachmiel Rabinowitz of Peshischa, son of the Yid HaKadosh, and Rabbi Moshe Mordechai Twersky of Lublin-Trisk, both on the 8th of Iyar; Rabbi David Twerski of Tolna, son of Rabbi Mordechai of Chernobyl, on the 10th; and Rabbi Masoud Abuchatzeira, son of the Abir Yaakov and father of the Baba Sali, on the 12th.

222.title: Securing Our Connection to the Land in the Face of the Enemy
body: The Song's verses are the nations' praises again, and they are full of places in the region, where so many came to attack us: "Your neck is like an ivory tower; your eyes are [like] pools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bath-Rabbim; your face is as the tower of Lebanon, facing towards Damascus." "Your head upon you is like Carmel, and the braided locks of your head are like purple; the king is bound in the tresses." "How fair and how pleasant you are, a love with delights!" Heshbon is in Jordan; and there is Lebanon, and Damascus.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the thirty-second is Jahleel, whose name means to wait for, to yearn for G-d. Yachel also carries forgiveness, and nullification, and desecration. This week is about the nations finally acknowledging Israel after so many years, and its animal is the mule, which belongs to Bilaam — who was trying to nullify the oath G-d made to Abraham, and was in many ways the anti-Abraham. And it is the heart, since 32 is Lev. We yearn for Hashem with all our hearts and to return to our land, and in that, He nullifies those who fight our connection to the Land of Israel.
Daf Lamed Beit of Shevuoth keeps on with who is excluded from liability for a court oath — which is last week's three oaths again.

Jeremiah's thirty-second chapter says the return openly, and the prophet himself is told to redeem his family's portion of the Land by buying it. "Behold, Hanamel, the son of Shallum your uncle, is coming to you, saying: Buy for yourself my field that is in Anathoth, for the right of redemption is yours to buy it." Then the deed, witnessed and put away to last: "Take these scrolls, this deed of purchase and the signed one and this open scroll, and put them into an earthen vessel so that they remain many years. For so says the Lord of Hosts, the God of Israel; Houses and fields and vineyards shall be purchased again in this land." Then the gathering: "Behold I will gather them from all the lands where I have driven them with My anger and with My wrath and with great fury, and I will restore them to this place and I will cause them to dwell safely. And they shall be My people, and I will be their God." Then the covenant: "And I will form for them an everlasting covenant, that I will not turn away from them to do them good, and My fear I will place in their heart, not to turn away from Me. And I will rejoice over them to do good to them, and I will plant them in this land truly with all My heart and with all My soul." And the measure of it: "As I have brought upon this people all this great evil, so will I bring upon them all the good that I speak concerning them." And the fields bought in a land now called desolate: "Men shall buy fields for money and inscribe deeds and sign [them] and appoint witnesses in the land of Benjamin and in the environs of Jerusalem."

223.title: Reviewing the Second Week of Iyar - Psalms 94-96; 90:14-16; 89:33
body: The second week of Iyar in psalms: the ninety-fourth, ninety-fifth and ninety-sixth, with three verses of Psalm 90 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 94 is a prayer any individual can use for the redemption, and an important moral teaching with it. "The Lord is a G-d of retribution; O G-d of retribution, reveal Yourself! Judge of the earth, arise; render to the arrogant their recompense. How long shall the wicked, O Lord, how long shall the wicked exult?" What they do, and what they say about it: "They kill the widow and the stranger, and murder the orphans. And they say, 'The Lord does not see, the G-d of Jacob does not perceive.'" Then the answer, which is made of questions: "Shall He who implants the ear not hear? Shall He who forms the eye not see? Shall He who chastises nations not punish?" Then the fortunate man: "Fortunate is the man whom You chastise, O Lord, and instruct him in Your Torah, bestowing upon him tranquillity in times of adversity, until the pit is dug for the wicked. For the Lord will not abandon His people, nor forsake His heritage." And the holding up: "When I thought that my foot was slipping, Your kindness, O Lord, supported me. When my [worrisome] thoughts multiply within me, Your consolation delights my soul."

Psalm 95 speaks of the time when a man will say to his fellow, come, let us sing and offer praise to G-d for the miracles He has done for us. "Come, let us sing to the Lord; let us raise our voices in jubilation to the Rock of our deliverance." Whose everything is: "in His hands are the depths of the earth, and the heights of the mountains are His. Indeed, the sea is His, for He made it; His hands formed the dry land." Then the flock, and the condition: "For He is our G-d, and we are the people that He tends, the flock under His [guiding] hand-even this very day, if you would but hearken to His voice!" And the warning from the wilderness: "Do not harden your heart as at Merivah, as on the day at Massah in the wilderness, where your fathers tested Me; they tried Me, though they had seen My deeds. For forty years I quarreled with that generation."

Psalm 96 is the same time coming: come, let us sing to G-d. "Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth. Sing to the Lord, bless His Name; proclaim His deliverance from day to day. Recount His glory among the nations, His wonders among all the peoples." Then the call to the families of nations to bring an offering and come to His courtyards. And then the whole world joining in, which is how it ends: "The heavens will rejoice, the earth will exult; the sea and its fullness will roar. The fields and everything therein will jubilate; then all the trees of the forest will sing. Before the Lord [they shall rejoice], for He has come, for He has come to judge the earth; He will judge the world with justice, and the nations with His truth."

Psalm 90's verses ask for joy to match the affliction: "Satiate us in the morning with Your kindness, then we shall sing and rejoice throughout our days. Give us joy corresponding to the days You afflicted us, the years we have seen adversity. Let Your work be revealed to Your servants, and Your splendor be upon their children." And Psalm 89's verse completes the condition of the last two weeks: "then I will punish their transgression with the rod and their misdeeds with plagues."

224.title: The Mule Is Saying
body: The mule opens, and the week sets broken bows against the kings who acknowledge Him.

The breaking and the acknowledging first: "The bows of the mighty are broken" / "And those who stumbled, are girded with strength" / "All the kings of earth shall acknowledge You, G-d" / "For they have heard the sayings of Your mouth."

Then the towers and the pools, with the asking for joy: "Your neck is like an ivory tower" / "Your eyes are [like] pools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bath-Rabbim" / "Your face is as the tower of Lebanon, facing towards Damascus" / "Your head upon you is like Carmel" / "Give us joy corresponding to the days You afflicted us" / "The years we have seen adversity."

Then the vine of Sodom, and those who did not come: "For their vine is of the vine of Sodom" / "And of the field of Gemorrah" / "Because they came not to the aid of the Lord" / "To the aid of the Lord against the mighty" / "For who is G-d, save the Lord?" / "And who is a rock, save our G-d?"

Then the braided locks, and the splendour upon the children: "And the braided locks of your head are like purple" / "The king is bound in the tresses" / "Let Your work be revealed to Your servants" / "And Your splendor be upon their children."

And the end is the meat and the bread, with the bitter clusters between: "The Lord spoke to Moses, saying, I have heard the complaints of the children of Israel" / "Their grapes are grapes of rosh, and they have bitter clusters" / "Speak to them, saying, 'In the afternoon you shall eat meat'" / "'And in the morning you shall be sated with bread'" / "Satiate us in the morning with Your kindness" / "Then we shall sing and rejoice throughout our days" / "And you shall know that I am the Lord, your G-d" / "How fair and how pleasant you are, A love of delights!"

225.title: To Recognize the Spiritual Treasures Hidden within Each One of Us
body: Week thirty-three is the week of Pesach Sheini and Lag Ba'Omer. Lag Ba'Omer is a day of great celebration, because it was then that the students of Rabbi Akiva stopped perishing. It is also the yahrzeit of Rabbi Shimon Bar Yochai — Yesod ha'Olam, the foundation of the world — and the custom is to light a bonfire in his honor, representing the great light he brought to the world through his teachings of Kabbalah.

In Perek Shirah the creature of this week is the donkey, which proclaims: “Yours, O Lord, are the greatness, and the might, and the glory, and the victory, and the majesty, for all that is in the heavens and on the earth is Yours; Yours is the kingdom and You are He Who is exalted over everything as the Leader.” (I Chronicles 29:11) King David recited this verse when he was at the height of his glory, reiterating that everything is from Hashem: glory and kingship, the Heavens and the earth.

In the Counting of the Omer this is the week of hod, acknowledgement — Hod shebeHod — so it is quite appropriate that the song of the donkey should so gracefully acknowledge that everything comes from G-d. The song contains all seven emotional sefirot: gedulah is a reference to chesed; then come gevurah, tiferet, netzach and hod; hakol is a reference to yesod; and mamlachah, a reference to malchut.

From Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Yochanan the son of Berokah: whoever desecrates the Divine Name covertly is punished in public, and regarding the desecration of the Name the malicious and the merely negligent are one and the same.
Pesach Sheini is the yahrzeit of Rabbi Meir.

226.title: Chabakuk and Torah that Comes from Suffering
body: The thirty-third week is the week of Pesach Sheini and Lag Ba'Omer, and in Haazinu the verse speaks again of the bitter punishment faced by the Jewish people, comparing it to wine: “Their wine is the bitterness of serpents, and the bitterness of the ruthless cobras.” (Deuteronomy 32:33) Read in a positive light, their deep Torah wisdom came from the bitter serpents, and their ability to be a head — to have a deep mind — from dealing with ruthless cobras.

Wine is also a known metaphor for the essence and the hidden part of the Torah, associated primarily with the works of Rabbi Shimon Bar Yochai. The joy of Lag Ba'Omer comes in contrast to the suffering and the mourning of the Omer period, with the passing of twenty-four thousand of Rabbi Akiva's students. Rabbi Shimon Bar Yochai himself acquired this wine through much suffering, and in the end he said that the suffering he endured was very much worth it.

The haftorah verse: “G-d is He who has fortified me with strength; and He looseth perfectly my path.” (II Samuel 22:33) The word for strength is chayil, a known reference to the Torah, the source of King David's power. The verse also carries a word written differently from how it is spoken — darchoh, His way, rather than darchi, my way — so that it reads: G-d makes clear to me His perfect way. The word for perfect is tamim, itself a reference to the Torah, as David says, Torat Hashem Tmimah Meshivat Nafesh.
The quality of this week is Ohev et HaBriot, loving the creations, the third term Rabbi Meir uses of those who study Torah lishmah. The prophet is Chabakuk; the Levitical city, Jarmuth.
226.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 33.

227.title: Blessed Above All Others
body: Week thirty-three is the week of Pesach Sheini and Lag Ba'Omer, and the Torah portion section for this week first introduces the Mannah: “It came to pass in the evening that the quails went up and covered the camp, and in the morning there was a layer of dew around the camp.
