The layer of dew went up, and behold, on the surface of the desert, a fine, bare substance as fine as frost on the ground.”

The Mannah is fine as frost and compared to the dew, in contrast with the physicality of the quail. That contrast is also one between the revealed Torah, nigleh, and the Kabbalah, nistar. In nigleh there is back and forth and room for digestion — setting aside certain opinions and coming to conclusions. When it comes to Kabbalah there is no need for separating the good from the bad. There is also an opinion that the Mannah began falling on Lag Ba'Omer, and that this is the reason for its celebration.

The haftorah: “Blessed above women shall Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, be; above women in the tent shall she be blessed.” The women in the tent are a reference to the blessings given to the matriarchs (Talmud, Sanhedrin 105). Similarly, Rabbi Shimon Bar Yochai is said to be praiseworthy above all of his colleagues.

Daf Lamed Gimmel of Sotah continues the discussion of statements that must be said in Hebrew to be valid and those that may be said in any language, and the blessings and curses said at Mount Grizim and Mount Eival. It goes into the language of angels and heavenly voices, and contains a story of what Shimon HaTzadik heard in the Kodesh HaKodashim.
The generation is David. The journey: they journeyed from Ezion geber and camped in the desert of Zin, which is Kadesh.

228.title: Health
body: Channah's fifth verse keeps last week's reversals going and turns them to the body: "They that were full have hired out themselves for bread; and they that were hungry have ceased; while the barren hath borne seven, she that had many children hath languished." Physical wealth and health, and above all the ability to have children.
Pirkei Avot, on the greatness of the Torah, stays physical too, and seems to point the same way: "It shall be health to your navel, and marrow to your bones."

Ecclesiastes 2 is the pleasures of the body and physical wealth, told by the one man who could afford all of them. "I said to myself, 'Come now, I will mix [wine] with joy and experience pleasure'; and behold, this too was vanity. Of laughter, I said, '[It is] mingled'; and concerning joy, 'What does this accomplish?'" Then the building: "I made myself great works; I built myself houses, and I planted myself vineyards. I made myself gardens and orchards, and I planted in them all sorts of fruit trees. I made myself pools of water, to water from them a forest sprouting with trees." Then the having: slaves and household and cattle and flocks, silver and gold and the treasures of kings and provinces, every kind of musical instrument, wagons and coaches — "So I became great, and I increased more than all who were before me in Jerusalem; also my wisdom remained with me. And [of] all that my eyes desired I did not deprive them; I did not deprive my heart of any joy." And then the accounting: "Then I turned [to look] at all my deeds that my hands had wrought and upon the toil that I had toiled to do, and behold everything is vanity and frustration, and there is no profit under the sun."

The week holds many yahrzeits, among them two prominent rebbes of the Chernobyl line. Rabbi Mordechai, Mottel, of Chernobyl, on the 20th of Iyar, succeeded his father Rabbi Nachum, and was the son-in-law of Rabbi Aharon the Great of Karlin and afterwards of Rabbi David Seirkes, an important disciple of the Baal Shem Tov. All eight of his sons became major Chasidic leaders. One of them, Yaakov Yisrael Twerski of Cherkassy, the first Hornsteipel Rebbe, married Devora Leah, one of the six daughters of Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch, son of Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi — a match the two grandfather-Rebbes arranged, to make the most of the prediction that the Moshiach would be born of the elder disciple of the Maggid of Mezritch or the youngest. His grandson, named after him, Rabbi Mordechai, Mottele, Twersky of Rachmistrivka, on the 17th of Iyar, moved to Jerusalem from Europe in 1908; he was known for a sharp mind, and many businessmen sought his advice, and he was himself a skilled craftsman who did complex engravings in silver and copper. His father, Rabbi Yochanan Twerski, son of the famous Rebbe Mottele of Chernobyl, was the first Rebbe of Rachmistrivka.

Also this week: R' Chaim Meir Yechiel Shapira, the Saraph of Moglenitz, and Rabbi Shmuel of Karov-Vinagrov on the 15th of Iyar; Rabbi Moshe Chaim Ephraim of Sudylkov, the Degel Machaneh Ephraim, on the 17th; Rabbi Moshe Isserles, the Ramah, on the 18th; Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Riminov and Rabbi Shmuel Abuchatzeira, forefather of the Abuchatzeira dynasty, on the 19th; and Rabbi Yechi ben R' Avrohom Abuchatzeira on the 20th.

229.title: The Tzadik
body: Lag Ba'Omer, and the counting enters a new stretch in which most people stop all signs of mourning. The Song changes speakers with it. Rashi: until this point the nations praise Him; from here on are the words of the Shechinah, to reveal Israel, who are among the nations. And Lag Ba'Omer is a day of tremendous revelation, the day of the Tzadik Yesod Olam, Rabbi Shimon Bar Yochai.

The verses are the palm. "This, your stature, is like a palm tree, and your breasts are like clusters [of dates]. I said: Let me climb up the palm tree, let me seize its boughs, and let your breasts be now like clusters of the vine and the fragrance of your countenance like [that of] apples." The Tamar is the metaphor for the upright Tzadik Yesod Olam, and the vav, which is Yesod, stands upright too; in Perek Shirah the Tamar's own verse is "Tzadik KaTamar Yifrach, K'Erez BaLevanon Yizgueh." The vine is the hidden Torah, and the fragrance of apples is the fragrance of Gan Eden, which is known to be like an apple orchard. The third verse belongs here as well: "And your palate is like the best wine, that glides down smoothly to my beloved, making the lips of the sleeping speak." That is revelation — the inner secrets that gave the Jewish people life in times when they were spiritually asleep, and made their lips speak.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the thirty-third is Dinah, the last directly descended from Leah; from here the count turns to Rachel's descendants, beginning with Joseph's family. The first listed, after Rachel, Joseph and Binyamin, who are left for the end, is Joseph's wife, Asenath daughter of Poti-phera Chief of On, whom the Midrash teaches is Dinah's own daughter.

The lesson of the Counting of the Omer and of Lag Ba'Omer is love and respect for one another, and Dinah is the great example of it. Leah foresaw that Dinah was to have been a boy, and prayed that she be turned into a girl so that Rachel could still merit two sons, founders of tribes. Asenath — daughter of Dinah, who came from Leah, and mother of Efraim and Menasheh by Joseph, who came from Rachel — holds that same union; and Efraim and Menashe are the link between the two sides of the people, Rachel and Leah, Yehudah and Yosef, which is why Jacob says those two will be to him like Reuven and Shimon. Dinah endured a great deal and was redeemed in the end, marrying Shimon and seeing her daughter marry Joseph. Dinah means judgement, strictness, and the Hey at the end of her name adds mercy. Asenath's name is harsh too: "And Dinah gave birth to a daughter and named her Asenat, saying, 'To my woe did I bear her for Shechem the son of Chamor who had taken me by force to his house.'" And her name carries an added Heh as well, since she is not called Bat Potiphar but Bat Potipherah.

Daf Lamed Gimmel of Shvuot keeps on with who is excluded from liability for a court oath, especially where there are two pairs of witnesses, with a long discussion of liability for fines, of claiming on behalf of someone else, and of oaths applying only to monetary claims. Lag Ba'Omer is the day we celebrate how the merit of Rabbi Shimon Bar Yochai and his son, Rabbi Elazar, spared the whole world from judgement: in Rabbi Shimon's days there was never a rainbow in the sky, because the rainbow is the reminder of the oath never to destroy the world again, and in his time no such sign was needed. Fittingly, one of the main principles of this daf comes from an opinion of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon Bar Yochai, and the next daf opens with words of Rabbi Shimon Bar Yochai himself.

Jeremiah's thirty-third chapter is joy after desolation, and purification from sin, with the House of David and the Kohanim in it, and even the idea of counting. Iyar is a month of healing and Lag Ba'Omer a day of festivity, weddings among them. "Behold, I will bring it healing and cure, and I will cure them, and I will reveal to them a greeting of peace and truth." "And I will purify them of all their iniquity that they sinned against Me." Then the sound returning to the empty streets: "There shall again be heard in this place, concerning which you say, 'It is desolate without man and without beast,' in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem that are desolate... the sound of mirth and the sound of joy, the voice of a bridegroom and the voice of a bride, the sound of those saying, 'Thank the Lord of Hosts, for the Lord is good, for His loving-kindness endures forever.'" Then the shepherds, and the counting: "flocks shall again pass under the hands of one who counts them." And the plant: "In those days and in that time I will cause to grow for David a plant of righteousness, and he shall execute justice and righteousness in the land." And the two lines that will not be cut off, the throne and the priesthood.

230.title: Reviewing the Third Week of Iyar - Psalms 97-99; 90:17, 105:1-2; 89:34
body: The third week of Iyar in psalms: the ninety-seventh, ninety-eighth and ninety-ninth, with the last verse of Psalm 90, the opening of Psalm 105, and one verse of Psalm 89.

Psalm 97 is the revealing of His kingship. "When the Lord will reveal His kingship, the earth will exult; the multitudes of islands will rejoice. Clouds and dense darkness will surround Him; justice and mercy will be the foundation of His throne." Then the melting: "The mountains will melt like wax before the Lord, before the Master of all the earth." Then the idols: "All who worship graven images, who take pride in idols, will be ashamed." And the end, which is sown rather than given: "You who love the Lord, hate evil; He watches over the souls of His pious ones, He saves them from the hand of the wicked. Light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart."

Psalm 98 is how Israel will praise Him for the Redemption. "Sing to the Lord a new song, for He has performed wonders; His right hand and holy arm have wrought deliverance for Him." Then the seeing of it: "He has made known His salvation; He has revealed His justice before the eyes of the nations. He has remembered His kindness and faithfulness to the House of Israel; all, from the farthest corners of the earth, witnessed the deliverance by our G-d." Then the instruments — harp, trumpets, the sound of the shofar — and then the world joining: "The sea and its fullness will roar in joy, the earth and its inhabitants. The rivers will clap their hands, the mountains will sing together."

Psalm 99 refers to the wars of Gog and Magog, which come before the Redemption. "When the Lord will reveal His kingship, the nations will tremble; the earth will quake before Him Who is enthroned upon the cherubim." Then the three who were answered: "Moses and Aaron among His priests, and Samuel among those who invoke His Name, would call upon the Lord and He would answer them. He would speak to them from a pillar of cloud; they observed His testimonies and the decrees which He gave them." And both halves of the answer: "Lord our G-d, You have answered them; You were a forgiving G-d for their sake, yet bringing retribution for their own misdeeds."

Psalm 90 ends here, on our own hands: "And may the pleasantness of the Lord our G-d be upon us, and the work of our hands establish for us, and the work of our hands establish it." Psalm 105 begins: "Give thanks to the Lord, call out in His name; make His deeds known among the peoples. Sing to Him, play music to Him, speak of all His wonders." And Psalm 89's verse holds, as it has through the condition of the last three weeks: "But I shall not cancel My kindness from him, and I shall not betray My faith."

231.title: The Donkey is Saying
body: The donkey opens with everything being His, and the week's books come in around it.

The greatness and the palm first: "Yours, G-d, is the greatness, and the might" / "And the splendor, and the victory, and the glory" / "This, your stature, is like a palm tree" / "And your breasts are like clusters [of dates]" / "Sing to Him, play music to Him, speak of all His wonders" / "For everything in the Heavens and earth [is Yours]" / "Yours, G-d, is the kingship, and the exaltation over all."

Then the blessing on Jael, with the bitter wine: "Blessed above women shall Jael" / "The wife of Heber the Kenite, be" / "Their wine is the bitterness of serpents" / "And the bitterness of the ruthless cobras" / "While the barren hath borne seven" / "She that had many children hath languished."

Then the clusters and the apples, and the strength: "And let your breasts be now like clusters of the vine" / "And the fragrance of your countenance like apples" / "Above women in the tent shall she be blessed" / "G-d is He who has fortified me with strength" / "And He loosened perfectly my path" / "And may the pleasantness of the Lord our G-d be upon us."

Then the quails and the dew, with the kindness not cancelled: "It came to pass in the evening that the quails went up and covered the camp" / "But I shall not cancel My kindness from him" / "And I shall not betray My faith" / "And in the morning there was a layer of dew around the camp" / "The layer of dew went up" / "I said: Let me climb up the palm tree" / "Let me seize its boughs" / "And behold, on the surface of the desert, a fine bare [substance] as fine as frost on the ground."

And the end is the hungry who have ceased, and the work of our hands: "They that were full have hired out themselves for bread" / "And they that were hungry have ceased" / "Give thanks to the Lord, call out in His name" / "Make His deeds known among the peoples" / "And the work of our hands establish for us" / "And the work of our hands establish it."

232.title: To Work in a Focused Manner and without Ego
body: The ox is saying, "Then Moses and the Children of Israel sang this song to G-d, and they said, I shall sing to G-d, for He has triumphed; He has thrown the horse and its rider into the sea." (Exodus 15:1) The month of Iyar is linked to Taurus, and the ox is the last of the farm animals to sing, with a verse from the opening of the Song of the Sea.

The sheep and the goat, the first farm animals, also sang a verse from the Song of the Sea, on Rosh Chodesh Nissan. The cow, which came next, sang a verse that calls the people Jacob, the more fragile and humble side — Yaakov is from Ekev, heel. The ox uses the name Israel, the stronger side. Across this journey of liberation, from the start of Nissan until now, we make the whole transformation from Jacob to Israel. The Hebrew for ox is Shor, which is near Shir, song, and Yashar, upright — and Israel itself reads as Yashar-El, the upright one of G-d, and, with the letters turned around, Shir-El, the song of G-d, and even Li-Rosh, to me is the head. The ox's song is in the future tense, which points to the World to Come.

There is the same journey inside Iyar. The first animal of the month was the horse, and now at its end the ox sings about the horse and its rider being thrown into the sea. Both are strength. But the horse's power is a somewhat unrestrained military might, where the ox is marked by humbly accepting its yoke; the ox's meat is kosher and the horse's is not. That firm acceptance of the yoke of Heaven is what is most precious in His eyes. The ox belongs to the conquest of the Land too, which is this month: "Moab became terrified of the people, for they were numerous, and Moab became disgusted because of the children of Israel. Moab said to the elders of Midian, 'Now this assembly will eat up everything around us, as the ox eats up the greens of the field.'" And Joseph is called an ox, and Joshua descended directly from Joseph.

Thirty-four is twice 17, the gematria of tov, good — the 17 years Jacob lived with Joseph in Israel and the 17 more he lived with Joseph in Egypt, the best years of his life. It is also the gematria of Vayechi, the portion that tells of Jacob's passing. So 34 is that journey from Yaakov to Yisrael, and the healing Jacob found on being reunited with his son. And it is the gematria of ga'al, redeemed.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yossi: one who learns Torah in order to teach is given the opportunity to learn and teach; one who learns in order to do is given the opportunity to learn, teach, observe and do. That bears on the death of Rabbi Akiva's students during the omer. They died because they did not respect one another enough: those who thought they knew more believed the respect should come to them rather than from them. The thing that matters in learning is learning in order to teach and to do, not in order to feed one's own ego — which leads a person to think his knowledge makes him better than others, and defeats the whole purpose of having learned.

The combination is yesod shebehod. Joseph, who is yesod, is called an ox by Jacob in the blessing on his deathbed, in the portion of Vayechi. The lesson from the ox is to work on ourselves in a concentrated and humble way, remembering His omnipotence — and to keep in mind that He saved us from our enemies before, and does it again in every generation, so there is nothing to fear.

233.title: Zephaniah and Loving Tzedakot
body: The last week of Iyar. Haazinu asks a question: "Is it not stored up with Me, sealed up in My treasuries?" (Deuteronomy 32:34) By Rashi's plain reading, the sins of the Jewish people have not been forgotten; He has stored and preserved them. And there is room for another reading, because why would sins be sealed in His treasuries, which implies something He treasures rather than something He despises? Perhaps what is stored is not their sins but their suffering for His sake, which He does treasure. And that suffering gives access to His treasuries, as it did for Rabbi Shimon Bar Yochai, and to the return to the Holy Land.

The Haftorah: "He makes my feet like hinds; And sets me upon my high places." (II Samuel 22:34) He set King David in Jerusalem, Ir David, which stands on a mountain, Mount Zion. As in the verse before it, the kri differs from the ksiv: it is read as making David's feet swift like hinds, presumably for battle, and the ksiv speaks instead of G-d's feet. The Torah says the Earth is the place of His feet, and His representatives on Earth are the Jewish people; Moshe once calls them feet. The word for hinds, Ayalot, is spelled like Ayalut, strength — as in Psalm 22, with Ayaluti, my strength — so the first half can read that He gives the people the power to overcome the enemy and conquer the Land, which fits the second half, David established in Jerusalem. It also recalls Moshe's final blessing, "Ve Atah Al Bamoeimoh Tidroch," and you shall trample upon their high places, which Rashi reads as Yehoshua, commanded in the conquest to place his own feet on the neck of the Cana'anite enemies — and the neck is also the Temple. And there is an almost identical verse at the end of Chabakuk's prayer, last week's prophet, where G-d comes gloriously to save the people and their anointed leader: "G-d the Lord is my strength. He made my feet [as swift] as the hind's, and he guides me on my high places. To the conductor [to play] with my melodies!"

Perhaps because Lag Ba'omer has passed, the quality is no longer one of the marks of someone who studies Torah for its own sake, though love continues in it: loves the ways of righteousness, ohev et hatzedakot. Righteousness stands in the plural and the feminine, which suggests it should also be read as loving the many givings of tzedakah. Charity is called tzedakah because it is not first of all an act of generosity but an act of righteousness and justice. It is a quality found in every Jew, not only the observant ones — plainly so in the efforts to support the Jews of the Holy Land, and in the Zionist endeavour as a whole.

The prophet is Zephaniah, whose prophecy is full of it. "Seek the Lord, all you humble of the earth who executed His judgment; Seek righteousness, seek humility! Perhaps you will be concealed on the day of the Lord's wrath." "The Lord is just in her midst; He commits no injustice. Every morning He brings His judgment to light. It does not fail. But the one who commits injustice knows no shame." "The remnant of Israel shall neither commit injustice nor speak lies; neither shall deceitful speech be found in their mouth, for they shall graze and lie down, with no one to cause them to shudder." He also names what tzedakah stands against, the lust for money and the trust placed in it: "Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to save them on the day of the Lord's wrath."

The levitical city is 'Ein Gannim, the fountain of gardens. Ein also means eye, and it is the letter Ayin, whose value is seventy; one who gives tzedakah generously is said to have an Ayin Tovah. The Tanya draws the connection between Tzedakah and gardens — the Upper and the Lower Garden of Eden — and the letter Ayin. Charity is greater than all the commandments, because performing them produces garments for the soul: garments that let the soul withstand the intense Divine revelation it will meet in Gan Eden instead of being nullified by it, drawn from the light of the Ein Sof, so that having an infinite source they can bear an infinite revelation. And this is the meaning of "He who sows tzedakot brings forth yeshuot," salvations — the drawing down of the light of the shin-ayin nehorin, the three hundred and seventy lights spoken of in the holy Zohar: shin, three hundred, for the three intellectual faculties of ChaBaD at the level called hundreds, and ayin, seventy, for the seven emotive attributes, each holding ten. That illumination, the helmet of salvation, is drawn onto the head, the beginning, of the Ten Sefirot.

Like Dobrath, 'Ein Gannim has its own connection to the Zionist endeavour: it was the name of Israel's first Moshav Poalim, a worker's settlement, a model a little different from the kibbutz, and among its residents were prominent members of the Zionist movement, David Ben-Gurion among them.
233.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 34.

234.title: Feeling "Shalem" (Whole)
body: Beshalach describes what the Mannah actually was: "When the children of Israel saw [it], they said to one another, It is manna, because they did not know what it was, and Moses said to them, It is the bread that the Lord has given you to eat. This is the thing that the Lord has commanded, Gather of it each one according to his eating capacity, an omer for each person, according to the number of persons, each one for those in his tent you shall take." There was a social side to it, which had people talking to each other — and some commentaries say it had them not recognising one another, because after such spiritual food they stood at a higher level. And there was the miracle in it: each was to take one omer a person, and whatever anyone took came out according to his eating capacity. Him filling the people's needs with bread belongs to the healing of Iyar. "Omer lagulgolet" also looks toward Lag Ba'Omer, the main day of this month, since it holds the word omer, and lagulgolet in Hebrew has two Lamed Gimmels in a row — lag, lag.

The Haftorah sates thirst and hunger: "Water he requested, (but) milk she gave him: in a lordly bowl she brought him cream." Out of the context of Yael killing Sissera, which is a worthy event in itself, the verse hints at the motherly kindness of women, who offer milk and cream when only water was asked for. The mannah is the same: instead of simply giving bread from the earth, He gave heavenly bread, with its own powers and blessings.

Daf Lamed Dalet of Sotah keeps on with crossing the Jordan, the spies, and Hebron. Week 34 is the completion of a cycle, with the Jews now ready to enter the Land — and with the disaster of the spies to keep in mind.

The generation is Solomon, Shlomoh, whose name comes from Shalom, peace, and is also near Shalem, whole, complete. We finish Iyar with the sense of being whole again, healed. And Shlomoh lived to see his father's work completed and the Temple finished — and on that day he wrote the Song of Songs.

The journey is from Kadesh to Mount Hor, at the edge of the land of Edom. Hor HaHar is a double mountain, a small apple atop a big apple, and it is the place where Aharon HaKohen passed away. Rabbi Simon Jacobson explains that the double mountain is Aharon's love — love within love. That love and harmony is what is needed to receive the Torah on another mountain, Mount Sinai, where the Jews camp in week 35. The personal journey moves from living with people's faults to the love and peace of Aharon, Rosh Chodesh Sivan, and the giving of the Torah.

235.title: The Tree of Life
body: Channah's sixth verse holds both ends: "The Lord kills and makes alive; He brings down to the grave and raises up." Which is the whole difference between those He heals and those He does not.
Pirkei Avot, on the greatness of the Torah, is also about life this week: "She is a tree of life for those who hold fast to her, and happy are those who support her."

Ecclesiastes 3 opens on the same contrast. "Everything has an appointed season, and there is a time for every matter under the heaven. A time to give birth and a time to die; a time to plant and a time to uproot that which is planted. A time to kill and a time to heal; a time to break and a time to build." The third of those is striking: it sets killing against healing — because healing is ultimately the sparing of life itself.

The week holds two prominent yahrzeits from the line of Kosov, two brothers who passed away on the same date, the 25th of Iyar: Rabbi Chaim Hager of Kosov and Rabbi David of Zubeltov, sons of Rabbi Menachem Mendel Hager of Kosov. Rabbi Chaim succeeded his father as Rav and Rebbe in Kossov in 1827 and wrote the Toras Chayim; a prominent synagogue in Tsfat is named after him, and his son Menachem Mendel became the first Rebbe in Vishnitz. Rabbi David of Zubeltov was the son-in-law of Rabbi Moshe Leib of Sassov and became a rebbe in his own right at the young age of 29, held in great respect for his wisdom even by the other rebbes of his generation. Also this week: Rabbi Mordechai Shraga of Husyatin and Rabbi Shlomo-Eliezer Alfandri on the 22nd of Iyar, Rabbi Benyamin Mendelson on the 24th, and Rabbi Yitzchak-Isaac of Homil, Rabbi Shmuel Eliyahu of Zvolin — son of Rabbi Yecheskel of Kuzmir and father of the first Modzhitzer Rebbe — and Rabbi Shlomo of Zivhil on the 26th.

236.title: Healing and Rabbi Shimon's "Wine"
body: The last week of Iyar, the end of the journey from Yaacov to Yisrael that began in Nissan, with Shavuot ahead. The Song's verse is wine: "And your palate is like the best wine, that glides down smoothly to my beloved, making the lips of the sleeping speak." Wine is the inner secrets of the Torah, and those secrets are what gave the Jewish people life in hard times when they were spiritually asleep, bringing them back and making their lips speak. Which is Lag Ba'Omer and the Kabbalah revealed by Rabbi Shimon Bar Yochai, and the healing of Iyar. The verses that follow belong here too: "I am my beloved's, and his desire is upon me. Come, my beloved, let us go out to the field, let us lodge in the villages. Let us arise early to the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has blossomed, the tiny grapes have developed, the pomegranates have lost their flowers; there I will give you my love." Closeness, with His desire upon us; and the tiny grapes developed and ready to give and receive His love at Mt. Sinai.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the thirty-fourth is Gad, son of Zilpah, and with him Menasheh, son of Joseph. Gad was known as a fierce warrior, and his name means good luck. Menashe's name has the verb to forget at its root, for Joseph forgetting the hardships of his past; and Menashe also means to sustain, since he was Joseph's main assistant in sustaining Egypt and running the affairs of the empire. Both of them are the healing of Iyar, and the journey from hardship to strength and relative independence.

Daf Lamed Dalet of Shvuoth keeps on with oaths applying only to monetary claims, and takes up witnesses who did not see or know the facts, and deriving the laws of an oath over a pikadon from the laws of court oaths. The theme again is the move from a poor and weak position to one of strength and order. Rabbi Shimon Bar Yochai is by far the most quoted rabbi on this daf, from beginning to end.

Jeremiah's thirty-fourth chapter is going from slave to free, in the seven-year cycle, and then the promise broken. "The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord after King Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people who were in Jerusalem, to proclaim freedom to them; That every man should let his manservant and every man his maidservant, a Jew and a Jewess go free, that none should hold his Jewish brother as a slave." They did it: "then they obeyed and let them go." And then they undid it: "But afterwards they turned and brought back the manservants and the maidservants whom they had let free, and forcibly made them into manservants and maidservants." He reminds them where the law came from — "I made a covenant with your fathers on the day that I brought them forth out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slaves" — and what they have just done: "And now this day you turned and did what was right in My sight by proclaiming liberty every man to his neighbor, and you made a covenant before Me in the House upon which My Name is called. But then you turned and profaned My Name." And the sentence is made out of their own word: "You have not hearkened to Me to proclaim freedom, every one to his brother and every one to his neighbor; behold I proclaim freedom to you, says the Lord, to the sword, to the pestilence, and to the famine."

237.title: Reviewing the Fourth Week of Iyar - Psalms 100-102; 105:3-5; 89:35
body: The fourth week of Iyar in psalms: the hundredth, hundred and first and hundred and second, with three verses of Psalm 105 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 100 is for the hearts of those who suffer in this world: let them serve G-d with joy all the same, because all of it is for their good, as in the verse, "He whom G-d loves does He chastise." It also refers to the thanksgiving sacrifice, the only one to be offered in the Messianic era. It is five verses long. "Serve the Lord with joy; come before Him with exultation. Know that the Lord is G-d; He has made us and we are His, His people and the sheep of His pasture. Enter His gates with gratitude, His courtyards with praise; give thanks to Him, bless His Name. For the Lord is good; His kindness is everlasting, and His faithfulness is for all generations."

Psalm 101 is David keeping himself apart from others, and his conduct inside his own house. "I will pay heed to the path of integrity-O when will it come to me? I shall walk with the innocence of my heart [even] within my house. I shall not place an evil thing before my eyes; I despise the doing of wayward deeds, it does not cling to me." Then whom he will not have near him: "He who slanders his fellow in secret, him will I cut down; one with haughty eyes and a lustful heart, him I cannot suffer." And whom he will: "My eyes are upon the faithful of the land, that they may dwell with me; he who walks in the path of integrity, he shall minister to me. He that practices deceit shall not dwell within my house."

Psalm 102 is the prayer of the exiled, and the right prayer for anyone in distress: "A prayer of the poor man when he is faint [with affliction], and pours out his tale of woe before the Lord." The body of it: "For my days have vanished with the smoke; my bones are dried up as a hearth. Smitten like grass and withered is my heart, for I have forgotten to eat my bread." The loneliness: "I am like the bird of the wilderness; like the owl of the wasteland have I become. In haste I fled; I was like a bird, alone on a roof." The food: "For I have eaten ashes like bread, and mixed my drink with tears." And then it turns, and the turn is the whole psalm: "But You, Lord, will be enthroned forever, and Your remembrance is for all generations. You will arise and have mercy on Zion, for it is time to be gracious to her; the appointed time has come. For Your servants cherish her stones, and love her dust." What the nations will see: "Then the nations will fear the Name of the Lord, and all the kings of the earth Your glory, when [they see that] the Lord has built Zion, He has appeared in His glory." Who it is written for: "Let this be written for the last generation, so that the newborn nation will praise the Lord." Why He looked: "to hear the cry of the bound, to untie those who are doomed to die." Then the asking not to be taken mid-life: "My G-d, do not remove me in the midst of my days! You Whose years endure through all generations." And the comparison that answers it: "In the beginning You laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands. They will perish, but You will endure; all of them will wear out like a garment; You will exchange them like a robe, and they will vanish. But You remain the same; Your years will not end. The children of Your servants will abide; their seed shall be established before You."

Psalm 105's verses are the seeking: "Glory in His holy Name; may the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice. Search for the Lord and His might; seek His countenance always. Remember the wonders that He has wrought, His miracles, and the judgments of His mouth." And Psalm 89's verse holds again: "I will not abrogate My covenant, nor change that which has issued from My lips."

238.title: The Ox is Saying
body: The ox opens on remembering the wonders, and the week comes in around it.

The remembering and the manna first: "Remember the wonders that He has wrought" / "His miracles, and the judgments of His mouth" / "When the children of Israel saw, they said to one another, 'It is manna'" / "Because they did not know what it was" / "And your palate is like the best wine" / "That glides down smoothly to my beloved."

Then the seeking, and the sleeping lips: "May the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice" / "Search for the Lord and His might" / "Seek His countenance always" / "Making the lips of the sleeping speak" / "Glory in His holy Name."

Then the bread and the covenant: "And Moses said to them, It is the bread that the Lord has given you to eat" / "This is the thing that the Lord has commanded" / "I will not abrogate My covenant" / "Nor change that which has issued from My lips" / "Is it not stored up with Me, sealed up in My treasuries?"

Then the song itself, and the feet set high: "Then Moses and the Children of Israel sang this song to G-d" / "And they said, 'I shall sing to G-d, for He has triumphed" / "He has thrown the horse and its rider into the sea'" / "He makes my feet like hinds" / "And sets me upon my high places."

And the end is the gathering by capacity, and the milk in the lordly bowl: "Gather of it each one according to his eating capacity" / "An omer for each person, according to the number of persons" / "Each one for those in his tent you shall take" / "Water he requested, (but) milk she gave him" / "In a lordly bowl she brought him cream" / "The Lord kills and makes alive" / "He brings down to the grave and raises up."

239.title: To Thank G-d in Unison
body: The wild animals say: "Blessed is the One Who is good and bestows good." (Talmud, Brachot 48b) This week holds Yom Yerushalayim and Rosh Chodesh Sivan.

Their song is the blessing Jewish law gives when something substantially good happens. It is called HaTov veHaMetiv, and it stands above the more familiar She'ychianu, because it is said when the good reaches not only the person but others as well. That all the wild animals, with their strong and ferocious instincts, can sing in unison a song that shows concern for others belongs directly to Rosh Chodesh Sivan. Sivan carries the giving of the Torah, which was made possible by the unity of the Jewish people then: the Torah tells that on Rosh Chodesh Sivan they all camped at Mount Sinai "as one man with one heart."

Sivan belongs to Zevulun, known for merchant skill and for the ability to survive in the outside wild jungle that is the commercial world. That prowess also kept his brother's tribe, Issachar, whose life was insular and wholly given to Torah; Zevulun supported Issachar fully. The Torah explicitly compares the Jewish women in Egypt to wild animals, and Rashi explains further that the whole people is called wild animals, since Benjamin is a wolf, Judah a lion, Dan a lion cub. For all our strong personalities and different ways of thinking — two Jews, three ideas, as the saying goes — we manage to get along. That closeness, among ourselves and with Him, is also in the month's sign: Gemini, twins.

On Yom Yerushalayim we mark Israel's miraculous victory in the Six-Day War, when Jerusalem was reunited — a day when something substantially good happened to all of the Jewish people, which is the blessing exactly. Today we say HaTov veHaMetiv only when something very good happens, and when something very bad happens, or what looks bad to us, we say Baruch Dayan Emet, Blessed be the True Judge. The Talmud teaches that in Messianic times we will say HaTov veHaMetiv in all circumstances, because we will understand that what we once took for bad was ultimately for the good. Yom Yerushalayim is that too. The term appears in the Psalms as a reference to the destruction of the Temple and of Jerusalem, perhaps the worst event in our history; since 1967 it names the day Jerusalem was liberated. The meaning of that destruction is still hard to understand, and we know at least that the second use of the name could not exist without the first.

The song also holds a double tov — HaTov veHaMetiv. The gematria of tov is 17, and twice that is 34, which was last week; this week builds on it. Thirty-five is the gematria of yehudi, which names every Jew even though its root is only the tribe of Judah — the whole people able to unite behind one tribe. Its first appearance in the Tanach is in Megillat Esther, of Mordechai, who was of Benjamin; and the Megillah calls the whole people Am Mordechai. Thirty-five is also lamed and heh, the only two letters in the word Hallel, the song of praise said on Rosh Chodesh Sivan, and said by many on Yom Yerushalayim.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Tzadok: do not separate yourself from the community; do not act as a counselor-at-law when serving as a judge; do not make the Torah a crown to magnify yourself with, or a spade with which to dig. So would Hillel say, one who makes personal use of the crown of Torah shall perish — and one who benefits himself from the words of Torah removes his life from the world. That is the unity of Rosh Chodesh Sivan. And Rabbi Tzadok fasted for forty years to prevent the destruction of the Temple; Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai said of him that had there been one more tzadik like him, Jerusalem would not have been destroyed. His words falling in the week of Yom Yerushalayim is fitting indeed.

This week completes another cycle of seven, and the combination is malchut shebehod. Malchut is taking abstract ideas and applying them in the real world; this week we bring our service and our pursuit of peace to fruition. The lesson from the wild animals is that everything He does is for the good, and what looks bad for us will prove in the end to have been for our good.

240.title: Uriah and Loving the "Just"
body: Yom Yerushalayim and Rosh Chodesh Sivan. Sivan, the month of Shavuot, belongs to Zevulun, who could combine the study of Torah with making a living, and kept not only himself but Issachar, who was immersed in learning.

Haazinu speaks of vengeance and reckoning: "Vengeance is poised with Me, and it will pay at the time their foot stumbles. For the appointed day of their reckoning is near, and what is destined for them hastens." (Deuteronomy 32:35) And a positive message is there too: the vengeance read as against the enemy, and the payment as for the good deeds of the Jews and for their suffering. On Rosh Chodesh Sivan we feel the day of payment for the work of the omer, Shavuot, coming fast. On receiving the Torah the people collapsed, feeling the soul leave the body and return. The revelation of the final day of judgment will be one in which we are overawed by His kindness toward His people — and a glimmer of that kindness was seen in the Six-Day War and the conquest of Jerusalem, which was a victory we stumbled into.
The Haftorah: "He trains my hand for war, so that mine arms do bend a brass bow." (II Samuel 22:35) Another reference to His kindness on Yom Yerushalayim.

The quality is loves justice, Ohev Et HaMeisharim — and as last week, Meisharim is not the usual word for justice. Meishar means levelled or plowed, a levelled plain or field, and it comes from yashar, straight, so it means a straight and righteous path. A tzadik is called that for fulfilling the positive commandments, and a yashar for fulfilling the negative ones. Working at being both is part of preparing to receive the Torah. On Rosh Chodesh Sivan the whole people could be like one man with one heart because of the harmony those two produce — above all the negative ones, in not harming one another. And yashar is the root of Yisrael and of Yeshurun. The omer is a personal transformation from Ha'Akov l'Mishor, from Yaakov to Yisrael.

The prophet is Uriah, whose prophecy is tied to this quality and to Jerusalem: it was Uriah who said in the name of G-d that Zion would be plowed like a field, and Meishar is a levelled, plowed field. As Rabbi Akiva explained, his prophecy is linked to the good outcomes for Jerusalem as well: just as Uriah's prophecy had been fulfilled, so would the positive prophecy of Zechariah be fulfilled. Chassidic thought explains that sometimes a descent is needed for a greater ascent, Yeridah L'Tzorech Aliyah. Given the corruption and crookedness of the time, Jerusalem had to be plowed and made straight and upright again — and out of that plowed field would come the foundation of the Jerusalem of today, and of the Jerusalem of Messianic times, with the Temple rebuilt. His own story is tragic: because of his negative prophecies he runs to Egypt, is brought back, and is killed by the king of Judah. His message is not in a book of his own but inside the Book of Jeremiah, and his prophecy is described chiefly as being "like all the words of Jeremiah" — and Jeremiah is next week's prophet. His murder was a Yeridah L'Tzorech Aliyah too.

The levitical city is Yokneam, whose name looks like a contraction of Yikneh Am, He will acquire a nation — which can also be read as a nation shall acquire. On Shavuot Hashem acquired us as a nation, and on Shavuot we acquired the Torah. The verse stands in the future tense all the same, because that acquiring was to be felt again: in the days of Purim, when the Jews took the Torah on themselves at a higher level, and with the coming of Mashiach. Yokneam today is an important high-tech centre and an extensive archeological site.
240.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 35.

241.title: To Be United and Not Divided
body: Yom Yerushalayim and Rosh Chodesh Sivan. Beshalach: "And the children of Israel did so: they gathered, both the one who gathered much and the one who gathered little. And they measured [it] with an omer, and whoever gathered much did not have more, and whoever gathered little did not have less; each one according to his eating capacity, they gathered." That is how harmony is reached — each one doing his share. The unity is Sivan, and it is Yom Yerushalayim. One link to the Six Day War may be how much was done in how little time: in six days Israel's territory more than tripled, which belongs with whoever gathered little not having less, because with miracles the time and effort are not necessarily in proportion to the outcome.

The Haftorah is Yael's hand: "She put forth her hand to the pin, and her right hand to strike the weary." She struck Sissera at the right moment, and one of the great miracles of the Six Day War was striking bravely and effectively at the right time.

Daf Lamed Heh of Sotah keeps on with the spies, Calev in particular, and takes up transporting the Aron and the rocks used for writing the Torah and as signs for later generations. Calev suits Yom Yerushalayim, since he showed the spirit it takes to conquer the land, as was done in 1967. Part of the discussion of the Aron is bringing it to Jerusalem. And setting up those rocks to write the Torah on reads like the encampment at Har Sinai.

The generation is Rehoboam, son of Solomon, king when the kingdom split in two. His name is from Rehav, wide and expansive, and Am, nation. His counterpart is Jeroboam, crowned king of the Kingdom of Israel, whose name also holds Am and can be read as one who will increase, or will fight for, the nation. The division between the two kingdoms increased nothing. So it is fitting that Rehoboam is the link for week 35, when the nation was united on Rosh Chodesh Sivan, and when Jerusalem and Judea and Samaria were reunited under Jewish sovereignty. Both kings' ways were sinful. In Rehoboam's time idol worship and adultery spread in the Kingdom of Judah; Jeroboam caused still more idol worship in the Kingdom of Israel, and Pirkei Avot cites him as the standing example of one who sinned and made others sin, future kings included — he even set up golden calves to be worshipped in a temple set against the one in Jerusalem. Getting ready to accept the Torah has to include banishing the idols and the adulterous behaviour of our own time.

The journey is from Mount Hor to Zalmonah, from Zalmon, darkness. Rabbi Jacobson connects it to the verse in Psalms about becoming whitened from the dark shadows of exile. That is close to the song of the deer next week: "And I shall sing of Your strength, I shall rejoice of Your kindness in the morning, for You were a refuge to me, and a hiding place on the day of my oppression." On Shavuot we think of all the darkness we had to come through to reach this light. The personal journey moves from the love and peace of Aharon to the light about to arrive after the dark.

242.title: True Wealth and Honor
body: Channah's seventh verse: "The Lord impoverishes and makes rich. He humbles; He also exalts." He gives wealth and standing, and He takes them away.

Pirkei Avot, on the greatness of the Torah, turns to the true wealth and the true standing, which come from the Torah, and uses ornament for it: "For they shall be a garland of grace for your head, and necklaces about your neck."

Ecclesiastes 4 sets physical wealth against the wealth that comes of wisdom, and shows that even a king without wisdom is humbled in his own kingdom: "Better a poor and wise child than an old and foolish king, who no longer knows to receive admonition. For out of the prison he has come to reign, for even in his kingdom, he becomes humble."
The week holds three prominent yahrzeits: Rav Meir'l of Premishlan on the 29th of Iyar, Rabbi Yisroel of Vizhnitz and Rabbi Chaim-Elazar Spira, the Munkaczer Rebbe, both on the 2nd of Sivan.

Reb Meir'l and Reb Yisroel of Ruzhin were very good friends, for all that they served Hashem in very different ways: the Rizhiner lived in grand luxury and Reb Meir with the bare minimum. One day Reb Meir'l was riding in a simple wagon drawn by a lone horse and met R' Yisroel of Rizhin in a wagon drawn by four powerful horses. He asked why he needed them. The Rizhiner answered that if he got stuck in the mud, those horses could pull him out easily. Reb Meir replied: since I have one weak horse, I am careful not to get stuck in the mud in the first place. He was also on very good terms with Gedolim of the non-chassidic world, such as Reb Shlomo Kluger and Reb Yosef Shaul Natanson, and many Divrei Torah and exchanges between them are recorded. He lived in abject but patient poverty and exerted himself tirelessly for the needy and the suffering; his divine inspiration and his ready wit have become legendary. He wrote no works, and some of his teachings were collected and published by his Chassidim after his death.

Rabbi Yisroel of Vizhnitz, in Bukovina, had many thousands of followers over the 43 years he served as Rebbe, and after WWI he headed a major yeshiva in Hungary. For his warmth and friendliness to every Jew he was known as the Ahavas Yisrael. Rabbi Chaim-Elazar Spira, the Munkaczer Rebbe, wrote and published over twenty books on law, Torah, chasidism, religious philosophy and custom; the work that made him world famous is the Minchas Elazar, in six volumes.

243.title: Feeling Hashem's Desire
body: The Song's verse is one line, and it is about being wanted: "I am my beloved's, and his desire is upon me." That desire was certainly felt in the days just before the giving of the Torah, and again when we were able to re-conquer Jerusalem. The verses that follow belong here too: "The pots [of figs] have given forth [their] fragrance, and on our doorways are all manner of sweet fruits, both new and old, which I have hidden away for you, my beloved." "O, that you were like my brother, who sucked my mother's breasts! I would find you outside, I would kiss you, and they would not despise me." "I would lead you, I would bring you to the house of my mother, who instructed me; I would give you to drink some spiced wine, of the juice of my pomegranate." Rosh Chodesh Sivan is the sign of twins — like my brother — and the house of my mother looks like Jerusalem.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the thirty-fifth is Ziphion, son of Gad, and with him Ephraim, son of Joseph. Ziphion looks related to Letzapot, to see into the distance, like the name of a mountain in Jerusalem, Har HaTzofim, which saw some of the greatest battles for the city in 1948 and 1967. Ephraim comes from being fruitful and multiplying, and Israel's size certainly multiplied after the Six Day War; Ephraim was also the ancestor of Joshua, who conquered the Land the first time. Ephraim and Menashe, last week, were partners much as Issachar, of Iyar, and Zevulun, of Sivan: of the two brothers Ephraim is the one associated with spiritual pursuits and the acquiring of Torah, and Menashe with running the affairs of the kingdom.

Daf Lamed Heh of Shvuot takes up exemptions, when oaths are not made, the wording of an oath, the holy names of G-d, and whether an oath must include His name. Those names belong to the revelation and the giving of the Torah on Shavuot — and the Torah itself is one of His names.

Jeremiah's thirty-fifth chapter holds the story of the Rechabites, sons of Jonadab the son of Rechab, children of Yitro. "And I placed before the sons of the house of the Rechabites goblets full of wine, and cups, and I said to them, 'Drink wine.' And they said, 'We will not drink wine, for Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us saying, "You shall not drink wine, you or your children forever. And you shall not build a house, neither shall you sow nor shall you plant a vineyard, nor shall you have [any], but you shall dwell in tents all your days."'" And they kept it: "And we have dwelt in tents, and we have hearkened and done according to all that Jonadab our father has commanded us." Yitro's story, a convert's story, belongs to the giving of the Torah — it is in Parashat Yitthro that we read of it. And the Rechabites show the unity of children all obeying their father's wish together; they were converts themselves, as the whole Jewish people were like converts on Shavuot.

244.title: Reviewing the Week of Rosh Chodesh Sivan - Psalms 103 -105; 105:6-8; 89:36
body: The week of Rosh Chodesh Sivan in psalms: the hundred and third, hundred and fourth and hundred and fifth, with three verses of Psalm 105 again and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 103 is David's prayer when he was ill, and the right prayer for the sick, above all said by the sick person himself while his soul is still in his body, so that he can bless G-d from his depths, body and soul. "Bless the Lord, O my soul; and all my being, His holy Name. My soul, bless the Lord; forget not all His favors: Who forgives all your sins, Who heals all your illnesses; Who redeems your life from the grave, Who crowns you with kindness and mercy; Who satisfies your mouth with goodness; like the eagle, your youth is renewed." Then the measures of His patience: "He has not dealt with us according to our transgressions, nor requited us according to our sins. For as high as heaven is above the earth, so has His kindness been mighty over those who fear Him. As far as the east is from the west, so has He distanced our transgressions from us. As a father has compassion on his children, so has the Lord had compassion on those who fear Him. For He knows our nature; He is mindful that we are but dust." Then our side of the comparison: "As for man, his days are like grass; like a flower of the field, so he sprouts. When a wind passes over him, he is gone; his place recognizes him no more." And then everything is called to bless Him — the angels, the hosts, all His works — and the last line returns where it started: "My soul, bless the Lord!"

Psalm 104 tells the beauty of creation, what was made on each of the six days, and the awesomeness of the One who sustains all of it, from the horns of the wild ox to the eggs of the louse. "You enwrap [Yourself] with light as with a garment; You spread the heavens as a curtain." The waters put in their place: "You set a boundary which they may not cross, so that they should not return to engulf the earth." The drinking: "He sends forth springs into streams; they flow between the mountains. They give drink to all the beasts of the field; the wild animals quench their thirst." What grows: "He makes grass grow for the cattle, and vegetation requiring the labor of man to bring forth food from the earth; and wine that gladdens man's heart, oil that makes the face shine, and bread that sustains man's heart." Who lives where: "The high mountains are for the wild goats; the rocks are a refuge for the rabbits." The clock of it: "He made the moon to calculate the festivals; the sun knows its time of setting. You bring on darkness and it is night, when all the beasts of the forest creep forth. The young lions roar for prey, and seek their food from G-d. When the sun rises, they return and lie down in their dens. Then man goes out to his work, to his labor until evening." The accounting: "How manifold are Your works, O Lord! You have made them all with wisdom; the earth is full of Your possessions." The sea, with the Leviathan created to frolic in it. And the dependence of all of it on one hand: "They all look expectantly to You to give them their food at the proper time. When You give it to them, they gather it; when You open Your hand, they are satiated with goodness. When You conceal Your countenance, they are terrified; when You take back their spirit, they perish and return to their dust. When You will send forth Your spirit they will be created anew, and You will renew the face of the earth."

Psalm 105 David composed when he brought the Holy Ark up to the City of David, and sang before the Ark. It recounts the miracles done for the Jews in Egypt, beginning with Joseph sent ahead of them, imprisoned and then freed, until he could imprison the princes of Egypt without consulting Pharaoh. The covenant first: "He remembers His covenant forever, the word which He has commanded to a thousand generations; the covenant which He made with Abraham, and His oath to Isaac. He established it for Jacob as a statute, for Israel as an everlasting covenant, stating, 'To you I shall give the land of Canaan'-the portion of your inheritance, when they were but few, very few, and strangers in it." The protection on the road: "He permitted no one to wrong them, and admonished kings for their sake: 'Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not harm my prophets.'" Then Joseph: "He sent a man before them; Joseph was sold as a slave. They afflicted his foot with chains, his soul was put into iron; until the time that His words came, the decree of the Lord purified him." Then the plagues told one after another — darkness, blood, frogs, beasts and lice, hail and flaming fire, grasshoppers and locusts without number, and every firstborn. Then the leaving: "And He took them out with silver and gold, and none among His tribes stumbled. Egypt rejoiced at their leaving, for the fear [of Israel] had fallen upon them." Then the desert: the cloud for shelter and the fire for the night, the quail and the bread of heaven, the rock opened so that waters streamed through dry places like a river — "for He remembered His holy word to Abraham His servant." And the point of all of it: "He gave them the lands of nations, they inherited the toil of peoples, so that they might keep His statutes and observe His laws. Praise the Lord!"

The Tikkun HaKlali verses are the seed of Abraham and the covenant remembered to the thousandth generation. And Psalm 89's verse is the oath: "One thing have I sworn by My holiness, that I will not fail David."

245.title: The Wild Animals Say
body: The wild animals open, and the week sets the oath beside the hand trained for war.

The swearing and the hands first: "One thing have I sworn by My holiness" / "That I will not fail David" / "He trains my hand for war" / "So that mine arms do bend a brass bow" / "She put forth her hand to the pin" / "And her right hand to strike the weary."

Then the reckoning, and the raising and lowering: "For the appointed day of their reckoning is near" / "And what is destined for them hastens" / "The Lord impoverishes and makes rich. He humbles; He also exalts" / "Vengeance is poised with Me" / "And it will pay at the time their foot stumbles."

Then the gathering that came out even: "And the children of Israel did so" / "They gathered, both the one who gathered much" / "And the one who gathered little" / "And they measured [it] with an omer" / "And whoever gathered much did not have more, and whoever gathered little did not have less" / "I am my beloved's, and his desire is upon me" / "Each one according to his eating capacity, they gathered."

And the end is the blessing itself, with the covenant under it: "Blessed is the One Who is good and bestows good" / "The seed of Abraham His servant, the children of Jacob, His chosen ones" / "He is the Lord our G-d; throughout all the earth are His judgments" / "He remembered His covenant forever, the word He had commanded to the thousandth generation."

246.title: To Have Emunah
body: The gazelle is saying, "And I shall sing of Your strength, I shall rejoice of Your kindness in the morning, for You were a refuge to me, and a hiding place on the day of my oppression." (Psalms 59:17) This week holds Shavuot, and the whole week is also known as Shivah Yemei Miluim, in which the Shavuot sacrifices could still be brought to the Temple.

The Hebrew for gazelle is Tzvi, which has the same gematria as emunah, complete faith. Its three letters — tzadi, beit, yud — are an acronym for "tzadik b'emunatoh yichieh," a tzadik lives through his faith, a verse of the prophet Habakkuk; and the Talmud explains that this verse is a summary of the whole Torah given to Moses at Mount Sinai on Shavuot. The song holds faith in both directions, in the morning and in trouble, which is night. Psalm 92 opens the same way: "It is good to give thanks to the Lord, and to sing to Your name, O Most High; To declare in the morning Your kindness and Your faith at night." After the troubles of the Counting of the Omer, which belongs to the night, on Shavuot the revelation comes clear as day.

The horns of a gazelle are like a double crown, and the Jewish people received a double crown on Shavuot, as a reward for their faith. The Midrash teaches that other nations refused the Torah, and the Jews did not even ask first what was in it: they said "Na'aseh veNishmah," we will do and we will listen, accepting the commandments before knowing what they were. So each Jew was given two crowns, one for Na'aseh and one for Nishmah — crowns that were later removed after the sin of the golden calf.

Thirty-six is the thirty-six hidden tzadikim who sustain the world. It is also the total number of Chanukah candles lit over the eight days. Both belong to the light revealed on Shavuot, when, through the work of the omer, we all stand closer to the level of tzadikim — and those thirty-six are literally the foundation of the world.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Yossi: whoever honors the Torah is himself honored by the people, and whoever degrades the Torah is himself degraded by the people. That belongs to the giving of the Torah and to what happened soon after. When we accepted it we were shown great honour; when we dishonoured it with the golden calf, the honour was taken away.

The combination is chesed shebeyesod, kindness within foundation. On Shavuot the people had to stand firm — not coming too close to the mountain, not letting their souls expire altogether from the revelation — in order to receive the great good that is the Torah. The lesson from the gazelle is to have faith at night, in the hard times, knowing that the night will pass and we will thank Him in the open light of day.

247.title: Accepting the Truth
body: The week of Shavuot. Haazinu: "When the Lord will judge His people, and will reconsider His servants, when He sees that the power is increasing, and none is controlled or strengthened." (Deuteronomy 32:36) Shavuot is not usually thought of as a day of judgment, and in many ways it has much of one, like Rosh Hashanah. How a person's studies will go through the year is largely settled on Shavuot. As we try not to sleep much on Rosh Hashanah, on Shavuot we stay up all night learning. And for all that it is a day of celebration, what happened immediately after the giving of the Torah — the sin of the golden calf — needed His great mercy, and Moshe begging on our behalf.

The Haftorah points at Shavuot plainly: "And You have given me the shield of Your salvation; And You have increased Your humility for me." (II Samuel 22:36) At Mount Sinai He lowered Himself, which is increased humility, so that He could be revealed to the people.

The quality is loves reproof, Ohev Et Hatochachot. Every year before Shavuot we read the Tochachah in the portion of Bechukotai. This week is tied to the events just after the giving of the Torah, which hold much reproof. And only by being open to reproof can a person learn and grow; it is one of the main teachings of the Book of Proverbs: "Reprove not a scorner lest he hate you; reprove a wise man and he will love you. Give a wise man, and he will become yet wiser; teach a righteous man, and he will increase in learning. The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and the knowledge of the holy ones is understanding."

The prophet is Jeremiah, whose prophecy is more associated with reproof than any other: he spoke so strongly about the destruction of the Temple, the devastation of Jerusalem and the Babylonian exile, and he lived to see them. He also recorded the Book of Lamentations, which sets out G-d's reproof as vividly as it has ever been set out. He stood at a level few prophets reached, which also suits the week of Shavuot. And his message belongs to the day: "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might; let not the rich man glory in his riches. But let him that glorieth, glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth Me, that I am the L-rd Who exercises mercy, justice, and righteousness on the earth; for in these things I delight, saith the L-rd."

The levitical city is Kartah, which means city in Aramaic. Perhaps the point is that receiving the Torah means knowing the simple truth, even when the truth is painful. The Jewish people come from Shem, whose name means name, which points to the same plain truth he stood for. The ruins of Kartah, outside Haifa, are an important and beautiful archeological site today.

There is also an opinion that Kartah is Tavor, a city of the tribe of Issachar — and Mount Tabor was shared by Issachar and Zevulun, so the two brothers share the levitical city of the week of Shavuot, which is the brotherly love the giving of the Torah needed; and the sign of Sivan is gemini, twins. Mount Tabor also thought itself worthy of being the mountain where the Torah would be given, and was later the scene of miracles in the days of Devorah. Rashi, on "I, to the Lord I shall sing," notes that the word is repeated, and gives an Aggadic reading: the Holy One did not withhold the reward of Mount Tabor and Mount Carmel, who came to the giving of the Torah expecting it to be given upon them and turned away in shame. He said to them, I will pay you double fold. At Sinai it was said, "I am the Lord your G-d"; at Tabor it will be said, "I… I…". At Sinai it was said, "I am the Lord your G-d"; at Carmel it will be said twice, "The Lord He is G-d, the Lord He is G-d," in the days of Elijah.
247.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 36.

248.title: Not Leaving the Learning for the Morning
body: Beshalach: "And Moses said to them, Let no one leave over [any] of it until morning. But [some] men did not obey Moses and left over [some] of it until morning, and it bred worms and became putrid, and Moses became angry with them." Which is Shavuot itself, where at the first giving of the Torah the people overslept and Moshe reprimanded them for it — and that is the basis of the custom of spending the whole night studying, not leaving it until morning.

The Haftorah is Yael again: "she struck Sisera, pierced his head, and wounded and penetrated his temple." Taken out of the context of her act, as in week 34, the words could describe the experience of Mount Sinai, where the Torah pierced and penetrated our minds in a way that left a mark in every Jewish soul.

Daf Lamed Vav of Sotah keeps on with how the people entered the Land, how the tribes stood at Mount Grizim and Mount Eival, and how the names of the tribes were inscribed on the Ephod — a symbol of unity, which is Shavuot and Sivan. There is discussion of there being 50 letters in the Ephod, and 50 belongs to Shavuot too. The daf also spends a good deal of time on Yosef and the tests he came through. Shavuot is about miracles, and about all of Israel standing at a mountain and entering a covenant; and Yosef is the consummate example of one who followed the Torah, the very definition of a Tzadik.

The generation is Abijam, son of Rehoboam, also known as Abijah, which means my father is Hashem. As we received the Torah through unity, he sought to reunite the kingdoms of Judah and Israel — and for all his military victory he could not reach it. He followed his father's wicked ways, and the people were steeped in idolatry. Jeroboam, the sinful king of Israel who built an alternate temple with golden calves, also had a son named Abiyah; that child fell critically ill, died, and was eulogized by all of Israel — and even a eulogy for the son of an evil king shows the unity of this week.

The journey is from Zalmonah to Punon, the place where the people complained and were bitten by snakes, and were healed through Moshe's copper snake. Punon comes from the word for directed, or faced, and also means death in Greek. At the giving of the Torah the people died and were revived at once: facing Hashem and hearing Him speak, their souls left their bodies. Punon also has two letter Nuns, which may point to the fiftieth day of the omer, which is Shavuot. The personal journey is to take in the light of Shavuot against the darkness of the omer, and to be revived by the Torah as well.

249.title: The Crown(s) of Torah
body: Channah's eighth verse lifts people off the ground: "He lifts the poor from the dust; From the dunghill, He raises the pauper, To seat them with princes, And a seat of honor He causes them to inherit, For the pillars of the earth are the Lord's, And He placed the world upon them." He is the one who decides who deserves honour and nobility.

Pirkei Avot, on the greatness of the Torah, speaks of honour again and makes it an ornament: "She shall give to your head a garland of grace, a crown of glory she shall grant you." It was on Shavuot that the people were crowned with a double crown, one for Na'aseh, we will do, and one for Nishmah, we will listen.

Ecclesiastes 5, like chapter 4, sets wealth against poverty, and names cases where a king is the one who is subservient: "If you see oppression of the poor and deprivation of justice and righteousness in the province, wonder not about the matter, for the Highest over the high waits, and there are higher ones over them. And the loftiness of the earth is in everything; even the king is subservient to the field."

The week holds the yahrzeit of the Baal Shem Tov on the 6th of Sivan, and of Rabbi Avraham Mordechai Alter, the third Gerrer Rebbe, on the same date. Rabbi Yisrael ben Eliezer, the Baal Shem Tov, master of the good Name, a unique and seminal figure in Jewish history, revealed the Chassidic movement and his own identity as an exceptionally holy person on his 36th birthday, the 18th of Elul 1734. He wrote no books, though many claim to hold his teachings; one available in English is the annotated translation of Tzava'at Harivash. Rabbi Avraham Mordechai Alter, son of the Sfas Emmes, was the third Rebbe of Gur, spiritual leader of over 250,000 Chassidim in pre-WW II Poland. In 1940 he managed to escape with three of his sons to Israel, though the vast majority of his followers did not survive; he began to rebuild the Gerrer community in Jerusalem and died there during the siege of the city on Shavuos, 1948. He was known as the Imrei Emmes, after the title of his major book.

Also this week: Rabbi Yitzchak Issac son of Rabbi Yisachar Beirish of Ziditchov on the 9th of Sivan, Rabbi Moshe of Rozvadov on the 10th, Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Alter Yechezkel Horowitz of Dzhikov on the 11th, and Rabbi Avraham son of Rabbi Noach Weinberg of Slonim on the 12th.

250.title: Chag (Festival)
body: The Song's verse goes out of doors: "Come, my beloved, let us go out to the field, let us lodge in the villages." The field and the villages look toward Eisav, who was a man of the field, and Rashi comments that Kefarim, villages, should be read Kofrim, disbelievers — because at the giving of the Torah He offered it to the other nations, Yishmael and Eisav among them, and they refused. Shavuot belongs to the field in its own right as well: it is Chag HaKatzir, the Harvest Festival, and Chag HaBikkurim, the Festival of the First Fruits.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the thirty-sixth is Haggi, and with him Bela, son of Benjamin. Haggi comes from Chag, festival: Chagi means my festival, or Chag-Yud, the festival of G-d. Chag covers all the festivals and especially those with a pilgrimage to Jerusalem — Shavuot, Pessach and Sukkot. Bela means swallowed up, for how Joseph disappeared from Benjamin when he was still a child; Benjamin naming his sons after Joseph is evidence of the brotherly love that existed and still exists among the Jewish people, which is a key part of our meriting to receive the Torah.

Daf Lamed Vav of Shvuot keeps on with the wording of an oath and the holy names of G-d, and opens a new chapter on the oath of a pikadon, a gift or deposit. The names belong to the revelation and the giving of the Torah — and the Torah was the gift itself, given at Sinai.

Jeremiah's thirty-sixth chapter is the writing of a scroll, which is in fact the Book of Lamentations, spoken by Jeremiah and written down by Baruch ben Neriah. "And Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote from Jeremiah's mouth all the words of the Lord that He had spoken to him, on a roll of a book." He could not go himself: "I am imprisoned; I cannot enter the House of the Lord. And you shall come and read in the roll that you have written from my mouth, the words of the Lord, in the ears of the people." Then the king destroyed it: "And it came to pass, when Jehudi read three or four verses, he rent it with a scribe's razor, and cast [it] onto the fire which was on the brazier until the entire roll was consumed." And nobody flinched: "And the king and all his servants who heard all these words were neither frightened nor did they rend their garments." Then it was written again, longer: "And Jeremiah took another roll and gave it to Baruch the son of Neriah the scribe, and he wrote on it from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the book that Jehoiakim the king of Judah burnt with fire, and there were yet added to them many words like those." There is a strong parallel there with the giving of the Torah.

251.title: Reviewing the Second Week of Sivan - Psalms 106-108; 105:9-11; 89:37
body: The second week of Sivan in psalms: the hundred and sixth, hundred and seventh and hundred and eighth, with three verses of Psalm 105 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 106 carries on from the last one, praising Him for the miracles it did not mention, because who can recount the mighty acts of G-d? Were we to try, we could not name them all. "Praise the Lord for He is good, for His kindness is everlasting. Who can recount the mighty acts of the Lord, or proclaim all His praises? Fortunate are those who preserve justice, who perform deeds of righteousness all the time." Then the confession, and it is long: "We have sinned as did our fathers, we have acted perversely and wickedly. Our fathers in Egypt did not contemplate Your wonders, they did not remember Your abundant kindnesses, and they rebelled by the sea, at the Sea of Reeds. Yet He delivered them for the sake of His Name, to make His strength known." Then the forgetting: "Then they believed in His words, they sang His praise. They quickly forgot His deeds, they did not wait for His counsel." Then the calf: "They made a calf in Horeb, and bowed down to a molten image. They exchanged their Glory for the likeness of a grass-eating ox." And the one man standing in the way: "He said that He would destroy them-had not Moses His chosen one stood in the breach before Him, to turn away His wrath from destroying." Then the land despised, Baal Peor, Phineas rising and the plague stayed, the waters of Merivah, and the nations not destroyed but mingled with. And then, after all of it, the turn: "But He saw their distress, when He heard their prayer; and He remembered for them His covenant and He relented, in keeping with His abounding kindness, and He caused them to be treated mercifully by all their captors." And the ending, which is the end of the fourth book of psalms: "Deliver us, Lord our G-d; gather us from among the nations, that we may give thanks to Your Holy Name and glory in Your praise. Blessed is the Lord, the G-d of Israel, forever and ever. And let all the people say, 'Amen! Praise the Lord!'"

Psalm 107 is for those saved out of four particular dangers — imprisonment, sickness, desert travel and sea travel — who must give thanks, because their sins brought the trouble and only His kindness brought them out, so it is right that they praise Him and tell everyone of their salvation. The desert: "They lost their way in the wilderness, in the wasteland; they found no inhabited city. Both hungry and thirsty, their soul languished within them." The prison: "Those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in misery and chains of iron... He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and sundered their bonds, for He broke the brass gates and smashed the iron bars." The sickness: "Their soul loathes all food, and they reach the gates of death... He sent forth His command and healed them; He delivered them from their graves." And the sea, which is the longest of them: "Those who go down to the sea in ships, who perform tasks in mighty waters; they saw the works of the Lord and His wonders in the deep. He spoke and caused the stormy wind to rise, and it lifted up the waves. They rise to the sky, plunge to the depths; their soul melts in distress. They reel and stagger like a drunkard, all their skill is to no avail." And then: "He transformed the storm into stillness, and the waves were quieted. They rejoiced when they were silenced, and He led them to their destination." Four times over comes the same line: "Let them give thanks to the Lord for His kindness, and [proclaim] His wonders to the children of man." Then the turning of places into their opposites — rivers into desert and desert into lake, fruitful land into salt-marsh and parched land into springs — and the last line, which asks for a reader: "Let him who is wise bear these in mind, and then the benevolent acts of the Lord will be understood."

Psalm 108 is a steadfast heart and a man waking the dawn: "My heart is steadfast, O G-d; I will sing and chant praises even with my soul. Awake, O lyre and harp; I shall awaken the dawn. I will thank You among the nations, Lord; I will sing praises to You among the peoples." Then the dividing up of the land again, Gilead and Manasseh, Ephraim and Judah, Moab and Edom and Philistia. And the close, which gives the fighting back where it belongs: "Give us help against the adversary; futile is the help of man. Through G-d we will do valiantly, and He will trample our oppressors."
Psalm 105's verses are the covenant and the land promised. And Psalm 89's verse is the throne: "His seed will endure forever and his throne will be [resplendent] as the sun before Me."

252.title: The Gazelle Is Saying
body: The gazelle opens, and the week goes out to the field with it.

The field and the refuge first: "Come, my beloved, let us go out to the field, let us lodge in the villages" / "And I shall sing of Your strength" / "I shall rejoice of Your kindness in the morning" / "For You were a refuge to me, and a hiding place on the day of my oppression" / "And You have given me the shield of Your salvation" / "And You have increased Your humility for me."

Then the lifting out of the dust, with the judging between: "He lifts the poor from the dust" / "From the dunghill, He raises the pauper" / "When the Lord will judge His people" / "And will reconsider His servants" / "To seat them with princes" / "And a seat of honor He causes them to inherit" / "When He sees that the power is increasing" / "And none is controlled or strengthened."

Then what must not be left until morning, and the pillars of the earth: "And Moses said to them, Let no one leave over [any] of it until morning" / "For the pillars of the earth are the Lord's, And He placed the world upon them" / "But [some] men did not obey Moses" / "And left over [some] of it until morning" / "And it bred worms and became putrid" / "And Moses became angry with them."
