And the end is the piercing and the covenant: "She struck Sisera, pierced his head" / "And wounded and penetrated his temple" / "The covenant which He made with Abraham" / "And His oath to Isaac" / "He established it for Jacob as a statute, for Israel as an everlasting covenant" / "Stating, 'To you I shall give the land of Canaan'" / "His seed will endure forever and his throne will be as the sun before Me" / "The portion of your inheritance."

253.title: To Maintain our Humility and Not Forget the Greatness We Experienced
body: The elephant is saying, "How great are your works, G-d; Your thoughts are tremendously deep." (Psalms 92:6) The word for great is gadlu, from gadol, big — and the elephant is the largest of the land animals. The verse is from Psalm 92 again, as last week's was.

On Shavuot we were all deeply impressed by the greatness of Hashem and His Torah, and after a day of such revelation we all stand higher. The elephant presses that greatness on us, and that it matters not to let ourselves forget it; elephants are famous for their memory. Physical greatness belongs to the week after Shavuot in another way too, since that is when we read Nasso, the largest portion in all the Five Books of Moses.

Thirty-seven is the gematria of the root of gadol. It is also the numerical difference between the name of Moses, 345, and Korach, 308. The deep thoughts of the verse may be Korach's rebellion against Moses and Aaron. Korach wanted the leadership for himself and persuaded a substantial number of his tribesmen and neighbours to rebel; in the confrontation he and his congregation were miraculously sucked into a deep pit, which Pirkei Avot says was thought of and created in the very first week of Creation. The Rebbe explains that they were brought into the pit still alive so that they could repent and return to G-d, as Korach's sons did. It happened on Rosh Chodesh Sivan, the beginning of this month, and the portion of Korach, which tells it, is often read in the last days of Sivan.

It is fitting that Moses goes with the elephant, the largest land animal, because he also goes with the eagle, the largest bird, and the Leviathan, the largest sea animal. He was and always will be the greatest of all prophets.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Yishmael: one who refrains from serving as a judge avoids hatred, thievery and false oaths, and one who frivolously hands down rulings is a fool, wicked and arrogant. He also says: do not judge on your own, for there is none qualified to judge alone, only the One; and do not say, "You must accept my view," for that is the majority's right, not yours. That belongs to the unity of Sivan, and to the humility the commandments need. We have to do everything in our power not to make ourselves great at the Torah's expense, remembering that only G-d is truly great. And it points straight at Moses and Korach. Korach was enormously rich, with a deep-set enlarged view of himself, and his claim rested on something like the last part of this teaching — that Moses and Aaron should follow the majority rather than keep the key positions for themselves. Moses explained that the rebellion was ultimately against G-d Himself, who had chosen the two of them. And G-d does, and will, judge alone.

The combination is gevurah shebeyesod. This week we work with strength and discipline to keep a solid foundation in study and in the mitzvot, and the elephant is that foundation: who can move an elephant against its will? The lesson from it is that even the largest animal recognises the infinite greatness and depth of Hashem.

254.title: Strength and Stability that Come From Humility
body: The third week of Sivan. Haazinu asks the question: "Then He will say, 'Where is their deity, the rock in which they trusted,'" (Deuteronomy 32:37) and read positively it is asked not of the Jewish people but of the other nations — which fits the verse of week thirty-one, that our Rock is not like theirs.

The Haftorah is the footing: "You have enlarged my step[s] beneath me; And my ankles have not slipped." (II Samuel 22:37) That support is a stable rock. It also runs parallel to the elephant's verse about the works of G-d being great — Gadol, big, like the elephant, and Gimmel Dalet Lamed have the numerical value of 37.

The quality is keeping far from honor. Pirkei Avot teaches that seeking honor takes a person out of this world. Honor, or anything that feeds the ego, is an enormous obstacle in serving G-d; haughtiness is the opposite of holiness. For all the honor given the Jewish people at Mount Sinai, the experience was so awe-inspiring that it led to greater humility. It is the same thing the Pirkei Avot of Book 1 says, about not handing down judgments needlessly — and seeking honor is what brought Korach down.

The prophet is Ezekiel, who is bound closely to keeping far from honor. G-d commands him to do things so far against what we would call kevod habriot, the honour and dignity of a person, that it is hard to imagine anyone capable of them: Ezekiel is commanded to eat excrement. And it is Ezekiel who has the most exalted visions of G-d — the Haftorah of the first day of Shavuot is his vision of the Heavenly Chariot, the opening lines of his book. He was a kohen too, like Uriah and Jeremiah, the prophets of the two weeks before.
The levitical city is Dimnah, which literally means dunghill: staying away from honor again.
254.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 37.

255.title: Remembering the Shavuot Experience
body: Beshalach: "They gathered it morning by morning, each one according to his eating capacity, and [when] the sun grew hot, it melted. It came to pass on the sixth day that they gathered a double portion of bread, two omers for [each] one, and all the princes of the community came and reported [it] to Moses." Each took what he could hold. The sixth day is not only the sixth of the week but Shavuot, which fell on the sixth of Sivan; the double portion may be the two crowns of Torah; and all the princes of the community coming together is the unity of this month.

The Haftorah is Sissera going down: "At her feet he sank, fell, lay; at her feet he sank (and) fell." It is remarkable how often the words repeat — karah three times in the whole verse, and nafal three times, and in the part given to this week a whole phrase comes twice with "lay" set between. Taken out of the context of his death and set in Shavuot, it is perhaps the people's own experience at Mount Sinai: there we bowed and fell and lay at the feet of the Shechinah, our souls left our bodies, and we had to be revived.

Daf Lamed Zayin of Sotah takes up the splitting of the Red Sea, including the initiative and self-sacrifice of the tribe of Benjamin and of Nachshon ben Aminadav; then Har Grizim and Har Eival again, with where the Levi'im and the Kohanim stood; and then the number of covenants made with the Jewish people, the one at Har Sinai among them, and the blessings and curses. The parallels with Shavuot are many: the initiative and self-sacrifice of saying Na'aseh veNishmah, and the covenant at the mountain.

The generation is Asa, son of Abijam, an extremely righteous king who returned the kingdom to the ways of Hashem and rid it of idol worship — he even removed his own mother from her position for worshipping Ashera trees. He overlaps briefly with Jeroboam, and with all the kings of Israel who fought over Jeroboam's succession: Nadav, Baasa, Elah, Zimri, Tivni, who was never an undisputed king, and Omri. All of them ruled for very short times, Tivni never ruling at all, except Omri, who ruled for 12 years. Asa reigned for forty-one years, and except for one brief lapse of faith in dealing with Baasa he was righteous and faithful and led Judah on a good path — fitting for the week after Shavuot.

The journey is from Punon to Oboth. Rabbi Jacobson explains that Oboth means enemies, and also necromancy, as in the practice of Ovoth and Yidonim. After the giving of the Torah we begin to be tested by our enemies, who work to bring us down from the height we reached, and it matters to stay firm. Oboth is also spelled like Avoth, the patriarchs — and it was by visiting Hebron, the Cave of the Patriarchs, that Caleb was able to stay faithful to his mission and bring back a true report. The personal journey moves from being revived by the Torah to staying connected to our roots and true to our mission.

256.title: Years of Life and Length of Days
body: Channah's ninth verse: "The feet of His pious ones He will guard, And the wicked shall be cut off in darkness, For not by strength will man prevail."

Pirkei Avot, on the greatness of the Torah, also weighs life against death: "With me, your days shall be increased, and years of life shall be added to you." Days and years look like a repetition, and they are not — a person can live many years and have little quality in his days.

Ecclesiastes 6 is length of days, and the darkness inside even a long life. "Should a man beget one hundred [children] and live many years, and he will have much throughout the days of his years, but his soul will not be sated from all the good, neither did he have burial. I said that the stillborn is better than he. For he comes in vanity and goes in darkness, and in darkness his name is covered." And then: "For who knows what is good for man in his lifetime, the number of the days of his life of vanity, that he do them like a shadow, for who will tell man what will be after him under the sun?"
The week holds the yahrzeits of Rav Aharon of Karlin, the Beis Aharon, on the 17th of Sivan, and Rabbi Yissachar Dov of Radoshitz, the Sabba Kadisha, on the 18th.

Rebbe Aharon of Karlin was the son of Rebbe Asher of Stolin and grandson of Rebbe Aharon HaGadol of Karlin, and is known as the Second Rebbe Aharon. He was chosen as Karliner Rebbe at only 26, and led the Karlin Chassidim with prodigious scholarship and unparalleled piety and humility; tens of thousands thronged around him seeking the blessings of a man said to be endowed with ruach hakodesh, and some even claimed he had the soul of King David. His leadership fell in the dark days of the reign of Czar Nikolai I, and he knew how to cheer his Chassidim and help them carry their burdens. Some powerful residents of Karlin objected to how much song and dance filled his court, and in 1864 he was run out of town; he resettled in Stolin, and since then the dynasty has been known as Karlin-Stolin. By family tradition he was born on Rosh Chodesh Sivan, 1802, and he led the Karliner Chassidim for nearly fifty years. A gifted organiser, he worked at the bonds between himself and his followers, visiting them often in their towns and welcoming them warmly in his court. He had a striking natural simplicity and sense of humour, and regularly made jokes in the Russian vernacular even while teaching at his table; he mixed freely with people of all kinds, and his confident presence was admired even in non-Chassidic circles.

Rabbi Yissachar Dov, the Sabba Kadisha, the holy grandfather, of Radoshitz, was a disciple of the Seer of Lublin and of the Holy Yid of Peshischa. Famed as a miracle maker, he lived in poverty as a simple tutor. Also this week: Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin on the 14th of Sivan and Rabbi Dovid Twersky, Second Rebbe of Skver, on the 19th.

257.title: First Fruits
body: The Song goes out early: "Let us arise early to the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has blossomed, the tiny grapes have developed, the pomegranates have lost their flowers; there I will give you my love." This one belongs to Chag HaBikkurim, the festival of the first fruits, gathered from the field and brought as an offering. Rashi explains that the pomegranates losing their flowers means they had become ripe, and he connects each of the fruits named with the knowledge and study of Torah, the study of Mishnah in particular.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the thirty-seventh is Shuni, whose name looks related to LeShanot, to go over, to study. And with him Becher, son of Benjamin, whose name is near Bechor, firstborn, and Bikkurim, first fruits.
Daf Lamed Zayin of Shvuot keeps on with the oath of a pikadon, a gift or deposit — and the Torah is the gift itself, given at Sinai.

Jeremiah's thirty-seventh chapter has the king of Judah finally listening to the prophet, and the first signs of all his prophecies coming true, and of his vindication against the false prophets. "Deceive not yourselves, saying, 'The Chaldeans shall surely withdraw from us,' for they shall not withdraw." Then the king, in private: "And King Zedekiah sent and took him, and the king asked him secretly in his house, and he said, 'Is there a word from the Lord?' And Jeremiah said, 'There is.' And he said, 'You shall be given into the hand[s] of the king of Babylon.'" And then Jeremiah's own question: "What have I sinned against you and against your servants and against this people, that you have put me into the prison? And where are your prophets who prophesied to you, saying, 'The king of Babylon shall not come upon you or upon this land'?"

258.title: Reviewing the Third Week of Sivan - Psalms 109-111; 105:12-14; 89:38
body: The third week of Sivan in psalms: the hundred and ninth, hundred and tenth and hundred and eleventh, with three verses of Psalm 105 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 109 David composed while fleeing from Saul, facing many enemies who acted friendly in his presence and spoke only evil of him — so he curses them bitterly. "O G-d of my praise, be not silent. For the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of the deceitful have opened against me; they spoke to me with a false tongue." The exchange that hurts: "In return for my love they hate me; still, I am [a man of] prayer. They placed harm upon me in return for my favor, and hatred in return for my love." Then the long curse, which runs from his days to his children to his name. Then the reason: "Because he did not remember to do kindness, and he pursued the poor and destitute man and the broken-hearted, to kill [him]." And the curse as clothing: "He donned the curse like his garment, and it came like water into his innards, like oil into his bones." Then his own state: "For I am poor and destitute, and my heart has died within me. Like the fleeting shadow I am banished, I am tossed about like the locust. My knees totter from fasting." And the asking: "Let them know that this is Your hand, that You, Lord, have done it. Let them curse, but You will bless." And the last line, which says where He stands: "when He stands at the right of the destitute one to deliver him from the condemners of his soul."

Psalm 110 records the answer of Eliezer, servant of Abraham, to those who asked how Abraham managed to defeat the four kings; he tells of Abraham killing the mighty kings and their armies. Read it and you will find that the whole psalm is about Abraham, who merited prominence for recognising G-d in his youth. "The Lord said to my master, 'Sit at My right, until I make your enemies a stool for your feet.' The staff of your strength the Lord will send from Zion, to rule amid your enemies." The youth kept: "because of your splendid sanctity from when you emerged from the womb, you still possess the dew of your youth." And the oath: "The Lord has sworn and will not regret: 'You shall be a priest forever, just as Melchizedek!'"

Psalm 111 is written in alphabetical sequence, two letters to a verse, except the last two, which have three each. It is short and prominent, and it is about the works of G-d and their greatness. "Great are the works of the Lord, [yet] available to all who desire them. Majesty and splendor are His work, and His righteousness endures forever. He established a memorial for His wonders, for the Lord is gracious and compassionate." The works that hold: "The works of His hands are true and just; all His mandates are faithful. They are steadfast for ever and ever, for they are made with truth and uprightness." And the last line: "The beginning of wisdom is fear of the Lord; sound wisdom for all who practice it-his praise endures forever."

Psalm 105's verses are the few strangers on the road: "When they were few in number, hardly dwelling in it. And they walked from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people. He let no man oppress them, and He reproved kings on their account." And Psalm 89's verse is the witness in the sky: "Like the moon, which is established forever, and it is a witness in the sky, eternally true."

259.title: The Elephant Is Saying
body: The elephant opens, and the week sets a widened step beside thoughts too deep to follow.

The step and the depth first: "You have enlarged my step[s] beneath me" / "And my ankles have not slipped" / "How great are your works, G-d" / "Your thoughts are tremendously deep" / "Let us arise early to the vineyards" / "Let us see whether the vine has blossomed."

Then the gathering, and what strength cannot do: "They gathered it morning by morning" / "For not by strength will man prevail" / "And they walked from nation to nation" / "From one kingdom to another people" / "A double portion of bread, two omers for one" / "And all the princes of the community came and reported to Moses" / "Each one according to his eating capacity" / "And [when] the sun grew hot, it melted."

Then the question about their rock, and the falling at her feet: "Then He will say, 'Where is their deity'" / "'The rock in which they trusted?'" / "At her feet he sank, fell, lay" / "At her feet he sank (and) fell" / "The feet of His pious ones He will guard" / "And the wicked shall be cut off in darkness."

And the end is the ripe fruit and the moon: "The tiny grapes have developed" / "The pomegranates have lost their flowers" / "Like the moon, which is established forever" / "And it is a witness in the sky, eternally true" / "When they were few in number, hardly dwelling in it" / "It came to pass on the sixth day that they gathered" / "He let no man oppress them, and He reproved kings on their account" / "There I will give you my love."

260.title: To Be Strong and Courageous in order to Defend the Common Good
body: The Lion is saying, "G-d shall go out as a mighty man, He shall arouse zeal, He shall cry, even roar, He shall prevail over His enemies." (Isaiah 42:13) The verse belongs to Sivan, where the whole people trembled at the voice giving the Ten Commandments at Mount Sinai. It belongs to Zevulun too, who went out to sea to trade — and our sages draw an interesting line between going out to war and going out to make a living, which can be its own kind of war.

The week of the lion is the last of Sivan and the last of spring. The two summer months that follow, Tammuz and Av, are intense, and closely tied to the destruction of the Temple — and also to its rebuilding and the coming of Mashiach.

Here Hashem Himself is the lion. The Temple is often called a lion too, Ariel, which means lion of G-d. And the lion is the symbol of the tribe of Judah, from whom come King David and Mashiach. A Midrash runs all three together: the lion, Nebuchadnezzar the Babylonian emperor, came during the lion, the month of Av, and destroyed Ariel, the Temple, so that the Lion, G-d, will appear during the lion, the month of Av, and rebuild Ariel. The verse itself compares Him to a man at war, a roaring lion who will defeat His enemies and redeem His people. In the last week of Sivan we get ready, spiritually and physically and in our minds, for what is coming. Tammuz and Av can hold much pain, and they hold the spirit of redemption; it depends how they are approached. To come through, we have to reach the spark of the lion of Judah, of David, of Mashiach, that each of us carries. Prepared well, with everything learned from Passover to Lag Ba'Omer to Shavuot, we will be strong as lions, and with G-d beside us there is nothing at all to fear.

Thirty-eight is the gematria of Bul, the biblical name of Cheshvan. The Torah says that "in the month Bul, which is the eighth month, the house [of G-d] was finished throughout all the parts thereof, and according to all the fashion of it, and he built it in seven years." In week twenty-three we had the gematria of Ziv, the biblical name of Iyar, the month Solomon's Temple was begun. Having lived the redemption of Adar and Nissan, worked on ourselves in Iyar, and received the Torah in Sivan, our inner Temple should feel finished now — and it is our work to protect it, and to bring about the rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem.

Thirty-eight is chet and lamed, which spell chol, sand, recalling the blessing Abraham received that his offspring would be as many as the sand of the sea. Chol also means profane, which belongs to the destruction, the exile, and the profanation of His name in the months after Sivan. And the same letters spell lach, wet or fresh: we leave Sivan, and spring, fresh and full of water — a metaphor for Torah — and ready for the summer heat.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Yonatan: whoever fulfills the Torah in poverty will ultimately fulfill it in wealth, and whoever neglects the Torah in wealth will ultimately neglect it in poverty. This week holds the same thing. If we break the Torah so soon after its revelation in Sivan, it will be harder still to keep it in the poverty that Tammuz and Av may bring. Keep it through those months of poverty, and they turn into months of tremendous enrichment, with the coming of Moshiach — and our commitment through the spiritual poverty of exile will be repaid with the ability to keep the Torah in the spiritual wealth of the Messianic era. The teaching also belongs to Zevulun, whose wealth provided for Issachar, and who, for all his professional activity, stayed faithful to the Torah and devoted to studying it.

The combination is tiferet shebeyesod. This week we feel the beauty and the balance of the Torah inside us and strengthen our foundations for the hard months. The lesson from the lion is that we have to be brave and willing to go out beyond our own sheltered worlds in order to help the people around us.

261.title: Daniel and Not Acting Arrogantly with One's Knowledge
body: The last week of Sivan. Haazinu continues last week's questions: "who ate the fat of their sacrifices and drank the wine of their libations? Let them arise and help you! Let them be your shelter!" (Deuteronomy 32:38) Read positively, the questions are still being put to Israel's enemies. The Haftorah supports that directly: "I have pursued my enemies and have destroyed them; Never turning back until they were consumed." (II Samuel 22:38) They found no refuge at all.

The quality is that he does not act arrogantly with his knowledge. Haughtiness is the opposite of holiness and of Torah, so being arrogant on the strength of what one knows is the plainest case of behaving wrongly — the knowledge does not belong to the individual but to G-d. It can also be read as not acting arrogantly with His knowledge, because the knowledge is all His. That is a central message of Sivan.

The prophet is Daniel — and this is the week of the lion, and Daniel is known above all for being thrown into the den of hungry lions and miraculously saved. His reading of Nebuchadnezzar's dream is this quality at work, because the interpretation of dreams comes from G-d. "And to these youths, the four of them, G-d gave knowledge and understanding in every script and wisdom, and Daniel understood all visions and dreams." Asked for the dream, he first asked for time, told Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, and prayed; and when the secret was revealed to him in a vision of the night, he blessed the G-d of heaven: "May the Name of G-d be blessed from everlasting even to everlasting, to Whom are wisdom and might. And He changes the times and the seasons, He removes kings and sets up kings; He grants wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who know understanding. He reveals the profound and secret things; He knows what is in the dark, and light dwells with Him." And standing before the king he said it plainly: "The secret that the king asks, no wise men, astrologers, necromancers, or demonologists can tell the king. But there is a G-d in heaven Who reveals secrets." And: "And I-not with wisdom that I possess more than all living, did He reveal this secret to me." Which is what his predecessor Joseph said to Pharaoh: "Not I; G-d will give an answer [that will bring] peace to Pharaoh."

Rashi notes that the sages discuss whether Daniel should count as a prophet, so some put Shemaiah here instead. The prophet Shemaiah, who prophesied in the days of Rehavam, would be well out of chronological order; another Shemaiah, a kohen, the father of Uriah, is somewhat closer and still out of order. Perhaps the name is a further hint at the quality of the week, since Shemaiah comes from Lishmoah, to hear, with the Name of Hashem in it — heard G-d, or G-d heard. It points at the humility a prophet needs: to remember that his job is to be a conduit, to hear the word of G-d when G-d hears His people. Which is Sivan as well.
The levitical city is Nahalal, whose name holds hallel, to praise. Praising G-d for everything He has done for us is the ultimate form of humility.
261.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 38.

262.title: Preparing for the Summer Months
body: Beshalach: "So he said to them, That is what the Lord spoke, Tomorrow is a rest day, a holy Sabbath to the Lord. Bake whatever you wish to bake, and cook whatever you wish to cook, and all the rest leave over to keep until morning. So they left it over until morning, as Moses had commanded, and it did not become putrid, and not a worm was in it." The sixth day is special again, and this is preparing for the Sabbath — which is the preparing for the hard summer months, and it has to be done in Sivan.

The Haftorah finishes Sissera and turns to a window: "where he sank, there he fell down dead. Through the window looked forth, the mother of Sisera [peered] through the window." Out of the context of his death, the verse looks like Sinai again. And a mother peering through a window brings to mind the verse of the Song of Songs where G-d peers through the window to see our suffering, ready to return His Shechinah to its place — which points at the coming months too.

Daf Lamed Cheit of Sotah is all the blessing of the Kohanim, and how the blessing given outside the Temple differed from the one given inside. That blessing, which by halachah must be given out of love, as the brachah before it says, is the ultimate example of brotherly love and peace among the Jewish people.

The generation is Jehoshaphat, son of Asa, another extremely righteous king; his counterparts in Israel were Omri, Ahab, and Ahaziah. His name means G-d is Judge — and in Book 2 this week's prophet is Daniel, whose name also means G-d is my Judge. His one mistake was growing too friendly with the evil rulers of the northern kingdom and at times seeking alliances with them, which is the other side of this month's brotherly love: one has to know when to keep a distance. Overall he was extremely righteous and led the people through 25 years of real peace and prosperity. Set his name against Ahab's, which makes no reference to G-d and suggests possible incest, meaning brother-father. Ahab seems to correct that in naming his own son Ahaziah, one who holds on to G-d, with Hashem's name in it; Ahaziah is also the name of one of the kings of Judah. He followed his father's evil ways all the same, was involved in idolatry, and died after only two years.

The journey is from Oboth to the ruins of Abarim, on the Moabite boundary. Abarim comes from Aveirah, transgression. Because of our sins in the summer months of Tammuz and Av, our Temple lies in ruins — and Rashi himself draws the parallel to Jerusalem in one of his few comments on the journeys, reading the ruins of Abarim as an expression of waste and ruin, as in "into a heap in the field," and "they have turned Jerusalem into heaps." Moab was a nation known for its immorality, and like Ahab's, its name suggests incest, and was given for that reason: Moab means from the father, because the nation began when Lot had relations with his own daughter. It is our work to fight such immorality, and so to raise the sparks hidden in that nation's kelipah. And after Ahab's death it was Moab that revolted against Israel. The personal journey moves from staying true to our mission to repenting of, and fighting, the sins that brought the Temple down.

263.title: Strength and Long Life
body: Channah's tenth verse closes her song: "Those who strive with the Lord will be broken; Upon him will He thunder in Heaven; The Lord will judge the ends of the earth. And He will grant strength to His King, And raise the horn of His anointed one." Judgment, and then strength given to the king.
Pirkei Avot, on the greatness of the Torah, raises those who come near it: "Long days in her right hand; in her left, wealth and honor."

Ecclesiastes 7 is the standing and the length of days that wisdom brings: "Be not overly wicked, and be not a fool; why should you die before your time? It is good that you should take hold of this, and also from this you shall not withdraw your hand, for he who fears God will discharge himself of them all. Wisdom affords strength to the wise more than ten rulers who were in the city."
The week holds the yahrzeits of Rebbe Yisrael Dan of Modzitz on the 20th of Sivan, Rebbe Shlomo Shapira of Munkatch on the 21st, and Rabbi Mordechai-Tzemach Eliyahu on the 25th.

Reb Israel Dan was born in 1928 in Warsaw, the capital of Poland, and made Aliya to Eretz Yisrael with his parents in 1936, as a child of 7. He married Rachel, daughter of HaRav Shmuel Aharon Shadrovitzki from Byalistok, a great talmud chacham among the heads of Agudas Yisrael in Poland. He was chosen to replace the Imrei Aish on his passing, and his deep knowledge of the Torah became evident to many when he became the Admor on his father's death; at his Tishim people heard many beautiful Divre Torah, pleasant to the ear. For some years he led the Chasidim in Tel-Aviv, where his father had lived, and on Lag Ba'omer 1995 he moved to a new building the Chasidim had built in Bnei Brak. Like his fathers he composed Nigunnim, many of which are already sung regularly in Jewish homes. He was very active in the public interest and a member of the Moetzet G'Dolei Hatorah, where his opinions were looked up to.

Rabbi Shlomo Shapira, author of the Shem Shlomoh, was the first Rebbe of Chassidut Munkach, son of Rabbi Elazar Shapira and grandson of Rabbi Zvi Elimelech Shapira of Dynow, the Bnei Yissachar; he was also the rabbi of the town of Munkatch. His biography is set down in a work by David Kahane called Beit Shlomoh.

Rabbi Mordechai-Tzemach Eliyahu, the former Chief Sephardic Rabbi of Israel, was born in Iraq. A noted sage in every area of Torah study and a significant kabbalist, he was considered one of the leading authorities on Jewish law in Israel. His son, Rabbi Shmuel Eliyahu, is Chief Rabbi of Tsfat.

264.title: Unity and Captivity
body: The Song's verse keeps to the first fruits, with fruit new and old: "The pots [of figs] have given forth [their] fragrance, and on our doorways are all manner of sweet fruits, both new and old, which I have hidden away for you, my beloved." Rashi comments that before, there were two kinds of fruit, good and bad, and now both of them have given forth their fragrance; they all seek Your countenance. Sivan is the height of both Jewish unity and the revelation that follows it.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the thirty-eighth is Ezbon, whose name looks related to Etzbah, finger. A finger is not an independent thing: it is part of a hand and has to be joined to it. And with him Ashbel, son of Benjamin, whose name means taken captive — another of the names Benjamin gave as a sign of unity with his brother, mourning that Joseph had been sold as a slave.

Daf Lamed Cheit of Shvuot keeps on with the oath of a pikadon and opens a new chapter on Shevuas HaDayanim, the oath of judges, on partial admission, and on how an oath is administered. Most of the daf is the collective oath — and this week and this month are about collectivity.

Jeremiah's thirty-eighth chapter has the king receptive again, and promising not to punish him for his words. "And King Zedekiah sent and took Jeremiah the prophet to him, to the third entrance, that was in the house of the Lord, and the king said to Jeremiah, 'I ask you a word; do not conceal a word from me.'" Jeremiah's answer: "If I tell you, will you not put me to death? And if I advise you, you will not listen to me." So the king swore secretly: "As the Lord lives who made for us this soul, I will neither put you to death nor will I deliver you into the hand[s] of these men who seek your life." Then the choice, laid out plainly: "If you go out to the officers of the king of Babylon, your soul shall live, and this city shall not be burnt with fire, and you and your household shall live. But if you do not go out... this city shall be delivered into the hand[s] of the Chaldeans, and they shall burn it with fire." The king was afraid of the Jews who had defected. And then the picture of what refusing would bring, down to the women and the children: "Behold, all the women who remained in the house of the king of Judah shall be taken out to the officers of the king of Babylon, and they shall say, 'Your cohorts have enticed you and prevailed over you. Your feet have sunk into the mire; they have turned back.'" The last verse of the chapter says what happened: "And Jeremiah stayed in the prison yard until the day that Jerusalem was taken, and he was [there] when Jerusalem was taken."

265.title: Reviewing the Last Week of Sivan - Psalms 112-114; 105:15-17; 89:39
body: The last week of Sivan in psalms: the hundred and twelfth, hundred and thirteenth and hundred and fourteenth, with three verses of Psalm 105 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 112 also follows the alphabet, two letters to a verse except the last two, which have three each. It is about the good traits a man should choose, and about how to give charity — whose reward is never having to rely on others. "Fortunate is the man who fears the Lord, and desires His commandments intensely." The light in the dark: "Even in darkness light shines for the upright, for [He is] Compassionate, Merciful, and Just." The measure of the man: "Good is the man who is compassionate and lends, [but] provides for his own needs with discretion." The steadiness: "He will not be afraid of a bad tiding; his heart is steadfast, secure in the Lord." And the giving: "He has distributed [his wealth], giving to the needy. His righteousness will endure forever; his might will be uplifted in honor."

Psalm 113 recounts some of the wonders of the exodus. "From the rising of the sun to its setting, the Name of the Lord is praised. The Lord is high above all nations; His glory transcends the heavens. Who is like the Lord our G-d, Who dwells on high [yet] looks down so low upon heaven and earth!" And what He does when He looks: "He raises the poor from the dust, lifts the destitute from the dunghill, to seat them with nobles, with the nobles of His people. He transforms the barren woman into a household, into a joyful mother of children."

Psalm 114 explains why the tribe of Judah merited kingship. "When Israel went out of Egypt, the House of Jacob from a people of a foreign tongue, Judah became His holy [nation], Israel, His domain." Then the world running: "The sea saw and fled, the Jordan turned backward. The mountains skipped like rams, the hills like young sheep." Then the question put to all of them — what is the matter with you, sea, that you flee; Jordan, that you turn backward; mountains, that you skip — and the answer: "[We do so] before the Master, the Creator of the earth, before the G-d of Jacob, Who turns the rock into a pool of water, the flintstone into a water fountain."

Psalm 105's verses are the protection and the famine and the man sent ahead: "Do not touch My anointed ones, and do not harm My prophets." "He called a famine upon the land; He broke every staff of bread. He sent a man before them; Joseph was sold as a slave." And Psalm 89's verse turns hard: "But You abandoned and You rejected; You became wroth with Your anointed."

266.title: The Lion is saying
body: The lion opens, and the week sets a roar against a mother at a window.

The roaring and the pursuing first: "He shall arouse zeal, He shall cry" / "Even roar, He shall prevail over His enemies" / "I have pursued my enemies and have destroyed them" / "Those who strive with the Lord will be broken" / "Upon him will He thunder in Heaven."

Then what was left until morning, and the famine: "So they left it over until morning" / "As Moses had commanded" / "He called a famine upon the land" / "He broke every staff of bread" / "Who ate the fat of their sacrifices" / "And drank the wine of their libations?" / "Through the window looked forth, the mother of Sisera [peered] through the window."

Then the gods called on to help, and the dead man: "Let them arise and help you! Let them be your shelter!" / "And all the rest leave over to keep until morning" / "Where he sank, there he fell down dead" / "The Lord will judge the ends of the earth" / "And He will grant strength to His King" / "And raise the horn of His anointed one."

Then the anointed twice over, and Joseph sold: "'Do not touch My anointed ones, And do not harm My prophets'" / "But You abandoned and You rejected; You became wroth with Your anointed" / "He sent a man before them; Joseph was sold as a slave."

And the end is the Sabbath and the fragrance: "So he said to them, That is what the Lord spoke" / "Tomorrow is a rest day, A holy Sabbath to the Lord" / "The pots [of figs] have given forth [their] fragrance" / "And on our doorways are all manner of sweet fruits" / "Bake whatever you wish to bake" / "And cook whatever you wish to cook" / "G-d shall go out as a mighty man" / "Never turning back until they were consumed" / "And it did not become putrid, and not a worm was in it" / "Both new and old, Which I have hidden away for you, my beloved."

267.title: To See the World in a Positive Light in Order to Elevate It
body: This week holds Rosh Chodesh Tammuz and Gimmel Tammuz, the date of the Lubavitcher Rebbe's passing and also the beginning of the liberation of the Sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe.

Tammuz belongs to Reuven, Jacob's firstborn. His name comes from reiyiah, sight, and the month is the tikkun of our sense of sight. Reuven belongs to teshuvah in general: the Midrash says of him that he was the first to repent out of love, without being chastised first. The month is also the tikkun for the sin of the spies. Moses sent them, and they travelled through the Land of Israel for the whole month of Tammuz, and apart from Joshua and Caleb they saw it in a negative light. Tammuz carries the tragedies of the 17th day of the month — among them the destruction of the first tablets of the Ten Commandments, and the breaching of the walls of Jerusalem — and it also carries the final redemption, when, after we repent and are redeemed, the 17th of Tammuz will no longer be a day of fasting and mourning but a day of celebration. That turnaround is Reuven's own. Jacob took away his firstborn rights after a severe mistake involving one of his father's concubines, and Reuven spent his whole life doing teshuvah for it — and the Torah recognises that repentance, still calling him Jacob's firstborn long after.

The Bear is saying, "Let the wilderness and its cities lift up their voice, the village that Kedar inhabits; let the inhabitants of the rock sing, let them shout from the peaks of the mountains. Let them give glory to G-d and tell of His praise in the islands." (Isaiah 42:11-12) The song is about looking at the world with good eyes. The Bear sees that the deserts, the cities, the villages, the mountains and the islands all hold the great potential of praising G-d. That is how the world should be seen — everyone has it, and we only need to open our eyes. One of the Rebbe's main accomplishments, which began with the Previous Rebbe, was always to see in each follower and in every Jew that enormous potential for good; it is how he formed so many leaders and reached so many people, spreading the light of Judaism and Chassidism to the far corners of the world — cities and spiritual deserts, mountains and isolated islands.

Eliyahu HaNavi, who will announce the coming of Mashiach, also goes with the Bear. As in week 12, the Tanach tells that before Elijah ascended, Elisha asked for a double portion of his strength. Soon after, when Elisha purified the waters of a city, he was insulted by some young men who had made their money carrying clean water from elsewhere, and whose trade his miracle had made useless. They began taunting him, calling him bald, to set him against Elijah, who had a head full of hair. Elisha cursed them, and two bears — an apparent reference to that double portion — came out of the wilderness and killed them. And just as the bear's song names Arabia, Kedar, the Talmud has various stories of Elijah disguising himself as an Arab when he appeared before tzadikim, to test them or to help them.

Thirty-nine is the number of kinds of work forbidden on Shabbat, which parallel the thirty-nine kinds of work done in building the Mishkan, a miniature Temple where the Divine Presence rested. The Mishkan is a microcosm of the world: as G-d rested on the seventh day of creation, the Jewish people rested on the same day while building it. And the bear's song is about distant, uninhabited places that hold the potential to praise Hashem, and so to make Him a home in this world. The Midrash Tanchumah teaches that His main object in creating the world was to make a home for Himself in the lowly realms — and that home is the Mishkan. The letters lamed and tet, which make thirty-nine, spell tel, mountain; the laws of Shabbat are known as mountains on a wire, because a vast number of prohibitions are drawn from a few explicit verses.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Meir: engage minimally in business and occupy yourself with Torah; be humble before every man; if you neglect the Torah there will be many more causes for neglect before you, and if you toil much in Torah there is much reward to give you. The Talmud says that whoever saw Rabbi Meir studying saw him take mountains and grind them into each other. He was known for miracles, many of them involving Eliyahu HaNavi. He is teshuvah too, and seeing the potential in people and in far places: he was himself a descendant of Roman converts, and when a certain group of people mistreated and insulted him, he followed his wife Beruria's advice and, instead of praying for their destruction, prayed that they do teshuvah — which in the end they did. His words belong to Tammuz and to Reuven: humbly turning any lack of dedication to the Torah, which brought our people such obstacles and tragedies, into full dedication and toil, and so into enormous reward.

The combination is netzach shebeyesod. We have to be persistent in keeping our foundation in Torah and mitzvot. Joseph, who is yesod, endured the constant attempts of Potiphar's wife to seduce him and resisted her in the end — and Rashi compares her to a bear. There will always be bears trying to pull us off our purpose; we have to stand as firm as one ourselves. And from the bear we learn that wherever we are, we should try to speak of the Torah and raise the place we are in as far as we can.

268.title: Baruch and Not Being Happy in Handing Down Decrees
body: Rosh Chodesh Tammuz and Gimmel Tammuz. Tammuz is marked by the fast of the 17th, when the walls of Jerusalem were breached, and the month belongs to Reuven, Jacob's firstborn.

Haazinu: "See now that it is I! I am the One, and there is no G-d like Me! I cause death and grant life. I strike, but I heal, and no one can rescue from My Hand!" (Deuteronomy 32:39) That verse is Tammuz exactly — before the times of Mashiach a month of death and suffering, and after them a month of life and healing.

The Haftorah picks up the last words of it: "And I have consumed them, and I have crushed them that they cannot rise; Yes, they are fallen under my feet." (II Samuel 22:39) In this month we have been crushed and consumed in the past, and in the future the enemies of the Jews will fall under their feet.

The quality is that he does not take pleasure in handing down halachic decisions, Einoh Sameach B'hora'ah — not using the Torah for one's own honor. More literally, the person is not happy in making rulings. Tammuz has been a month in which the Jewish people were not happy, having been handed difficult decrees in it. And it is in our power to reverse those decrees, through Teshuvah.

The prophet is Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, who was given the task of reading those dire prophecies to the people — a task he certainly took no pleasure in, and he handed the decrees down all the same, according to his master's will. All four prophets of the month of Tammuz are related to Baruch: after him comes his father, then his brother, then his grandfather.

The levitical city is Betzer, also a city of refuge. Betzer means fortification, which suits the week, since it was in Tammuz that the fortifications of Jerusalem were breached. All the cities of this week are connected to Moab, and to Jeremiah's prophecy against that nation. Moab is the kelipah of broad powers, physical and intellectual, and the fear of losing them — which is Reuven's own.
268.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 39.

269.title: Challenges to Faith in the Times of Exile
body: Beshalach: "And Moses said, Eat it today, for today is a Sabbath to the Lord; today you will not find it in the field. Six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day [which is the] Sabbath on it there will be none." The mannah did not fall on the Sabbath, and it made the people nervous. Rashi sets the scene: in the morning, when they were used to going out to gather, they came to ask whether they should go out or not, and he said, what you have in your possession, eat. In the evening they came again and asked, and he said, today is the Sabbath. He saw they were worried that the manna had perhaps stopped and would not come down again, so he said, today you will not find it — meaning today you will not find it, and tomorrow you will.

Tammuz is a difficult month. In it the spies looked at the Land with negative eyes. In it, because of Moshe's brief delay in coming down the mountain, the grave sin of the golden calf happened, and then the breaking of the Luchot HaBrit. It is a month in which our Emunah is tested. And in Messianic times it will be a month of celebration. The mannah, the source of physical and spiritual substance, is not readily to be had at this time of year — in Moshe's words, today you will not find it, but tomorrow you will.

The Haftorah asks after a son who has not come home: "why is his chariot late in coming? Why tarry the strides of his chariots?" That is a challenge to faith too. And out of the context of Sissera's death, the chariot can mean something else: the visions of the Divine Presence, Ezekiel's and Isaiah's, and all the esoteric literature on them, are known as Ma'aseh Merkavah, the Workings of the Chariot. From Tammuz on, we think about how late the Shechinah is in returning to its holy place.

Daf Lamed Tet of Sotah gives the laws of proper behaviour in a synagogue, during the reading of the Torah and the blessing of the Kohanim. It mentions the verses the congregation says during the priestly blessing, which are about Zion, and the verses of the blessing said on the afternoon of a fast day, which plead to be saved from exile. A synagogue is known as a mikdash me'at, a miniature Temple — and this is the time of year we turn to Zion, to the destruction, and to the rebuilding.

The generation is Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat, whose reign was a complete disaster. His counterparts in Israel were Ahaziah and another king named Jehoram, son of Ahab, who was also wicked. Jehoram of Judah married Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, two of the most wicked and idolatrous people in all of Jewish history; she was idolatrous to an extreme and led her husband the same way, and soon idols and their priests were brought to Jerusalem. She then convinced him to kill his own six brothers. The kingdom was so steeped in crime and idolatry that all the nations that had been tributaries of Judah rebelled, ransacking every house including the royal palace; his wives and all but one of his children were captured and killed, and he himself died of an incurable disease. His name means G-d is exalted, and as this difficult month opens his reign shows how low we sometimes fall, and how much repentance matters.

The journey is from the ruins to Dibon gad. Dibon looks related to daveh, pining or moaning, and gad means good fortune, like the tribe of Gad, which belongs to Elul and to teshuvah. The secret is connecting Tammuz and Av to Elul, turning the word Dal, poor, into Dalet, door, which is the gates of teshuvah. The personal journey moves from fighting the sins that destroyed the Temple to pining for the good tidings that such repentance brings.

270.title: Years of Fullness and Peace
body: Channah's story ends quietly: "And Elkanah went to Ramah, to his house, and the child was serving the Lord before Eli the priest." It is a peaceful end to her life's dream of having children — and the end is really a beginning, a life full of meaning, with Shmuel now spending his days in the service of the leader of the generation.
Pirkei Avot, on the greatness of the Torah, adds peace to the length of days: "For long days, years of life, and peace, they shall add to you."

Ecclesiastes 8 says the days of the wicked will not be long: "But it will not be well with the wicked, and he will not prolong [his] days, like a shadow, because he does not fear God." And the days he does have hold no peace: "When I applied my heart to know wisdom and to see the conduct that is done upon the earth, for neither by day nor by night does he see sleep with his eyes."
Besides the Lubavitcher Rebbe's yahrzeit, the week holds Rabbi Shlomo of Bobov on the 1st of Tammuz, and Rabbi Nachman Horodenker and Rabbi Avraham of Trisk on the 2nd.

Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, the Lubavitcher Rebbe, became the seventh Rebbe of Chabad after his father-in-law, Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, passed away in Brooklyn on the 10th of Shvat 1950. He is widely acknowledged as the greatest Jewish leader of the second half of the 20th century. A dominant scholar in both the revealed and the hidden Torah, fluent in many languages and scientific subjects, he is best known for an extraordinary love and concern for every Jew on the planet; his emissaries around the globe number in the thousands, and hundreds of volumes of his teachings have been printed, with dozens of English renditions.

Rabbi Shlomo of Bobov was the first rebbe of the Bobover dynasty, which he took up shortly after the death of his renowned grandfather, the Divrei Chaim of Sanz. He was noted for strengthening the Judaism of the younger generation and for founding numerous yeshivas, and his chasidim numbered in the thousands. Rabbi Avraham of Trisk was one of the eight sons of Rabbi Mordechai of Chernobyl, all of whom became chasidic rebbes in their own right; besides being well known for the success of his blessings, his approachability and friendliness to all comers drew thousands to the court he conducted for some fifty years at Trisk, and his book, Magen Avraham on the Torah and the festivals, is popular among Chasidim and among yeshiva students for the guidelines it offers.

Rabbi Nachman Horodenker, Rebbe Nachman's grandfather, was associated with the pious scholars of Brody. Around 1740 he travelled with his son Reb Shimshon to Eretz Yisrael and left two years later. When Rabbi Elazar Rokeach, rabbi in Amsterdam and later Tzfat, heard that Rabbi Nachman was in Eretz Yisrael, he said that if they were both there together they would be able to bring the Mashiach, and he rushed to join him — but Rabbi Nachman had already left. And when Rabbi Nachman, back in Europe, heard that Rabbi Elazar was in Israel, he travelled back to Tsfat to join him, and Rabbi Elazar had died. When his wife passed away he returned to Europe and became one of the closest followers of the Baal Shem Tov; around that time he remarried, and Rabbi Simcha, Rebbe Nachman's father, was born. The Baal Shem Tov said that Rabbi Nachman Horodenker had prayed not to be able to hear anything unnecessary to his service of G-d, and that his request was granted. He was known for remarking on every occurrence that it was for the best, and he is quoted several times in the works of Rabbi Yaakov Yosef of Polonnoye and in Degel Machaneh Ephraim. The Baal Shem Tov held him back from returning to the Land of Israel, and in 1764, after visiting the Baal Shem Tov's grave, he said the Baal Shem Tov had appeared to him and granted permission. Rabbi Pinchas of Koretz said that as long as Rabbi Nachman was in what was then Poland, the Cossaks could not enter the country — and it was while he was on his way to Eretz Yisrael that the massacre in Uman took place. He is buried in the old cemetery in Tiveria.

271.title: Feeling the Harshness of Exile
body: The Song begins its last chapter wishing for a brother: "O, that you were like my brother, who sucked my mother's breasts! I would find you outside, I would kiss you, and they would not despise me." Fitting, now that Sivan and its twins are over and Tammuz has come, a month tied to exile, when we were despised outside our land. Rashi's comment points to Joseph: that you were like my brother, meaning that you would come to console me as Joseph did his brothers, who had done evil to him, and of whom it is said, "and he consoled them." And Rosh Chodesh Tammuz is Joseph's yahrzeit.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the thirty-ninth is Eri, whose name looks related to being awake — as in "I am asleep, but my heart is awake," on which our Sages comment: although I am sleeping in exile, my heart is awake for the Holy One, blessed be He. And with him Gera, son of Benjamin, whose name means a foreigner, which is Joseph becoming a stranger in a strange country, as the Jewish people did in this season. Er is also the name of Judah's son who was killed by G-d for his sins — and the harsh punishments of these months serve as a wake-up call.

Daf Lamed Tet of Shvuot describes the harsh punishments for false oaths. Even the family of the one who swears falsely is punished, and the punishment is immediate: water and fire do not wear away the wood and rocks of his house, but false oaths do; and regarding false oaths Hash-m does not cleanse without punishment even if he repents. The daf connects this to the oaths taken at Sinai.

Jeremiah's thirty-ninth chapter begins the description of the atrocities. It says it was in the tenth month that Nebuchadnezzar's army besieged Jerusalem, and in the fourth month that it breached the walls. Here the months are counted from Nissan, so the fourth is Tammuz; and though Tammuz is also called the tenth month, counting from Rosh Hashanah, here the tenth is Teveth. Tammuz belongs to Reuven and to sight — and after the walls are breached the king of Judah is blinded. "And the king of Babylon slaughtered Zedekiah's sons in Riblah before his eye, and the king of Babylon slaughtered all the nobles of Judah." Rashi: all the nobles of Judah are the Sanhedrin, because they had annulled the oath. "And he blinded Zedekiah's eyes, and he bound him with copper chains to bring him to Babylon. And the king's palace and the houses of the people the Chaldeans burnt with fire, and they demolished the walls of Jerusalem."

272.title: Reviewing the Week of Rosh Chodesh Tammuz - Psalms 115-117; 105:18-20; 89:40
body: The week of Rosh Chodesh Tammuz in psalms: the hundred and fifteenth, hundred and sixteenth and hundred and seventeenth, with three verses of Psalm 105 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 115 asks Him to end this long exile for the sake of His Name, that it not be desecrated. "Not for our sake, Lord, not for our sake, but for the sake of Your Name bestow glory, because of Your kindness and Your truth. Why should the nations say, 'Where, now, is their G-d?'" Then the idols, made of silver and gold by human hands, taken apart sense by sense: "They have a mouth, but cannot speak; they have eyes, but cannot see; they have ears, but cannot hear; they have a nose, but cannot smell; their hands cannot touch; their feet cannot walk; they can make no sound in their throat." And then the warning: "Those who make them will become like them-all who put their trust in them." Then the three who are told to trust instead — Israel, the House of Aaron, those who fear the Lord — and the blessing on the small with the great. And the end: "The dead cannot praise the Lord, nor any who descend into the silence [of the grave]. But we will bless the Lord from now to eternity."

Psalm 116 is David's love for G-d in the light of all the miracles done for him, and his not knowing how to repay any of it. "The pangs of death encompassed me and the misery of the grave came upon me; I encounter trouble and sorrow. I invoke the Name of the Lord, 'Lord, I implore you, deliver my soul!'" Then the saving: "The Lord watches over the simpletons; I was brought low, and He saved me. Return, my soul, to your tranquility, for the Lord has bestowed goodness upon you. For You have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling." The faith held in the worst of it: "I had faith even when I declared, 'I am greatly afflicted'; [even when] I said in my haste, 'All men are deceitful.'" Then the question the psalm is built on: "How can I repay the Lord for all His beneficences to me? I will raise the cup of deliverance and proclaim the Name of the Lord." And the line that reads differently in this month: "Grievous in the eyes of the Lord is the death of His pious ones."

Psalm 117 is two verses, and it points at the Messianic era, when the Children of Israel will have their former glory and all will praise G-d, in fulfilment of the verse that all will then call in the Name of G-d: "Praise the Lord, all you nations; extol Him, all you peoples. For His kindness was mighty over us, and the truth of the Lord is everlasting."

Psalm 105's verses are a man in irons and then released: "They afflicted his foot with fetters; his soul was placed in irons. Until His word came, the saying of the Lord purified him. A king sent and released him, a ruler of peoples [sent] and loosed his bonds." And Psalm 89's verse is the crown thrown down: "You abrogated the covenant of Your servant; You profaned his crown to the ground."

273.title: The Bear Is Saying
body: The bear opens by calling on every place there is, and the week comes in around it.

The wilderness and the wish for a brother first: "Let the wilderness and its cities lift up their voice" / "The village that Kedar inhabits" / "O, that you were like my brother" / "Who sucked my mother's breasts!" / "And Moses said, 'Eat it today, For today is a Sabbath to the Lord; Today you will not find it in the field.'"

Then the rocks and the islands, and the going home: "Let the inhabitants of the rock sing" / "Let them shout from the peaks of the mountains" / "Let them give glory to G-d and tell of His praise in the islands" / "And Elkanah went to Ramah, to his house" / "I would find you outside, I would kiss you, and they would not despise me."

Then I am the One, with the six days and the child serving: "See now that it is I! I am the One, And there is no G-d like Me!" / "Six days you shall gather it, But on the seventh day, the Sabbath, on it there will be none" / "And the child was serving the Lord before Eli the priest" / "They afflicted his foot with fetters; His soul was placed in irons" / "You abrogated the covenant of Your servant."

And the end is the late chariot, the striking and the healing: "Why is his chariot late in coming?" / "Why tarry the strides of his chariots?" / "I cause death and grant life. I strike, but I heal" / "And no one can rescue from My Hand!" / "And I have consumed them, And I have crushed them that they cannot rise" / "Yes, they are fallen under my feet" / "You profaned his crown to the ground" / "Until His word came, the saying of the Lord purified him" / "A king sent and released him, A ruler of peoples [sent] and loosed his bonds."

274.title: To Fight for Truth
body: The wolf is saying, "For every matter of iniquity, for the ox, the donkey, the lamb, the garment, for every lost item which he says, 'This is it,' the matter of both of them shall come before the judge; he who the judge finds guilty shall pay double to the other." (Exodus 22:8)

The song belongs to Reuven. As last week, he lost the double portion that was his as firstborn, because of a mistake in moving the bed of one of Jacob's concubines. And on another occasion, when Jacob refused to let his children take Benjamin to Egypt, Reuven said that if he did not bring Benjamin back himself he would be willing to give up his two sons — which would be a double loss.

The wolf is also the symbol of Benjamin, who is close to this song too: arriving in Egypt, Benjamin is accused of theft by the viceroy, Joseph. And of all Jacob's children Benjamin is the one most bound to the Land of Israel, because he alone was born there.

The song runs parallel to the conquest of the Land as well. Rashi's first comment in the Torah explains why the Torah begins with the creation of the world rather than with the first mitzvah, blessing the new moon, given at our departure from Egypt: so that when the nations of the world accuse us of being thieves, claiming we are stealing the land, we can answer that the world and everything in it belongs to G-d, and it is He who decides which land to give to whom.

Forty intensifies the firmness of four. It is also deeply tied to taking in His eternal truth, the Torah: forty days and nights that Moses spent on Mount Sinai to receive it, forty years the Jews wandered in the desert, forty days and nights of the Flood, forty seah of water for a kosher mikvah. In Pirkei Avot the age of forty is understanding — it takes forty years to truly understand one's master's teaching. A pregnancy is forty weeks, the time in which an angel teaches the fetus the whole Torah. And the spies spent forty days scouting the Land, from Rosh Chodesh Tammuz to Tisha B'Av, this week among them.
The wolf sings the verdict on a thief, and it is known that the Flood only began once people began to steal — and the Flood also served as a mikvah to purify the world.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Eliezer the son of Yaakov: he who fulfills one mitzvah acquires for himself one angel-advocate, and he who commits one transgression acquires against himself one angel-accuser; repentance and good deeds are a shield against retribution. Theft is exactly the transgression that brings an accuser. And the teaching belongs to Tammuz and the tikkun of sight: it matters to look favourably on other people and on what they own, because jealousy is often what leads to theft — and to look at people favourably in order to be a good advocate ourselves. Teshuvah runs through it, which is Reuven.

The combination is hod shebeyesod, glory and gratefulness within foundation and firmness. This week we should be thankful, dedicated and grounded in our moral ways. The lesson from the wolf is that we cannot give in to corruption: we have to stand firm so that justice and truth win out over falsehood.

275.title: Neriah and "Bearing the Burden with One's Friend"
body: The second week of Tammuz. Haazinu is an oath: "For I raise up My hand to heaven, and say, 'As I live forever.'" (Deuteronomy 32:40) The wolf's song this week also refers to an oath. An oath adds weight and power, and determination and foundation — yesod.

The Haftorah girds for battle again: "For You have girded me with strength for the battle; You have subdued under me those that rose up against me." (II Samuel 22:40) King David's verses have been about being fortified and victorious ever since the week of Lag Ba'omer. Perhaps the repetition is there to say that in conquest it is often not enough to win once: one has to have yesod, to meet the same situation again and again and come through it without budging.

The quality is bearing the burden with one's friend, noseh b'ol im chaveroh. Not bearing the friend's burden — both are to share the burden together. That yoke might even be the yoke of Torah, which has to be taken up again day after day, an ongoing battle across a whole life. In Tammuz the burden is heavy; through love of our fellow we help each other and repair the root of what brought this on in the first place, which is baseless hatred. The qualities of this week and of every week until Rosh Chodesh Av are about how to act toward one's friend.

The prophet is Neriah, of whom little is known beyond his being the father of Baruch, last week's prophet. He was related to and a contemporary of the other prophets of this month — Baruch, Machseyah, Serayah, and Huldah — who all carried the burden of telling the news of the coming destruction. Neryah means the candle of G-d, and that is what we all are at our essence, one soul.

The levitical city is Jahaz, where Israel destroyed Sihon, king of the Amorites, told in the portion of Chukat, which is always read at this time of year. Yachatz is also mentioned in the Tanach in connection with Moab: it was conquered under Moshe and apparently retaken by Moab later. Which is the idea again that conquering something once is not enough; there has to be ongoing vigilance, a foundation, to keep it. Reuven had that struggle himself — given the firstborn's right and unable to hold it, and after his sin always in a state of Teshuvah. Yachatz also means will apportion, divide, break, like the Yachatz step of the Seder: the matzah is broken to show its brokenness and its standing as the poor man's bread. And Tammuz is tied to poverty — the letter Dalet of Tammuz and the Lamed of Av spell Dal, poor, and connecting them to Elul, with its Tav, spells Delet, door, the gates of repentance.
275.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 40.

276.title: Returning to Ourselves
body: Beshalach: "It came about that on the seventh day, [some] of the people went out to gather [manna], but they did not find [any]. The Lord said to Moses, How long will you refuse to observe My commandments and My teachings?" The stubbornness is the point. As the Rebbe would often repeat, the reason for our suffering is "Mipnei Chata'eynu Galinu Me'Artzeinu," because of our sins we were exiled from our Land — and the moment we stop and turn around, we are redeemed.

The Haftorah: "The wisest of her princesses answer her, she too returns answers to herself." The wisest of princesses is the Neshamah, the soul, called a princess because she is the daughter of the King. Despairing over the exile, the soul wakes and brings us to return, to teshuvah. In Tammuz we have to see that it is time to come back to ourselves — our true selves, our Neshamah.

Daf Mem of Sotah keeps on with laws of Birkat Kohanim, the public's prayer of thanks, and the Kohen Gadol reading the Torah on Yom Kippur, and includes a story about R. Avahu and R. Aba and their humility. The Temple again, and the ways of restoring it: humility and thanks.

The generation is Ahaziah, son of Jehoram, who reigned a very short time and continued his father's evil ways under his mother's terrible influence. His counterpart in Israel was Jehoram, with whom he sought a close alliance at her urging. Both were killed by Jehu, anointed king by the Prophet Elisha — and the death of the two of them shows that without repentance there is no hope of salvation. He was apparently named after his maternal uncle, the son of Ahab; his name means one who holds to G-d, and he held fast to idolatry instead.

The journey is from Dibon gad to Almon diblathaimah, which means hidden sweetness. Almon comes from He'elem, concealment, and Diblathaimah from sweetness, specifically deveilah, pressed cake figs. So the name holds a dichotomy, like Tammuz itself: it may be a place of death and mourning, and through teshuvah the month's concealed sweetness is revealed. The personal journey moves from the good tidings of repentance to the concealed sweetness that repentance uncovers.

277.title: Getting to the Root of the Matter, the Torah
body: A new verse opens a new part of the story: "Now the sons of Eli were base men; they knew not the LORD." The main way of knowing G-d is through the Torah, and their behaviour shows a real deficit there; their lack of connection to it and respect for it was their downfall.

Pirkei Avot turns to G-d's acquisitions — He acquired five in His world, and the first is the Torah: "G-d acquired me as the beginning of His way, before His works of yore." His way begins with the Torah.

Ecclesiastes 9 holds the same thing, that everything depends on wisdom and righteousness: "For all this I laid to my heart and to clarify all this, that the righteous and the wise and their works are in God's hand; even love, even hate, man does not know; everything is before them."

The week holds the yahrzeits of three relatively recent figures: Rabbi Menachem-Mendel Futerfas on the 4th of Tammuz, 1995; Rabbi Simcha Bunim Alter, the Lev Simcha, fifth Rebbe of Ger, on the 7th, 1992; and Rabbi Yekutiel Yehuda Halberstam, the Klausenberger Rebbe, on the 9th, 1994.

Reb Mendel Futerfas was a near legendary Lubavitcher chasid, even to those who knew him personally. In 1947 he was arrested for running networks of underground yeshivas and Jewish schools, and for helping thousands of Soviet Jews reach Poland after WWII, and sentenced to 8 years in Soviet prisons and labor camps, which he came through without compromising any religious observance despite cruel pressure to do so. After another six years in Siberian exile he was allowed to emigrate to England, thanks to an appeal for family repatriation made by prime minister Harold Wilson at his summit meeting in Moscow with Chairman Nikita Khrushchev. In 1973 he settled in Kfar Chabad for the rest of his life.

Rav Simcha Bunim Alter, also known as the Lev Simcha after the works he wrote, was the fifth Rebbe of Ger, from 1977 until 1992. The Alter mishpacha managed to escape Poland during the Holocaust to Eretz Yisroel. Before becoming Rebbe he was said to have been extremely successful as a businessman, though it is not known in what line. Ger grew greatly in Eretz Yisroel under him; he carried on the family tradition of vigorous leadership of the Agudas Yisroel party in the Knesset, and he instituted the daily learning of a page of Talmud Yerushalami.

Rabbi Yekutiel Yehuda Halberstam, the Klausenberger Rebbe, also became the post-war Rebbe of the Sanz Chassidim. One of the foremost Chasidic leaders of his generation, he is best known for reviving the study of Talmud through Mifal Shas, and for building a hospital, Laniado in Netanya, which works to the highest standards of Jewish law and medical practice. Also this week: Rabbi Pinchas HaLevi Horowitz, brother of Rabbi Shmuel Shmelke of Nicholsburg and teacher of the Chattam Sofer, and Rabbi Boruch Frankel-Tumim, father-in-law of R' Chaim of Sanz, both on the 7th of Tammuz.

278.title: Upholding our Morality in Exile
body: The Song's verse names the Temple as a house: "I would lead you, I would bring you to the house of my mother, who instructed me; I would give you to drink some spiced wine, of the juice of my pomegranate." Tammuz is bound to exile and to the destruction of that house. Forty is the gematria of the letter Mem, and next week, 41, is Alef Mem, which spells Em, mother. The verse also names the pomegranate, and this season belongs to the pomegranate in Perek Shirah.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the fortieth is Arodi, whose name seems related to Lered, to descend, which is also exile. And with him Naaman, son of Benjamin, whose name means pleasant, for how Joseph's deeds were seemly and pleasant. Like Joseph, we have to hold to the ways of righteousness even in exile.

Daf Mem of Shvuot describes admission in paying someone back. It belongs with the wolf of this week, who names "the ox, the donkey, the lamb, the garment, for every lost item" — and the daf too takes up all sorts of disputed items, ox and sheep and vessels and land. The focus again is keeping our moral standards in exile.

Jeremiah's fortieth chapter introduces Gedaliah, a righteous leader, through whose righteousness life regains some normalcy despite the great destruction. "And Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan swore to them and to their men, saying, 'Fear not to serve the Chaldeans. Dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will go well with you. And I, behold I dwell in Mizpah to stand before the Chaldeans who will come to us, and you gather wine and dried figs and oil and put [them] into your vessels and dwell in your cities, which you have taken.'" And they came back: "And all the Jews returned from all the places they had been driven, and they came to the land of Judah to Gedaliah to Mizpah, and they gathered very much wine and dried figs." He was so righteous that he would not believe another leader meant to assassinate him: "Do not do this thing for you speak falsely about Ishmael."

279.title: Reviewing the Second Week of Tammuz - Psalms 118-120; 105:21-23; 89:41
body: The second week of Tammuz in psalms: the hundred and eighteenth, hundred and nineteenth and hundred and twentieth, with three verses of Psalm 105 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 118 is David's immense trust, and praise for what He has already fulfilled. It begins with four voices saying the same thing — Israel, the House of Aaron, those who fear the Lord, each declaring that His kindness is everlasting. Then the distress: "From out of distress I called to G-d; with abounding relief, G-d answered me. The Lord is with me, I do not fear-what can man do to me?" The comparison: "It is better to rely on the Lord than to trust in man. It is better to rely on the Lord than to trust in nobles." The surrounding, three times over: "They surrounded me like bees, yet they shall be extinguished like fiery thorns." Then the living: "I shall not die, but I shall live and recount the deeds of G-d. G-d has indeed chastised me, but He did not give me up to death." Then the gates: "Open for me the gates of righteousness; I will enter them and praise G-d. This is the gate of the Lord, the righteous will enter it." And the lines everyone knows: "The stone which the builders scorned has become the chief cornerstone. From the Lord has this come about; it is wondrous in our eyes. This is the day which the Lord has made; let us be glad and rejoice on it. We implore You, Lord, deliver us. We implore You, Lord, grant us success."

Psalm 119 is the long one, composed in alphabetical sequence with eight verses to each letter, and every verse holds one of the words for an aspect of Torah — way, Torah, testimony, precept, commandment, statement, word, judgment, righteousness, statute. Replete with morals and prayers, it should be said daily, as a powerful preparation for the service of G-d. Its first line sets the whole: "Fortunate are those whose way is artless, who walk with the Torah of the Lord." Then, over and over, the asking to be taught and to be kept: "Unveil my eyes, that I may behold wonders from Your Torah." "I am a sojourner on earth; do not hide Your commandments from me." "Your statutes have been my songs in the house of my wanderings." "At midnight, I rise to thank You for Your righteous judgments." The affliction turned to account: "It is for my good that I was afflicted, so that I might learn Your statutes." The worth of it: "The Torah of Your mouth is better for me than thousands in gold and silver." What it is for a man walking: "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path." "How sweet are Your words to my palate, [sweeter] than honey to my mouth!" "O how I love Your Torah! All day it is my discussion." What it holds off: "Had Your Torah not been my delight, I would have perished in my affliction." The peace in it: "There is abundant peace for those who love Your Torah, and there is no stumbling for them." And the last verse, which does not end in confidence but in asking to be found: "I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek out Your servant, for I have not forgotten Your commandments."

Psalm 120 rebukes slanderers, and shows how the deadly effect of slander reaches further than weapons. "I have called out to the Lord in my distress, and He answered me. O Lord, rescue my soul from the lips of falsehood, from a deceitful tongue. What can He give you, and what [further restraint] can He add to you, O deceitful tongue? [You resemble] the sharp arrows of a mighty one, and the coals of broom-wood." And the end, which is a whole position in two lines: "Too long has my soul dwelt among those who hate peace. I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war."

Psalm 105's verses are the rise to power and the coming down to Egypt: "He made him the master of his household and the ruler over all his possessions. To bind up his princes with his soul, and he made his elders wise. Israel came to Egypt, and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham." And Psalm 89's verse is the breach: "You breached all his fences; You made his fortifications a ruin."

280.title: The Wolf Is Saying
body: The wolf opens on the breached fences, and the week comes in around it.

The ruin and the disputed goods first: "You breached all his fences" / "You made his fortifications a ruin" / "For every matter of iniquity" / "For the ox, the donkey, the lamb, the garment" / "For every lost item which he says, 'This is it'" / "Some spiced wine, of the juice of my pomegranate."

Then the going before the judge, and the seventh day: "The matter of both of them shall come before the judge" / "To bind up his princes with his soul" / "It came about that on the seventh day" / "The people went out to gather, but they did not find" / "And he made his elders wise" / "He who the judge finds guilty shall pay double to the other."

Then the sons of Eli, and the master of the household: "Now the sons of Eli were base men" / "They knew not the Lord" / "He made him the master of his household" / "And the ruler over all his possessions" / "The Lord said to Moses, How long will you refuse" / "To observe My commandments and My teachings?"

And the end is the princess answering herself, the oath, and the house of my mother: "The wisest of her princesses answer her" / "She too returns answers to herself" / "For I raise up My hand to heaven" / "And say, 'As I live forever'" / "Israel came to Egypt and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham" / "For You have girded me with strength for the battle" / "You have subdued under me those that rose up against me" / "I would lead you, I would bring you to the house of my mother" / "Who instructed me; I would give you to drink."

281.title: Not to Become Corrupt
body: The fox is saying, "Woe to him that builds his house without justice and his chambers without lawfulness; that uses his friend's service without wages, and does not give him for his hire."
