(Jeremiah 22:13) This week, beginning with the fast of the 17th of Tammuz, opens the three weeks of mourning for the destruction of the Temple, the House of G-d — a destruction that came of the injustice and lawlessness of the Jews of that time.

The week also holds the Chassidic holiday of the 12th and 13th of Tammuz, which marks the Sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe, Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn's birthday and the day he was freed from prison in Communist Russia. Among Chabad Chassidim it is called Chag HaGeulah, the Festival of Redemption.

The fox is a symbol of the destruction, as the Talmud in Makkot tells. A group of rabbis gathered soon after the Temple fell and saw a fox walk into the place on the Temple Mount where the holiest part had stood. The others wept; Rabbi Akiva saw it in a positive light — which is the month of Tammuz — so much so that he laughed. He explained that the Torah makes the prophecy of Jerusalem's destruction depend on the prophecy of its redemption: now that the first has been fulfilled, the second will be fulfilled too. And explaining his laughter, he was able to truly comfort them.

At Yud Beit-Yud Gimmel Tammuz the Sixth Rebbe took on the whole Soviet empire and won. Despite open defiance, refusal to obey orders, and insisting on not giving up an inch of his religiosity, he was eventually released and his death sentence commuted. Years later the Soviet Union itself, full of injustice and G-dlessness, collapsed along with the Berlin Wall — and the Seventh Rebbe, Menachem Mendel Schneerson, had predicted that fall many years earlier, when few thought it even possible.

Forty-one spells em, mother. That suits the start of the three weeks, whose second half falls in Av, which means father. In this historically hard stretch it matters to remember that the difficulties He gives us are ultimately for our good, as a father and a mother sometimes have to be strict with a child. In Judaism the mother is the akeret habayit, the anchor of the house, responsible for its values and its atmosphere — and the upkeep and the moral atmosphere of the Temple, G-d's house, was mainly the responsibility of the kohanim. Much of their extremely holy service paralleled housework: the daily sacrifices, the lighting of the Menorah, the upkeep of the building were close to cooking, cleaning and lighting candles for Shabat. By the time of the Second Temple the priestly class had become enormously corrupt — even the position of High Priest was open for sale to the highest bidder — and the Temple could not stand, in great part because of that.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar: every gathering that is for the sake of Heaven will endure, and one that is not for the sake of Heaven will not. Which is the same thing: not becoming corrupt or divided out of selfish motives. The firmness of a community comes from rock-solid commitment to our principles and the desire to do His will, and the best example is the Sixth Rebbe himself, whose work kept Judaism alive through intense Communist oppression. Where we do not follow His word, the whole community suffers and our structures do not stand, as at the destruction of the Temple.

The combination is yesod shebeyesod: absolute firmness in our Jewish values. The lesson from the fox is not to let ourselves be dragged down by dishonesty and the thought of immediate gain. Walking in the path of Torah, we will be more solid and more secure.

282.title: Judgement followed by Teshuvah
body: The week of the 12th and 13th of Tammuz, and of the 17th. Haazinu sharpens: "When I sharpen the blade of My sword, and My hand grasps judgment, I will bring vengeance upon My adversaries and repay those who hate Me." (Deuteronomy 32:41) The Haftorah holds the same: "And of my enemies You have given me the back of their necks; them that hate me, that I may cut them off." (II Samuel 22:41) Judgment and Divine wrath are central to the 17th of Tammuz.

The quality is judging him favorably, Machrioh Lechaf Zechut, which belongs to the repair of sight. The phrase literally means tips him to the side of merit. Rebbe Nachman teaches that focusing on someone else's good points actually tips the person to that side. Maimonedes puts the principle more broadly, in the context of Teshuvah, which this month needs: throughout the entire year a person should look at himself as equally balanced between merit and sin, and the world as equally balanced; if he performs one sin he tips his own balance and the world's to the side of guilt and brings destruction upon himself, and if he performs one mitzvah he tips his own and the world's to the side of merit and brings deliverance and salvation to himself and others. As last week, the action is not only about the friend: the person puts himself in the balance, and by acting justly tips his friend's balance too.

The prophet is Seraiah, Baruch's brother, who went into exile with Zedekiah the King of Judah. Like Baruch, Jeremiah gave him dire prophecies to read to the king — only this time the harsh words were against Babylon itself. So the king and the people were being judged favourably, since the prophecy assured that their suffering would one day end and be avenged.

The levitical city is Kedemoth. The desert of Kedemoth was where Moshe sent messengers to Sihon, king of Heshbon, with words of peace; after Sihon refused, it was at Kedemoth that he was miraculously defeated. His refusal came out of deep Sinat Chinam, gratuitous hatred, which is what destroyed the Temple these days commemorate. Kedemoth is from Kedem, days of yore, often used of the Garden of Eden and the pristine state humanity once had — and in this month we begin our Teshuvah and try to reach back to it.
282.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 41.

283.title: Standing One's Ground
body: Beshalach: "See that the Lord has given you the Sabbath. Therefore, on the sixth day, He gives you bread for two days. Let each man remain in his place; let no man leave his place on the seventh day. So the people rested on the seventh day." The weight falls on staying still, not leaving one's place. In a way it is the reverse of the 17th of Tammuz, when the Jews, running out of food, had no choice but to stay where they were — and then, when the walls were breached, were forced to surrender and were led into exile, unable to stay in place even on the Sabbath. And the message of Yud Beit/Yud Gimmel Tammuz has its own parallel: for all the oppression he suffered in prison, the Sixth Rebbe stood his ground and remained in his spiritual place.

The Haftorah has the enemy counting his winnings: "'Are they not finding (and) dividing the spoils? A damsel, two damsels to every man.'" Which is what happened when the walls were breached. The word used for women, Rechem, is related to womb and to mercy, and brings to mind the verse of Lamentations: "The hands of compassionate women boiled their own children." And 41 is the gematria of em, mother.

Daf Mem Alef of Sotah gives laws of the Torah reading on Yom Kippur and how the King reads the Torah in the Temple — the Temple again — and then the trait of flattery. Flattery causes corruption and leads to destruction: from the day that flattery became rampant, judgments became distorted, deeds became spoiled, and no one can say "My deeds are better than yours." The destruction itself is tied to flattery: we learn from Yirmeyahu, who supported Chananyah's false prophecy, and Chananyah's grandson later seized Yirmeyahu and handed him to the Babylonian officials. The Rebbe Rayatz on the 12th of Tammuz is the opposite of flattery — he spoke his mind about the evil of the Soviet empire, endured torture, and did not move.

The generation is Athaliah, who took the kingdom after her son Ahaziah's death; her counterpart in Israel was Yehu. Her reign was absolute terror, and her hatred after her own son's death drove her to try to destroy the whole House of David. She managed to kill every descendant of King David but one, Jehoash, who miraculously survived. Her story shows how cruel and ruthless a mother, who is naturally merciful, can be, and how distorted and corrupt Israel had become — and a mother's mercy appears in it too, in the saving of Jehoash. The corruption parallels the 17th of Tammuz, and the hope in Jehoash parallels how the Rebbe Rayatz was saved out of the embers and the Chabad dynasty was able to go on. And Athaliah did enormous damage to the Temple, damage which Jehoash would repair.

The journey is from Almon diblathaimah to the mountains of Abarim, in front of Nebo. As in week 38, Abarim comes from aveirah, transgression — and now instead of the ruins of Abarim it is the mountain of Abarim, which is the height teshuvah reaches. The Temple itself is also called a mountain. Nebo is nun boh, the fiftieth gate Moshe reaches at his passing; that gate is beyond nature, and belongs to teshuvah, where G-d lifts us out of our sins in a way nature does not allow. The personal journey moves from the sweetness repentance uncovers to the supernatural heights it can reach.

284.title: Not Corrupting G-d's World
body: The verse is the priests' due: "And this was the due of the priests from the people: (whenever) any man would slaughter a sacrifice, the servant of the priest would come when (one) cooked the flesh, with a three-pronged fork in his hand." The sons of Eli had set up a rule by which anyone bringing a sacrifice had to give them an extra portion, more than Torah law allots. It was a Hillul Hashem, a desecration of His name, and it lowered the Mishkan in the eyes of the people. The seventeenth of Tammuz is largely about the corruption of the Jewish people of that time, the Temple's priests in particular, which brought it down.

This week's acquisition in Pirkei Avot is the heavens and the earth: "So says G-d: The heavens are My throne and the earth is My footstool; what house, then, can you build for Me, and where is My place of rest?" And: "How many are your works, O G-d, You have made them all with wisdom; the earth is filled with Your acquisitions." The verses name the Temple and the limits of it as His house — and against the account above, the point is sharp: since everything is His, and the Temple is His house, how dare the sons of Eli take more for themselves of what plainly belongs to the Master and Owner of all heaven and earth.

Ecclesiastes 10 has a passage on the same centrality, and on not abusing what is in it. "Woe to you, O land whose king is a lad, and your princes eat in the morning. Fortunate are you, O land, whose king is the son of nobles, and your princes eat at the proper time, in might and not in drinking. Through laziness the rafter sinks, and with idleness of the hands the house leaks." And the last verse, which is watched: "Even in your thought, you shall not curse a king, nor in your bedrooms shall you curse a wealthy man, for the bird of the heaven shall carry the voice, and the winged creature will tell the matter." Rashi: the bird of the heaven is the soul, placed within you, which will ultimately fly up to the heaven.

The week holds the yahrzeits of Rebbe Tzvi-Hirsh Eichenstein, first rebbe of Zhidachov, on the 11th of Tammuz, and Rabbi Chaim Ibn Atar, the Ohr HaChaim, on the 15th. Rebbe Tzvi-Hirsh, founder of the Zhidachov dynasty, was a prominent disciple of the Seer of Lublin, and championed the position that the practice of Chasidism had to rest firmly on the study of the Kabbala of the holy Ari of Safed. He wrote and published numerous commentaries on Kabbala, including Ateret Tzvi on the Zohar, and several on the weekly readings; the Malbim was a student of his, and he was succeeded by three nephew-disciples, among them Yitzhak-Isaac of Zhidachov and Yitzhak-Isaac-Yehuda-Yechiel of Komarno. Rabbi Chaim Ibn Atar is best known as the author of one of the most important and popular commentaries on the Torah, the Ohr HaChaim; he established a major yeshiva in Israel after moving there from Morocco. Chassidic tradition holds that the main reason the Baal Shem Tov twice tried so hard, and failed, to reach the Holy Land was that he said if he could join the Ohr HaChaim there, together they could bring Moshiach. His burial site outside the Old City of Jerusalem, on the Mount of Olives, is considered a propitious place to pray. Also this week: Rabbi Elazar of Reishe on the 15th of Tammuz, Rabbi Avrohom Yehoshua Heschel of Kopischnitz on the 16th, and Rabbi Shmuel Yaacov Weinberg on the 17th.

285.title: G-d's Right and Left "Hands"
body: The Song's verse is one line and it is held in both arms: "His left hand would be under my head, and his right hand would embrace me." It is often quoted in the Tanya and in Chassidic and Kabbalistic sources. At the same time that His left hand, which is gevurah, discipline, is under our heads, His right hand, Chesed, kindness, is around us. He held us through our exiles, and He held the Sixth Rebbe through what he faced.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the forty-first is Areli, whose name holds the same letters as Ariel, the Lion of G-d, one of the names of the Temple. And with him Ehi, son of Benjamin, whose name means my brother, Achi, for Joseph being Benjamin's brother. Brotherly love is what will rebuild the Temple.

Daf Mem Alef of Shvuot keeps on with the repayment of loans and whether it has to be done in front of witnesses, and then the difference between an oath that is d'rabbanan and one that is d'oraisa, and how a d'rabbanan oath can be reversed though payment is taken by other means. Which belongs to the 17th of Tammuz, when payment is taken for our spiritual debts.

Jeremiah's forty-first chapter is the murder of Gedaliah — for which we still fast, as for the 17th of Tammuz — and the divisions inside the Jewish people that kept the suffering going. "And Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the ten men who were with him arose and smote Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan, with the sword, and he slew him, whom the king of Babylon had appointed in the land, and all the Jews who were with him." Then the pilgrims: "men came from Shechem, from Shiloh, and from Samaria, eighty men, with shaven beards and rent garments and having cut themselves, with a meal-offering and frankincense in their hand[s], to bring to the house of the Lord." And Ishmael came out to meet them weeping, and said, "Come to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam" — and killed them in the city. Ten of them were spared for saying they had stores in the field, wheat and barley and oil and honey. And the pit he filled with the bodies was the one King Asa had made because of Baasa, king of Israel.

286.title: Reviewing the Third Week of Tammuz - Psalms 121-123; 105:24-26; 89:42
body: The third week of Tammuz in psalms: the hundred and twenty-first, hundred and twenty-second and hundred and twenty-third, with three verses of Psalm 105 and one of Psalm 89. All three are songs of ascents, and all three are short.

Psalm 121 alludes to the Lower Paradise, from which one ascends to the Higher, and speaks of how He watches over us. "I lift my eyes to the mountains-from where will my help come? My help will come from the Lord, Maker of heaven and earth. He will not let your foot falter; your guardian does not slumber. Indeed, the Guardian of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps." And the last line covers everything: "The Lord will guard your going and your coming from now and for all time."

Psalm 122 sings the praises of Jerusalem and the miracles that happened there. "I rejoiced when they said to me, 'Let us go to the House of the Lord.' Our feet were standing within your gates, O Jerusalem; Jerusalem that is built like a city in which [all Israel] is united together." What stood there: "For there stood the seats of justice, the thrones of the house of David." And the asking, which is the line this week needs: "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem; may those who love you have peace. May there be peace within your walls, serenity within your mansions. For the sake of my brethren and friends, I ask that there be peace within you."

Psalm 123 laments how long the exile has already run. "To You have I lifted my eyes, You Who are enthroned in heaven. Indeed, as the eyes of servants are turned to the hand of their masters, as the eyes of a maid to the hand of her mistress, so are our eyes turned to the Lord our G-d, until He will be gracious to us." And then: "Be gracious to us, Lord, be gracious to us, for we have been surfeited with humiliation. Our soul has been overfilled with the derision of the complacent, with the scorn of the arrogant."

Psalm 105's verses are the growing of the people and the turn against them: "And He made His people very fruitful, and He made it stronger than its adversaries. He turned their heart to hate His people, to plot against His servants. He sent Moses His servant, [and] Aaron whom He chose." And Psalm 89's verse is the plundering: "All wayfarers have plundered him; he was a disgrace to his neighbors."

287.title: The Fox Is Saying
body: The fox opens on the sharpened sword, and the week sets a house built without justice beside it.

The sword and the house first: "When I sharpen the blade of My sword" / "And My hand grasps judgment" / "Woe to him that builds his house without justice" / "And his chambers without lawfulness" / "When (one) cooked the flesh, With a three-pronged fork in his hand."

Then the spoils divided, and the bread for two days: "Are they not finding (and) dividing the spoils" / "A damsel, two damsels to every man" / "He gives you bread for two days" / "Let each man remain in his place" / "The servant of the priest would come" / "[And] Aaron whom He chose" / "And this was the due of the priests from the people" / "(Whenever) any man would slaughter a sacrifice."

Then the unpaid wages, and the vengeance: "That uses his friend's service without wages" / "And does not give him for his hire" / "I will bring vengeance upon My adversaries" / "And repay those who hate Me" / "Them that hate me, that I may cut them off" / "And of my enemies You have given me the back of their necks."
Then the plundering, and the hearts turned: "All wayfarers have plundered him" / "He was a disgrace to his neighbors" / "He turned their heart to hate His people" / "To plot against His servants."

And the end is the Sabbath and the two hands: "See that the Lord has given you the Sabbath" / "Therefore, on the sixth day" / "He sent Moses His servant" / "His left hand would be under my head, And his right hand would embrace me" / "Let no man leave his place on the seventh day" / "So the people rested on the seventh day" / "And He made His people very fruitful" / "And He made it stronger than its adversaries."

288.title: To Be Loyal and Pursue Justice
body: The hound is saying, "Let the righteous rejoice in G-d; praise is befitting to the straight." (Psalms 33:1) We are in the middle of the three weeks of mourning.

The hound stands for uprightness, and it often hunts last week's animal, the fox, who stands for corruption and injustice. It is also the standing example of loyalty. In this period, for all our outward mourning, we also come to see that after so many centuries of exile and so many tragedies the Jewish people, like the hound, has kept its loyalty and faith in G-d — and that G-d has kept His faith in us. That loyalty on both sides is worth recognising and praising.

The Talmud ties the verse to the Temple as well. The word for befitting, na'avah, can be read naveh, habitation, pointing to how the enemies of the Jewish people had no power over the parts of the Temple that King David and Moses had built. And it matters to remember that the world has no power over the holy habitation inside each one of us.

Released from prison, the Previous Rebbe was sent into exile by the Soviet regime. At the Leningrad train station Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn parted with these words, quoting his father: this all the nations of the world must know, that only our bodies were sent into exile and subjugated to alien rule; our souls were not given over into captivity and foreign rule. In any matter affecting the Jewish religion, the Torah, and its mitzvot and customs, we are not subject to the dictates of any power.

Forty-two is the number of journeys in the desert. Through them He tested His people several times and we kept our loyalty and proved worthy of His love; the people also tested Him several times, and He did not give up hope in them. Forty-two is mem and beit, which spell bam, in them. The Ba'al Shem Tov teaches that the words "vedibarta bam" in the Shemah point to the forty-two personal journeys each person makes in a life, parallel to the forty-two in the desert.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Eliezer the son of Shamua: the dignity of your student should be as precious to you as your own, the dignity of your colleague as your awe of your master, and your awe of your master as your awe of Heaven. Which is Tammuz again, and the ability to look deeper and see the value and the potential in each person, student or colleague or teacher. And the hound is itself a perfect example: its devotion to its master is like what is due to G-d.

Completing the cycle of yesod, the combination is malchut shebeyesod. This week we hold a solid foundation in our Judaism and use it to influence the world around us. The lesson from the hound is that as it sings of being upright and pursues the fox, we have to pursue justice at all costs: "Tzedek Tzedek Tirdof," justice, justice you shall pursue.

289.title: Mehsiah and Being Placed in the Path of Truth
body: The last week of Tammuz. Haazinu: "I will intoxicate My arrows with blood, and My sword will consume flesh, from the blood of the slain and the captives, from the first breach of the enemy." (Deuteronomy 32:42) The Haftorah holds the same theme: "They looked about, but there was no one to save them; [Even] to the Lord, but He answered them not." (II Samuel 22:42) And in the future this month's fortunes will be reversed for the good.

The quality is placing him in the path of truth, Ma'amidoh Al Ha'Emet. The verb does not mean place but raise — the same verb as in the opening of Pirkei Avot, where the Men of the Great Assembly advise raising up many students. Raise, because students have to be able to stand on their own two feet, and truth is by definition the foundation a person needs to stand on. The letters of emet say it too: each one has a stable base and can stand on its own, while the three letters of sheker, falsehood, cannot — they are unstable and they fall. Which is the fox of last week, woe to him that builds his house without justice; and this week the hound, praise is befitting to the upright.

The prophet is Mehsiah, grandfather of Baruch and Seriah. His name appears in two chapters of the Book of Jeremiah, and in both the punishment named is ultimately what is needed to set the Jewish people on a path of truth and goodness.

The levitical city is Mepha'ath, also one of the cities named in the prophecy against Moab. The word means to shine. This month is about working on our sense of sight, and as we refine ourselves and look at things the right way, we can see beauty shine out, in others and in ourselves.
289.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 42.

290.title: Remembering to Repent in the Face of Destruction
body: Beshalach describes the manna and then has it kept: "The house of Israel named it manna, and it was like coriander seed, [it was] white, and it tasted like a wafer with honey. Moses said, This is the thing that the Lord commanded: Let one omerful of it be preserved for your generations, in order that they see the bread that I fed you in the desert when I took you out of the land of Egypt." It came in different forms — a seed, a dough, a finished bread — according to a person's spiritual standing, so that for anyone not fully righteous the manna was itself a call to repent. And Rashi explains that the omerful was kept specifically for the times of Jeremiah and the destruction of the Temple.

The Haftorah divides the spoils: "a spoil of dyed garments to Sisera, a spoil of dyed garments of embroidery." When the walls were breached and the Temple destroyed, the enemy took its spoils — and dyed garments recall the clothes the Kohen Gadol wore in the Temple.

Daf Mem Beit of Sotah finishes with flattery and opens a new chapter on the Mashuach Milchamah, the Kohen anointed for war. Mashuach shares a root with Mashiach. The daf tells how that Kohen says to the people that this war is not against their brethren, and that if they are taken captive the enemy will show no mercy — as it was at the destruction. And these three weeks belong to Mashiach too, since the birth of Mashiach takes place on Tisha B'Av.

The generation is Jehoash, who replaced Athaliah once she was removed and killed, and who was still a boy. He was tutored and counselled by the righteous Kohen Yehoiadah; his counterparts in Israel were Yehu and Jehoahaz. While Yehoiadah lived he served G-d faithfully, and after Yehoiadah died he turned to idols. Yehoiadah's son, the prophet Zachariah, condemned him, and Jehoash had him killed in the Temple — stoned to death on Yom Kippur itself. That blood was not forgiven. He was severely punished, with the Syrians overrunning and sacking most of the country; and when the Temple fell the matter came up again. Our Sages say that when Nebuzaradan entered the Temple he found the blood of Zechariah seething, and asked the Jews what it meant; they tried to conceal the scandal, and he threatened to comb their flesh with iron combs, so they told him: there was a prophet among us who chastised us, and we killed him, and for many years now his blood has not rested. Nebuzaradan said, I will appease him. He killed the members of the Great and Small Sanhedrins, then youths and maidens, then school-children, 940,000 people in all. Still the blood boiled, until he cried, "Zechariah, Zechariah! I have slain the best of them; do you want all of them destroyed?" And at last the blood sank into the ground. So Jehoash holds both sides of Jewish behaviour toward the Temple: in his early years exemplary piousness, and repairs to the building; in his later years, bad influences and such disrespect that his acts were a significant factor in its destruction. His name apparently means fire of G-d — and fire can be used either way.

The journey is from the mountains of Abarim to the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, camping along the Jordan from Beth jeshimoth to Abel shittim. Arvot Moav has a double meaning, as Rabbi Jacobson explains: Arvot comes from erev, night, and from arev, mixture or confusion, and marks the most difficult part of the forty-two-part journey — and the 42nd week of the year is often a difficult one, part of the three weeks. And arev also means sweet, and teshuvah can turn these harsh days sweet. He reads Jordan-Jericho, Yarden Yerichoh, as a reference to Mashiach, whose birth is near, on the ninth of Av. Crossing the Jordan is finally leaving the wandering and entering the Land — and so leaving the more spiritual existence of the desert and engaging fully with the physical world. That is also the sense of Beth Yeshimoth, from yeshimon, wasteland, and of Abel Shitim, which he translates as desolate plains, based on the Ramban. Abel Shitim also means mourning for follies, like the mourning of this season: the folly of impurity, since the Talmud in Sotah says a person does not sin unless a spirit of folly enters him. And the Rebbe Rayatz explains that there is also a positive spirit of folly, Shtus d'Kedushah, a folly of holiness, whose work will bring a mourning of the yetzer harah, which will then be gone from the world for good. All of it depends on Arvoth Moav, turning the darkness of Av into light. The personal journey moves from the heights teshuvah reaches to engaging the physical world, conquering the Land, and lifting it through holy folly and through the spark of Mashiach each of us holds.

291.title: The Importance of Giving (not Taking By Force)
body: The verse goes further into what the sons of Eli took: "And he would thrust into the fire-pot, or into the pot, or into the cauldron, or into the pan, everything which the fork would pick up, the priest would take therewith; so would they do to all Israel who came there in Shiloh." A disproportionate part of every person's sacrifice, taken — which runs against the Torah, that is above all about love and about giving. The main reason the Second Temple was destroyed was Sinat Chinam, gratuitous hatred, caused by acts like these.

Pirkei Avot's acquisition this week is Abraham: "And he blessed him, and said: Blessed be Abram to G-d Most High, acquirer of heavens and earth." Abraham's whole essence was giving and love — and that verse comes immediately before he gives a tenth of everything he has to Malchitzedek, a priest. He gave to the priest of his own will, where the sons of Eli took by force, and took more than was theirs.

Ecclesiastes 11 opens on the same thing: "Send forth your bread upon the surface of the water, for after many days you will find it. Give a portion to seven and even to eight, for you do not know what evil will be on the earth." Rashi reads it: do goodness and kindness to a person about whom your heart tells you that you will never see him again, like one who casts his food upon the surface of the water — and days will yet come, and you will receive your recompense. Note what is said about Jethro: "Call him that he should eat bread," and he thought Moses was an Egyptian whom he would never see again; and in the end he became his son-in-law and brought him under the wings of the Shechinah, and his sons and grandsons merited to sit in the Chamber of Hewn Stone. And: if you have shared your food and drink with seven who need kindness, share further with eight who come after them, and do not say, "Enough" — because days may yet come when you need them all, and then you will be saved from the evil by this charity; and if not now, when?

The week holds the yahrzeits of three important figures in Chassidism and Kabbalah: Rabbi Avraham Mattisyahu Fridman of Shtefanesht on the 21st of Tammuz, Rabbi Shlomo of Karlin on the 22nd, and Rabbi Moshe Kordevero on the 23rd. Rabbi Avraham Mattisyahu, in Romania, was the grandson of the holy Rabbi Yisroel of Rhzhin, and succeeded his father, Rabbi Menachem Nochum, as the second Rebbe of the dynasty in 1869. Famed for miraculous powers and with thousands of followers, he was also considered one of the true hidden tzadikim of his generation; in 1969 his remains — which witnesses alive today testify were still as whole and fresh as the day he died — were moved from Romania to Nachlas Yitzchok in Tel Aviv, where his grave is still a holy site of prayer for thousands. R. Shlomo of Karlin was a student of the Maggid and of Reb Aharon the Great of Karlin, whom he succeeded in 1772; most of the Chassidic leaders of the next generation in the Lithuanian region were his disciples. He died Kiddush HaShem, stabbed by a Cossack in the middle of the Amida prayer. Rabbi Moshe Kordevero, known by the acronym of his name, Ramak, was considered the head of the Tsfat Kabbalists until his death shortly after Rabbi Yitzchak Luria arrived; he wrote many major works of Kabbalah, among them Pardes Rimonim, Orchard of Pomegranates, in which he systematised all the kabbalistic knowledge revealed until then.

292.title: Faithfulness in Exile
body: The Song's verse tells the others to leave it alone: "I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem; why should you awaken, and why should you arouse the love until it is desirous?" The Jewish people adjuring the nations not to interfere in its relationship with G-d. Which is the hound: the people keeping their loyalty through the difficulties of exile, and G-d keeping His faithfulness to us. Rashi puts it that way too: now the congregation of Israel addresses the nations — even though I complain and lament, my Beloved holds on to my hand, and He is my support in my exile; therefore, I adjure you.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the forty-second is Asher, which means happy. And with him Rosh, son of Benjamin, whose name means head, for Joseph being Benjamin's superior. When Mashiach comes and the Temple is rebuilt, this week will be a happy one, in which we feel like a head and not a tail. Asher and Rosh hold the same letters, Reish and Shin, in reverse — and with the slightest change those letters spell Rash, poor, which these weeks tend to be.

Daf Mem Beit of Shevuoth keeps on with the repayment of loans, and takes up one who is established as a liar, questionable documents, and other breaches of trust. Which belongs to the 17th of Tammuz, when payment is exacted for our spiritual debts.

Jeremiah's forty-second chapter is faithfulness, and His help in exile. "And they said to Jeremiah, 'May the Lord be a true and faithful witness against us if we do not do according to the entire matter that the Lord your God shall send you to us. Whether good or bad, we will hearken to the voice of the Lord our God.'" And the answer: "If you dwell in this land, I will build you up and I will not pluck you up, for I have repented of the evil that I have done to you. Fear not the king of Babylon whom you fear; fear it not, says the Lord, for I am with you to redeem you and to save you from his hand."

293.title: Reviewing the Last Week of Tammuz - Psalms 124-126; 105:27-29; 89:43
body: The last week of Tammuz in psalms: the hundred and twenty-fourth, hundred and twenty-fifth and hundred and twenty-sixth, with three verses of Psalm 105 and one of Psalm 89. Three more songs of ascents, all short.

Psalm 124 is what would have happened otherwise. "Were it not for the Lord Who was with us-let Israel declare- were it not for the Lord Who was with us when men rose up against us, then they would have swallowed us alive in their burning rage against us. Then the waters would have inundated us, the torrent would have swept over our soul." And then the escape: "Our soul is like a bird which has escaped from the fowler's snare; the snare broke and we escaped. Our help is in the Name of the Lord, the Maker of heaven and earth."

Psalm 125 is what holds. "Those who trust in the Lord are as Mount Zion which never falters, but abides forever. Mountains surround Jerusalem, and the Lord surrounds His people from this time and forever." And why that matters: "For the rod of wickedness will never come to rest upon the lot of the righteous; therefore the righteous need not stretch their hand to iniquity." It ends in three words: "Peace be upon Israel."

Psalm 126 speaks of the future, comparing our service in exile to a man who sows arid land and then cries and begs for rain so the seed is not wasted, and who gives thanks when he merits to reap. "When the Lord will return the exiles of Zion, we will have been like dreamers. Then our mouth will be filled with laughter, and our tongue with songs of joy; then will they say among the nations, 'The Lord has done great things for these.'" And the last two verses, which are the whole of it: "Those who sow in tears will reap with songs of joy. He goes along weeping, carrying the bag of seed; he will surely return with songs of joy, carrying his sheaves."

Psalm 105's verses are the signs and the first plagues: "They placed upon them the words of His signs and His miracles in the land of Ham. He sent darkness and it darkened, and they did not disobey His word. He turned their water into blood, and it killed their fish." And Psalm 89's verse is the enemy raised up: "You raised the right hand of his adversaries; You caused all his enemies to rejoice."

294.title: The Hound Is Saying
body: The hound opens, and the week sets rejoicing against the plunder of a Temple.

The rejoicing and the adjuring first: "Let the righteous rejoice in G-d" / "I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem" / "Why should you awaken, and why should you arouse the love until it is desirous?" / "And he would thrust into the fire-pot" / "Or into the pot, or into the cauldron, or into the pan" / "They looked about, but there was no one to save them" / "[Even] to the Lord, but He answered them not."

Then what the fork picked up, and the arrows: "Everything which the fork would pick up" / "The priest would take therewith" / "I will intoxicate My arrows with blood" / "And My sword will consume flesh" / "He turned their water into blood" / "And it killed their fish."

Then the dyed garments, and what was done to all Israel: "A spoil of dyed garments to Sisera" / "A spoil of dyed garments of embroidery" / "So would they do to all Israel" / "Who came there in Shiloh" / "From the blood of the slain and the captives" / "From the first breach of the enemy" / "You raised the right hand of his adversaries" / "You caused all his enemies to rejoice" / "He sent darkness and it darkened, And they did not disobey His word."

And the end is the omerful kept, and the taste of it: "In order that they see the bread that I fed you" / "In the desert when I took you out of the land of Egypt" / "They placed upon them the words of His signs" / "Let one omerful of it be preserved for your generations" / "And His miracles in the land of Ham" / "Moses said, 'This is the thing that the Lord commanded'" / "The House of Israel named it manna" / "Praise is befitting to the straight" / "And it was like coriander seed" / "White, and it tasted like a wafer with honey."

295.title: To Pursue the Enemy and to Pursue Peace
body: The Cat is saying, "If you rise up like a vulture, and place your nest among the stars, from there I shall bring you down, says G-d." (Obadiah 1:4) And when it catches the mouse, the cat says, "I have pursued my enemies and overtaken them, and I did not return until they were destroyed." (Psalms 18:38) This is the week of Rosh Chodesh Av, and we begin the Nine Days leading to Tisha b'Av, a mourning more intense, and with greater hardships, than the rest of the Three Weeks.

A cat is a miniature lion. In this month we all have the potential to be lions; Mashiach will be born in Av and will reign on earth like a lion. Rosh Chodesh Av is the yahrzeit of Aaron, one of the few yahrzeit dates named explicitly in the Torah, and Aaron was known for his incessant pursuit of peace. The month's sign is Leo, and the Midrash Yalkut Shimoni quoted in week 38 shows how plainly Av belongs to the lion.

The month belongs to the tribe of Shimon, known for severe judgment, and it is the tikkun of the sense of hearing: Shimon comes from Shmiah, hearing, and the month repairs the sin of listening to the report of the spies. It was in Av that the spies came back and described the Land, and instead of holding to Kalev and Joshua's good report the people took up the bad report of the other ten and wept bitterly. Our sages teach that because they cried for no reason, He gave them a reason to cry for generations: that night was Tisha B'Av, the day both Temples were destroyed.

The cat and the mouse can be read at least two ways. Through history the Jews have played the mouse, prey to our enemies inside the nations we were exiled among; for roughly the past two thousand years we have been in the exile of Esau and Edom. In messianic times the roles reverse, and we will be the ones pursuing, specifically Amalek, a descendant of Esau, who stands for the height of immorality and G-dlessness. The cat's song comes from the prophet Obadiah, a convert from the nation of Edom, whose whole prophecy is directed against it — and Edom is Rome and its descendants, which destroyed the Second Temple. The prophet says that one day Edom will be punished for what it did.

Forty-three is gimmel and mem, which look toward the war of Gog uMagog, whose root letters they are. By tradition that will be the last war before the coming of Mashiach, and is believed to involve the descendants of Esau and Yishmael. Mem and gimmel also spell gam, also — a word that stands out in the Psalm most tied to Aaron, whose yahrzeit is this week: "Hineh Mah Tov uMah Naim Shevet Achim Gam Yachad," behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers also to dwell together, as the good oil on the head runs down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron. Rav Ovadia Yosef asks why gam is there at all, since it seems superfluous, and explains that when brothers sit together family problems usually come to the surface — and that also is for the good: we should sit together despite them, and do our best to solve them. Like the cat, Aaron also pursued enemies, and only in order to make peace between them and bring them nearer the Torah. As Hillel says in Pirkei Avot, be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving your fellow creatures and bringing them closer to Torah. That is how the negative forces of this month are turned. The Temple was destroyed through Sinat Chinam, baseless hatred, and will be rebuilt through Ahavat Chinam, baseless love.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Yehudah: be careful with your studies, for an error of learning is tantamount to a willful transgression. It is well known that the First Temple fell because Torah study was not given its weight. And Rabbi Yehudah is a perfect example of peace being possible between Jacob and Esau, the Jewish people and the Romans. He once met a Roman stranger who had just survived a shipwreck as its only survivor, and without knowing who he was gave him his own clothes. The man turned out to be a powerful Roman legislator, and because of that kindness he annulled all the harsh decrees that were about to be imposed on the Jewish people.

The week also holds Rabbi Shimon Bar Yochai: there are three crowns — the crown of Torah, the crown of priesthood and the crown of sovereignty — but the crown of a good name surmounts them all. All three belong to the figures of this month: Aharon HaKohen the priesthood, Mashiach the kingship, and Rabbi Shimon himself the Torah. It is fascinating that his words sit beside Rabbi Yehudah's, since unlike him Rabbi Shimon did not get on with the Romans. When Rabbi Yehudah once praised them for building bridges, Rabbi Shimon said he should not, because everything they do is for their own benefit; the emperor heard of it, and Rabbi Yehudah was given a high position while Rabbi Shimon had to flee, and famously spent the next 12 years in a cave with his son, Rabbi Elazar. There is a tradition that he descends from the tribe of Shimon, this month's tribe, and his own life is a transition and a tikkun of Shimon's strict justice. In the cave he and his son were concerned with pure spirituality; coming out, he could not understand how people spent so much time on material concerns, to the point that everything they looked at was consumed by fire, and he was sent back for another year. The second time he came out he understood the value of being involved with the material world. His sayings in Pirkei Avot seem to follow that: the earlier ones insist on Torah above material things, and these later ones include qualities other than Torah. They also seem to complete his saying in week 16, where he mentions three without saying three of what; here he says there are three crowns. Both sayings begin with the word shloshah, three, and the number most associated with him is thirty-three, since Lag Ba'Omer is the 33rd day of the omer. So the earlier saying can be read: a person with all three crowns on his table — Torah, priesthood, kingship — should be praised and seen as a true example, which is the crown of a Good Name. And there is a well-known story in which Rabbi Shimon Bar Yochai gave an interpretation of "Hineh Mah Tov" and ended a drought — again, having understood the need for material concerns too.

The combination is chesed shebemalchut, kindness within kingship. Like Rabbi Yehudah, we try to do good deeds that land directly in this material world. And the lesson from the cat is that as it chases the mouse, we should be like Aaron and pursue the people around us in a friendly way, to bring them closer to unity, love, peace and truth.

296.title: Destruction that Leads to Peace
body: Rosh Chodesh Av. Av belongs to Shimon, and Rosh Chodesh itself is the yahrzeit of Aharon the Kohen. It is the month of Tisha B'Av, which marks the destruction of both Temples and is also the day the Messiah is born.

Haazinu keeps to retribution and turns to praise: "Sing out praise, O you nations, for His people! For He will avenge the blood of His servants, inflict revenge upon His adversaries, and appease His land [and] His people." (Deuteronomy 32:43) The Haftorah stays with it, and with the physical Land: "Then I ground them as the dust of the earth, as the mud of the streets I did tread upon them, I did stamp them down." (II Samuel 22:43)

The quality is placing him in the path of peace, ma'amidoh al hashalom. Aharon is peace itself; Hillel says we should all be students of Aharon, who loves peace and pursues peace. As last week, the verb ma'amidoh belongs to raising students — hinted at in the lighting of the menorah at the start of Beha'alotchah, where Aharon is told to raise the lights until they stand on their own.

The prophet is Haggai, whose prophecy is the destruction of the Temple and its rebuilding, and whose words are peace. "Who among you is left, who saw this house in its former glory? And as you see it now, is it not as nothing in your eyes? And now, be strong, Zerubbabel, says the Lord; and be strong, Joshua the son of Jehozadak the High Priest; and be strong, all the people of the land." And the promise: "And I will shake up all the nations, and they shall come [with] the precious things of all the nations. And I will fill this House with glory, said the Lord of Hosts. The silver is Mine, and the gold is Mine, says the Lord of Hosts. The glory of this last House shall be greater than the first one, said the Lord of Hosts. And in this place I will grant peace, says the Lord of Hosts."

The levitical city is Jattir, from Yeter, the remains, what is left after destruction — a fitting name for Av. Yeter can also mean an addition, close to Yoter, more: with the coming of Mashiach, Av will be a month of added importance and celebration.
296.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 43.

297.title: Facing Esau (Edom)
body: Rosh Chodesh Av, and the more intense part of the Three Weeks. Rosh Chodesh Av is Aharon's yahrzeit, one of the few named in the Torah — and this is the first Torah section to mention Aharon since the week of Moshe's yahrzeit, in Adar: "And Moses said to Aaron, Take one jug and put there an omerful of manna, and deposit it before the Lord to be preserved for your generations. As the Lord had commanded Moses, Aaron deposited it before the testimony to be preserved." The keeping of the omer again, which belongs to the times of Jeremiah and the destruction.

The Haftorah divides spoils and then turns: "dyed garments of embroidery for the neck of the spoiler.' So may perish all Your enemies, O Lord; but they that love Him (should be) as the sun when he goes forth in his might." Devorah prays that this be the fate of His enemies — which is Av, to be turned from a month of Jewish suffering into one of Jewish triumph. And those who love Him are to be as the sun in its might: Av is the hottest month, and the sun is usually associated with the gentile nations rather than the Jewish people, who go with the moon. She is hinting at the transformation of Jacob into Israel, who also stands for the sun.

Daf Mem Gimmel of Sotah has Pinchas as the Mashuach Milchamah in the war against Midian, and then those exempt from fighting a milchemet reshut, a non-mandatory war, mostly the case of a man who planted a vineyard and had not redeemed its fruit. Pinchas could not suit this week better: a Kohen, Aharon's grandson, and tied to Mashiach, born on Tisha B'Av, both by being the anointed for war in the last battle the Torah describes and by being the same person as Eliyahu HaNavi, who will accompany Mashiach. The daf also discusses how he descends from Joseph — and the Torah makes clear that it is the strength of Joseph that can defeat Esau. Pinchas looks like the ultimate archetype of Mashiach ben Yosef.

The generation is Amaziah, son of Yehoash, who began his kingship very righteous, and whose righteousness earned him a tremendous victory over none other than Edom, which he treated particularly severely. His counterparts in Israel were Jehoahaz, Jehoash and Jeroboam ben Jehoash. The victory led to haughtiness and then to idolatry, and he was castigated by his own brother Amoz, the father of the prophet Isaiah. His haughtiness led to a disastrous war against the King of Israel, Jehoash, and because of that loss Jerusalem itself was looted and Amaziah taken captive. The destruction of Jerusalem is the main theme of the week, and the other is sinat chinam.

The forty-third week goes with conquering the Chittites, whose name comes from Chet, sin. They belong to the negative side of Chesed, which shows itself mostly in improper relations — as in the story of David and Batsheva, who was married to Uriah HaChiti, Uriah the Chittite. Esau himself married two Chittites, Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite and Basemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite, and made life bitter for Isaac and Rebeccah.

298.title: Israel, an Acquisition of G-d
body: The verse shows the sons of Eli pressing further: "Also, before they would make the fat smoke, and the servant of the priest would come, and would say to the man who slaughtered, 'Give meat to roast for the priest, and he will not take from you cooked meat, but raw.'" They sent a servant of the priests to force the portion out of a man before the offering was even ready, which showed disdain both for the person bringing the sacrifice and for those who served in the Tabernacle.

Pirkei Avot's acquisition this week is the people of Israel: "Till Your nation, O G-d, shall pass, till this nation You have acquired shall pass." And: "To the holy who are upon earth, the noble ones, in whom is all My delight." The verses are about the Jews being acquired as His servants after being freed from Egyptian servitude, and about their holy and noble character. The sons of Eli denigrated both: they used the priests' servants for their own motives and belittled the holiness of what the people brought.

Chapter 12 ends Ecclesiastes, and the book closes on the relationship itself: "The end of the matter, everything having been heard, fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the entire man. For every deed God will bring to judgment-for every hidden thing, whether good or bad." Rashi: what you can, do, and let your heart be to Heaven; and keep His commandments, for this is the entire man — because for this matter the entire man was created.
The week holds the yahrzeits of Rabbi Shlomo Ganzfried on the 26th of Tammuz, Rabbi Moshe Teitelbaum, the Yismach Moshe, on the 28th, and Rabbi Shlomo Halberstam of Bobov on Rosh Chodesh Av.

Rabbi Moshe Teitelbaum, known as the Yismach Moshe after the title of his book of Torah commentary, was famed both as a scholar and a wonderworker. A disciple of the Seer of Lublin, he was instrumental in spreading Chasidut in Hungary, and his descendants founded the dynasties of Satmar and Sighet.

Rabbi Shlomo Ganzfried was born in Ungvar, Hungary, in 1804. His father, Rabbi Yossef Ganzfried, died in his childhood, and the orphan was brought up by one of the great men of the generation, Rabbi Tzvi Hirsch Heller, better known as Rabbi Hirsch Charif, the Rav of Ungvar, who saw in the boy the potential of becoming one of the great authorities of Israel. Through all the years beside his teacher his soul thirsted to get to the bottom of Halachah until a clear answer was reached, and that is what drove his Halachic books. Above all of them he earned merit with the Kitzur Shulchan Aruch. From 1864, when it was first printed in Ungvar, it has been reprinted dozens of times in hundreds of thousands of copies, which has never been the case with any other book of its kind; it has become one of the most popular works of all time, worthy of every Jew. It fits Rabbi Yossef Caro's own hope that young students consult the Shulchan Aruch constantly, studying it by heart and keeping that study of youth well in their mouths in order to know the Halachah in each case, and so as not to distance themselves from it in old age. Study groups have formed in hundreds of cities and towns to learn it and spread its teachings. One of the great masters of Lithuanian Jewry said of him that he was a man aided by Providence: none of the great men of Israel have ever seen in their own lifetime, as he did, their work crowned with Halachic commentaries and new Dinim by other Rabbis. The Kitzur was printed 14 times in his lifetime, and at each reprint he added numerous new Dinim; during his lifetime Rav Ishaya Hacohen encircled the work with a commentary called Misgeret HaShulchan, the Border of the Table, printed with his permission alongside it. Though his own Shulchan had grown vast in scope, he kept the title Kitzur, abridged. When a close friend asked why he clung to that name, he answered with a smile: in the book of Psalms it is written, "You prepare a table before me" — it is not written, "You will lengthen a table before me."

Rabbi Shlomo Halberstam of Bobov survived the Holocaust along with only 300 chasidim, succeeding his father, who was among those martyred. Settling in Manhattan and then in different parts of Brooklyn, he served as the third rebbe of Bobov for over 50 years and rebuilt it to even more thousands than his father had before the war. Besides being wise and pious he was noted for his steadfastness in not taking sides in disputes — and he passed away on the same Hebrew date as Aharon the High Priest, the first Jew known for loving peace and pursuing peace.

299.title: Holding On Through the Birthpangs of Mashiach
body: The Song asks who this is, coming up out of the desert: "Who is this coming up from the desert, embracing her beloved?" "Under the apple tree I aroused you; there your mother was in travail with you; there she that bore you was in travail." The Jewish people holding tightly to Hashem under an apple tree — this twenty-two-day period belongs to the apple, the Tapuach, whose song is from Shir HaShirim — and then the travail, the birthpangs. Which is this week exactly: the closeness Aharon stands for, and the difficulty of these days, which are the birthpangs of Mashiach.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the forty-third is Imnah, whose name looks related to Yemin, right, the right hand: His great might, with which He redeemed us at the Exodus. In these days through history we have felt that might against us, and in the future it is in Av that Mashiach will be born and we will see a greater redemption and a greater might. Imnah also looks to come from Limnot, to count. And with him Muppim, son of Benjamin, whose name refers to Joseph's exceeding beauty. It was Aharon's work to count the Jewish people with Moshe — attending to their good points, their strength and their beauty.

Daf Mem Gimmel of Shvuot takes up when a shomer, a guardian, is exempt from paying, how claims must be quantified, and what happens when a security is lost. Which reads onto Aharon as a guardian of the Jewish people who quantified them in the desert, and onto the loss of the security G-d entrusted to us, the Temple, which happened at this time of year.

Jeremiah's forty-third chapter gathers everyone who had stayed in the land, and sets the people against their guardian, the prophet. They did not listen to him; they listened to Johanan the son of Kareah, who gathered them and took them to Egypt. "And Johanan the son of Kareah and all the officers of the armies and all the people did not hearken to the voice of the Lord to dwell in the land of Judah." They took everyone — "the men and the women and the children and the king's daughters and all the people whom Nebuzaradan the chief executioner had left with Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan, and Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch the son of Neriah" — "And they came to the land of Egypt, for they did not hearken to the voice of the Lord."

300.title: Reviewing the Week of Rosh Chodesh Av - Psalms 127-129; 105:30-32; 89:44
body: The week of Rosh Chodesh Av in psalms: the hundred and twenty-seventh, hundred and twenty-eighth and hundred and twenty-ninth, with three verses of Psalm 105 and one of Psalm 89. Three more songs of ascents.

Psalm 127 is King David instructing his generation, and his son Solomon above all, that everything a person does should be for the sake of Heaven; and it criticises those who toil day and night after a livelihood. "If the Lord does not build a house, then its builders labor upon it in vain. If the Lord will not guard a city, the vigilance of its watchman is in vain. It is in vain for you, you who rise early, who sit up late, and who eat the bread of tension, for in fact He gives His loved ones sleep." Then the inheritance: "Behold, the heritage of the Lord is children; the fruit of the womb is a reward. As arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the children of youth."

Psalm 128 praises the man who lives off his own labour, avoiding theft and deception and even refusing gifts, and describes how the G-d-fearing live. "Fortunate is every man who fears the Lord, who walks in His ways. When you eat of the labor of your hands, you will be happy, and you will have goodness. Your wife will be like a fruitful vine in the inner chambers of your house; your children will be like olive saplings around your table." And the blessing at the end: "May the Lord bless you out of Zion, and may you see the goodness of Jerusalem all the days of your life. And may you see children [born] to your children; peace upon Israel."

Psalm 129 laments Israel's troubles. "Much have they persecuted me from my youth on. Let Israel declare it now- 'Much have they persecuted me from my youth on, [but] they have not prevailed against me.'" The image is agricultural and brutal: "The plowmen plowed upon my back; they wished to make their furrow long. But the Lord is just; He cut the cords of the lawless." And the haters of Zion get the grass of a rooftop, which withers before anyone pulls it, which no reaper ever fills his hand with and no passer-by ever blesses.

Psalm 105's verses are more of the plagues: "Their land swarmed with frogs in the rooms of their monarchs. He commanded and a mixture of noxious beasts came, lice throughout all their boundary. He made their rains into hail, flaming fire in their land." And Psalm 89's verse turns the sword back: "You even turned back the sharp edge of his sword, and You did not raise him up in battle."

301.title: The Cat Is Saying
body: The cat opens on the pursuit, and the week comes in around it.

The pursuing and the avenging first: "I have pursued my enemies and overtaken them" / "And I did not return until they were destroyed" / "Sing out praise, O you nations, for His people!" / "For He will avenge the blood of His servants" / "Inflict revenge upon His adversaries, And appease His land [and] His people" / "Their land swarmed with frogs In the rooms of their monarchs."

Then the meat demanded raw, and the nest among the stars: "And [they] would say to the man who slaughtered, 'Give meat to roast for the priest'" / "'And he will not take from you cooked meat, but raw'" / "Dyed garments of embroidery for the neck of the spoiler" / "If you rise up like a vulture, and place your nest among the stars" / "From there I shall bring you down, says G-d."

Then the grinding into dust, and the sword turned back: "Then I ground them as the dust of the earth" / "As the mud of the streets I did tread upon them, I did stamp them down" / "You even turned back the sharp edge of his sword" / "And You did not raise him up in battle" / "So may perish all Your enemies, O Lord" / "But they that love Him [are] as the sun when it goes forth in its might" / "He commanded and a mixture of noxious beasts came, Lice throughout all their boundary."

And the end is the jug of manna and the apple tree: "Also, before they would make the fat smoke, And the servant of the priest would come" / "And Moses said to Aaron, take one jug and put there an omerful of manna" / "And deposit it before the Lord to be preserved for your generations" / "He made their rains into hail, flaming fire in their land" / "Who is this coming up from the desert, embracing her beloved?" / "As the Lord had commanded Moses, Aaron deposited it before the testimony to be preserved" / "Under the apple tree I aroused you; there your mother was in travail with you" / "There she that bore you was in travail."

302.title: To Recognize Our Mistakes and Change
body: The Mouse says, "I shall exalt you, G-d, for You have impoverished [uplifted] me, and You have not let my enemies rejoice over me." (Psalms 30:2) And once it is caught: "You are just for all that comes upon me, for You have acted truthfully, and I have been wicked." (Nehemiah 9:33) This is the week of Tisha B'Av.

The song belongs to Shimon and to the day. Shimon, the man and the tribe, made serious mistakes: he was instrumental in the sale of Joseph, and the tribe, its prince included, openly rebelled against Moses. And through repentance Shimon will be fully redeemed. As the mouse is caught through its own iniquities, our Temple was destroyed on Tisha B'Av through our sins, and the first step toward redemption is recognising that fault — it is said that in any generation in which the Temple is not rebuilt, it is as if that generation destroyed it.

The word the mouse uses, dilitani, for having been impoverished or uplifted, is near Dal, poor, and Delet, door. The Bnei Yissachar teaches, from the writings of the Arizal, that Tammuz is the letter dalet and Av the letter lamed, which spell Dal — and Elul, the month of Teshuvah, is the letter Tav, which makes Delet. The secret of being lifted in the poor months is to join them to the doors of Elul. That is in the words of Selichot: "kdalim uchrashim dafaknu dlatecha," like the poor and destitute we knock on Your door.

The letters of forty-four, mem and dalet, spell dam, blood, and mad, from limdod, to measure. Av has been a month in which much blood was spilled; once the Jewish people learn the lesson, measure their actions and improve, it will be a month of light and joy. The same letters spell dom, to be silent — a word often used in praise of how our greatest sages met tragedy. Of Aaron, learning that his two eldest sons had died, the Torah says "yehidom Aharon," Aaron was silent and did not complain. Our Chassidic masters explain that King David's way went further still: after great suffering he says, "l'man yezamerchah velo yidom," I will sing to You and not be silent. There is much to learn from both approaches about how to keep this day. And dom has a brighter side: pursuing the enemies of the Jewish people, Joshua calls to the sun and commands it, "Dom!" — telling it to stop its song to G-d, which makes the sun stand still, and gives the people time to finish before the Sabbath begins.

Pirkei Avot gives Rabbi Nehora'i: exile yourself to a place of Torah; do not say that it will come after you, that your colleagues will help you retain it; rely not on your own understanding. Tisha B'Av is about exile in general, and about one exile in particular, to a place of Torah: Yavneh. By establishing Yavneh and bringing our sages there, Rabbi Yochanan Ben Zakkai made sure Judaism continued long after the Roman Empire had stopped existing. And since the suffering of this week is so hard to understand, it is fitting to be told not to lean on our own limited understanding but to stay joined to the rest of our people.

The combination is gevurah shebemalchut. This week we work on the strength to reach goals in this material world against obstacles. As in the week of Yom Kippur, gevurah shebechesed, we fast — and not feeling like angels this time; more like the mouse. On Yom Kippur, one of the happiest days of the year, the fast is for spiritual reasons; on Tisha B'Av we fast in mourning. The day belongs to gevurah because of how many tragedies fell on it, the decree of forty years in the wilderness and the destruction of both Temples among them — and to malchut, because it is exactly out of that tragedy that Mashiach is born.

The lesson from the mouse is that He can raise us up at any moment, and that to come out of sadness we should increase our prayers and direct them to Him alone. Any fall, personal or national, is an opening for teshuvah. And judging oneself is only good if it leads to better behaviour rather than to sadness: there is a fine line between being temporarily broken-hearted over one's sins, which is a good regret, and sadness, which should be avoided at all costs. Broken-heartedness should lead to greater joy.

303.title: Zechariah and Settling One's Heart
body: The week of Tisha B'Av. Haazinu ends: "And Moses came and spoke all the words of this song into the ears of the people he and Hoshea the son of Nun." (Deuteronomy 32:44) Av is the tikkun of hearing, and into the ears of the people is how the song arrives. Perhaps Yehoshua stands beside Moshe here because of all of them he was the one best able to absorb Moshe's teaching. This week holds the birth of Mashiach, on the 9th of Av, and the Midrash teaches that Moshe is the first redeemer and the final redeemer; Yehoshua is likewise a prototype for Mashiach Ben Yoseph.

The Haftorah is plainly about that coming: "And You have allowed me to escape from the contenders amongst my people; You shall keep me as head of nations; a people whom I have not known serve me." (II Samuel 22:44) Mashiach will be not only king of Israel but will stand for the Kingdom of G-d on earth.

The quality is he deliberates in his study, Mityashev Liboh Betalmudoh. A great part of the destruction on the 9th of Av came of the hot-headedness of the zealots of that time, where the Torah scholars sought calm and compromise. More literally the phrase is that he settles his heart with his study. The Midrash says that Mashiach is a metzorah, one who suffers a form of spiritual skin disease, and that he cures one wound at a time. The Alter Rebbe explains that the cure for the metzorah is Torah — which is why the verse says "this shall be the Torah of the metzorah on the day of his purification," where the plainer wording would have been "this is the purification of the metzorah." The metzorah is a man whose heart is unsettled, and it is the Torah that settles it. The line can also be read about a friend's heart, continuing the qualities of the past weeks. And Mashiach will be known for his Torah and for his power of speech: the word Mashiach is spelled like Mesiach, one who speaks.

The prophet is Zechariah. We read in the kinot of Tisha B'Av about an earlier Zechariah, killed at the time of the First Temple's destruction, whose blood had to be avenged — and that is settling of another kind. Our Sages say that when Nebuzaradan entered the Temple he found the blood of Zechariah seething, and asked what it meant; the Jews tried to conceal it, and under threat told him there was a prophet among them who chastised them and whom they killed, and that for many years his blood had not rested. He said, I will appease him, and killed the members of the Great and Small Sanhedrins, then youths and maidens, then school-children, 940,000 people in all; and still the blood boiled, until he cried, "Zechariah, Zechariah! I have slain the best of them; do you want all of them destroyed?" — and at last it sank into the ground.

This Zechariah's own prophecy makes some of the most direct references to Mashiach: "Be exceedingly happy, O daughter of Zion; Shout, O daughter of Jerusalem. Behold! Your king shall come to you. He is just and victorious; humble, and riding a donkey and a foal, the offspring of [one of] she-donkeys." And in the story of Rabbi Akiva laughing while the other rabbis mourn, it is Zechariah's prophecy that consoles them: old men and women shall yet sit in the streets of Jerusalem.

The levitical city is Holon, from chol, which means sand and also profane. As at the destruction, when something is emptied of its holiness it is chol, a vacuum, dead like the sand of the sea. And in the Torah almost nothing stands for life, and for children, as the sand does; we are promised to be as many as they are one day. One day our tears of sadness will be tears of joy, and the earth will be filled with the knowledge of G-d as the water covers the sea, and the sand. The numerical value of chol is forty-four. Holon is also a city in modern Israel, the country's second largest industrial area.
303.teaser: Book 3 · Song of the Sea, week 44.

304.title: War and Conquest
body: Tisha B'Av, the only twenty-four-hour fast besides Yom Kippur, marks the destruction of both Temples and many other tragedies. It was on Tisha B'Av that the spies came back with a negative report, and after the people reacted as they did it was decreed that they would spend 40 years in the desert.

Beshalach ends with exactly that span: "And the children of Israel ate the manna for forty years until they came to an inhabited land. They ate the manna until they came to the border of the land of Canaan. The omer is one tenth of an ephah." Once the forty-two journeys are done and we reach that border, in Av, the manna stops and sustenance has to come from working the Land. And that conquest belongs to the coming of Mashiach, which belongs to this week.

The Haftorah rests the land forty years: "And the land rested forty years. And the children of Israel did that which displeased the Lord, and the Lord delivered them into the hand of Midian (for) seven years." Those forty years stand against the forty in the desert. And as the last battle of the desert years was against Midian, Israel now faced oppression from Midian after forty years of relative calm. Like Tisha B'Av, they were given into their enemies' hands because they displeased Him — which reads back onto last week's daf, where Pinchas is the anointed for war against Midian.

Daf Mem Dalet of Sotah gives the laws of the impurity of a dead body, then more of those exempt from a milchemet reshut — the engaged, and the afraid — and then opens a chapter on the Eglah Arufah, the beheading of a calf for an unsolved murder outside a Jewish city. The first and the last belong to a date marked by death. And Tisha B'Av belongs to those who fear war, like the fear that took hold when the people heard the spies.

The generation is Uzziah, also called Azariah, son of Amaziah, one of the most successful kings of Judah. His counterparts in Israel were Jeroboam ben Jehoash, Zechariah, Shallum, Menachem ben Gadi, Pekahiah ben Menahem and Pekah ben Remaliah. The start of his reign, while he was young, saw great devastation, with attackers plundering Judah from every border; once he came of age and held his throne firmly he developed the country extensively, militarily and economically. For all his piety he made one grave mistake that became the defining event of his kingdom: over repeated warnings he tried to play the part of a kohen and offer incense in the Temple, and was immediately struck with tzara'at. He stayed a metzorah for the rest of his life, living in isolation near a cemetery — and there is a well-known story in the Talmud that Mashiach, born on Tisha B'Av, is a Metzorah by the gates of Rome. Uzziah means G-d is my strength, and Azariah G-d is my help. The word for strength, Oz, is near Az, bold: there is a boldness on the side of holiness, as in being bold like a leopard, and a boldness on the side of impurity, as in the saying that those who are bold go to gehinnom. Uzziah showed both, and both belong to this day. And the Haftorah of Shabat Hazon, read this week, opens by saying it was prophesied by Isaiah, Uzziah's uncle, during his reign.

The forty-fourth week goes with conquering the Girgashites, whose name comes from Girgash, a kind of red clay. That recalls the making of man from the earth: Adam comes from Adamah, earth, and is near Adom, red, like Edom. The Girgashites belong to the negative side of Gevurah, which shows itself in violence and murder, which is Eisav's own characteristic. King David, who is also described as red, is the tikkun of it: he used his gevurah for the good, against Goliath and in all his other battles for G-d and Israel.

305.title: Building G-d's House
body: The verse ends with a threat: "And (if) the man said to him, 'Let them make the fat smoke now, and (then) take for yourself, as your soul desires,' And he would say, 'No, but now you shall give. And if not, I shall take by force.'" Taking the portion by force, before the offering was ready — a great disdain for the laws of sacrifice and for the person bringing one, which recalls the baseless hatred and the corrupt priests of the time of the destruction.

Pirkei Avot's acquisition this week is the Holy Temple: "The base for Your dwelling that you, G-d, have achieved; the Sanctuary, O L-rd, that Your hands have established." And: "And He brought them to His holy domain, this mount His right hand has acquired." His dwelling, which He established and acquired with His own hands — where the sons of Eli spoke as though the Tabernacle and the sacrifices were theirs, putting their own will before His.

Psalm 127 was said by King Solomon, and it is about building the Temple and how its success depends entirely on His will: "If the Lord will not build a house, its builders have toiled at it in vain." Failing to keep His will leads to the destruction that came on Tisha B'Av.

The week holds the yahrzeits of two of the greatest masters of Kabbalah and Chassidut: Rabbi Yitzchak Luria, the Arizal, on the 5th of Av, and Rabbi Yaakov Yitzchok Horowitz, the Chozeh of Lublin, on the 9th. Rabbi Yitzchak Luria, known as the holy Ari, revolutionised the study of Kabbalah and its place in mainstream Judaism in the two years he spent in Zefat before his death at 38; much of Chasidic thought rests on his teachings as recorded by his main disciple, Rabbi Chaim Vital. Rabbi Yaakov Yitzchok Horowitz, the Chozeh of Lublin, succeeded R. Elimelech of Lizensk and led the spread of chassidus in Poland. Many great Rebbes of the next generation came out of his followers: the Yid HaKodesh, Simcha Bunim of Peshischa, Meir of Apta, David of Lelov, the Yismach Moshe, the Sabba Kadisha of Radoshitz, the Bnai Yisasscher, Rabbi Naftali Zvi of Ropshitz, the Maor Vashemesh and Sar Shalom of Belz. Many of his insights were published after his death, in Divrei Emmes, Zichron Zos and Zos Zichron.

Also this week: Rabbi Shimshon Ostropolier, Rabbi Chaim Yechezkel Taub of Ozorov, and Rabbi Yitzchak Twersky, the first Skverer Rebbe in America, on the 3rd of Av; and Rabbi Ephraim Taub of Kuzmir and Rabbi Benzion Halberstam, the second Bobover Rebbe, on the 4th.

306.title: "Love is as Strong as Death"
body: Tisha B'Av, which marks the destruction of both Temples and the enormous destruction that came with them, remembered every year with fasting and intense mourning, and on which we remember every tragedy of Jewish history, the Holocaust among them.

The Song's verse is hauntingly close to it: "Place me like a seal on your heart, liked a seal on your arm, for love is as strong as death, zeal is as strong as the grave; its coals are coals of fire of a great flame!" Death and the grave; a seal on your arm, like the numbers etched on the arms of Jews in the concentration camps; a great fire, like the one that burned the Temples. And love is stronger than death. We survived, and the great flame of our people burns still.

Of the seventy souls that descended to Egypt, the forty-fourth is Ishvah, whose root is the same as Leshavot, and which looks related to this week's quality, Mityashev Liboh Betalmudoh, to settle one's heart in study. Much of the destruction on the 9th of Av came of the hot-headedness of the zealots, where the Torah scholars of that time sought calm and compromise. And with him Huppim, son of Benjamin, whose name is near Chuppah, a wedding canopy, for Benjamin never seeing Joseph's wedding. The Chuppah is the great symbol of peace and normalcy, in the prophecy of Jeremiah that is part of the Shevah Brachot said under it: "There shall again be heard in this place, concerning which you say, 'It is desolate without man and without beast,' in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem that are desolate... the sound of mirth and the sound of joy, the voice of a bridegroom and the voice of a bride, the sound of those saying, 'Thank the Lord of Hosts, for the Lord is good, for His loving-kindness endures forever.'" Those words hold both the tragedy of Tisha B'Av and the redemption. And the Chuppah belongs to love, and to Tu B'Av next week, which is a day of marriage and love — the high that comes directly after these lows.

Daf Mem Dalet of Shvuot keeps on with a mashkon, a security, that was lost, like the Temple, and opens a new chapter on oaths taken in order to receive payment. Much of it is about someone entering another person's house without permission: a case where he takes vessels from the owner, and a case where the owner wounds him. Which reads onto Tisha B'Av, when our house, the House of G-d, was entered without permission and its vessels taken, and when those who entered were punished and will be punished again. And there is a discussion of partial admission — admitting to taking one vessel rather than two, or to wounding once rather than twice — which reads onto two Temples destroyed, both on the same day.

Jeremiah's forty-fourth chapter is the destruction brought on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, and not listening to the prophets, which is the sense this month repairs. "You saw all the evil that I brought upon Jerusalem and upon all the cities of Judah, and behold, they are waste, and there are no inhabitants in them, because of their evil, which they did to provoke Me, to go to burn incense to worship other gods, which they did not know." And the sending that went unheard: "And I sent to you all My servants the prophets, sending them betimes, saying: Now do not do this abominable thing which I hate. But they did not hearken, nor did they incline their ear[s] to repent of their evil." And the question: "Why do you do this great evil to your souls, to cut off from you man and woman, child and suckling from the midst of Judah, not to leave over a remnant for yourselves?"

307.title: Reviewing the Week of Tisha B'Av - Psalms 130-132; 105:33-35; 89:45
body: The week of Tisha B'Av in psalms: the hundred and thirtieth, hundred and thirty-first and hundred and thirty-second, with three verses of Psalm 105 and one of Psalm 89.

Psalm 130 prays for an end to this long exile, and it begins as low as a psalm can begin: "Out of the depths I call to You, O Lord. My Lord, hearken to my voice; let Your ears be attentive to the sound of my pleas." Then the thing that makes any of it possible: "G-d, if You were to preserve iniquities, my Lord, who could survive? But forgiveness is with You, that You may be held in awe." Then the waiting: "I hope in the Lord; my soul hopes, and I long for His word. My soul yearns for the Lord more than those awaiting the morning wait for the morning." And the last line: "And He will redeem Israel from all its iniquities."

Psalm 131 is David saying that in all his life he was never haughty and never chased greatness or the pleasures of the world.
